title: 009 Api Design
text:
## Context

The Artifact Registry API design has the following constraints:

1. **Three API categories**: Management APIs to interact with registry concepts, Artifact Management Client APIs that follow strict specifications to be used by specific clients, and a GitLab API for platform-to-registry communication.
1. **Follow the database data organization**: The API endpoints are organized by artifact format, matching the database schema, where each format family has its own tables and fields (`docker` and `oci` form one family). This mapping simplifies implementation by avoiding complex multi-format abstractions and enables format-specific optimizations.
1. **Three repository types**: The registry supports three repository types: hosted (private storage for pushed artifacts), remote (proxy/cache for external registries), and virtual (aggregated pull endpoint combining hosted and remote upstreams). This model matches industry practice. All three types are standalone, independently manageable entities.

The Artifact Registry is scoped to Organizations (see [ADR-001](001_organizations_as_anchor_point.md) for rationale) through an immutable, customer-chosen slug ([ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md)) that appears in all customer-facing URLs. All client and management endpoints include the `/:slug` path segment after the API version prefix (or protocol prefix for client APIs), scoping every request to a specific slug. The slug provides stable [Cells](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/cells/) routing via the topology service without depending on organization path resolution. Two exceptions: the OCI-mandated `GET /v2/` version probe (see [Container](#container)) and the GitLab API endpoints (see [GitLab API](#gitlab-api)).

The Artifact Registry is served on a dedicated domain (for example, `artifact-registry.gitlab.com`), separate from the main GitLab application domain. This improves our security posture against [XSS](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/xss/) and [SSRF](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Server_Side_Request_Forgery) vulnerabilities by isolating the registry from the main application's cookies, credentials, and internal network context.

This ADR defines the API surfaces and the rules that apply to them. The OpenAPI specifications and the per-format specifications in the Artifact Registry codebase define the routes and their payloads.

### Versioning

The Artifact Registry runs on a dedicated domain, so the `/api/v4` prefix used in the GitLab Rails monolith does not apply. The monolith uses `/api/v4` to separate API routes from web UI routes on the same domain and to reflect its API version lineage (v3 to v4).

Management API routes use an `/api/v1` path-based version prefix. The `/api/` prefix separates management routes from protocol-specific client routes on the same domain, preventing namespace collisions if the management API version is ever bumped (e.g., OCI mandates `/v2/`, so a bare `/v2` management prefix would collide). This is consistent with industry practice. Path-based versioning keeps the version visible in URLs, logs, and routing rules without requiring header inspection.

Client APIs do not use a version prefix. Protocol-specific versioning is handled by the clients themselves if necessary. This keeps client-configured URLs as short as possible.

GitLab API routes use an `/api/gitlab/v1` prefix. The explicit `gitlab` segment keeps the surface visible in URLs, logs, and routing rules, and lets the edge apply dedicated path rules to it. This follows the Container Registry precedent, whose registry-to-platform surface uses a `/gitlab/v1/` prefix.

### API Classification

The API surface is divided into three distinct categories which have different rules:

1. **Management APIs**: REST and GraphQL APIs for CRUD operations on registry concepts (repositories, artifacts, policies, etc.)
   - Authentication: the GitLab standard REST/GraphQL authentication
   - Purpose: UI, automation scripts, administrative tools
   - Format: JSON responses with standard GitLab API patterns. A route that returns a stored JSON document, such as a container manifest, returns it unchanged under the document's own media type
   - Pagination: All list endpoints are paginated, preferably using a keyset pagination strategy. A list that a limit keeps below one page, such as a virtual repository's upstreams, is not paginated

1. **Artifact Management Client APIs**: Protocol-specific APIs implementing industry-standard specifications
   - Authentication: Protocol-specific (Bearer tokens for OCI, Basic auth for Maven, etc.)
   - Purpose: Native client compatibility (`docker`, `npm`, `mvn`, `go` commands)
   - Format: Protocol-specific responses (OCI Distribution Spec, Maven Repository Layout, NPM Registry API, GOPROXY protocol)

1. **GitLab API**: REST endpoints for platform-to-registry communication
   - Authentication: Service-to-service credentials; no end-user identity
   - Purpose: Namespace provisioning, resolution, and service conditions; resource verifications
   - Format: JSON
   - Exposure: Trusted platform callers only

Management and Client APIs serve all three repository types: hosted, virtual, and remote. Client APIs are organized per protocol (one set of endpoints per protocol; the OCI Distribution Spec endpoints serve repositories of both the `docker` and `oci` formats), while Management APIs share a unified repository CRUD with format appearing only in format-specific sub-resources.

### URL Structure Design

Management API routes are **anchored at the repository**. The `/api/v1/:slug` prefix is mandatory for all routes and is not counted as a conceptual level. Repository endpoints accept a unique repository name as the `:repository_name` parameter.

All repository-level resources (artifacts, lifecycle policies, upstream associations) are scoped to a repository because hosted and remote repositories store data in separate, per-format-family tables.

The `:format` segment appears **after a repository** for all format-specific sub-resources: `/api/v1/:slug/repositories/:repository_name/:format/...` (e.g., listing images, lifecycle policies). Repository-level sub-resources are dedicated to a specific format, allowing higher flexibility in endpoints organization and customization of the returned structure. Namespace-level format-specific operations use `:format` as a prefix: `/api/v1/:slug/:format/statistics`.

Repository CRUD itself is format-free because every format and kind shares one repository resource. Format and kind are properties of the repository resource, not URL segments.

For example:

- Listing all repositories: `GET /api/v1/:slug/repositories`
- Creating a repository: `POST /api/v1/:slug/repositories`
- Reading/updating/deleting a repository: `GET/PATCH/DELETE /api/v1/:slug/repositories/:repository_name` (top-level route using the target concept identifier)
- Listing images in a container-family repository: `GET /api/v1/:slug/repositories/:repository_name/:format/images` (format-specific sub-resource; `:format` is `docker` or `oci`)
- Getting an image by ID: `GET /api/v1/:slug/repositories/:repository_name/:format/images/:image_id` (artifact detail, scoped to the repository)

### Repository Name Immutability

Repository names are set at creation time and cannot be changed. Repository descriptions remain mutable. This prevents broken client configurations, authorization bypass through name reclaim, and silent misrouting. It also enables name-based URLs (see [below](#human-friendly-urls)) and simplifies authorization rules. This is consistent with industry practice.

### Human-Friendly URLs

Repository names must be globally unique within the slug, regardless of format or repository type. This global uniqueness constraint matches industry practice and avoids ambiguous name-based lookups. It can be relaxed to per-format uniqueness later without breaking anyone; tightening would be a breaking change. Name immutability (see [above](#repository-name-immutability)) makes name-based URLs safe as stable path segments. Slugs are immutable ([ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md)), so every segment in a URL path is human-readable and permanently stable.

## API Organization

### Management APIs

Management APIs use GitLab [REST API authentication](https://docs.gitlab.com/api/rest/authentication/).

**Note:** `:format` is the repository's `format` value. The `docker` and `oci` formats form the container family and share one artifact model: images, tags, and manifests. A request whose `:format` segment does not match the repository's format returns `404 Not Found`.

#### Namespace-level APIs

Namespace-level routes sit directly under `/api/v1/:slug`: the repository collection, namespace and per-format statistics, the namespace lifecycle policy, and the namespace itself. The repository list spans every format and kind, and filters by both.

The repository resource is polymorphic by format and kind. Fields every repository shares sit at the top level. Format-specific and kind-specific fields nest under a single `settings` object, and `format` and `kind` act as its discriminators. Create and update bodies take the same nesting.

A virtual repository's create and update bodies can carry an ordered list of upstream repository IDs, which states its upstreams after the write, in resolution order. It is the one kind-specific key outside `settings`, because no response returns it. It requires the upstream abilities of [ADR-021](021_authorization.md) as well as the repository ability, so it grants no write that the upstream routes would refuse.

Permission verdicts embed in the domain responses that carry the resources they gate, opt-in through a boolean query parameter. [ADR-021](021_authorization.md#permission-checks-for-ui-gating) defines the semantics, including which responses carry them.

##### Repository Deletion

Deleting a repository **requires** a destructive-intent query parameter that carries exactly `true` or `false`. It has no default: a request that omits it, or carries any other value, returns `400 Bad Request`. This ADR fixes the contract, not the parameter's name.

| Value   | Behavior                                                                                              |
|---------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `false` | Deletes an empty repository and returns `204`, unless a virtual repository lists it as an upstream, in which case it returns `409 Conflict`. A repository that still holds artifacts returns `409 Conflict` |
| `true`  | Cascades: deletes the repository and its contents (`204` when already empty, `202` otherwise), unless a virtual repository lists it as an upstream, in which case it returns `409 Conflict`         |

Deleting an empty repository is synchronous and returns `204` under either value. The cascade against a non-empty repository is asynchronous: the request returns `202 Accepted`, the repository becomes unreachable at once (its name stays reserved until the deletion completes), and storage reclamation follows in the background.

The two values give two levels of protection: the caller declares destructive intent, and `false` still refuses to touch contents.

A repository that a virtual repository lists as an upstream returns `409 Conflict` under **either** value. Destructive intent does not reach it: the association is the virtual repository's configuration, not this repository's contents. The caller removes the association first. The `409` names the condition without listing the virtual repositories that hold the reference.

The parameter is required so that its removal fails loudly. GA makes soft delete the only delete path ([ADR-010](010_data_retention.md#release-phasing)), so the API drops the parameter, and a closed-beta integrator who still sends it gets an **explicit rejection that names the trash as the recovery path**, not a generic unknown-field `400`.

#### Repository-level APIs

Repository-level routes sit under `/api/v1/:slug/repositories/:repository_name`. Repository statistics and the remote connection test are format-free. Upstreams and lifecycle policies sit under the `:format` segment.

An upstream of a virtual repository references an existing hosted or remote repository, whose `kind` sets the upstream type. The upstream list follows resolution order. The upstream routes change one association at a time. The whole-list form on the repository body states the full list instead, and the registry applies it against the current set atomically.

Repository-level lifecycle policies override the namespace-level defaults.

#### Format-Specific Artifact APIs

Each format exposes its own artifact hierarchy under the `:format` segment: images and tags for the container family, and packages, versions, and files for Maven and npm.

Artifact routes are scoped to the repository. Routes, verbs, and pagination are the same for hosted and remote repositories. A route whose data the remote cache keeps as one document rather than per row, such as npm dist-tags, answers `404` on a remote repository.

Artifact responses are polymorphic by repository `kind`, like the repository `settings` object: a remote repository adds upstream freshness metadata to the rows that track it, and a hosted repository returns the same shape without it.

Verb semantics on a remote repository describe the cached row, not the upstream:

- `DELETE` evicts the cached row (no upstream effect; the artifact is re-fetched on the next pull through the client API).
- `PATCH .../quarantine` flags the cached row as blocked: client pulls return `404 Not Found` even if upstream still has the artifact. The flag follows the cached row's lifecycle, so eviction clears it. Persistent or digest-level blocks are out of scope, because they are a lifecycle-management concern, not an API one.
- `GET` is identical for both kinds, apart from that freshness metadata.

### Artifact Management Client APIs

Client API URLs are the same for all repository types (hosted, remote, virtual). The registry resolves the repository kind internally and applies type-specific behavior (e.g., rejecting writes on remote and virtual repositories, and refusing reads a repository kind cannot serve).

Each format implements its client protocol under `/:slug/:format/:repository_name/`. The container family is the one exception (see [Container](#container)).

#### Container

Implements [OCI Distribution Spec v1.1](https://github.com/opencontainers/distribution-spec/blob/main/spec.md). Authentication: [Bearer token](https://docs.docker.com/reference/api/registry/auth/).

Container routes live under `/v2/:slug/container/:repository_name/:image_name/`. The literal `container` path segment is fixed at the protocol level: one set of `/v2` endpoints serves repositories of both the `docker` and `oci` formats. It is a fixed literal, not the repository's `format` value (see [Management APIs](#management-apis)).

**Note:** The OCI-mandated `GET /v2/` endpoint has no `/:slug` prefix, so the [Cells](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/cells/) router cannot pick a Cell from its path. Any Cell can serve it, because it is a stateless version probe that answers `200 OK` for OCI compliance or `401 Unauthorized`. Every other client request carries a `/:slug` segment, which the Cells router uses to pick the target Cell. Clients get credentials through [`glab`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cli) (see [ADR-020](020_authentication_flow.md)) and send a Bearer token from the first request, so the registry never uses the OCI `401 WWW-Authenticate` challenge.

#### Maven

Implements [Maven Repository Layout](https://maven.apache.org/repositories/layout.html). Authentication: Basic auth.

#### NPM

Implements [NPM Registry API](https://github.com/npm/registry/blob/main/docs/REGISTRY-API.md). Authentication: Bearer token.

#### Go

Implements the [GOPROXY protocol](https://go.dev/ref/mod#goproxy-protocol) for reads, plus an upload route, because the protocol has no publish operation.

### GitLab API

The GitLab API serves platform callers, initially the Rails monolith. Requests authenticate the calling service, never an end user: user checks belong to the platform flows that trigger the calls, and user-facing traffic uses the management and client APIs instead ([ADR-014](014_frontend_to_artifact_registry.md), [ADR-021](021_authorization.md)). "GitLab" names the caller: a GitLab platform deployment, in the hybrid deployment model a customer-hosted monolith, so the surface is internet-facing yet never customer-facing.

[ADR-020](020_authentication_flow.md) and [ADR-021](021_authorization.md) cover how callers authenticate to this surface, including in the hybrid deployment model, where a Self-Managed or Dedicated monolith calls the SaaS registry.

#### Namespace Lifecycle

These endpoints are slug-exempt: provisioning runs before a slug is claimed, resolution turns a UUID into the slug, and service conditions must work regardless of the slug's state. They reference namespaces by owner anchor ([ADR-001](001_organizations_as_anchor_point.md)) or UUID ([ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md)).

The platform provisions a namespace for an owner anchor and persists the namespace UUID it gets back. Provisioning is idempotent on the anchor. The platform resolves a namespace by UUID to its owner anchor, slug, and status, and caches the slug and status ([ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md), [ADR-014](014_frontend_to_artifact_registry.md)). It applies and lifts the reversible service conditions of [ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md#namespace-lifecycle) through one endpoint per action.

Slug-exempt routes do not weaken [Cells](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/cells/) routing. Namespace creation cannot be routed by key: nothing exists yet to route by. A cell-resident monolith calls its cell-local registry directly, and the namespace lands in that cell; a hybrid caller has no cell, so its call enters at the edge, which decides the target Cell. Both paths register the namespace UUID as a routing key, and the slug becomes a second key when claimed. All other GitLab API endpoints are keyed by that UUID and route through the same topology mechanism as slug-prefixed requests, wherever the caller sits. If UUID-keyed routing ever proves insufficient, GitLab API requests can also embed the owner anchor as a routing hint.

#### Resource Verifications

Platform authorization flows must confirm that resources targeted by bulk role grants belong to a namespace. Namespace-targeted grants need no registry call: the platform verifies ownership against its persisted mapping. Repository-targeted grants use a batch verification scoped by the namespace UUID. It succeeds only when every id belongs to the namespace, and otherwise lists exactly the failing ids without saying why one failed, so an id that exists nowhere and an id another namespace owns look the same.

The registry returns no organization data: the caller supplies the namespace scope and already knows its owner. Each future assignable resource type follows the same pattern, `POST /api/gitlab/v1/namespaces/:uuid/<resource_type>/verifications`.

The GitLab API must stay backward compatible across the platform versions it serves: in the hybrid deployment model, a Self-Managed monolith can lag the SaaS registry ([ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md)).

## Consequences

### Positive

- **Clear separation of concerns**: The three API surfaces have distinct purposes, authentication mechanisms, and target audiences, reducing confusion and enabling independent evolution
- **Permanently stable, human-readable URLs**: Slugs and repository names are both immutable, so every URL path segment is human-readable and never changes. No numeric IDs appear in any client-facing URL
- **Unified hybrid list**: A single endpoint lists all repositories (hosted, virtual, remote) across all formats with filtering, enabling a cross-format governance and auditability view for platform engineers
- **Remote repositories as standalone entities**: Remote repositories are independently manageable, reusable across multiple virtual repositories, and have their own lifecycle, matching industry practice (JFrog Artifactory, Sonatype Nexus, Google Cloud AR)
- **Uniform hosted and remote artifact structure**: Remote repositories reuse the hosted artifact hierarchy, routes, and verbs, so API clients and the UI handle both kinds the same way
- **Simplified upstream model**: Virtual repository upstreams reference existing repositories by ID rather than using separate endpoint hierarchies per upstream type, reducing API surface and implementation complexity
- **API evolution outside the ADR**: Routes and payloads live in the OpenAPI and per-format specifications, so a new route or field needs no ADR change unless it breaks a rule here
- **Future extensibility**: The design accommodates additional package formats (PyPI, NuGet, Helm, etc.) without architectural changes. Management and Client APIs can evolve independently based on their respective requirements

### Negative

- **Repository name immutability limits flexibility**: A typo or organizational rename requires creating a new repository and migrating artifacts rather than simply renaming
- **Global name uniqueness is restrictive**: Names like `my-app` cannot be reused across formats (e.g., a Docker and a Maven repo both called `my-app`), which may lead to naming conventions like `my-app-docker` and `my-app-maven`
- **Format-specific API surface**: Dedicating endpoints per format means some duplication across formats and no unified cross-format operations for management tasks

## References

- [ADR-001: Organizations as Anchor Point](001_organizations_as_anchor_point.md)
- [ADR-010: Data Retention](010_data_retention.md#release-phasing) - Delete phasing across closed beta and GA
- [ADR-022: Namespace Decoupling](022_namespace_decoupling.md)
- [Cells Architecture](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/cells/)
- [Container Registry Routing Service (Cells)](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/content-sites/handbook/-/merge_requests/14825)
- [GitLab REST API Authentication](https://docs.gitlab.com/api/rest/authentication/)
- [OCI Distribution Spec v1.1](https://github.com/opencontainers/distribution-spec/blob/main/spec.md)
- [Docker Registry Bearer Token Authentication](https://docs.docker.com/reference/api/registry/auth/)
- [Maven Repository Layout](https://maven.apache.org/repositories/layout.html)
- [NPM Registry API](https://github.com/npm/registry/blob/main/docs/REGISTRY-API.md)
- [Repository Name Immutability Proposal](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/592582)

title: 010 Data Retention
text:
<!-- Design Documents often contain forward-looking statements -->
<!-- vale gitlab.FutureTense = NO -->

## Context

The Artifact Registry manages data through two complementary mechanisms:

1. **Retention**: Time-based expiration that sets the maximum lifespan for artifacts
1. **Cleanup**: Active processes that remove data (lifecycle policies, garbage collection)

These mechanisms operate independently. Retention defines when artifacts become eligible for deletion; cleanup executes the deletion.

| Mechanism          | Purpose                                                     | Scope                    | Configurable |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------|--------------|
| Default retention  | Maximum artifact lifespan                                   | Organization-wide cap    | Yes          |
| Lifecycle policies | User-defined cleanup rules                                  | Repository or Org level  | Yes          |
| Garbage collection | Infrastructure cleanup                                      | Namespace                | No           |
| Soft delete        | Recovery window before hard delete ([GA](#release-phasing)) | Organization-wide        | No           |

### Release Phasing

Closed beta ships permanent delete only: every delete permanently removes its target with no recovery path, and deleting a repository deletes its contents. Closed beta accepts that risk and guards it with a typed repository-name confirmation in the UI and an explicit destructive intent on the API (see [ADR-009](009_api_design.md#repository-deletion)).

Soft delete, restore, trash, and expiration ship together at GA as one feature, API and UI. Soft delete stays the target state this ADR describes, so the sections below apply from GA unless they name closed beta.

### Deletion Precedence

From GA, every deletion trigger (manual deletion, lifecycle policy, retention expiration) goes through soft delete. This provides a consistent recovery window regardless of the trigger, protecting against bugs or misconfigured retention periods. The lifecycle purger permanently removes soft-deleted artifacts after the soft delete window expires, and garbage collection reclaims the blobs they leave. In closed beta every trigger deletes permanently.

## What Must Always Hold

These rules bind every feature that deletes or retains data.

| # | Constraint | Machine-checkable? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **From GA, every deletion trigger goes through soft delete.** Manual deletion, lifecycle policy and retention expiration all mark artifacts for deletion rather than removing them. Soft delete is always on and not user-configurable. | Yes: a test per trigger that no path deletes permanently |
| 2 | **Closed beta deletes permanently.** Every delete removes its target with no recovery path, and deleting a repository deletes its contents. | Yes: a test that no delete path offers a restore |
| 3 | **Default retention is an Organization-level cap.** It applies to all artifacts regardless of tags or lifecycle policies, and a download resets it. Lifecycle policies can delete sooner, never later. | Yes: tests on the expiry computation |
| 4 | **Garbage collection reclaims only unreferenced blobs.** A blob is reclaimable only when no attachment in its deduplication boundary references it. Garbage collection is not user-configurable. | Yes: a test that no setting reaches it, and one that it reads only attachments |
| 5 | **Every deletion audit entry records its trigger.** The trigger is manual, lifecycle policy, retention expiration or garbage collection. | Yes: a test per trigger on the audit entry |
| 6 | **Every permanent deletion uses the storage provider's deletion.** The object is deleted through the provider's API and the database record is hard-deleted. | Yes: tests on each permanent-deletion path |
| 7 | **A deletion propagates to every replica.** No replica keeps a deleted blob or its metadata. | Yes: a drift check comparing the blobs and metadata of every replica |
| 8 | **A suspended namespace accepts no writes.** It follows the three phases of the [Subscription Expiration](#subscription-expiration) table: pull is allowed and push is blocked at first, then access ends. | Yes: tests per phase |

## Artifact Retention

Retention defines the maximum time an artifact can exist without being accessed.

### Default Retention Period

Artifacts unused for 365 days are automatically deleted. This default prevents unbounded storage growth, while [extending retention](#extending-retention) accommodates customers with longer retention needs. This Organization-level default:

- Applies to all artifacts regardless of tags or lifecycle policies
- Acts as a cap: lifecycle policies can delete sooner, but cannot extend retention beyond this limit
- Resets when an artifact is downloaded

Organization administrators can adjust the default period. The 365-day value applies unless explicitly changed.

## Soft Delete

Soft delete ships at GA. Closed beta deletes permanently (see [Release Phasing](#release-phasing)).

From GA, soft delete is always enabled and not user-configurable. All deletions (manual, lifecycle policy, retention expiration) mark artifacts for deletion rather than removing them immediately. Users can restore soft-deleted artifacts until the hard deletion window expires. Optional soft delete leads to accidental permanent data loss.

Whether soft-deleted artifacts are visible in the UI is a display concern, not a retention concern.

## Virtual Repository Caches

Virtual repositories cache packages from upstream registries. Cached content has separate retention and cleanup rules from hosted artifacts. How long cached metadata stays fresh controls staleness, not deletion.

## Audit Log Retention

Audit logs capture security-relevant operations:

| Log Category                                                    | Default Retention | Rationale               |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------|-------------------------|
| Security events (auth failures, permission changes)             | 365 days          | Matches the GitLab [Records Retention & Disposal](/handbook/security/policies_and_standards/records-retention-deletion/) policy for production audit logs (1 year) |
| Administrative operations (policy changes, repository creation) | 365 days          | Matches production audit log retention for consistent change tracking |
| Artifact operations (upload, download, delete)                  | 60 days           | Most operational issues surface within this window; Meets the 60-day minimum for critical system activity logs |

Deletion audit entries must record the trigger (manual, lifecycle policy, retention expiration, or garbage collection) to support debugging and compliance investigations.

Background jobs purge logs exceeding retention periods.

## Garbage Collection

Garbage collection reclaims blobs that no artifact references any longer, within its deduplication boundary (see [ADR-002](002_storage_deduplication_scope.md)). Unlike retention and lifecycle policies, garbage collection is not user-configurable.

Deleting an artifact removes its attachment record. Once a blob has no attachments left within the boundary, garbage collection deletes the object from storage and then the blob record. Reclamation is deferred rather than immediate, so a re-push can rescue a recently dereferenced blob. [ADR-025: Garbage Collection](025_garbage_collection.md) records the full model, the coordination protocol, and the safety properties.

### Soft Delete Expiry

Background jobs permanently remove soft-deleted artifacts after the soft delete window expires. GA sets the window length together with the trash design.

### Secure Disposal

All permanent deletions (garbage collection, soft delete expiry, retention expiration) rely on the storage provider's secure deletion mechanisms, in accordance with the [Records Retention & Disposal](/handbook/security/policies_and_standards/records-retention-deletion/) policy. For object storage, this means the physical file is deleted through the provider's API. Database records are hard-deleted from PostgreSQL. Audit log entries for the deletion itself are retained per the [audit log retention](#audit-log-retention) periods.

## Backup Retention

Backup retention for the Artifact Registry's PostgreSQL database and object storage is a platform responsibility and follows the deployment's standard backup policies: GitLab.com follows the existing GitLab backup schedules, and GitLab Dedicated and GitLab Self-Managed administrators configure their own.

Backups may contain artifacts that retention policies, lifecycle policies, or garbage collection have already deleted. Restoring from backup may reintroduce them. This is expected behavior and the normal retention and cleanup cycle will re-process them.

## Storage Class Transitions

Storage class management is a **platform responsibility**. The Artifact Registry does not manipulate storage classes; deployment administrators configure transitions on their storage provider when supported, for example with GCS [Autoclass](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/autoclass) or S3 [Intelligent-Tiering](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/storage-classes/intelligent-tiering/). The service is able to see and operate with artifacts regardless of their storage class.

Storage class transitions are independent of retention and cleanup:

- Artifacts in archive storage are still subject to retention limits and lifecycle policies
- Soft-deleted artifacts retain their storage class until hard deletion
- Virtual repository caches follow the same transitions as hosted artifacts

## Cross-Cutting Concerns

### Multi-Region Replication

When artifacts are deleted by retention policies, lifecycle policies, or garbage collection, the deletion must propagate to all replicas. Whatever replication mechanism the Artifact Registry adopts must ensure that deleted blobs and metadata are removed from all replicas to avoid storage drift and stale data.

### Subscription Expiration

The Artifact Registry is available on Premium and Ultimate and is billed through GitLab Credits.
Only a plan lapse suspends the namespace: the [subscription expires](https://docs.gitlab.com/subscriptions/manage_subscription/#expired-subscription) or is downgraded below Premium.
Reaching the usage limit does not suspend the namespace (see [Usage Limit Block](#usage-limit-block)).
Usage during the suspension is written off and not billed.
Renewing the plan lifts the suspension.
The suspension starts a three-phase lifecycle, which reuses the existing [soft delete](#soft-delete) and [garbage collection](#garbage-collection) mechanisms:

| Phase | Duration | Access | Description |
|-------|----------|--------|-------------|
| Write-blocked | 30 days after suspension (day 0-30) | Read only (pull allowed, push blocked) | No usage is billed. Existing artifacts remain accessible, so CI/CD pipelines keep pulling and teams can migrate or renew. [Retention policies](#artifact-retention) and [lifecycle policies](#lifecycle-policies) continue to run. Renewing the plan within this window lifts the suspension. |
| Soft delete | 30 days after write-blocked ends (day 30-60) | No access, data recoverable | Data enters the existing [soft delete](#soft-delete) pipeline. Renewing the plan within this window restores all data. |
| Hard deletion | After soft delete window (day 60+) | N/A | The lifecycle purger permanently removes the data, and [garbage collection](#garbage-collection) reclaims its blobs. |

The namespace's slug (registry handle) follows these phases and is permanently retired at hard deletion. See [ADR-015: Slug Policy (internal)](https://internal.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/decisions/015_slug_policy/#slug-lifecycle) for the slug-specific semantics, including reclaim within the soft-delete window.

Notifications follow the same framework defined in the [Notifications](#notifications) section:

- At suspension: the namespace is read-only, with soft deletion in 30 days
- 14 days before write-blocked phase ends: upcoming soft deletion
- 14 days before soft delete window ends: upcoming permanent deletion

This timeline is more generous than existing GitLab precedents: [GitLab Duo add-ons retain seat assignments for 28 days](https://docs.gitlab.com/subscriptions/subscription-add-ons/#at-subscription-expiration) after expiration with features unavailable immediately, and standard [GitLab subscription expiration](https://docs.gitlab.com/subscriptions/manage_subscription/#expired-subscription) immediately downgrades to the free tier.
Unlike stateless features such as GitLab Duo, the Artifact Registry stores customer data that cannot be re-created, and losing read access can break production deployments.
Unlike the GitLab core platform, it has no free tier to fall back to: once the read-only phase ends, the customer loses access completely, not to a degraded experience.

This section covers involuntary suspension (a lapsed plan). Intentional cancellation, where a customer actively opts out and controls their exit timeline, may warrant a different offboarding path, which this ADR does not decide.

### Usage Limit Block

A namespace that reaches its usage limit gets the usage-limit block, not a suspension:

- Pulls are served and pushes are refused.
- Usage is still billed.
- No deletion clock starts: the block never leads to soft delete or hard deletion.
- The block lifts when the usage limit is raised or the monthly usage resets.

The usage-limit block applies on GitLab.com only.
On Self-Managed and Dedicated, a plan lapse is the only restriction.

A subscription without accepted overage terms gets the same kind of block.
That block lifts once the terms are accepted.

Suspension and the usage-limit block show their own reason in the UI and in client errors.

### Billing and Retention by Condition

[ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md#namespace-lifecycle) defines the namespace service conditions and lets several apply at the same time.

- Usage is not billed while the namespace is suspended, even when another condition also applies: it is written off.
- Under every other condition, usage is billed until deletion or purge.
- Retention applies under every condition, until deletion or purge.

## Deferred to Later Iterations

No release builds these yet. Each rule below binds its feature when it ships. The spec that builds the feature takes over its values; until then they live here.

### Extending Retention

By default, all repositories must comply with the Organization's retention policy through strict enforcement. Organization Owners can optionally enable:

- Repository-level exceptions: Allow repositories to extend retention beyond the Organization default
- Indefinite retention: Allow critical artifacts to be retained indefinitely

These mechanisms are designed for regulated industries where multi-year retention is required (for example, SOX or HIPAA).

### Cache Retention

Cached artifacts are automatically deleted once unused for a set number of days since their last download. Cache retention is more aggressive than hosted artifact retention because cached content can be re-fetched from upstream.

| Setting          | Options                        | Default |
|------------------|--------------------------------|---------|
| Retention period | 1-365 days since last download | 7 days  |
| Cleanup cadence  | Daily, weekly, monthly         | Daily   |

Cache retention is enabled by default.

### Lifecycle Policies

Lifecycle policies are user-defined rules that actively delete artifacts matching specific criteria. They execute more aggressive cleanup than the default retention period:

- Lifecycle policies can delete artifacts before the retention period expires
- Retention deletes artifacts that lifecycle policies miss or ignore
- Neither mechanism can resurrect destroyed artifacts

#### Supported Strategies

| Strategy                | Description                             | Example                                    |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Keep last N versions    | Retain the N most recent versions       | Keep last 10 versions                      |
| Age since last download | Delete artifacts unused within a period | Delete if unused for 90 days               |
| Pattern matching        | Retain artifacts matching a pattern     | Keep `release-*` names; keep `v*` versions |

An artifact that was never downloaded counts as last downloaded at the oldest possible time, so an age-since-last-download rule can delete it.

Lifecycle policies use **keep semantics only**: patterns define what to retain, and everything not matched is eligible for deletion. Conflicting keep and expire rules are hard to reason about.

#### Artifact Targeting

Pattern matching uses one targeting model shared with access rules and virtual repository filters. Each rule specifies a **pattern** and a **target field**, and a rule can combine several target fields. Available target fields vary by artifact type:

| Artifact type    | Target fields                            |
|------------------|------------------------------------------|
| npm              | Scope, package name, version             |
| Maven            | `groupId`, `artifactId`, version         |
| Container images | Image name, tag                          |
| Generic          | Package name, version                    |
| Go               | Module path (decoded), version           |

Using the same targeting model across lifecycle policies, access rules, and virtual repository allow/deny filters enables implementation reuse and a consistent user experience.

### Notifications

The Artifact Registry notifies users before every scheduled permanent removal:

| Trigger                | Description                                                  |
|------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Retention expiration   | Artifacts approaching the retention limit                    |
| Lifecycle policy match | Artifacts matching a lifecycle policy scheduled for deletion |
| Soft delete expiry     | Soft-deleted artifacts approaching permanent removal         |

A minimum advance notice of 30 days before retention expiration should be enforced to give users time to download or extend retention on critical artifacts.

### Export and Import

GitLab project export/import may reference artifacts stored in the Artifact Registry. If artifacts have been deleted by retention or lifecycle policies before an export, the export should handle missing artifacts gracefully (for example, by excluding them and logging the omission rather than failing).

### Dependent Features

CI pipelines, merge requests, and other GitLab features may reference artifacts managed by the Artifact Registry. When retention or lifecycle policies delete these artifacts, the **service or application that holds the reference** is responsible for handling the missing artifact gracefully:

- Links to deleted artifacts should display clear messaging rather than generic errors
- API responses for deleted artifacts should return appropriate status codes
- Soft-deleted artifacts should remain resolvable (with a "scheduled for deletion" indicator) until hard deletion

The Artifact Registry does not proactively notify dependent features when an artifact is deleted. Dependent services resolve references at query time and handle missing artifacts accordingly.

## Consequences

### Positive

- **Predictable costs**: Default expiration prevents unbounded storage growth
- **Automatic cost optimization**: Storage class transitions reduce costs for aging artifacts without manual intervention
- **Flexibility**: Organization and repository overrides accommodate diverse needs
- **Recovery capability**: Soft delete protects against accidental deletion
- **Compliance support**: Configurable retention meets regulatory requirements
- **Cache efficiency**: TTL-based management balances freshness with storage

### Negative

- **Onboarding friction**: Users must understand default expiration to avoid surprise deletions
- **Complexity**: Multiple retention levels (Organization, repository, rule) require clear documentation
- **Background load**: Cleanup jobs consume additional resources

## Alternatives Considered

### Require Explicit Policy Before Publishing

Users must configure a lifecycle policy before publishing artifacts.

**Trade-offs**: Prevents accidental storage growth but increases onboarding friction and may discourage adoption.

### Indefinite Retention by Default

Artifacts persist forever unless explicitly deleted.

**Why rejected**: Leads to unbounded storage growth and cost surprises. Most users forget to configure cleanup policies, resulting in accumulated stale artifacts.

### API-First Soft Delete

Ship soft delete on the API in closed beta and defer restore, trash, and expiration to GA.

**Why rejected**: Five flows break once the UI is absent:

1. An invisible record holds a repository name that is immutable and globally unique ([ADR-009](009_api_design.md)).
1. The same Delete button acts reversibly for npm and permanently for containers.
1. A republished version leaves the original impossible to restore.
1. A delete frees no storage.
1. Admin-only purge becomes the only cleanup path.

Soft delete, restore, trash, and expiration therefore ship as one feature at GA (see [Release Phasing](#release-phasing)).

## References

- [ADR-001: Organizations as Anchor Point](001_organizations_as_anchor_point.md)
- [ADR-007: Database Schema](007_database_schema.md) - Blob attachments and cleanup
- [ADR-009: API Design](009_api_design.md#repository-deletion) - Destructive intent on repository delete
- [GitLab Audit Events Documentation](https://docs.gitlab.com/administration/compliance/audit_event_reports/)
- [Records Retention & Disposal](/handbook/security/policies_and_standards/records-retention-deletion/) - GitLab security policy for records retention and secure disposal
- [Data Retention Guidelines for Feature Development](/handbook/engineering/architecture/guidelines/data_lifecycle/data_retention/) - Architecture guidelines for data retention in new features

title: 011 Data Reconciliation
text:
<!-- Design Documents often contain forward-looking statements -->
<!-- vale gitlab.FutureTense = NO -->

## Context

Content-addressable storage ([ADR-008](008_content_addressable_storage.md)) keeps two sources of truth: records in the database and objects in storage.
They can diverge:

- A crash between the storage write and the database commit leaves an object with no record.
- A delete that fails after the move leaves the staging object behind.
- An operator or another process changes or deletes an object outside the registry, so a record points at missing or wrong content.
- A reference-tracking bug keeps a reference after its artifact is gone, so the blob is never reclaimed, or removes one too early, so the next garbage collection loses data.

Remote caches diverge the same way.
Content-addressable storage stores every blob the same way, whatever its origin, so the same features cover them.

Three features address divergence:

| Feature | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Garbage collection (GC) | Reclaims blobs whose last reference is gone |
| Upload purging | Deletes the staging objects and the records of abandoned uploads |
| Data validation | Finds and reports objects with no record, references kept after their artifact is gone, and other divergence between records and objects. Other documents call it the reconciliation service |

[ADR-010](010_data_retention.md) decides what GC reclaims, and [ADR-025](025_garbage_collection.md) decides how.
This ADR decides when each feature ships, and what the schema and the storage layout must keep so the deferred one can ship later.
Expiring soft-deleted artifacts is retention, not reconciliation: both sources agree on the data's state, and only the policy says it should go.

## Decision

**GC and upload purging ship before data validation. Data validation is deferred, and the schema and the storage layout keep what it needs, so it can ship later without tracking of its own.**

Upload purging runs as one of the [GC jobs](025_garbage_collection.md#jobs).

### What must always hold

| # | Constraint | Machine-checkable? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **GC and upload purging find their work in the database.** They select candidates from database records, never by listing storage, and each sweep is scheduled once for the fleet, not once per instance. | Yes: neither lists storage, and running more instances does not run any sweep more often |
| 2 | **An abandoned upload is found from its record.** Every upload session has an expiry in the database, so upload purging needs nothing else to find what to delete. | Yes: every upload session record has an expiry, and the purge finds every expired session from the records alone |
| 3 | **A storage key maps back to its records.** A blob key holds the namespace hash and the content hash, and a staging key holds the namespace hash and the upload ID, so both read back without a database lookup ([ADR-008](008_content_addressable_storage.md)). Hashing a blob again verifies its content. Data validation matches objects and records both ways without a mapping of its own. | Yes: every key the layout produces parses back to the namespace hash, and the content hash or upload ID, it was built from |
| 4 | **A namespace's blobs can be read page by page.** GC and data validation both work one namespace at a time ([ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md)), so the schema serves one namespace's blobs in bounded pages. | Yes: a page of one namespace's blobs reads a bounded number of rows |
| 5 | **One mechanism for every origin.** Each feature treats a blob the same way, whether a client uploaded it or a remote cache fetched it, with no per-format variant. | Yes: no feature reads where a blob came from |

### Why GC ships first

- **Retrofitting GC is the costly path.** The Container Registry added [online GC](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/container-registry/-/blob/master/docs/spec/gitlab/online-garbage-collection.md) after years in production, to a system with billions of objects and nothing tracking their references. A new service can build it in from the start.
- **The window is now.** With little data, a GC bug puts fewer objects at risk, GC competes less with API traffic for storage and database connections, and the data is small enough to inspect by hand. The races between GC and the API exist at any scale, but they cost least while the service is new, and that window does not come back.
- **Orphans only grow.** Without GC, nothing frees a blob that nothing references. The Container Registry grew to billions of objects and tens of petabytes on GitLab.com ([ADR-003](003_system_requirements.md), [ADR-002](002_storage_deduplication_scope.md)).
- **GC proves the reference tracking.** It is the only consumer of the whole reference lifecycle: add a reference, remove it, confirm none is left, delete. Running it early shows the schema tracks references correctly ([ADR-007](007_database_schema.md)) before data volume makes a bug costly.

### Why data validation can wait

Data validation finds divergence after it happens and prevents none.
GC reclaims blobs that nothing references, and upload purging reclaims abandoned uploads.
Validation catches objects left with no record by a crash or by a failed delete after the move, references kept after their artifact is gone, storage corruption, changes made outside the registry, and bugs in GC or upload purging.
Telling those apart from correct state needs a production baseline, and running GC first gives one.
Constraints 3 and 4 keep anything that diverges in the meantime detectable from the database and storage alone.
If either were missing, validation would need tracking of its own and would have to ship earlier.

### Adoption path

1. GC and upload purging ship first. GC turns on its deletes in the [phases of ADR-025](025_garbage_collection.md#adoption).
1. Data validation starts by reporting: logs and metrics for each divergence it finds, and no automated repair.
1. Repair follows in a later iteration.

## Alternatives Considered

### Do nothing: defer all three

Rejected: it trades the one-time chance to build GC into an empty service for a permanent retrofit, ships the reference-tracking schema unproven under real traffic, and lets orphaned blobs grow with nothing to correct them.

### Ship data validation with GC

It would close the window in which divergence goes unnoticed.
Rejected: validation needs the production baseline that only running GC gives, and unlike GC it has no one-time window, so it adds scope without matching risk reduction.

### Defer upload purging

Abandoned uploads would leave staging objects and session records to pile up: a hygiene cost, not a correctness one.
Rejected: nothing can reference a staging object, so the purge needs no review delay and no recheck under a lock.
It runs as one more GC job.

### Find candidates by listing storage

Walk storage and compare each object with the database.
Rejected: in the Container Registry, listing storage used memory that grew with storage, and a sweep on every instance repeated the same work, until it rebuilt its schema to track references in the database.
The cost grows with total storage, not with what changed.

## Consequences

### Positive

1. GC shows that reference tracking is correct under real traffic before data volume grows.
1. Concurrency bugs in GC are cheapest to find and fix while data volume is low.
1. Data validation can ship later without tracking of its own.

### Negative

1. GC's schema support and background jobs are built before data volume needs them.
1. Until data validation ships, divergence other than unreferenced blobs and abandoned uploads goes unnoticed.
1. Until data validation ships, a GC bug that deletes a referenced blob too early is found only when a client asks for the artifact. Low data volume bounds how many artifacts it hits, not how long it goes unnoticed.

title: 012 Usage Data Collection
text:
<!-- Design Documents often contain forward-looking statements -->
<!-- vale gitlab.FutureTense = NO -->

## Context

The Artifact Registry requires usage data collection for product analytics and business intelligence, and separately, billing events. Usage data answers critical questions: which artifact formats are most adopted, how many artifacts are pushed and pulled, how storage grows over time, how many unique users interact with the registry, and what virtual repository cache hit rates look like.

The Artifact Registry is a standalone Go service deployed outside the Rails monolith ([ADR-006](006_technology_stack.md)). The GitLab primary instrumentation framework — [Internal Event Tracking](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/development/internal_analytics/) backed by Snowplow — is designed around Rails monolith integration. Collecting usage data from a satellite service requires a deliberate strategy.

Collection must work across all deployment types:

- **GitLab.com (SaaS)**: Multi-tenant, GitLab-operated infrastructure with full access to analytics pipelines
- **Self-Managed**: Customer-hosted instances where data collection is on by default and administrators can opt out
- **GitLab Dedicated**: Single-tenant cloud instances managed by GitLab, functionally similar to self-managed for data collection purposes

### Internal Event Tracking via Snowplow

The GitLab primary instrumentation framework. Events are sent to Snowplow collectors, flow through an AWS pipeline with pseudonymization, and land in a data lake to be ingested into the Snowflake data warehouse.
Available on SaaS always, and on self-managed/Dedicated from GitLab 18.0+, on by default unless an administrator opts out.

For Go satellite services, [LabKit v2](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/labkit) provides a native Snowplow tracker (`v2/events/snowplow/`) with:

- Custom usage events using the [`custom_event`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/iglu/-/tree/master/public/schemas/com.gitlab/custom_event/jsonschema) schema, with one or more self-describing custom contexts attached to carry typed, schema-validated attributes.
- Billable usage events using the [`billable_usage`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/iglu/-/tree/master/public/schemas/com.gitlab/billable_usage/jsonschema) schema, whose first-class fields include the billing keys (the `billing_entity_type` and `billing_entity_id` pair, `root_namespace_id`, `unique_instance_id`), `realm`, `deployment_type`, `quantity`, and `unit_of_measure`, plus a free-form `metadata` object for dimensions the schema does not model.
- Asynchronous batch sending with automatic retry and FIFO queue management
- Built-in Prometheus metrics for emitter observability
- In-memory event storage (10,000 event capacity) with overflow protection

This is the same mechanism used by other satellite services (AI Gateway, GitLab Language Server) and is the organizationally recommended path for Go services.

### Context schemas for custom events

Every AR custom event attaches two contexts, layered by scope:

- **[`gitlab_standard`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/iglu/-/tree/master/public/schemas/com.gitlab/gitlab_standard/jsonschema)** — universal identity and environment fields (`environment`, `realm`, `instance_id`, `deployment_type`, `organization_uuid`, `user_id`). The Artifact Registry stores only the Organization's UUID ([ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md)), so it populates `organization_uuid` and never the integer `organization_id`. Lands AR events in the same warehouse columns as monolith events for cross-product analysis.
- **[`artifact_registry_context`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/iglu/-/tree/master/public/schemas/com.gitlab/artifact_registry_context/jsonschema)** — AR-specific dimensions: `ar_instance_version` (required), `ar_namespace_id` (namespace UUID) and `ar_namespace_slug`, `format`, `repository_kind` (`hosted`/`virtual`/`remote`), `repository_id` (repository UUID) and `repository_name`, `cache_hit`, `upstream_type` (`hosted`/`remote`). Namespace and repository each carry their UUID plus a human-readable identifier. The UUIDs are the stable join keys for analytics, because the slug, while immutable for customers, can change through administrative reclamation (squatting disputes, legal claims).

Event-specific one-offs (for example `auth_method`, `deletion_type`, `artifacts_removed_count`) go in the event's own `custom_event` payload rather than in either context.

## Decision

**The Artifact Registry will use the LabKit v2 Snowplow tracker as its sole usage data collection mechanism.** Usage data is best effort. Events are emitted directly from the Go service to the Snowplow collector endpoint. No Rails monolith integration is required for analytics data flow.
Billing is not usage data and must be reliable, so it follows its own rules (see [Billing events](#billing-events)).

This is the simplest path that delivers event-level product analytics for the MVP. It mirrors the approach already used by other Go satellite services (AI Gateway, GitLab Language Server). Aggregated metric collection (for example via Service Ping) is intentionally out of scope; if a future need arises for self-managed instances that opt out of Snowplow, it can be addressed in a follow-up ADR.

### Event-Level Tracking via LabKit v2 Snowplow

**What to track** (initial set, expanded iteratively). Every event carries both `gitlab_standard` and `artifact_registry_context` as custom contexts. Universal fields (`organization_uuid`, `realm`, `deployment_type`, `instance_id`, `environment`, `user_id`) come from `gitlab_standard` and are not repeated below.

| Event | `artifact_registry_context` fields | Event payload (one-off) fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `artifact_registry_artifact_pushed` | `format`, `repository_kind=hosted`, `repository_id`, `ar_namespace_id` | `auth_method` |
| `artifact_registry_artifact_pulled` | `format`, `repository_kind` (`hosted`/`virtual`), `repository_id`, `ar_namespace_id`, `cache_hit` (virtual only) | `auth_method`, `delivery_mode` (`proxy`/`redirect`) |
| `artifact_registry_artifact_deleted` | `format`, `repository_kind`, `repository_id`, `ar_namespace_id` | `deletion_type` (`manual`/`lifecycle_policy`) |
| `artifact_registry_namespace_created` | `ar_namespace_id` | — |
| `artifact_registry_repository_created` | `format`, `repository_kind`, `repository_id`, `ar_namespace_id` | — |
| `artifact_registry_repository_deleted` | `format`, `repository_kind`, `repository_id`, `ar_namespace_id` | — |
| `artifact_registry_virtual_cache_miss` | `format`, `repository_kind=virtual`, `repository_id`, `ar_namespace_id`, `upstream_type` (`hosted`/`remote`) | — |
| `artifact_registry_lifecycle_policy_executed` | `format`, `repository_kind`, `repository_id`, `ar_namespace_id` | `artifacts_removed_count` |

#### When a pull event fires

The catalog above names the dimensions but not the moment. "Download success" is ambiguous once a response can fail after its status is committed, and each format slice resolved that ambiguity independently, so the readings diverged. The rule is **each delivery mode reports the strongest signal it can observe**.

[ADR-005](005_artifact_delivery_mode.md) defines the two modes. Because it makes the mode an instance-level default with an always-available per-namespace override, the same artifact can be counted under either rule, depending on the namespace serving it. The event records how the response actually delivered, not the configured setting.

1. **Proxy mode**: the service streams the bytes, so it knows whether delivery completed. The event fires only after the payload copy finishes cleanly. Once the response status is committed, a client disconnect or a storage read fault emits nothing, because a partial transfer is not a download.
1. **Redirect mode**: the service hands the client a pre-signed storage or CDN URL and never sees the transfer. The event fires when the service issues the redirect. That is the only observable moment, and it counts as one pull for product usage.

Leveling proxy mode down to the redirect rule would discard a delivery signal the service holds; leveling redirect mode up to the proxy rule is impossible.

The two modes therefore carry different confidence. Redirect-mode pulls can over-count (the client may never follow the redirect) and under-count (one pre-signed URL may serve several transfers within its TTL, and a CDN may serve many clients from one origin fetch). The event payload carries the mode, per the catalog above, so analysis can separate the two; summing across both blends the confidence levels. Billable quantity in particular cannot rest on redirect-mode events; it needs storage or CDN access logs.

The AR namespace is the slug-anchored entity from [ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md) — an organization can own multiple AR namespaces. The [billing design doc](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/usage-billing/design-doc/-/merge_requests/27) sets the metering boundary at the AR namespace: billable events carry `ar_namespace_id` in `billable_usage.metadata`, and analytics events carry it in `artifact_registry_context`, so both datasets aggregate at the same granularity. `organization_uuid` (in `gitlab_standard`) supports cross-namespace rollups.

**Configuration**: The Snowplow collector endpoint is provided in the service configuration file. On SaaS, this points to `snowplowprd.trx.gitlab.net`.
On self-managed and Dedicated instances that do not opt out, this is configured to point to the same collector.
On instances that opt out, the analytics emitter is disabled (no analytics events are sent).
Billing events do not depend on the opt-out (see [Billing events](#billing-events)).

**Coverage**: SaaS (always), self-managed and Dedicated (on by default, administrators can opt out).

**Data destination**: Events flow through the standard Snowplow pipeline (collector, enricher, pseudonymization, S3) into the Snowflake data warehouse. No custom pipeline infrastructure is required.

### Billing events

Billing usage is not telemetry and must be reliable, so billing events follow their own rules:

- **Opt-out**: billing events ignore the product usage data opt-out. The opt-out applies to analytics events only.
- **Destination on GitLab.com**: the service sends billing events on a separate billing tracker to an authenticated billing collector, separate from the analytics one.
- **Schema**: the service sends its own `billable_usage` context, not LabKit v2's billing API.
- **Delivery**: no billing event is lost silently. Delivery survives process restarts and collector outages, and a re-sent event keeps its event ID, so it is counted once.

The meters differ per deployment:

| Meter | GitLab.com | Connected Self-Managed and Dedicated | Air-gapped Self-Managed (offline license) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Component versions | Yes | Yes | No event. Rails pulls the service's daily component counts and includes them in the offline usage export |
| Storage | Yes, billed once blob reclamation ships | No | No |
| Egress | Yes | No | No |

The egress event carries the bytes sent for one namespace and one delivery mode in one hour.
The service counts the bytes it streams itself.
It never sees a redirected transfer, so those bytes come from storage and CDN access logs, as [When a pull event fires](#when-a-pull-event-fires) requires ([ADR-029 (internal)](https://internal.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/decisions/029_egress_metering/)).

The air-gapped pull is not the Service Ping API that [Alternative 3](#alternative-3-add-service-ping-integration-for-self-managed-opt-out-coverage) rejects: it reads one stored daily count per namespace, so its cardinality and query cost stay small.

On Self-Managed and Dedicated, how the component event reaches the billing collector and how it authenticates is open.

### Operational Metrics (Non-Product)

The Artifact Registry already uses LabKit v2 for Prometheus metrics (request latency, error rates, connection pool stats). These are operational metrics consumed by infrastructure dashboards and alerting, not product analytics. They are mentioned here for completeness but are not part of the usage data collection decision.

The LabKit Snowplow emitter itself exposes Prometheus metrics (enqueue counts, send success/failure, batch delivery duration, queue depth) that should be registered for operational visibility into the event pipeline health.

## Consequences

### Positive

1. **Full SaaS coverage from day one**: LabKit v2's Snowplow tracker is production-proven and provides event-level granularity with no additional infrastructure
1. **Simple, single-path instrumentation**: One mechanism, one codepath. No coordination with the Rails monolith for analytics data flow
1. **Organization-scoped context**: Every event carries `gitlab_standard.organization_uuid`, aligning with the Organization-anchored architecture ([ADR-001](001_organizations_as_anchor_point.md)). The integer `organization_id` fields stay unpopulated because the service stores only the UUID; billing joins key on the `billing_entity_type`/`billing_entity_id` pair (SaaS, from the namespace's billing anchor, [ADR-007](007_database_schema.md)) and `unique_instance_id` (Self-Managed and Dedicated)
1. **Privacy by default**: Events flow through the existing GitLab pseudonymization pipeline (HMAC-SHA256) without additional privacy engineering
1. **No custom infrastructure**: Uses the existing Snowplow pipeline and Snowflake warehouse
1. **Billing-ready**: the service sends its own `billable_usage` context on a separate billing tracker, not through LabKit v2's billing API ([Billing events](#billing-events)). This gives usage-based billing through GitLab Credits the fields it needs, such as realm, unit of measure, and quantity
1. **Aligned with satellite service precedent**: AI Gateway and GitLab Language Server already use LabKit v2 Snowplow directly. The Artifact Registry follows the same pattern.

### Negative

1. **Minimum LabKit v2 and iglu version dependency**: Emitting custom contexts on custom events requires a LabKit v2 release that supports it, and the `artifact_registry_context` schema must be deployed to the Snowplow enrichment pipeline before AR events using it pass validation.
1. **No analytics data from Snowplow opt-out instances**: Self-managed and Dedicated instances that opt out of Snowplow forwarding contribute no analytics data.
   Billing events do not depend on the opt-out ([Billing events](#billing-events)).
   This is acceptable for the MVP given the customer's explicit opt-out. If aggregated coverage of opt-out instances becomes a product requirement, a Service Ping integration can be added in a follow-up ADR.
1. **In-memory event buffer risk**: LabKit v2's Snowplow emitter uses in-memory storage (up to 10,000 events). Events are lost on process restart. For the Artifact Registry's expected event volume, this is acceptable for analytics events — they are analytics data, not transactional records. Billing events do not accept this loss ([Billing events](#billing-events)). Prometheus metrics on the emitter provide visibility into overflow or drop rates.

## Alternatives Considered

### Alternative 1: Route All Events Through the Rails Monolith

#### Approach

The Artifact Registry sends all usage events to the Rails monolith via an internal API. The monolith then fires `track_internal_event()` calls on behalf of the registry, using the existing Rails-integrated Snowplow pipeline.

#### Why Not Chosen

1. **Tight coupling**: Every tracked action would require an API call to the monolith, creating a runtime dependency for analytics on the critical path or a background job queue between the services
1. **Latency and availability risk**: If the monolith is slow or unavailable, event tracking degrades or blocks. LabKit's in-process emitter decouples tracking from any external service
1. **Unnecessary indirection**: LabKit v2 provides the same Snowplow tracker that the monolith uses internally, eliminating the need for a middleman
1. **Counter-pattern for satellite services**: Other Go services (AI Gateway, GitLab Language Server) already emit Snowplow events directly. Routing through Rails would be a regression from established patterns

### Alternative 2: OpenTelemetry (OTLP) to ClickHouse

#### Approach

Follow the [CI Job Telemetry](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/ci_job_telemetry/) pattern: emit OTLP traces/metrics to an OTEL Collector that writes to ClickHouse. Use ClickHouse as the analytics store instead of Snowflake.

#### Why Not Chosen

1. **Different use case**: CI Job Telemetry uses OTLP for operational performance traces (span-level timing of job stages). Artifact Registry usage data is product analytics (who uses what, how much, adoption trends). These are different domains with different query patterns and consumers
1. **ClickHouse availability**: ClickHouse is not yet universally available across all deployment types. Snowplow/Snowflake is the established product analytics infrastructure
1. **Organizational alignment**: The Analytics Instrumentation team owns the Snowplow pipeline and Snowflake warehouse. Product analytics consumers (product managers, data analysts) query Snowflake. Using ClickHouse would require building new query infrastructure and data models outside the established workflow
1. **Future compatibility**: If ClickHouse becomes the standard product analytics store, LabKit v2's Snowplow events can be rerouted at the pipeline level without changing application code. The decision is not mutually exclusive with future OTLP adoption

### Alternative 3: Add Service Ping Integration for Self-Managed Opt-Out Coverage

#### Approach

In addition to Snowplow, expose an internal API on the Artifact Registry that the Rails monolith queries during weekly Service Ping assembly to collect aggregated metrics. This would provide aggregated coverage even for instances that opt out of Snowplow event forwarding.

#### Why Not Chosen

1. **Cardinality problem**: Service Ping payloads aggregate to flat scalar metrics (one number per metric per week). The Artifact Registry's interesting dimensions — format, repository kind (hosted/virtual/remote), authentication method, organization, upstream type — explode into a large number of metric variants once cross-tabulated. Modeling this in Service Ping requires either flattening cardinality (losing analytical value) or registering hundreds of pre-aggregated metric YAML definitions (operational burden). Snowplow events handle high cardinality naturally because dimensions are stored alongside each event in the warehouse.
1. **Expensive SQL aggregations**: Service Ping computes its metrics via SQL queries on the live database. The Artifact Registry's tables (artifacts, blob references, cache entries) are partitioned by namespace and grow into the billions of rows at GitLab.com scale ([ADR-007](007_database_schema.md), [ADR-003](003_system_requirements.md)). Cross-namespace `COUNT`/`SUM` queries to populate weekly Service Ping metrics would scan large amounts of data on every cycle — an expensive operation we do not need to justify when Snowplow already provides the same information from the warehouse without touching the production database.
1. **Avoid Redis counter infrastructure**: The alternative to live SQL is to maintain Redis-backed counters incremented on every artifact operation, then read by Service Ping. This is the pattern the Rails monolith uses for HyperLogLog and Redis HLL metrics. Adopting it here would add a new operational dependency (Redis counters, expiry handling, recovery semantics on Redis flush) and a new instrumentation surface in the hot path of every push/pull. Snowplow already captures this data at the same instrumentation point, so the Redis counter layer would be pure duplication.
1. **Cross-service coordination**: Adds a dependency on the Rails monolith team for the YAML metric definitions, which is the kind of cross-service coupling we are trying to avoid in this ADR.
1. **Bounded gap**: Self-managed customers who opt out of Snowplow are explicitly choosing not to share data. The coverage gap is bounded and aligned with customer intent.
1. **Not foreclosed**: This option remains available as a follow-up if product requires aggregated coverage of opt-out instances. A separate ADR can revisit the tradeoff once we have data on opt-out rates.

## Implementation Sequence

1. **Phase 1 (MVP)**: Integrate the LabKit v2 Snowplow tracker. Emit events for core actions (push, pull, delete, repository create) with `gitlab_standard` and `artifact_registry_context` attached. Register emitter Prometheus metrics. Validate events arrive in Snowflake on staging with both contexts populated.
1. **Phase 2 (Billing)**:
   Emit billing events for the meters of each deployment ([Billing events](#billing-events)), conforming to the `billable_usage` schema:
   `billing_entity_type` and `billing_entity_id` identify the payer on SaaS (AR takes both values from the namespace's stored pair, [ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md)), `root_namespace_id` stays on SaaS events because the schema requires it and CustomersDot uses it as the fallback when the pair is absent (AR stores only the pair, so while the type is `top_level_group` it sends `billing_entity_id` as `root_namespace_id` too, and once the type changes it sends `null`, which the schema allows), and `ar_namespace_id` (the metering boundary per the [billing design doc](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/usage-billing/design-doc/-/merge_requests/27)) rides in the event's `metadata` object alongside `feature_qualified_name`.
   On Self-Managed and Dedicated, the transport of the component event is open, and with it where `unique_instance_id` comes from ([Billing events](#billing-events)).
   The billing pipeline reads only the top-level `billable_usage` fields and `metadata`, never the Snowplow custom contexts, so AR-specific billing dimensions belong in `metadata` rather than in `artifact_registry_context`.
   Independent of Phase 1.
1. **Phase 3 (Iteration)**: Expand event coverage based on product analytics requests — virtual repository usage patterns, lifecycle policy effectiveness, format-specific adoption. Extend `artifact_registry_context` (new minor version) if recurring AR-specific dimensions warrant first-class warehouse columns.

## References

- [Iglu `custom_event` schema](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/iglu/-/tree/master/public/schemas/com.gitlab/custom_event/jsonschema) — Schema for custom event payloads
- [Iglu `billable_usage` schema](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/iglu/-/tree/master/public/schemas/com.gitlab/billable_usage/jsonschema) — Schema for billable usage event payloads (billing keys: `billing_entity_type`, `billing_entity_id`, `root_namespace_id`, `unique_instance_id`)
- [Iglu `gitlab_standard` schema](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/iglu/-/tree/master/public/schemas/com.gitlab/gitlab_standard/jsonschema) — Universal identity/environment context attached to AR custom events
- [Iglu `artifact_registry_context` schema](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/iglu/-/tree/master/public/schemas/com.gitlab/artifact_registry_context/jsonschema) — AR-specific context schema (merged in [iglu!190](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/iglu/-/merge_requests/190))

title: 013 Storage Backend Interaction
text:
<!-- Design Documents often contain forward-looking statements -->
<!-- vale gitlab.FutureTense = NO -->

## Context

When the service redirects a download ([ADR-005](005_artifact_delivery_mode.md)), it answers with a signed URL, and the client fetches the bytes from a CDN or straight from blob storage.
So the service has to settle which CDN may front which storage, which clients skip the CDN, and how a download it never sees is attributed to a namespace.
When the service streams a download instead, it signs no URL, uses no CDN and sees the whole transfer, so this ADR does not apply.

The Container Registry has served downloads this way on GitLab.com for years, at tens of petabytes of egress a month and a CDN cache hit rate above 85%.
The Artifact Registry adopts the same design.
[ADR-006](006_technology_stack.md) chooses the blob storage and the CDN for each deployment, and this ADR sets the rules every pairing must meet.

## Decision

**The CDN fronts the same provider's blob storage, and the service signs every download URL for one whole object. A redirected download is attributed to its namespace from the object path in the provider's access logs, never from anything a client can change.**

### What must always hold

| # | Constraint | Machine-checkable? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **The CDN fronts its own provider's blob storage.** A deployment pairs a CDN only with the same provider's blob storage, for example Google Cloud CDN with GCS, or CloudFront with S3. | Yes: a configuration that puts a CDN in front of another provider's blob storage is refused at startup |
| 2 | **The CDN checks the signature before it serves, cache hits included.** A private blob never leaves the cache without a valid signature. | Yes: a request with a missing, altered or expired signature is refused, also when the object is cached |
| 3 | **Signing never splits the cache.** Every signed URL for one object reads the same cache entry, whatever its signature or expiry. | Yes: a second URL signed for a cached object is served from the cache |
| 4 | **The CDN caches large objects.** Container layers and other large artifacts reach tens of gigabytes, so a pairing caches objects of at least 50 GB. | No: the limit is set by the CDN provider |
| 5 | **A signed URL covers one whole object.** The service signs the full object URL, never a shorter prefix, so the signature covers the whole path, the namespace hash included. | Yes: every signed URL the service issues authorizes exactly one object |
| 6 | **Attribution comes from the path alone.** A signed URL carries no attribution data in its query string, because a client can edit anything the signature does not cover. | Yes: no signed URL carries attribution data, such as a namespace or a user, outside its path |
| 7 | **Every client request is logged with its full object path.** The access logs record the full object path of every client request, whether the CDN or blob storage served it. | Yes: a download by either route leaves an access-log entry that holds the full object path |
