| 8 | **Switching pairings is a configuration change.** Moving between supported pairings needs no change to the application. | Yes: each supported pairing runs on the same build, selected by configuration alone |

### Supported pairings

The CDN and the blob storage come from one provider, for same-network cache fills, native signed URL validation and operational alignment.
The service signs every URL itself, server-side: with the CDN's native scheme for a CDN URL, and with the storage provider's native scheme for a direct one.

### Interaction patterns

With a CDN in front, a redirect sends the client one of two ways:

- **A client outside the provider's network goes to the CDN.** The CDN checks the signature and serves a cache hit, or on a miss fills its cache from blob storage over the provider's network.
- **A client inside the provider's network can go straight to blob storage.** Serving it from blob storage over the provider's network costs less than CDN delivery. The bypass is optional for each pairing: where the price gap is small, the routing adds complexity without benefit.

### Download metadata propagation

After a redirect, the service cannot see the download: whether the client finished it, how many bytes it got, or whether it failed.
The provider's access logs record the outcome: the CDN's logs for a request the CDN served, and blob storage's logs for a direct one.
The object path holds the namespace hash ([ADR-008](008_content_addressable_storage.md#storage-path-strategy)), so every log entry names the namespace that owns the blob.
Constraints 5 to 7 keep that true for every pairing, present or future.

## Consequences

### Positive

1. **Proven at scale**: the design mirrors the Container Registry on GitLab.com.
1. **Attribution across the redirect**: the namespace in the signed path closes the visibility gap that redirect mode leaves on GitLab.com.

### Negative

1. **Coupled pairing**: the CDN is tied to the blob storage provider. Deployments are usually all-GCP or all-AWS, so this rarely limits anyone, and a [cross-provider CDN](#cross-provider-cdn-for-example-cloudflare) stays possible.
1. **CDN delivery cost at scale**: provider-native CDNs charge for each GiB delivered, in tiers, so at high traffic volumes the CDN can become a significant cost.

## Alternatives

### Do nothing: no CDN

Redirect every download straight to blob storage.
Rejected: at any non-trivial traffic volume, a CDN cuts blob storage egress, lowers download latency through edge caching, and raises availability.

### Cross-provider CDN (for example, Cloudflare)

One CDN in front of every storage provider, so deployments diverge less in configuration.
A cost analysis at Container Registry scale showed significant potential savings, from Cloudflare's unmetered delivery.

Deferred: Cloudflare needs custom infrastructure to validate signed URLs (a WAF rule or a Worker), manual cache key stripping, and a way to extract download metadata that nobody has validated.
Filling its cache across networks costs materially more than a same-network fill.
The Artifact Registry starts from zero traffic, so the savings do not matter yet.

The option is not foreclosed: a cross-provider CDN can be added later as a new pairing, by revisiting constraint 1.

title: 014 Frontend To Artifact Registry
text:
<!-- Design Documents often contain forward-looking statements -->
<!-- vale gitlab.FutureTense = NO -->

## Status

**Proposed.**

## Context

The Artifact Registry runs on a separate domain from the GitLab monolith
(for example, `artifact-registry.gitlab.com` while the monolith is at
`gitlab.com` or `gitlab.acme.com`).

This ADR addresses the browser frontend: the Vue UI that lists
namespaces, browses repositories, displays artifact metadata, and
exposes management actions.

[ADR-009](009_api_design.md) specifies that the Artifact Registry
exposes management APIs. [ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md) defines
how the registry resolves namespaces independently of Rails
identifiers. The authentication mechanism between Rails and the
Artifact Registry follows the [auth agreement](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/).
This ADR consumes those contracts.

The Artifact Registry is centralized today, with self-managed
deployments planned. Artifact Registry releases on a faster cadence than the Rails
monolith.

## Decision

**Adopt the Rails GraphQL resolver pattern, with a Ruby client in
the Rails monolith talking to Artifact Registry REST API directly.**

Rails resolvers talk to the registry through Ruby methods that map
one-to-one to Artifact Registry REST endpoints, the same way the
Container Registry's `lib/container_registry/client.rb` does.

### Authentication and request flow

The browser sends GraphQL queries and mutations to `/api/graphql`,
authenticated by the session cookie and CSRF token. The browser stays
same-origin; the Artifact Registry credential is acquired and held server-side by the
Ruby client and never reaches the browser.

The Ruby client handles authentication on its own. Given the current
Rails user, the client performs the token exchange and attaches the
resulting credential to the request. Artifact Registry's own authentication and
authorization middlewares validate the request.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant FE as Frontend (gitlab.com)
    participant GQL as Rails GraphQL (gitlab.com)
    participant ARC as ArtifactRegistry::Client
    participant AR as Artifact Registry (artifact-registry.gitlab.com)

    FE->>GQL: GraphQL query (session cookie + CSRF)
    GQL->>GQL: Authenticate user
    GQL->>ARC: Call (current_user, request args)
    ARC->>ARC: Acquire Artifact Registry credential for current_user
    ARC->>AR: HTTP call (Artifact Registry credential)
    AR->>AR: Authenticate and authorize the request
    AR->>ARC: Response (or 401/403)
    ARC->>GQL: Domain object
    GQL->>FE: GraphQL response
```

### Cross-service data joining

The Artifact Registry stores GitLab identifiers, not the data they
point to. When a user creates, updates, or publishes something, Artifact Registry
records the user's ID; related projects and commits are stored as
references too. The actual names, avatars, profile links, project
metadata, and commit details all live in the Rails database. Most
user-facing Artifact Registry views need at least one of those, so the join from
Artifact Registry's identifiers to Rails entities runs on every user-facing read.

Rails does the join itself. For each kind of reference, a resolver
uses `BatchLoader::GraphQL` to fetch records by ID, reusing the
existing `Types::UserType`, `Types::ProjectType`, and
`Types::CommitType`. The pattern is used elsewhere in the monolith;
see `app/graphql/types/container_registry/container_repository_type.rb`
for live examples. However many records are on the page, the view
costs one Artifact Registry call plus one Rails query per referenced type.

This holds no matter how Artifact Registry ships, what its compatibility policy is,
or how it's deployed. It comes from Artifact Registry's choice to keep identifiers
rather than copy user, project, and commit data into Artifact Registry.

### API contract

GraphQL is the surface for browser-driven reads and mutations,
matching Container Registry. Each Artifact Registry resource has a matching Rails
GraphQL type: Namespace, Repository, Artifact, Tag, and Version. The
resolver derives the target resource identifier from arguments such
as `namespacePath` and `repositoryPath`. Resolvers map Artifact Registry
authorization failures to a not-available error and transport
failures to a service-unavailable error, matching the Container
Registry resolvers.

### Rails-side components

Three Rails-side components, each with a Container Registry analogue:

| Component | Path | Container Registry analogue |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP client | `lib/artifact_registry/client.rb` | `lib/container_registry/client.rb` |
| GraphQL types and resolvers | `app/graphql/types/artifact_registry/`, `app/graphql/resolvers/artifact_registry/` | `app/graphql/types/container_registry/`, `app/graphql/resolvers/container_repositories_resolver.rb` |
| Vue entry | `app/assets/javascripts/packages_and_registries/artifact_registry/` | `app/assets/javascripts/packages_and_registries/container_registry/explorer/` |

Rails persists the organization-to-namespace mapping as the namespace
UUID, written at namespace creation ([gitlab#603023](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/603023)),
and resolves the slug and namespace status from the Artifact Registry,
caching both ([ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md#slug-discovery)).
The client and the navigation gating (whether registry entries appear
for an organization) read from this persisted mapping and its cached slug/status instead of
calling the Artifact Registry on every page load.

The Rails-side credential acquisition follows the
[auth agreement](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/); the specific service and
exchange protocol are open (see [Open Questions](#open-questions)).

Resolvers get the client through a cached helper on the loaded
resource (the same pattern as `ContainerRepository#registry`). Child
fields that fan out per parent use the same batched-lookup pattern
described in [Cross-service data joining](#cross-service-data-joining),
collapsing N parent resolutions into one Artifact Registry call per child field.

## Consequences

### Positive

1. **Reuses existing frontend infrastructure.** Session cookies,
   CSRF, axios defaults, the Apollo client, feature flags, and the
   error handling that's already in place all work as-is. It's the
   same pattern the Container Registry and Orbit (GKG) UIs use.
1. **Cross-service joins are cheaper.** Rails fetches the user,
   project, and commit data with existing GraphQL types and batches
   the lookups within a single request, so we avoid the extra
   round-trips and the merge code in the frontend that a
   frontend-side join would need. Batching on Artifact Registry's side is a
   separate question that depends on Artifact Registry's REST API (see Negative
   #3).
1. **Server-side authentication.** The Ruby client handles the token
   exchange from the Rails session identity.

### Negative

1. **Resolver surface scales with Artifact Registry's API.** Every Artifact Registry endpoint the
   frontend consumes needs a Rails GraphQL resolver.
1. **Domain model expressed twice.** Artifact Registry's domain is described in its
   own contract and again in Rails GraphQL types; drift is possible.
   Contract testing can mitigate this.
1. **Artifact Registry's API design is constrained.** The N+1 mitigation depends on
   Artifact Registry exposing bulk reads at every collection boundary the frontend
   renders.
1. **Additional latency.** Each request requires two network hops:
   Frontend to Rails, then Rails to Artifact Registry. This could be
   mitigated connecting the GraphQL calls to a gRPC endpoint instead of REST API.
   This could work when both services are co-located in the
   same platform (.com <-> .com for example). This involves Artifact Registry exposing
   gRPC which is additional work to do.
1. **Frontend release cadence is tied to Rails.** The frontend ships
   with the Rails monolith, so new Artifact Registry-facing features reach users
   only when their installation picks up the matching Rails release.
   Dedicated installations run on m-2, so Dedicated users see new Artifact Registry
   UI roughly two milestones after they're available on GitLab.com.

## Alternatives

### Alternative 1: Thin pass-through proxy

Rails would expose `/-/artifact_registry/proxy/graphql`, forward raw
GraphQL bodies to Artifact Registry, and attach a Rails-signed JWT. CustomersDot uses
this shape at `ee/app/controllers/customers_dot/proxy_controller.rb`.

**Pros:**

- Less Rails code; no per-resolver work.
- Artifact Registry's schema flows through directly. New fields show up in the
  frontend without a Rails change. Artifact Registry's additive-only commitment
  plus its faster release cadence keep schema drift away from the
  browser.

**Cons:**

- Cross-service joins move to the frontend: Artifact Registry stores GitLab
  identifiers rather than the underlying user, project, and commit
  data.
- Two sequential round trips per user-attributed view, plus a merge
  utility duplicated across many Vue components.
- Frontend depends on Artifact Registry's schema directly; no Rails-side error
  buffer.
- Introduces a second GraphQL endpoint in the frontend.
- Artifact Registry needs to implement an additional API: GraphQL. That's
  additional work to do on Artifact Registry.

**Why rejected:**

- The cross-service join becomes a frontend problem with no clean
  implementation path. Every user-attributed view costs an extra
  Rails round trip and a merge utility on the FE side.
- The duplication of merge logic across Vue components scales poorly
  with the frontend surface area.

### Alternative 2: GraphQL schema stitching

Rails uses a schema-stitching gateway to compose `GitlabSchema` with
the Artifact Registry's GraphQL schema into a unified supergraph at
`/api/graphql`. The stitching gem runs inside Rails; requests for Artifact Registry
types route to the Go service over HTTP, other queries stay with
`GitlabSchema`. A POC implementation using the `graphql-stitching`
gem exists at [gitlab-org/gitlab!227224](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/227224).

**Pros:**

- One GraphQL endpoint for the frontend (same as the chosen pattern).
- Artifact Registry's schema is consumed directly. Rails doesn't need a resolver
  for each Artifact Registry field, and new fields reach the frontend without a
  Rails MR once the gateway reloads its schema.
- Cross-service joins are expressed declaratively: Artifact Registry's SDL declares
  cross-service references (for example, `Repository.createdBy: User`),
  Rails declares it can resolve `User` by `id`, and the stitching
  gem plans the cross-service fetch and batching automatically.

**Cons:**

- Artifact Registry needs to implement an additional API: GraphQL. That's
  additional work to do on Artifact Registry.
- Adds the `graphql-stitching` gem and a schema composition pipeline
  to the monolith.
- Rails has to either sync Artifact Registry's SDL into the monolith repo
  (cross-repo coordination on every schema change) or introspect Artifact Registry
  at boot (Rails startup and its public GraphQL surface tied to Artifact Registry's
  deploy cadence).
- Each Rails entity type Artifact Registry references needs a boundary resolver on
  the Rails side and a `@key` declaration on the Artifact Registry side.

**Why rejected:**

- Adds gateway infrastructure without a clear advantage over the
  resolver pattern.
- Rails-side schema integration adds either a cross-repo SDL sync or
  a startup dependency on Artifact Registry.

### Alternative 3: Direct cross-domain with a browser-held credential

The frontend talks to Artifact Registry cross-origin, carrying its own credential to
Artifact Registry. Two variants that exist in the monolith were considered:
an identity-token bearer credential (the frontend obtains an identity
token, holds it in memory, and sends it as `Authorization: Bearer`
directly to Artifact Registry) and an encrypted session cookie (Rails sets an encrypted
cookie scoped to the Artifact Registry subdomain, similar to `KasCookie` in
`app/controllers/concerns/kas_cookie.rb`, which the browser sends on
cross-origin requests).

**Pros:**

- Artifact Registry serves the frontend directly; no per-resolver Rails work.

**Cons:**

- Cross-service join still falls to the frontend (same shape as
  Alternative 1).
- The browser crosses origin to Artifact Registry, so Artifact Registry must serve CORS for the
  monolith origin. The identity-token variant requires preflight for
  `Authorization`-bearing requests; the cookie variant requires
  `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, an explicit origin
  allowlist (no wildcards), and `SameSite=None; Secure` cookies.
- Identity-token variant: the credential lifecycle moves into
  JavaScript (acquisition, in-memory storage, expiration handling,
  refresh on 401, SPA navigation), and the double-exchange flow on
  cache misses (FE → Artifact Registry → Rails → Artifact Registry) is slower than a single
  FE → Rails → Artifact Registry call.
- Cookie variant: KAS uses the pattern for a long-lived WebSocket
  where one handshake amortizes across the connection lifetime; Artifact Registry
  exchanges are many short-lived REST calls, each requiring cookie
  re-validation. Reproducing Rails cookie encryption and key rotation
  in Go conflicts with the JWT-based auth direction in the
  [auth agreement](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/). Artifact Registry's authorization model is
  built around scoped JWTs with role enforcement; cookie auth would
  require a parallel authorization path inside Artifact Registry. The cookie domain
  would have to be scoped to a parent that includes both `gitlab.com`
  and `artifact-registry.gitlab.com` and potentially work with
  self-managed instances.

**Why rejected:**

- Leaves the cross-service join unsolved.
- Each variant adds a browser-side credential surface (a JS-held
  identity token or a parent-scoped encrypted cookie) and a parallel
  auth path inside Artifact Registry.

### Alternative 4: Iframe embed with `postMessage` credential delivery

The Artifact Registry serves a UI as an iframe with credentials passed
via `postMessage` at load time, similar to
`app/assets/javascripts/observability/utils/auth_manager.js`.

**Pros:**

- Lets Artifact registry service own its full UI.
- Decouples Rails instance versions from Artifact Registry versions: a new Artifact Registry
  backend feature with its UI reaches SaaS, Dedicated, and
  Self-Managed setups as soon as Artifact Registry ships, without waiting for a
  Rails release.

**Cons:**

- The iframe runs at Artifact Registry's origin and has no direct path to Rails
  (CORS plus no session sharing). The cross-service join has to
  happen either through `postMessage` requests back to the parent for
  user, project, and commit data, or it would need to be stored in
  Artifact Registry and kept in sync with Rails.
- Iframe communication breaks deep linking, browser-shell navigation,
  and accessibility patterns the GitLab monolith expects of in-shell
  views.

**Why rejected:**

- Cross-service join and CORS. The `postMessage` path costs the same
  as Alternative 3; the storage-and-sync alternative adds PII
  duplication, sync infrastructure, and GDPR-removal complications.
- Iframe-specific UX limitations apply across all in-shell views.

## Open questions

1. For self-managed deployments, how is the Artifact Registry endpoint
   URL surfaced to Rails? Possible mechanisms include a `gitlab.yml`
   config key or an Admin UI setting. Who owns the configuration
   contract between Rails and Artifact Registry for self-managed operators?
1. The token exchange between Rails and Artifact Registry is committed at the
   [auth agreement](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/) level, but the credential
   format, claim shape, and minting service are not yet specified.
   The Ruby client's credential acquisition step depends on those
   decisions and is deliberately left abstract in this ADR.
1. The per-element shape and pagination shape (cursor format,
   page-size limits) for Artifact Registry list endpoints are not yet
   specified in ADR-009. The N+1 mitigation in this ADR depends on list
   endpoints returning enough per-element data to render list views
   without per-element follow-up calls.

## Future work

When the GitLab Adaptive Trust Environment is finalized, the Rails-side
credential acquisition migrates to it. The frontend pattern in this ADR
carries over unchanged.

If a future product requirement establishes browser-side direct Artifact Registry
access (for example, signed-URL artifact uploads from the browser), it
warrants a follow-up ADR addressing CORS, credential lifecycle, and
the specific resources in scope.

## References

- [ADR-009: API Design](009_api_design.md)
- [ADR-022: Namespace Decoupling](022_namespace_decoupling.md)
- [Auth agreement](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/)
- Container Registry frontend: `app/assets/javascripts/packages_and_registries/container_registry/explorer/`
- Container Registry resolvers: `app/graphql/resolvers/container_repositories_resolver.rb`, `app/graphql/resolvers/container_repository_tags_resolver.rb`
- Container Registry auth service: `app/services/auth/container_registry_authentication_service.rb`
- Container Registry Ruby client: `lib/container_registry/client.rb`, `lib/container_registry/gitlab_api_client.rb`
- KAS cookie pattern: `app/controllers/concerns/kas_cookie.rb`
- CustomersDot proxy: `ee/app/controllers/customers_dot/proxy_controller.rb`, `ee/app/assets/javascripts/lib/customers_dot_graphql.js`
- GitLab Observability iframe and postMessage auth: `app/assets/javascripts/observability/utils/auth_manager.js`
- GraphQL schema stitching draft: [gitlab-org/gitlab!227224](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/227224)

title: 020 Authentication Flow
text:
<!-- Design Documents often contain forward-looking statements -->
<!-- vale gitlab.FutureTense = NO -->

## Status

**Proposed**

This ADR covers **authentication** only: how a caller's identity is established.
**Authorization** (roles, policy evaluation, role assignments) is covered by [ADR-021: Authorization](021_authorization.md).

## Context

Clients authenticate to the Artifact Registry with short-lived tokens issued by their GitLab Rails instance, through a dedicated API endpoint or, where Rails itself acts for the user, in process.
The Artifact Registry validates these tokens locally and is not involved in issuing them.

The contract with the Auth Platform team is the [Artifact Registry and Auth Platform interface agreement](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/), which sets six requirements (R1–R6).
This ADR consumes the authentication requirements: R1 (token exchange), R2 (token validation) and R3 (token payload).

## Decision

**The Artifact Registry authenticates clients by locally validating short-lived tokens issued by GitLab Rails, through a dedicated token-exchange API endpoint or in process where Rails itself acts for the user.**

### Iteration scope

The first iteration targets same-boundary topologies (`.com ↔ .com`, `SM ↔ SM`), where a single instance has a single trust anchor.
Rails signs the token with the Cloud Connector v1 key, every token names an organization as its principal's origin, and `gitlab_instance_uid` is omitted from the payload.
The cross-boundary topology, where many Self-Managed instances share one SaaS Artifact Registry, is a follow-up iteration.

### What must always hold

| # | Constraint | Machine-checkable? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **No callback to the GitLab instance while processing a request.** The issuer's keys are synced out of band. | Yes: once keys are cached, a request authenticates while the GitLab instance is unreachable |
| 2 | **Only a token from the trusted issuer authenticates an end user.** The Artifact Registry never accepts or exchanges a client's long-lived GitLab credential. | Yes: a token that fails the signature, algorithm, audience or expiry check is rejected, and so is a long-lived GitLab credential |
| 3 | **Tokens are short-lived.** No token lives longer than 12 hours, and one minted from a CI/CD ID token or issued into a CI job's payload does not outlive the job. | Yes: no issued token expires more than 12 hours after it is issued, and a token minted from an ID token or issued into a job payload expires no later than the job's timeout |
| 4 | **A token reaches only its own organization's namespaces.** The token's organization must equal the namespace's owner anchor, compared as opaque values. | Yes: a token for another organization is refused on every namespace-scoped route |
| 5 | **Build metadata never decides a request.** It comes only from a credential the CI job presents at the exchange, never from a database, and a missing or malformed value means no build metadata. | Yes: a token with missing or malformed build metadata authenticates the same as one without it |
| 6 | **A service-to-service call presents every layer its edge requires.** There is no anonymous mode. | Yes: a call missing a required layer is rejected |
| 7 | **A rejected service token reveals nothing.** A missing token and a wrong one look the same to the caller. | Yes: both get an identical response |
| 8 | **A service token rotates without downtime.** A current and a next value are accepted together. | Yes: both values authenticate during a rotation |
| 9 | **The development credential never runs beside token exchange or enforced authorization.** | Yes: a configuration that combines them fails to load |
| 10 | **A Kubernetes peer is admitted only when the path is on, its identity is allowlisted, and the route opts in.** A cluster-issued token that fails verification is never retried as an end-user token. | Yes: a peer missing any of these is rejected |

### Non-production development mode

The decision above governs every deployment that serves real artifacts.
The Artifact Registry also has a **non-production development mode**, so it can run where no GitLab instance can issue or sign tokens, such as a local checkout or a test rig.
It is off by default.

In this mode the Artifact Registry authenticates against a static development credential instead of a Rails-issued token.
Three of its properties cut against the decision above:

1. **It establishes no principal.** It carries none of the [R3 payload claims](#token-payload-r3), so a request it authenticates resolves to an identity with no subject.
1. **It is long-lived and static, not short-lived and issued**, so the short-lifetime reasoning under [Consequences](#consequences) does not apply to it.
1. **It is also the service token** on the [GitLab Rails to the Artifact Registry internal API](#gitlab-rails-to-the-artifact-registry-internal-api) edge, in the header a production deployment uses.
   The developer holds that edge's credential too, unlike the deployment credential [The two layers](#the-two-layers) describes; the service-token layer still applies, with the same comparison and opaque rejection.

All three are admissible because the mode admits no real principal and holds no production data, so there is nothing to impersonate and nothing of value to reach.
The topologies this ADR governs never run it.

One switch selects the mode together with the unenforced authorization posture, for the reason [ADR-021](021_authorization.md#non-production-development-mode) records.

## Architectural constraint

**No callbacks during request processing**, from the [interface agreement](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/#no-callbacks-during-request-processing), shapes this decision.
Everything needed to verify a request token MUST be in the token or already cached locally, which makes local, stateless validation a hard requirement rather than an optimization.
It matters most across boundaries, where a Self-Managed instance may be unreachable from a SaaS Artifact Registry.
The constraint targets the GitLab instance, not the dependencies the Artifact Registry is deployed with, and the periodic key sync (see [Token validation](#token-validation-r2)) runs outside request handling.

## Authentication flow

Rails issues the token (R1), and the Artifact Registry validates it locally against its trusted issuer's public keys, which it syncs periodically and caches (R2).
The client gets the token from its GitLab instance directly, so the Artifact Registry never sees the client's long-lived credentials.

## Token issuance (R1)

Rails exposes a dedicated token-exchange API endpoint that accepts client credentials and returns a short-lived token for the Artifact Registry.
Where Rails itself acts for the user, it issues the same token in process instead.

1. **Credentials.** The endpoint accepts standard GitLab API credentials that resolve to a `User`, the only principal type the first iteration issues tokens for.
   A credential that resolves to no user, such as a deploy token, is not accepted.
   The typed `sub` claim (see [Token payload](#token-payload-r3)) lets other principal types follow without changing its meaning.
1. **Client-side exchange.** The client obtains the token from its GitLab instance and presents it; the Artifact Registry never performs the exchange.
1. **Lifetime.** Tokens live 12 hours at most, with a short default.
   A client may request any lifetime up to that cap, so long builds do not expire mid-flight.
1. **Enablement.** Token exchange should fail for organizations that have not enabled the Artifact Registry (R1, a SHOULD).
   It is an availability gate only, checked at issuance on the Rails side, which owns the organization-level setting.
   Access does not rely on Unit Primitives or add-ons, since no Artifact Registry add-on exists under the credit-based billing model.
   On its side, the Artifact Registry binds the token to the namespace: the token's organization, `gitlab.origin_id`, must match the `entity_id` of the namespace's owner anchor ([ADR-001](001_organizations_as_anchor_point.md)).
   It is an opaque comparison that requires no organization awareness.
1. **CI/CD ID token exchange.** A CI job may present its CI/CD ID token as the credential.
   The ID token must carry a single fixed audience reserved for token exchange, matched exactly, so an ID token issued for another relying party cannot be exchanged.
   The principal is the user running the job, with the same checks as every other credential.
   The issued token cannot outlive the job.
   The job token stays accepted alongside it; a job-token exchange carries no build metadata.
1. **In-process issuance.** Where Rails already acts for a user and no client can call the endpoint, it may issue the token in process.
   Examples are the Ruby client acting for the signed-in user ([ADR-014](014_frontend_to_artifact_registry.md)) and the registry credential in a CI job payload, which the runner needs before any job script can exchange a credential.
   The token is the one the endpoint issues, with the same issuer, keys, claims and audiences, so the Artifact Registry validates it unchanged and is still not involved in issuing it.
   Each surface applies the endpoint's issuance rules: the user is a member of the organization the token names, that organization has the Artifact Registry activated, and the token lives at most 12 hours, a CI job's token no longer than the job's timeout.
   The endpoint's per-user rate limit does not apply to in-process issuance.
   When issuance moves into the IAM token service, these surfaces move with it.

## Token validation (R2)

The token is a JWT signed with the GitLab instance's Cloud Connector keys.
The Artifact Registry is configured with one **trusted issuer**, its GitLab instance, and syncs that issuer's public keys out of band.
It validates each token's signature against those cached keys, pins the signature algorithm, and rejects a token with the wrong audience or a past expiry.

Keys must be refreshed periodically, and a stale key kept briefly if a refresh fails, so a key-provider blip does not reject otherwise valid tokens ([R2](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/#r2--token-validation)).

Reusing the Cloud Connector v1 keys keeps the first iteration simple: it needs no new key-distribution infrastructure.
The target state moves key serving to GATE, but the Artifact Registry's action, verifying the signature against cached trusted keys, does not change.

## Token payload (R3)

[AUTH-021](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/auth-architecture/design-doc/-/blob/main/decisions/021-modular-service-token-payload-schema.md) defines the token's payload.
This ADR relies on these properties of it:

1. **The token is enough to authenticate.** Everything the Artifact Registry needs to establish the caller is in the token, so no callback is needed.
1. **The principal is typed.** `sub` names the principal with its type, so the claim can extend to principal types other than `User` without changing its meaning.
   The `gitlab` identity claims name the principal's origin, the origin's id and the principal's id within it.
1. **One token serves both services.** The token carries the Artifact Registry's audience and the relationships API's, so the Artifact Registry can forward it unchanged (see [Service-to-service authentication](#service-to-service-authentication)).
1. **Build metadata comes from the presented credential.** The `gitlab.job` claims are present only when the exchanged credential was a CI/CD ID token, and their values are copied from it, never from a database, so the IAM token service can make the same copy.
   They carry no authorization meaning.
   A consumer treats a missing or malformed value in any of these claims as "no build metadata" for the whole object, and never fails the request over it.
1. **Authorization-bearing claims belong to ADR-021.** This token establishes *who* the caller is; *what they may do* is evaluated separately.
   Whether authorization also considers the source credential type, for example a personal access token versus a CI job token, is ADR-021's question too.

## Service-to-service authentication

Calls between GitLab services, over more than one edge, need their own answer.
This section gives the shared pattern first, then what each edge carries.

### The two layers

1. **Service token.** Answers "is the calling process a trusted peer service?" A static, symmetric shared secret, compared in constant time.
   It carries no identity, so the result is only accept or reject.
1. **Caller identity.** Answers "who does the call act for?" Present only when the call acts for someone.
   Today that is the end user's token, verified as in [Token validation](#token-validation-r2).

Which layers apply depends on the edge.
A call made on behalf of an end user carries both.
A call that is not user-initiated has no identity for the second layer to carry, so the service token alone authenticates the caller.
Whichever layers apply, all of them are required: failing any one rejects the call as unauthenticated, and there is no anonymous mode.
The service token never authorizes anything on its own; where an end-user identity is present, authorization derives from that principal (see [ADR-021](021_authorization.md)).

1. **Credential names are per service.** Each service names the service-token credential it accepts, so request logs show which caller hit which service.
1. **The service token is a deployment credential.** It is provisioned as a secret to the calling service and is never visible to end users.
   The [non-production development mode](#non-production-development-mode) is the one exception.
1. **Health checks skip both layers**, so Kubernetes probes work without credentials.

### Artifact Registry to the relationships API

Both layers apply.
The relationships API is IAM's `iam-data-access` service.

Each side verifies the end-user token independently: the Artifact Registry on ingress against its own audience, and the relationships API again on its own.

On the data path, the Artifact Registry forwards the client's own token unchanged, so the user's identity flows end to end.
That includes the per-request lookup that bounds repository-list visibility by the caller's own grants, which IAM admits only for a subject in the caller's own organization.

Admin and UI flows that read or change role assignments go through a Rails GraphQL wrapper instead, which requests its own token for the relationships API from the Rails token issuer.

### GitLab Rails to the Artifact Registry internal API

The service token alone applies.
The internal API is the Rails-facing surface defined in [ADR-009](009_api_design.md#gitlab-api).
Its calls are not made on behalf of an end user, so there is no identity for the second layer to carry.
The service token is an interim mechanism here; see [Future work / open debates](#future-work--open-debates) for the direction.

### Services in the same cluster: Kubernetes service-account tokens

A service running in the same Kubernetes cluster as the Artifact Registry can call it as itself, with no Rails-issued token and no service token.
This path is the first step of a longer effort whose open items are under [Future work / open debates](#future-work--open-debates).
It is off by default, behind a switch an operator turns on per deployment.

1. **The credential is the caller's projected service-account token**, verified offline against the cluster's published keys, as an end-user token is.
1. **The issuer selects the verifier.** The end-user token travels in the same header, so the token's issuer decides which verification it gets.
   The issuer is read before verification only to choose; the chosen verifier still checks everything, and a token it rejects is refused with no fallback to the other path.
1. **Identity is the service account, as a SPIFFE ID**, derived from the token's subject.
   Every pod running as that service account shares it.
1. **An allowlist of SPIFFE IDs is the whole trust boundary.** A verified token whose ID is not listed is rejected.
   The caller acts for no end user and names no organization, so no GitLab principal is established; [ADR-021](021_authorization.md#services-in-the-same-cluster) records what an accepted caller may do.
1. **Each route opts in.** A route that does not admit this caller rejects it, whatever the token.

## Alternatives considered

The token mechanism follows from the [interface agreement](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/), and the Auth platform weighed its alternatives on its side.
On the Artifact Registry's side, two options lost:

1. **Do nothing: accept GitLab credentials directly.** The Artifact Registry would take personal access tokens and job tokens as clients send them today.
   Rejected because checking such a credential needs a call to the GitLab instance on every request, which the [no-callbacks constraint](#architectural-constraint) forbids, and because the Artifact Registry would then hold long-lived credentials.
1. **The Artifact Registry performs the exchange.** Rejected for the same two reasons: it would receive the long-lived credential and call the GitLab instance while handling the request.

The source of the `gitlab.job` build metadata was decided with the Authentication team ([AUTH-021](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/auth-architecture/design-doc/-/blob/main/decisions/021-modular-service-token-payload-schema.md)).
The exchange endpoint is to move into the IAM token service, which cannot read CI job records from the Rails database, and several package clients can send only one credential, so the claims must come from a credential the job presents at the exchange.
Three options were weighed:

1. **Self-attestation (SLSA or npm provenance).** The job builds and signs an in-toto statement binding the metadata to the artifact digest, and the Artifact Registry verifies it.
   It is the only option that binds the facts to the published bytes, and it remains the upgrade path if artifact substitution in the publish path becomes a threat to defend against.
   Rejected for now: it needs publish-side tooling for every package format, a statement schema and a new verification path.
1. **The Artifact Registry verifies the ID token as a second credential.** Same source of truth, presented alongside the access token.
   Rejected because Maven, npm and Docker clients can send only one credential; routing the ID token through the exchange keeps one token and one set of trusted keys.
1. **Claims from the database now and the JWT job token later.** Rejected because the token service is part of the auth infrastructure and must not depend on a feature's database tables, the JWT job-token rollout is a breaking change not scheduled before FY28, and it leaves Artifact Registry-specific claim assembly inside the generic issuer path.

The ID token is the only credential a CI job already holds that GitLab signs, that carries all of the `gitlab.job` claims, and whose issuance depends on no other rollout.
Because the claims prove nothing about the published bytes, they are called build metadata, not provenance.

## Consequences

### Positive

1. **Independent of Rails availability during request processing**: because validation is local and stateless, the Artifact Registry can authenticate requests even when the originating GitLab instance is unreachable.
1. **Short-lived tokens limit blast radius**: the Artifact Registry never handles the client's long-lived GitLab credentials, only short-lived tokens, so a leaked token expires quickly and exposes far less than a leaked personal access token.
1. **Aligned with platform direction**: the Artifact Registry consumes the platform's token-exchange and validation primitives rather than maintaining a bespoke flow.

### Negative

1. **Interim requires a connection to the GitLab instance**: to validate tokens, the Artifact Registry syncs issuer keys from the GitLab instance, out of band rather than per request.
   The end-state goal is no GitLab-instance connectivity at all, which the target state reaches by serving keys from GATE.
1. **Reuses Cloud Connector v1 machinery**: the interim relies on the existing Cloud Connector v1 keys rather than GATE-issued keys.
1. **Issued tokens cannot be revoked before expiry**: with local validation and no callback or blocklist, a token stays valid until it expires even if the originating credential is revoked moments after issuance, for example a phished personal access token exchanged for a 12-hour token.
   The short default lifetime mitigates it, and it is an accepted trade-off for the beta; stronger sender binding (such as DPoP) and key rotation are possible future hardening.
   The CI/CD ID token adds a second bearer credential with the same exposure: any holder of an exfiltrated ID token can exchange it until the job's timeout, including from another job, and the issued token then carries that token's build metadata and acts as its user.
   Authorization is no wider than the token already grants; the ID token is masked and redacted like the job token, each exchange is audited, and single-use tracking and sender binding in the token service close the gap.
1. **Every job in an organization with the Artifact Registry enabled gets an ID token by default**, a bearer credential GitLab itself accepts, held in an environment variable visible to every script in the job.
   It needs the same masking and documentation as the job token, can collide with jobs that already declare an ID token under the chosen variable name, and on Self-Managed and Dedicated it is instance-wide.
   This runs against the goal of [Ambient Credentials in CI](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/auth-architecture/design-doc/-/blob/main/proposals/004-ambient-credentials-in-ci.md); once ambient credentials exist, they replace this path.
   Build metadata exists only where an ID token was presented, so its coverage depends on default issuance.

### Mitigations

- The Artifact Registry's validation logic is the same for the interim and target issuers; only the source of the issuer's keys changes, which limits the blast radius of the migration.

## Future work / open debates

These authentication questions are open and out of scope for the first iteration.

1. **Cross-boundary issuer key and `gitlab_instance_uid`.** The cross-boundary follow-up has many Self-Managed instances behind one trust anchor, so a token must identify its issuing instance.
   Reintroducing `gitlab_instance_uid`, or an equivalent, and the resulting change to the validation model are open.
   Exchanging the job token automatically for remote runners that reach a SaaS Artifact Registry falls under this follow-up.
1. **Target-state service credentials.** The service token is an interim mechanism.
   The direction is to replace shared secrets with mutual TLS and workload identity, using SPIFFE-style caller identifiers, and to carry caller identity in a GitLab Unified Request Token ([URT](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/auth-architecture/design-doc/-/blob/main/glossary.md)).
   Neither direction is decided, and the URT does not exist yet.
   In-cluster transport security, including the terms for revisiting mutual TLS, is in [ADR-024](024_infrastructure_delivery.md#transport-security).
1. **Organization scoping for in-cluster service callers.** A service account [accepted in the same cluster](#services-in-the-same-cluster-kubernetes-service-account-tokens) acts in every organization the routes that admit it reach.
   Binding a caller to the organizations it serves, by configuration or by a signed claim, is open.

## References

1. [ADR-001: Organizations as Anchor Point](001_organizations_as_anchor_point.md)
1. [ADR-021: Authorization](021_authorization.md): the companion ADR for authorization
1. [ADR-022: Namespace Decoupling](022_namespace_decoupling.md)
1. [Artifact Registry and Auth Platform interface agreement](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/): the R1–R3 (authentication) requirements consumed here
1. [AUTH-021: Modular service token payload schema](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/auth-architecture/design-doc/-/blob/main/decisions/021-modular-service-token-payload-schema.md): the token payload, including the `gitlab.job` object
1. [AUTH-019: GATE identity federation](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/auth-architecture/design-doc/-/blob/main/decisions/019-gate-identity-federation.md): cross-boundary authentication

title: 021 Authorization
text:
## Status **Proposed** This ADR covers **authorization** only — what an authenticated caller may do. **Authentication** (how the caller's identity is established, and how the token is issued and validated) is covered separately by [ADR-020: Authentication Flow](020_authentication_flow.md). ## Context The Artifact Registry runs on a satellite service separate from the GitLab Rails monolith. [ADR-020](020_authentication_flow.md) establishes the caller's identity from a short-lived token that the Artifact Registry validates locally, without calling back to the GitLab instance during request processing. This ADR decides **what that caller can do**. The [Artifact Registry and Auth Platform interface agreement](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/) defines six requirements (R1–R6). ADR-020 consumes the authentication requirements (R1–R3). This ADR consumes the authorization requirements: **R4 (policy evaluation engine)**, **R5 (relationships API)**, and **R6 (bootstrapping)**. ### The permission model To grant or deny an operation, the Artifact Registry evaluates three parts: - **Principal**: the authenticated user, identified by the token's `sub` claim ([ADR-020](020_authentication_flow.md#token-payload-r3)). Every credential type (personal, OAuth, CI job, group, or project access token) resolves to the same `User` principal, so **closed beta authorizes by principal alone, independent of which credential was used**. A leaked CI job token therefore carries the user's full permissions; closed beta accepts this trade-off because tokens are short-lived by default. Differentiating authorization by credential type is an [open question](#open-questions). - **Operation**: a repository management operation or an artifact operation ([ADR-009](009_api_design.md)). - **Resource**: the namespace (the registry as a whole; see [ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md)) or an individual repository. The namespace maps one-to-one to the organization in closed beta. The Artifact Registry uses a **roles and permissions** model. **Roles** define _who the principal is_ in the context of a resource, through an assignment in the [relationships API](#role-assignment) (R5). **Permissions** define _what the principal can do_: each role maps to a fixed set of permissions, a [permission bucket](#default-permission-buckets). An operation is granted when the required permission is in the principal's effective permission set. ### Constraints Three constraints shape the decision: - **Closed-by-default.** Membership in the organization (or its groups and projects) does not grant any Artifact Registry access. A principal has no permissions until an Artifact Registry role is explicitly assigned. - **No inheritance from platform membership.** Top-level group and project roles do not map to Artifact Registry roles, which are product-specific and assigned independently. - **No callbacks to the GitLab instance during request processing.** Everything needed to authorize a request must be available without reaching the GitLab instance, which may be unreachable. The constraint targets _that instance_, not the dependencies the Artifact Registry is itself deployed and provisioned with — the relationships API, the GLAZ policy-engine sidecar, the key-value store, and the relational database — which share its failure domain (see the [interface agreement](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/#no-callbacks-during-request-processing)). If a dependency the decision needs an answer from is unavailable, authorization fails closed; the final fail-open versus fail-closed policy is an [open question](#open-questions). A cache is not such a dependency: losing one degrades to resolving the answer directly. ## Decision **Define product-specific Artifact Registry roles. Assign them to the namespace and to individual repositories through the auth platform's relationships API. Evaluate permissions through the co-located policy evaluation engine (GLAZ, a sidecar) using built-in role-to-permission defaults. Access is closed-by-default; Organization Administrators are bootstrapped with full access.** The auth platform stores role assignments (relationships) and provides the policy evaluation engine. The Artifact Registry owns the role definitions and the permission model, and drives every decision through the co-located engine. ### Roles The Artifact Registry defines its own **product-specific roles**, scoped to the Artifact Registry and distinct from platform roles. **Artifact Admin** is the only role that manages access. **Artifact Manager** manages repositories and artifacts, but not access. These are **user roles**, distinct from the platform **user types** (for example, Organization Administrator or Organization Member). A user type does not imply any Artifact Registry role; the two are assigned independently ([roles management work item](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/593455)). Organization Administrators are **bootstrapped** with access equivalent to namespace-level Artifact Admin (R6). The role definitions give their organization-level owner relationship, maintained as ownership changes, access to the organization's namespace and every repository under it. The grant cannot be revoked or downgraded while they remain an owner. It flows through ordinary relationship records, so it needs no special case, and an Organization Administrator can create repositories and assign roles before any other assignment exists. Custom roles are out of scope for closed beta; see [Custom roles](#custom-roles). ### Permissions Every operation requires one permission from a fixed set the Artifact Registry defines. Permissions follow [GitLab permission conventions](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/development/permissions/conventions.html): every permission names an action and a `resource(_subresource)`, and the action is one of `read`, `create`, `update`, or `delete`. Two consequences of applying that convention here: - **Reversible relationships are modeled as resources**, not bespoke verbs. A virtual repository's upstream is a `repository_upstream` — created to associate a hosted or remote repository, deleted to disassociate it. - **Caching reuses the artifact permissions** — there are no separate cache permissions. Remote repositories serve cached artifacts through the same endpoints ([ADR-009](009_api_design.md)), so viewing and evicting them take `read_artifact` and `delete_artifact`. Tags, such as container image tags and npm dist-tags, follow the artifact permissions by verb. Publishing covers re-publishing where the format's protocol permits it (Maven `SNAPSHOT` redeploys, OCI tag re-pushes); there is no separate overwrite permission, and preventing overwrites is a deferred [access-rule](#access-rules) capability. ### Default permission buckets Each role maps to a fixed set of permissions. A role holds the same permissions wherever it is assigned; what changes is _reach_ — a namespace assignment applies them across the registry, a repository assignment only to that repository. Each role is an independent permission bucket: it grants exactly its own permissions, with no hierarchy or inheritance between roles. Managing role assignments is not an Artifact Registry permission; only Artifact Admin holds it ([Role assignment](#role-assignment)). ### Repository visibility Each repository has a visibility level stored in the Artifact Registry database, not synced to any external entity. **Closed beta supports `private` only**: no access without an assigned role. `internal` (readable by organization members) and `public` (readable by anyone, including unauthenticated callers) each grant read without a role, which breaks the closed-by-default constraint: membership determines who _can_ be granted access, not the grant itself. Both are [deferred to GA](#public-and-internal-visibility). Write and management operations always require the corresponding permission from an assigned role, regardless of visibility. ### Namespace-level and repository-level resources Each permission is checked against the resource the operation addresses: the namespace or one repository. - **Namespace**: every management permission binds here and applies across the registry. `create_repository` acts only here and has no repository-level meaning. - **Repository**: every permission except `create_repository` binds here, for that repository and what it contains — its details, statistics, configuration, deletion, upstream associations, and artifacts. One permission name can therefore ask a different question per level: `update_repository` gates registry-wide settings on the namespace, and the repository's own configuration on a repository. ### Role assignment Roles are assigned through the auth platform's [relationships API](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/#r5--relationships-api) (R5) as `(subject, role, resource)` tuples, where the subject is the relationships-API [`Identity`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/auth/iam/-/blob/main/docs/relationships-api.md#subject-and-identity) type (`origin`, `origin_id`, `local_id`) resolved from the token, and the resource is an Artifact Registry namespace or repository. A role assignment binds the subject to a resource within that subject's organization. Any role can be assigned at either of **two resource levels**: - **Namespace**: the role applies to every repository in the registry. This is the baseline that lets administrators grant access to thousands of users at scale. - **Repository (direct, additive)**: the role applies to that repository only. It needs no namespace-level assignment, so a principal can hold access to a single repository and nothing else. With roles at both levels, the effective permissions on the repository are the **union** of the two: a repository-level assignment can only grant more, never less. Restricting access on a specific repository is [deferred](#reductive-repository-overrides). **Managing role assignments is reserved for Artifact Admin**, with the same capability at either level and only its scope differing. Artifact Manager manages repositories, not access: it grants no roles and writes no access rules. Assignments are managed in the GitLab UI, through the organization's access-management experience, where Rails provides the frontend and API (R5) and the relationships API authorizes each write. **Each request resolves against one resource.** The relationships lookup is filtered to the resource the request addresses and its ancestors (repository → namespace → organization), so an assignment on a _different_ repository never enters the decision. Because assignments only add, the effective role is the highest applicable one. A request served **through a virtual repository** resolves against the **virtual repository's** assignments, while a request addressed **directly** to a contained hosted or remote repository resolves against that repository's. A role on the virtual repository therefore grants access to the content it aggregates _as served through it_ — by design, not a bypass of a contained repository's assignments. How role assignments reach the Artifact Registry depends on the iteration: - **Closed beta**: the token carries no authorization claims. The Artifact Registry reads the principal's assignments from the relationships API and passes the tuples to the policy engine. It caches the lookup for a short, configured duration in the [key-value store it is provisioned](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/infrastructure/#isolation-levels), so one entry with one expiry serves the whole fleet. The cache is keyed on the lookup's inputs — the principal, the target resources, and the relationship kinds — so a result is never reused across a different principal or resource. Losing the store degrades the cache to direct lookups rather than failing the decision. - **Target state**: the auth platform's enrichment layer resolves role assignments and includes the authorization claims in the enriched token, so no lookup is needed. The shape of those claims, which ADR-020 defers to this ADR, is defined when the enrichment layer ships. **A role-assignment change, a revocation included, is not observed immediately.** The delay is up to one cache duration plus the relationships API's own write-to-read lag: a cache fill that lands after a write but before that write is readable serves the old answer for a further full duration. The relationships API's lag is not yet measured, so no total window is stated. Entries expire per key, and the key names the target resources, so a denial on one resource does not establish that a revocation has taken hold on another. ### Authorization flow Authorization begins after authentication: the Artifact Registry has already validated the token and established the principal ([ADR-020](020_authentication_flow.md)). It then reads the principal's role assignments from the relationships API and asks the co-located policy-engine sidecar to evaluate the requested action — without calling back to the GitLab instance. An unauthenticated request carries no token and is denied: closed beta has no public repositories (see [repository visibility](#repository-visibility)). ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Client participant AR as Artifact Registry participant Rel as Relationships API
(co-located) participant PE as Policy Engine
(co-located sidecar) Client->>AR: Request with validated token (principal + context) Note over AR: Identity established per ADR-020 Note over AR,Rel: Step 1 — Look up role assignments AR->>Rel: Look up role assignments
(target resource and its ancestors) Rel-->>AR: Membership tuples Note over AR,Rel: Target state: authorization claims arrive in the enriched token,
so this lookup is skipped Note over AR,PE: Step 2 — Evaluate the action AR->>PE: Role tuples + action + context (resource attributes) Note over PE: roles → permission buckets,
union, then check the requested action PE-->>AR: ALLOW / DENY (with policy ID) AR-->>Client: Response (403, or 404 if the resource is unreadable) ``` When an operation is denied, the status code depends on whether the principal may even see that the resource exists: - **The principal cannot read the resource** (for example, a private repository on which they hold no role): the Artifact Registry returns **404 Not Found**, so it does not confirm the resource exists. - **The principal can read the resource but lacks the specific operation** (for example, they hold a role but not `delete_repository`): the Artifact Registry returns **403 Forbidden**, since the resource's existence is already known to them. In neither case does the response reveal the permission or policy that caused the denial. The policy engine returns the policy ID that determined the decision (R4) for audit logging and debugging. ### List operations A list spans many resources at once, so it does not fit the single-resource evaluation above. **Listing repositories (namespace-scoped).** The Artifact Registry decides this from the principal's role assignments rather than one policy check per repository: - A principal holding **any namespace-level role** can list **all** repositories in the namespace. Every role includes `read_repository`, so this reduces to "does the principal hold a role at the namespace?"; the Artifact Registry then enumerates the repositories from its own database. - A principal with **no namespace-level role** sees only the repositories where they hold a **repository-level assignment** — closed beta has no visibility level that grants read without a role. The Artifact Registry asks the relationships service which resources the principal holds grants on, intersects them with the namespace's repositories, and evaluates only those, so the cost follows the principal's grants rather than the namespace's size. That lookup takes no namespace scope, so the bound is the principal's grants across the whole IAM instance. Viewing registry-wide statistics works the same way: they summarize the whole registry rather than a single repository, so they require a namespace-level role. **Listing within a repository (repository-scoped).** Browsing a repository's contents or sub-resources targets a single repository, so it is an ordinary point check on that repository. A list of a namespace's repositories omits the resources the principal cannot read rather than rejecting the request — an empty or partial list, with no error and no indication that hidden resources exist, preventing metadata leakage. A sub-resource list whose rows the addressed resource already names keeps them, with deny on every action ([Permission checks for UI gating](#permission-checks-for-ui-gating)). This is also the landing experience: the registry's navigation entry is not gated on any permission check ([ADR-014](014_frontend_to_artifact_registry.md)) — other gates, such as the Artifact Registry being enabled for the organization, still apply — so a principal with no access lands on the repository list and sees it empty. ### Permission checks for UI gating The frontend must know which actions to render — buttons, tabs, routes — before the user attempts any, and only the Artifact Registry can answer. It exposes **permission checks**: an allow or deny verdict per action for the calling principal. Checks name actions rather than enumerate permissions: the permission-to-action mapping belongs to the Artifact Registry. Verdicts **embed in the management API's domain responses**, opt-in: the repository detail response carries that repository's verdicts, and the repository list response carries the namespace verdicts and each row's — one call per page. **An embedded element can carry verdicts of its own**, answering for the resource that element represents. The namespace's verdicts embed in a namespace details response created for them ([ADR-009](009_api_design.md#management-apis)). It serves the namespace-scoped affordances on pages with no other domain call, and grows additively as the namespace becomes a user-facing entity. Each surface's action set follows its resource level and is published in the OpenAPI contract, which the frontend reads instead of inventing actions. A permission verdict follows the [resource levels](#namespace-level-and-repository-level-resources). A role verdict, for the `*_role_assignment` actions, applies the relationships API's rule for role-assignment writes: allowed only for an Artifact Admin on the repository or its namespace, or an Organization Administrator. Four rules govern the contract: - **Advisory only.** Verdicts pre-gate UI affordances; the Artifact Registry still authorizes every real request ([authorization flow](#authorization-flow)), so a stale verdict can mis-render a control, never grant access — which is why consumers may cache verdicts. Verdicts cover authorization only: rendering also requires the namespace status the platform caches ([ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md)), and the Artifact Registry enforces both on the real request. - **The caller is the end user.** The platform obtains a token for the current user and calls the management API as that user ([ADR-020](020_authentication_flow.md)). The Artifact Registry never accepts a service caller asserting a user identity, so verdicts stay off the GitLab API surface, which authenticates services, never end users ([ADR-009](009_api_design.md#gitlab-api)). No permission is needed beyond authentication: existence-hiding plus deny-by-default means a caller with no access learns nothing the gated endpoints would not reveal. - **Existence-hiding.** A repository the principal cannot read gets the domain response's own **404 Not Found**, indistinguishable from a missing one. The namespace endpoint answers any authenticated principal of the owning organization, with deny on every action when nothing is assigned; a caller from another organization, like an unknown slug, gets 404. **Embedded verdicts never change a row set**: a resource the principal cannot read stays listed, with deny on every action, wherever the addressed resource's response already names it — for example, the sibling repositories a virtual repository's upstream list resolves through. The omission rule under [List operations](#list-operations) still governs every list whose rows are not already named. Responses carry allow or deny only, never the deciding policy or reason. - **Embedded and opt-in.** Verdicts ride the response of the data they gate, only when requested, so the two cannot disagree and a consumer that renders nothing pays nothing. A sub-resource list gates only on the addressed resource, so its verdicts are evaluation the route would not otherwise do, bounded by the page and by the entity count caps of [ADR-004](004_data_and_application_limits.md#entity-count-limits). A row's verdicts come from that row's own evaluation: a failed row evaluation fails the whole request instead of dropping out silently, as does an unreachable dependency the decision needs. Consistency across a request's lookups is bounded by the role-assignment cache duration, not atomic. The shape follows [proposal 016](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/auth-architecture/design-doc/-/blob/main/proposals/016-batchcheck-ar-ui-authorization.md): verdicts embedded in the domain responses, resolved through its AR-GLAZ [`BatchCheck` contract](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/auth-architecture/design-doc/-/blob/main/proposals/016-batchcheck-ar-ui-authorization.md#interface). ### Non-production development mode The decision above governs every deployment that serves real artifacts. For local development and test rigs, the Artifact Registry also supports a **non-production development mode**, whose authorization half leaves authorization unenforced: nothing calls the relationships API or the policy engine, and every check a caller could reach — [point checks](#authorization-flow), [list filtering](#list-operations), and [UI gating verdicts](#permission-checks-for-ui-gating) — answers allow. It is an explicit operator opt-in, off by default: an omitted, empty, or disabled setting yields the enforcing posture. Three guards bound it: 1. **It is rejected alongside a configured IAM block** when configuration loads, so a deployment provisioned to enforce cannot also opt out. 1. **A boot with neither it nor an IAM block fails**, so serving without authorization is always something an operator asked for. 1. **A boot under it logs the posture once at WARN.** The enforcing posture is logged too, so an unenforced boot leaves a record of its own. **Unenforced is not anonymous access.** The mode makes no authorization decision, so it cannot widen one to admit callers without a role; a request presenting no credential is still rejected by authentication. It therefore does not reopen the [deferred](#public-and-internal-visibility) `public` and `internal` levels, which grant read to a caller holding no role while authorization is still evaluated. One switch selects this half together with ADR-020's [non-production development mode](020_authentication_flow.md#non-production-development-mode) for authentication. That mode's credential establishes no principal, which enforced authorization would deny on every request while the deployment looks healthy; one switch makes that state inexpressible. ### Services in the same cluster A caller authenticated by its Kubernetes service account ([ADR-020](020_authentication_flow.md#services-in-the-same-cluster-kubernetes-service-account-tokens)) has no role assignments. On a route that admits it, the policy engine evaluates it as an **Artifact Manager on the addressed resource**, with no relationships lookup. It names no organization, so the grant holds in every organization those routes reach. This first step stays off by default behind a switch; organization scoping is [open](020_authentication_flow.md#future-work--open-debates). Every other route denies it with **403 Forbidden**. This is not the unenforced posture above: authorization still runs under the enforcing posture. ## Deferred to later iterations The following capabilities are intentionally out of scope for closed beta. They are documented here so the design is on record, and will be revisited based on closed-beta customer demand. ### Public and internal visibility Closed beta supports only `private` visibility (see [Repository visibility](#repository-visibility)). Reintroducing `public` (read for anyone, including unauthenticated callers) and `internal` (read for organization members) requires deciding how to grant broad read access while remaining closed-by-default, so both are deferred to GA. ### Reductive repository overrides Closed beta repository-level assignments are **additive (raise-only)** (see [Role assignment](#role-assignment)). Lowering a principal's access on a specific repository (a reductive override) is out of scope, because it conflicts with role inheritance as it works across GitLab — a namespace-level assignment carries down to every repository. When this is added, the Artifact Registry will resolve precedence by reading the principal's permissions at both the namespace and repository levels and letting the repository level win outright — raising _or_ lowering access — instead of taking their union. ### Access rules Access rules let an Artifact Admin tighten _which roles hold an artifact permission_ — on the namespace, a repository, or artifacts matching a pattern — without naming a principal. They cover two customer use cases: protecting specific artifacts, and allowing or preventing duplicate uploads. Modeled as user-defined policies for the policy engine (R4), they can only tighten — never widen — the built-in defaults, and would be managed through a dedicated set of `*_access_rule` permissions introduced with the feature. Because they are deferred, closed beta cannot tighten any permission per repository. ### Custom roles Custom roles are deferred from closed beta. See the [custom roles roadmap work item](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/590721). Because roles are independent permission buckets, a custom role is a new bucket with any combination of Artifact Registry permissions (for example, a "CI Publisher" role with `read_artifact` and `create_artifact` but not `read_repository`). It is assigned through the same relationships API and can be referenced in access rules like a built-in role. ## Consequences ### Positive 1. **Aligned with the platform direction.** The Artifact Registry consumes the auth platform's relationships API and policy evaluation engine (R4, R5) rather than building a bespoke authorization system, matching the consolidation direction. 1. **Self-contained evaluation.** Once role assignments are available (resolved in closed beta, or carried in the enriched token in the target state), permission decisions are made through the dependencies the Artifact Registry is itself deployed and provisioned with, without calling back to the GitLab instance. 1. **Permission model preserved and portable.** Roles as independent permission buckets match the policy engine's "deny overrides" model, minimizing future migration effort. ### Negative 1. **Closed-beta role resolution.** Until the enrichment layer ships, the Artifact Registry resolves role assignments itself by querying the relationships API, which is more involved than reading a claim from the token. 1. **Onboarding overhead.** Closed-by-default requires explicit role assignment, which adds management effort. This is mitigated by bulk assignment workflows in the Organizations UI. 1. **Potential role proliferation.** Product-specific roles can grow into a large list over time. This is mitigated by Teams and group templates as the scaling mechanism, per the [roles management work item](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/593455) north star. 1. **No per-repository tightening in closed beta.** Without access rules or reductive overrides, a principal's access can only be raised on a repository, never lowered — a namespace-level assignment reaches every repository with no way to carve out exceptions. Both are [deferred](#deferred-to-later-iterations) and revisited on customer demand. ## Alternatives considered ### Organization Teams [Organization Teams](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/content-sites/handbook/-/merge_requests/17975) assign users a base role plus optional permission modifiers. The Artifact Registry could use a Team per organization for baseline access, and sub-teams for per-repository granularity. **Why not adopted now**: Organization Teams are in `proposed` status and not available in the Artifact Registry timeline. Teams remain the likely future scaling mechanism for role assignment (per the [roles management work item](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/593455) north star), and role assignments made through the relationships API are compatible with that direction. ### Artifact Registry-native authorization The Artifact Registry could maintain its own user-resource relationships and permission logic without relying on the auth platform. **Why not adopted**: it would introduce another authorization system alongside the platform's, adding fragmentation — the opposite of the consolidation direction. It would require building user management from scratch, produce an inconsistent user experience, and be harder to converge with the platform later. The relationships API (R5) provides the per-resource role assignment that this ADR needs without those downsides. ## Open questions 1. **Behavior when the relationships service is unavailable.** Closed beta fails closed (the request is denied), but the fail-open versus fail-closed policy is still being finalized. 1. **Organization-to-namespace resolution at scale.** Role assignments attach to the Artifact Registry namespace, which maps one-to-one to the organization in closed beta ([ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md)). If a future organization merge places multiple namespaces under one organization, define how organization-wide concerns — owner bootstrapping and the org-scoping invariant on assignments — resolve across them. 1. **Credential-type-aware authorization.** Closed beta authorizes by the `User` principal alone; all credential types resolve to the same principal (ADR-020), so a leaked CI job token carries the user's full permissions. Whether to constrain authorization by credential type — for example, limiting CI job tokens to publish-only — is deferred. It would require ADR-020 to carry the credential type in the token first, so it is a joint ADR-020/ADR-021 follow-up. 1. **Interface agreement alignment.** The [interface agreement](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/#gitlab-role-vocabulary) still states that the Artifact Registry uses the five built-in GitLab roles and "does not define its own roles", and its [no-callbacks constraint](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/#no-callbacks-during-request-processing) exempts co-located platform services by example rather than by its reachability rationale. Both need a companion update, coordinated with the Auth Platform team. 1. **Caching the repository-list authorization scan.** The repository list shows edit and delete controls on each row, so the list endpoint must both hide the rows a caller cannot read and return verdicts per row. Where the caller holds a grant on the namespace or its organization, that is an evaluation of every repository in the namespace (bounded by the repositories-per-namespace cap of [ADR-004](004_data_and_application_limits.md#entity-count-limits)), reachable by any such caller and repeated on every page load. How to cache and rate-bound that scan is unresolved ([proposal 016's open question](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/auth-architecture/design-doc/-/blob/main/proposals/016-batchcheck-ar-ui-authorization.md#open-questions)). ## References - [ADR-001: Organizations as Anchor Point](001_organizations_as_anchor_point.md) - [ADR-009: API Design](009_api_design.md) — management API and client API endpoints - [ADR-020: Authentication Flow](020_authentication_flow.md) — identity establishment and token validation - [ADR-022: Namespace Decoupling](022_namespace_decoupling.md) - [Artifact Registry and Auth Platform interface agreement](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/agreements/auth/) — the R4–R6 (authorization) requirements consumed here - [Relationships API](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/auth/iam/-/blob/main/docs/relationships-api.md) — the IAM relationships API contract;
