in closed beta it returns direct relationship tuples for a resource and its ancestors, which the policy engine evaluates as a union (additive repository-level assignments) - [GitLab permission conventions](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/development/permissions/conventions.html) — the naming and CRUD-decomposition rules these permissions follow - [Roles management and Artifact Registry onboarding](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/593455) — product-specific roles, closed-by-default, three-part model - [Proposal 016: BatchCheck](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/auth-architecture/design-doc/-/blob/main/proposals/016-batchcheck-ar-ui-authorization.md) — the AR-GLAZ batch evaluation contract behind the permission checks, and its UI flows - [UI gating direction (gitlab#602144)](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/602144#note_3532439195) — the agreement that UI gating uses action-based checks answered by the registry - [GATE Design Document](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/auth-architecture/design-doc/-/blob/main/design.md) — GitLab Adaptive Trust Environment

title: 022 Namespace Decoupling
text:
<!-- Design Documents often contain forward-looking statements -->
<!-- vale gitlab.FutureTense = NO -->

## Status

**Proposed.**

## Context

[ADR-001](001_organizations_as_anchor_point.md) makes Organizations the anchor point for the Artifact Registry.
Referencing the Rails organization directly, by its ID in tables and tokens and by its path in URLs, has two costs.

Organization paths are mutable: companies rename. With the path in Artifact Registry URLs, every rename breaks client
configurations (`.npmrc`, `settings.xml`, Dockerfiles, CI pipelines), invalidates cached references, makes token
scopes stale, and needs rename propagation and race handling between Rails and the Artifact Registry. Repository names
are immutable for the same reasons ([ADR-009](009_api_design.md#repository-name-immutability)), and the same principle
applies one level up.

The organizational hierarchy is also still developing: nested organizations and organization merges are possible, and
organization rollout is not universal. Tight coupling to the organization ID would be costly to undo if the anchor
entity changes. So the Artifact Registry references its anchor through an indirection it owns.

Organizations remain the default anchor. The question is how the Artifact Registry references them: directly, or
through an internal namespace with its own immutable identifier.

## Proposal

Introduce an internal namespace entity in the Artifact Registry with three properties:

1. **Immutable slug**: a globally unique, customer-chosen, human-readable identifier that appears in all URLs and never
   changes, like a storage bucket name.
1. **Virtual anchor tuple**: a `(platform, entity_type, entity_id)` tuple that links the namespace to an external
   entity without interpreting its semantics.
1. **UUIDv7 ID**: used for database partitioning, internal queries, and as the namespace's stable resource identifier
   for authorization, the resource that role assignments target ([ADR-021](021_authorization.md#role-assignment)). It
   is not an addressing identifier: the slug is the only namespace identifier in client-facing URLs, while the internal
   GitLab API is keyed by the UUID ([ADR-009](009_api_design.md)).

This does not change [ADR-001](001_organizations_as_anchor_point.md); it adds an indirection between the Artifact
Registry and the anchor entity. No Rails identifier appears in the Artifact Registry's partitioning or URLs.

### Anchors

- `entity_id` is numeric for some anchor types and a UUID for others. The Artifact Registry never interprets the
  external entity's semantics; `entity_type` tells a consumer which entity the value identifies.
- The anchor is unique among namespaces that are not purged. Purging frees it, so its owner can onboard a new
  namespace, while the old slug stays retired
  ([ADR-015 (internal)](https://internal.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/decisions/015_slug_policy/#slug-lifecycle)).
- For Organizations v1, every anchor is `('gitlab', 'organization', '<organizations.uuid>')`: the organization's
  UUIDv7, not its numeric ID. IAM's Relationships API rejects a non-UUIDv7 object id for the whole request it appears
  in, so the numeric ID could not name the organization ancestor.
- No other uniqueness may be placed on the organization value: [Organization Merges](#organization-merges) requires a
  surviving organization to hold more than one namespace.
- A new anchor type is a new `entity_type` value, with no schema change.
- A separate **billing anchor**, a `(billing_entity_type, billing_entity_id)` pair, identifies who pays for usage.
  The Artifact Registry stamps the stored pair on every billing event without interpreting its value, and checks only its type, when the pair is written.
  For Organizations v1 it is the top-level group, `('top_level_group', '<root_namespace_id>')`. Rails can replace it later when the payer changes (see
  [billing re-anchoring](#namespace-lifecycle)).
  The Artifact Registry accepts only the payer types it lists, so a new payer type, for example the organization when billing moves there, is an Artifact Registry change.
- The platform supplies every anchor and billing value at namespace creation.
  None has a schema default, so the Artifact Registry stays agnostic to the external identity and billing models beyond the payer types it accepts.

Partitioned tables key on `namespace_id`, or on the digest for blob storage
([ADR-007](007_database_schema.md#blob-storage-partitioning-strategy)), and neither changes. The Cells
[sharding key requirement](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/organization/sharding/#choosing-the-right-sharding-key)
applies to the Rails monolith's databases, not to a cell-local service: data movement across cells needs only that
rows are attributable to an organization, directly or indirectly. The namespace model provides
`namespace_id` → anchor → organization.

### Slug Design

The slug is chosen by the customer when creating a namespace and is exposed in every client surface. Its user-facing
name in customer documentation and UX is **registry handle**.

- **Immutable**: once set, it never changes.
- **Customer-chosen**: human-readable and typeable, since it appears in client configurations, CI pipelines, and
  Kubernetes manifests.
- **Globally unique**: no two namespaces can share a slug.
- **First in the path**: the slug is the first path segment after the API or protocol prefix in every client-facing
  URL except the OCI `GET /v2/` probe, and no numeric ID appears in any client-facing URL ([ADR-009](009_api_design.md)). With immutable repository names, the whole URL path
  is permanently stable.

Validation rules, default derivation from the organization name, reservation policy, and lifecycle controls (security
block and transfer) are defined in [ADR-015: Slug Policy (internal)](https://internal.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/decisions/015_slug_policy/).

A request resolves its slug to the namespace ID with one indexed lookup. The mapping is immutable, so it can be cached
freely.

### Namespace Lifecycle

**Creation:** the customer chooses a slug, the namespace is linked to their organization through the anchor, and the
slug is claimed with the topology service for Cells routing.

**Organization rename:** no impact. Nothing changes in the database, URLs, tokens, or client configurations.

**Anchor change:** re-anchoring a namespace to a different entity updates only the anchor. The slug, the URLs and the
partitioned data do not change. For Organizations v1, no such events exist.

**Billing re-anchoring:** Rails can replace the billing anchor when the payer changes, for example when a paid group becomes the nominated group.
Re-anchoring changes neither the slug nor the anchor tuple.

**Status:** A namespace has two one-way lifecycle events, deletion and purge, and four independent, reversible service conditions:

- Blocked (security).
- Disabled (the organization turned the registry off).
- Suspended (the plan lapsed, see [ADR-010](010_data_retention.md#subscription-expiration)).
- Usage-limit blocked (the namespace reached its usage limit, see [ADR-010](010_data_retention.md#usage-limit-block)).

Applying or lifting one condition never changes another, so several conditions can apply at the same time.
A suspended or usage-limit-blocked namespace serves reads (pulls) and refuses writes (pushes).
Any other event or condition stops all service.
[ADR-010](010_data_retention.md#billing-and-retention-by-condition) sets how billing and retention apply under each condition.
The Artifact Registry stores each condition and enforces the status on every request, whatever Rails has cached, and exposes it through its API (see [Slug Discovery](#slug-discovery)).
It never learns why Rails set a condition.

**Deletion:** The Artifact Registry soft-deletes the namespace. The slug is reserved and cannot be reclaimed
by another customer, to avoid the same security risks as repository name reclaiming (authorization bypass, cache
poisoning). See [ADR-015 (internal)](https://internal.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/decisions/015_slug_policy/#slug-lifecycle) for the full lifecycle (soft-delete window allowing
reclaim, hard-delete with permanent retirement) and the security-block and transfer controls.

### Organization Merges

If organizations merge, the namespace model needs no data migration:

1. The anchor on the absorbed organization's namespace is updated to point to the surviving organization: one metadata
   update per namespace.
1. The surviving organization holds several namespaces, each with its own repositories and its own deduplication
   boundary.
1. Nothing moves across database partitions or in object storage, because all stored data is keyed by namespace, not
   organization.
1. Slugs do not change, so URLs, tokens and client configurations stay stable.

Consolidating into a single namespace would be an explicit migration of repositories between namespaces, not an
automatic consequence of the merge.

Without the namespace, a merge would mean migrating all partitioned data from one organization ID to another,
changing every URL, reconciling deduplication boundaries, and handling stale token scopes.

### Cells Routing

The topology service maps claimed identifiers to cells, and the Artifact Registry claims slugs:

1. When a namespace is created, the Artifact Registry claims its slug, mapping it to the cell that holds its data.
1. The HTTP router extracts the slug from the URL and routes the request to that cell. The slug is readable without
   authentication, so it routes every slug-prefixed request. ADR-009 decides how the routes without a slug reach a
   cell: the OCI [`GET /v2/` probe](009_api_design.md#container) and the UUID-keyed
   [GitLab API](009_api_design.md#gitlab-api).

Only namespace creation needs the topology service to be writable. The read path needs only the routing lookup, which
can be cached.

### Slug Discovery

The GitLab frontend reaches the Artifact Registry through the Rails monolith ([ADR-014](014_frontend_to_artifact_registry.md)). Every Artifact Registry API call requires the slug in the URL, so Rails needs the slug before it can make any request.

Rails durably stores only the namespace UUID, one row per namespace, written at provisioning. For Organizations v1, that is a single row per organization; an [organization merge](#organization-merges) would add the absorbed namespace's row to the surviving organization. The UUID is immutable, so this reference never needs synchronization and survives merges and anchor changes.

The slug and the namespace status are not persisted on the Rails side. Rails resolves them from the Artifact Registry by UUID and caches them.
The slug can change only on the Artifact Registry's authority, through a legal escalation, the one exception to its immutability.
The service conditions ([Namespace Lifecycle](#namespace-lifecycle)) have two sources: Rails sets disabled, suspended and usage-limit blocked, and the Artifact Registry sets blocked (security).
The Artifact Registry is authoritative for enforcing every condition on each request.
In the hybrid deployment model (Self-Managed Rails against a SaaS Artifact Registry), slug changes and security blocks can only originate on the Artifact Registry side, so Rails cannot be their source of truth.

A stale cache never weakens enforcement: the Artifact Registry enforces the namespace status on every request. For the status, staleness only affects display (for example, the navigation briefly showing the registry while the namespace is disabled) until the next refresh. For the slug, a stale value can render broken links until the next refresh; slug changes are rare emergency events, and the cache refresh interval bounds that window.

## Consequences

### Positive

1. **Rails decoupling**: no Rails IDs in the Artifact Registry's partitioning or URLs. If Rails changes
   organization IDs or structure, the Artifact Registry is unaffected.
1. **Immutable URLs**: both the slug and repository names are immutable, so no rename breaks a URL, a token scope or a
   client configuration.
1. **Stable partitioning**: namespace IDs are internal and never change, even when the anchor changes.
1. **Anchor flexibility**: namespaces attach to organizations today and to other entities later, with no schema change
   or data movement.
1. **Cells-ready**: slug claiming gives a routing key that does not depend on organization path resolution.
1. **No Rails call on the request path**: the Artifact Registry resolves the namespace from its own data.
1. **Organization merges without data migration** ([Organization Merges](#organization-merges)).
1. **Standalone product potential**: because the Artifact Registry owns its namespace identity and treats the anchor as
   opaque, it does not structurally depend on GitLab Rails. It could be packaged as an independent product that relies
   on a third-party authentication and authorization provider.

### Negative

1. **Slug squatting**: globally unique slugs invite squatting, which needs a policy for reserved names, high-value
   slugs and minimum length ([ADR-015 (internal)](https://internal.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/decisions/015_slug_policy/)).
1. **Namespace creation is an explicit action**: a namespace must be provisioned before any client request can
   succeed. The Artifact Registry cannot serve an organization that has not set one up.
1. **Topology service dependency**: the Artifact Registry integrates the topology service to claim slugs.
1. **Slug discoverability**: unlike organization paths, which users already know from GitLab, the slug is a new
   concept. Client configuration documentation and the UI need to surface it.
1. **Deduplication boundary**: deduplication moves from the organization
   ([ADR-002](002_storage_deduplication_scope.md)) to the namespace. For
   Organizations v1 a namespace maps one-to-one to an organization, but an organization with several namespaces has an
   independent deduplication boundary in each. Cross-namespace deduplication is out of scope.

## References

- [ADR-001: Organizations as Anchor Point](001_organizations_as_anchor_point.md)
- [ADR-002: Storage Deduplication Scope](002_storage_deduplication_scope.md)
- [ADR-009: API Design](009_api_design.md)
- [ADR-014: Frontend to Artifact Registry Interaction](014_frontend_to_artifact_registry.md)
- [ADR-015: Slug Policy (internal)](https://internal.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/decisions/015_slug_policy/)
- [ADR-021: Authorization](021_authorization.md)

title: 023 Code Structure And Enforcement
text:
<!-- Design Documents often contain forward-looking statements -->
<!-- vale gitlab.FutureTense = NO -->

## Status

**Proposed.**

## Context

The Artifact Registry will support 15+ package formats (OCI, Maven, npm, PyPI, NuGet, and others)
developed by 20+ engineers. AI agents will write the format implementations, with engineers
writing specs, steering architecture, and reviewing output. The codebase needs a structure that
scales with format count, onboards new contributors quickly, and lets engineers find the relevant
code during incidents without tooling. It must enforce architectural boundaries mechanically
rather than through code review alone.

[ADR-006](006_technology_stack.md) sets Go as the implementation language. The format
extensibility mechanism (Module Pattern with Service Provider Interface and Capability Interfaces)
is out of scope. This ADR decides the project layout and the tooling that enforces it.

## Decision

We use a `cmd/` + `internal/` project layout with package-per-feature organization. These
conventions are widely adopted in production Go projects, the container registry included, and are
rooted in Go's own toolchain: `internal/` has
[compiler-enforced visibility](https://go.dev/doc/go1.4#internalpackages) and `cmd/` is the
conventional entry-point directory.

- A single entry point lives under `cmd/`. It is the composition root: it wires format packages,
  shared infrastructure, and the router.
- All application code lives under `internal/`.
- Each package format lives in its own package under `internal/format/<name>/`.
- Cross-cutting infrastructure (storage, auth, namespace resolution, data access, background jobs,
  and similar) lives in shared packages directly under `internal/`.

### Boundaries

Four rules hold the structure in place. Each is checked by a machine, not by review:

1. **No code outside the module imports its `internal/` packages**, and packages cannot import each
   other in a cycle. The Go compiler enforces both.
1. **A format package never imports another format package.** Behavior that spans formats is wired
   at the composition root. depguard's `format-isolation` rule enforces this in CI.
1. **A format package never uses the SQL driver directly.** SQL lives in `internal/datastore/`, and a
   format reaches it through the datastore's interfaces. depguard's `no-direct-db` rule enforces
   this in CI.
1. **Shared infrastructure never imports a format package.** A shared package defines the interface
   it needs, each format implements it, and the composition root injects the implementations. The
   dependency flows `cmd` → format → infrastructure and never back, so shared code stays
   format-agnostic and does not grow its imports with format count. depguard's
   `no-reverse-dependency` rule enforces this in CI. The one exception is `internal/authz`, which
   imports each format's route-grammar leaf (`internal/format/<name>/<name>route`) under its own
   depguard rule; each leaf imports nothing from `internal/format`.

The depguard rules match paths generically (every file under `internal/format/`), so adding a format
adds only two depguard entries for its route-grammar leaf: one that lets `internal/authz` import it, and
one that keeps it a leaf. Background processing for one format follows the same rules: its logic
lives in the format package, and shared scheduling infrastructure is built only once real formats
show which patterns they need.

### Locked paths

This ADR locks the enforcement rules and the paths they reference: `cmd/`, `internal/`,
`internal/format/<name>/`, `internal/datastore/`, and the shared packages the reverse-dependency
rule names. Renaming a locked path requires a paired update to the depguard configuration.

Everything else is a starting point: the files inside a format package and how they are named, the
organization of files within shared packages, and the names of other shared packages. A format
package is flat by default. Because the isolation rule matches by path prefix, a format that
imports its own sub-package needs an allow entry in that rule, and the entry opens the sub-package to
every format.

**The layout is a starting point, not a contract.** When it creates friction (for example, tests
pushing on package boundaries, or a format whose shape resists the default file split), the
expected response is to propose a layout change, not to work around it. AI agents in particular
should surface better organizations rather than force code into packages that are not its natural
home. Layout changes land in their own MRs, not bundled with feature or bug-fix work, so the
trade-off is reviewed on its merits. Revising the layout inside these paths does not require
revising this ADR.

### Comparative analysis

We built a demo of each pattern with five formats (see References). Three results decided the
choice:

- **Per-format cost follows format complexity.** Go Native pays 2-6 files per format; the
  alternatives impose 10-13 files on every format, simple ones included. Creating fewer files in
  one flat package is also cheaper for an AI agent adding a format: the DDD demo recorded
  the most agent backtracks, correlating with its file count and directory-spanning creation.
- **Enforcement barely grows with formats.** A new format adds only its route-grammar leaf's two
  depguard entries. A missing allow entry fails lint, but a missing leaf rule does not, so review
  has to catch that one. Both alternatives need a human to update the go-arch-lint configuration
  for each format, and a format added without that update is silently unchecked.
- **The contract surface held.** In all three demos, adding a format never changed a shared
  interface, so the choice of architecture does not trade away a stable contract.

Handler size varied with format complexity, not architecture. Go Native co-locates a format's
handler logic, so its handler files are the largest (797 lines for OCI and 916 for npm in the demo,
projecting to 1,200 to over 1,800 lines in production).

## Alternatives

### Clean Architecture (layer-first)

Clean Architecture organizes code into concentric layers (domain, usecase, adapter), and
go-arch-lint enforces the import direction between them. Each demo format needed 10-13 files, and
the composition root grows by ~30 lines per format.

The demo exposed an enforcement gap: in every format, management API endpoints bypassed the usecase
layer by reaching through service structs directly. go-arch-lint checks import graphs, not call
graphs, and no Go linter in production use catches a call to the wrong method on a correctly
imported package. At scale the usecase layer degrades into a mix of real logic and pass-through
stubs. Cross-cutting changes also touch two files per format (usecase and adapter) instead of one.

**Why rejected:** the usecase layer adds overhead without the isolation it promises, and current Go
tooling cannot close the gap.

### DDD + Hexagonal Architecture (bounded-context-first)

DDD + Hexagonal organizes code into one bounded context per format, each with domain entities,
application services, ports, and adapters, and go-arch-lint enforces boundaries between contexts and
layers. Every demo format needed exactly 13 files regardless of complexity.

The demo exposed forced duplication: every format adapter reimplemented the same credential
extraction, because the architecture prevents format adapters from importing shared adapters, and
no fix exists within it. DDD tactical patterns (aggregates, value objects, repositories) also map
poorly to Go's type system, so aggregate invariants depend on discipline, and the learning curve is
the steepest of the three.

**Why rejected:** the fixed 13-file structure taxes simple formats as much as complex ones, and it
forces duplication the architecture cannot resolve.

## Consequences

### Positive

- **Compiler-enforced isolation:** `internal/` visibility needs no configuration and has no false
  negatives.
- **Proportional per-format cost:** simple formats pay less than complex ones.
- **Minimal enforcement configuration:** a new format adds only its route-grammar leaf's two
  depguard entries.
- **Low cross-cutting amplification:** a cross-cutting change touches one file per format.

### Negative

- **No prescribed internal structure within format packages.** Format packages can drift apart in
  how they organize their files. This is a consistency problem, not a correctness one: the compiler
  and depguard still block every cross-boundary import. A reference implementation, a contributing
  guide, and conformance tests (each format implements the required interfaces, registers its
  routes, and passes behavioral contracts) carry consistency instead.
- **Large handler files need planned splitting.** At production scale a complex format's handler
  outgrows one file (the container registry's production manifests handler is 1,848 lines), and
  moderate formats may follow. The split is mechanical, such as separating client API handlers from
  management API handlers, and stays within the package. Plan for it rather than discover it under
  pressure.
- **Test overhead is unmeasured.** The demos had no tests, yet tests are the majority of production
  code (the container registry's handler test-to-code ratio is 2.3x) and regularly reshape package
  boundaries, interface placement, and file splits. The per-format layout may change once formats
  carry full test suites.
- **depguard cannot catch duplication.** Code duplicated within or across format packages still
  needs review, as it would under any of the three candidates.

## References

- [ADR-006: Technology Stack](006_technology_stack.md)
- [Go 1.4 `internal/` packages](https://go.dev/doc/go1.4#internalpackages)
- [depguard](https://github.com/OpenPeeDeeP/depguard)
- [go-arch-lint](https://github.com/fe3dback/go-arch-lint) (referenced in alternatives)
- Demo: [ar-guardrails-clean-arch](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/ci-cd/package-stage/ar-guardrails-clean-arch)
- Demo: [ar-guardrails-ddd-hex](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/ci-cd/package-stage/ar-guardrails-ddd-hex)
- Demo: [ar-guardrails-go-native](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/ci-cd/package-stage/ar-guardrails-go-native)
- Production reference: [container-registry](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/container-registry) (file size calibration)

title: 024 Infrastructure Delivery
text:
<!-- Design Documents often contain forward-looking statements -->
<!-- vale gitlab.FutureTense = NO -->

## Status

**Proposed.**

## Context

The target deployment model for the Artifact Registry
is a cell-based multi-tenant architecture
where each Cell is a self-contained regional data plane (GKE, PostgreSQL, Redis, GCS)
behind a shared edge (Cloudflare + Cloud CDN),
with slug-based routing through the Anchor Router and Anchor Topology services ([ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md))
and a Cell lifecycle managed by Terraform, Argo CD, and Fairway.

That target cannot be fully in place for the closed beta.
The beta has a fixed FY27-Q2 window,
and several of its dependencies are still in flight:

1. The **Anchor Router** and **Anchor Topology** services
   are not yet available for the Artifact Registry to route against.
   Until they exist,
   the registry owns slug uniqueness in its own database ([ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md)).
1. The **Theseus Platform Binding for Cells and Dedicated** — the mechanism that would let the registry be provisioned *inside* a Cell through the existing Instrumentor stack —
   is not ready.
   The Runway for GKE v2 work explicitly targets the Enterprise (non-Cellular) instance of Runway;
   Cells and Dedicated provisioning come later.
1. Per-Cell migration and rebalancing tooling does not exist.

## Decision

The Artifact Registry,
together with the Auth components it depends on,
is being used as the **thinnest viable platform** for building out [Theseus](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/content-sites/handbook/-/merge_requests/19702),
the GitLab internal developer platform.

AR is the first stateful GitLab Module heading to production,
so it exercises the parts of the platform — provisioning, service bindings, observability, build, and delivery —
that future Modular Components will reuse.
The Theseus platform teams **pave the path just ahead** of the AR and Auth teams:
they deliver the thinnest platform the beta needs,
rather than the full cell-based target,
and the product and the platform are built in parallel.

The Artifact Registry will be deployed using Fairway descriptors
on Runway's new "Runway for GKE v2" target.

Theseus allows application development teams to request backing stores for their components.
These are provisioned using automation, without the need for manual intervention.
The mechanism depends on the resource:
Runway provisions most backing stores directly,
while a small number are delivered as Artifact Registry
**[COM (Component Ownership Model) modules](/handbook/engineering/infrastructure-platforms/production/component-ownership-model/)** — owned by the relevant product engineering team,
integrated into Config-Mgmt, and managed outside Runway.

The split was agreed between the Artifact Registry and Runway teams:

| Infrastructure | How it is provided | Tracking |
|---|---|---|
| CloudSQL (database) | Runway provisions | Runway [`team#933`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/gl-infra/platform/runway/team/-/work_items/933) |
| Memorystore Redis (cache) | Runway provisions | Runway [`team#931`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/gl-infra/platform/runway/team/-/work_items/931) |
| Private Service Connect | Runway provisions; VPC peering was rejected as too complex and a net increase in scope | Runway [`team#934`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/gl-infra/platform/runway/team/-/work_items/934) |
| GCS bucket | Runway provisions in the general case; for the Artifact Registry it is a COM module, coupled with Cloud CDN | Runway [`team#932`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/gl-infra/platform/runway/team/-/work_items/932); COM [`production-engineering#28463`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/gl-infra/production-engineering/-/work_items/28463) |
| Cloud CDN | Artifact Registry COM module; no Runway provisioning. The GCS bucket ships in the same Terraform module, given the strong GCS–Cloud CDN coupling | COM [`production-engineering#28464`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/gl-infra/production-engineering/-/work_items/28464); [coupling decision](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/gl-infra/production-engineering/-/work_items/28464#note_3467903274) |
| YugabyteDB (IAM store) | Owned by the Auth team, delivered through config-management; reached over the Runway-provisioned Private Service Connect | [`gitlab#598250`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/598250) |

*Source: [Runway work item #44](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-com/gl-infra/platform/runway/-/work_items/44#note_3465201308).*

Runway-provisioned dependencies are consumed by the application through Fairway-generated service bindings.

### Strategy — Artifact Registry and Auth as the thinnest viable platform

AR and Auth are the first real Modular Components to be delivered using Theseus end to end,
and they are deliberately used as the **thinnest viable platform** for the platform itself:
the smallest workload that forces each Theseus capability
to be integrated.

The Theseus teams will pave the path just ahead of the AR and Auth teams,
delivering the thinnest platform each phase needs to deliver the Beta dotcom target.
Once that target is achieved, the focus will switch to the Self-Managed Beta target.

### Ways of working — early, continuous integration

The components are integrated **early and continuously**,
not assembled at the end.

Developers integrate locally against the full Cloud Native stack using **Caproni** ([`gitlab-org#22286`](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/22286)),
and a **weekly demo** brings together individual contributors representing the various teams — AR, Auth, and the Theseus platform teams —
to integrate their work as early as possible
and surface interface gaps while they are still cheap to fix.
This replaces a big-bang integration phase with a standing, demo-driven integration loop.

### Phase 1 — Dotcom closed beta

The Artifact Registry is deployed as a **single global service on Runway for GKE v2**
(the Enterprise, non-Cellular/non-Dedicated instance of Runway).

It is multi-tenant,
with tenants isolated by **namespace partitioning**:
the database is partitioned by namespace ([ADR-007](007_database_schema.md)),
and object-storage paths and deduplication are scoped per namespace ([ADR-008](008_content_addressable_storage.md)).

There is no per-Cell deployment,
no Anchor Router / Anchor Topology routing,
and no migration tooling in Phase 1.
The topology is shown in the [Phase 1 diagram](#architecture).

The following components are built and deployed:

1. The **Artifact Registry** (Go)
1. The **IAM Data Access** service (Go)
1. **GLAZ** (Rust authorization sidecar)
1. The **[Brand List Validator](https://internal.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/artifact_registry/decisions/015_slug_policy/)** Service (Go)

For the beta, non-FIPS binaries and container images are produced with GoReleaser.
FIPS images are out-of-scope for the Beta.

If the [TUBE proposal](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/content-sites/handbook/-/merge_requests/11660) is accepted
and when the TUBE build tooling is ready, it will be retrofitted into the projects.
Retrofitting is expected to be limited to build boilerplate
(CI/CD configuration and build scripts) rather than application code.
This may happen after the Beta period, or during development, but,
importantly, is not on the critical path.

The Artifact Registry and IAM Data Access service request backing stores through
their `FairwayManifest`s. Runway for GKE v2, acting as the Platform Binding, satisfies these dependencies,
and the application consumes them through provider-agnostic **service bindings**
(the Postgres and Redis bindings) surfaced through **LabKit v2**.

Note: Object storage is **not** consumed through a LabKit object-storage binding.
While Theseus will provide object-storage provisioning and service-binding in the general case,
the Artifact Registry will access **native cloud-provider SDKs (GCS/S3) directly, through HTTP requests**.
The registry depends on native object-storage primitives: specifically resumable, chunked uploads,
and this cannot currently be supported through a generic, provider-agnostic abstraction.
For the Artifact Registry, object storage will be delivered through a COM module rather than provisioned by Runway,
so the registry will configure the endpoint itself, and provider differences
(GCS on GitLab.com, S3 in Cells) will need to be handled in application configuration rather than hidden by a binding.
A LabKit object-storage abstraction that meets the Artifact Registry's and Container Registry's
requirements may be built in a later iteration, but it is not on the beta critical path.

The service bindings **must not** leak the provider-specific interface into the application manifest, for example
CloudSQL vs Amazon RDS vs Self-Managed Postgres,
so the same bindings carry over to Self-Managed
and the cellular target (Phase 2) without changes on the application side.

Driver selection sits behind the binding as well:
the application uses the Postgres-compatible `v2/postgres` client for its initial YugabyteDB integration,
and any future use of Yugabyte's cluster-aware smart drivers is handled by LabKit and Runway configuration
rather than chosen in the application manifest.
This keeps development, test, and production environments portable.

### Phase 2 — Cellular target

Once a Theseus Platform Binding for GitLab Dedicated and Cell is available,
the Artifact Registry will be deployed **as part of the Cell infrastructure, through Instrumentor**,
reaching the cell-based multi-tenant target.

This will build on the **existing** GitLab Cells and Dedicated automation (the Instrumentor stack)
rather than a new, parallel cellular fabric,
by accelerating the **Dedicated / Cells Platform Binding for Theseus** —
which also gives other GitLab Modules a route to the same platform underpinnings.

When the Artifact Registry moves into Cells,
customers are migrated **transparently** from the original global instance to the appropriate Cell,
aiming for the smallest customer-visible interruption the migration tooling can achieve.
This interim-to-target migration carries real cost and risk that grows the longer it is deferred — see [Negative consequences](#negative).

For GitLab.com / Cells customers,
the default placement is the Cell in the same isolation boundary as the customer's GitLab Cell (a rule of thumb, not a hard rule).

Authority for slug uniqueness moves from the registry's own database to the Anchor Topology service at this point;
slugs created during the single-instance era must be seeded into Anchor Topology before a second Cell can accept namespace creation.

The migration tooling required to move customers in is treated as **business-as-usual rebalancing capability**,
not throwaway one-off work.

## Consequences

### Positive

- The Dotcom beta ships on the FY27-Q2 timeline,
  without waiting on the Anchor Router, Anchor Topology, or the Theseus Platform Binding for Cells/Dedicated.
- Using AR and Auth as the thinnest viable platform builds Theseus against a real production workload:
  each capability is delivered just ahead of the product that needs it
  and in a form the next Modular Component can reuse.
  Early, continuous integration through Caproni and the weekly demo surfaces interface gaps while they are cheap to fix,
  rather than at a late integration milestone.
- Backing stores follow a consistent provisioning model with clear ownership:
  Runway provisions the database, cache, and Private Service Connect directly,
  consumed by the application through Fairway-generated service bindings;
  the Artifact Registry GCS bucket and Cloud CDN are delivered as self-contained,
  replaceable **COM modules** owned by product engineering.
- The Cells deliverables build on proven Cells and Dedicated automation,
  giving the registry — and future GitLab Modules — a single, shared deployment and operations path
  rather than two competing ones.
- The customer-migration work needed to move from the global instance into Cells
  doubles as the rebalancing tooling the cellular architecture needs anyway;
  nothing is wasted.

### Negative

- During the beta the registry is **not** Cellular:
  there is no per-Cell deployment, no request routing, and no migration tooling.
  Cells can, however, use Artifact Registry through the Global instance running in
  Runway for GKE.
  During this phase, Artifact Registry is a Global Service, but this is a [temporary state](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/content-sites/handbook/-/merge_requests/20067#note_3460179693).
  Various technical challenges will need to be overcome before Artifact Registry can be moved into the Cellular infrastructure.
  This includes the need to sync the [trusted issuer's public key](020_authentication_flow.md#authentication-flow),
  and the ability for each cell to call the [Relationships API](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/content-sites/handbook/-/merge_requests/18717).
- Tenant isolation in the Dotcom beta rests entirely on namespace partitioning within a single shared data plane;
  the stronger isolation and resiliency properties of the cellular model only arrive with the Cells/Dedicated Platform Binding
  and other work required to prepare the Artifact Registry for a cellular architecture.
- A later migration of Dotcom beta customers from the global instance into Cells is unavoidable,
  and the slug-authority handover (registry database → Anchor Topology) must be designed and executed carefully.
  The longer this migration is deferred, the higher the risk:
  - Vertical scaling of the global instance is only a temporary hedge;
    the longer the global instance grows, the larger and riskier the eventual migration.
  - The global instance runs in Google Cloud (GCS-backed) while the cellular instances run in AWS (S3-backed),
    so the move incurs cross-hyperscaler egress costs that scale with both customer activity and the delay before migration is supported
    (egress is on the order of USD 120 for the first TB and ~USD 1,000 for the first 10 TB).
  - Inter-Cell migration tooling should ideally be delivered as shared infrastructure for all teams building cellular (Modular) components,
    so that standardisation, security, and operational best practices are established once rather than reimplemented per component.
  - That shared infrastructure will take time to build. Depending on the urgency of the first migration,
    the tooling may be used before it is fully mature, with some disruption (minutes or even hours)
    before it can perform migrations with only seconds of customer-visible interruption.

  See the [CTO review migration planning notes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/12eJYdzyCcEUUeBjkV6wIL_5FymsUbh9Tb_yRDWHRWKo/edit?tab=t.i2jtfrt0twt9#bookmark=id.7n3stb68gv0a) for broader cross-Cell migration context.

## Alternatives considered

**Build a parallel cellular fabric for the registry.**
Stand up a registry-specific cell architecture independent of the existing Cells / Dedicated Instrumentor investment.
*Rejected:* it duplicates the most complex and costly part of the platform,
fragments the deployment and operations story,
and makes deploying modules into Single-Tenant, Dedicated, Dedicated for Government, and Self-Managed harder rather than easier.
Picking a cellular architecture for one part of the system and not the rest is the worst of both worlds —
the cost of making the hardest component cellular with none of the fleet-wide benefit.

## Architecture

### Phase 1 — Dotcom beta service architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  rails["GitLab Rails (legacy .com)"]

  subgraph cf["Cloudflare (edge: DDoS / WAF / rate limiting)"]
    arzone["Artifact Registry zone (Runway-provisioned)"]
    iamzone["IAM Data Access zone (Runway-provisioned)"]
  end

  subgraph gke["Runway for GKE v2 - single global deployment for Beta"]
    iam["IAM Data Access (Go service)"]
    blv["Brand List Validator (Go service, no backing-store dependencies)"]
    subgraph arpod["Artifact Registry pod"]
      ar["Artifact Registry (Go service)"]
      glaz["glaz (sidecar, Rust)"]
    end
    ardb[("Artifact Registry DB — CloudSQL (Runway-provisioned)")]
    redis[("Cache — Memorystore Redis (Runway-provisioned)")]
    psc{{"Private Service Connect (Runway-provisioned)"}}
  end

  subgraph gcscdncom["GCS + Cloud CDN COM module (Artifact Registry, outside Runway)"]
    gcs[("Object storage — GCS bucket")]
    cdn(["Cloud CDN (bucket origin, signed URLs)"])
  end

  subgraph yugacom["IAM store — owned by Auth team"]
    yuga[("YugabyteDB - exposed through Postgres binding")]
  end

  arzone -- "HTTPS" --> ar
  iamzone -- "HTTPS" --> iam
  rails -- "gRPC+TLS (via Cloudflare) — relationship management" --> iamzone
  rails -- "HTTPS (via Cloudflare) — REST API for frontend and admin operations" --> arzone
  ar -- "HTTPS, signed URL" --> cdn
  ar -- "gRPC" --> glaz
  ar -. "gRPC (K8s headless service, client-side LB; no internal gateway/LB)" .-> iam
  iam -- "SQL / TLS" --> psc
  psc -- "SQL / TLS" --> yuga
  ar -- "SQL / TLS" --> ardb
  ar -- "HTTPS" --> gcs
  ar -- "TCP / TLS" --> redis
  gke -. "Runway can provision object storage, not used for the Artifact Registry" .-> gcs

  %% Pastel colour-coding
  classDef edgezone fill:#FFE9DC,stroke:#F0A985,color:#5A2A1A;
  classDef svc fill:#DCE7FB,stroke:#6E97E0,color:#1E2F52;
  classDef dstore fill:#DDF3E4,stroke:#6FBF8E,color:#1E4031;
  classDef commod fill:#ECE0F7,stroke:#A87CC9,color:#3E2A52;
  classDef yugamod fill:#FCE1EC,stroke:#E892B5,color:#5A2238;
  classDef client fill:#FFF6D6,stroke:#D9B441,color:#5A4A12;

  class rails client;
  class arzone,iamzone edgezone;
  class ar,glaz,iam,blv svc;
  class ardb,redis,psc dstore;
  class gcs,cdn commod;
  class yuga yugamod;

  style cf fill:#FFF3EC,stroke:#F0A985,color:#5A2A1A;
  style gke fill:#F4F7FB,stroke:#9DB8E8,color:#1E2F52;
  style arpod fill:#EAF1FC,stroke:#6E97E0,color:#1E2F52;
  style gcscdncom fill:#F3EBFA,stroke:#A87CC9,color:#3E2A52;
  style yugacom fill:#FDEFF4,stroke:#E892B5,color:#5A2238;
```

### Transport security

Most edges in the diagram carry TLS: clients and Rails enter over HTTPS at Cloudflare, the Artifact Registry database accepts encrypted connections only, and object storage and the CDN serve HTTPS. Three hops are plain: the Artifact Registry to its GLAZ sidecar, loopback-only by configuration; to IAM Data Access, pod to pod; and to Redis, served by Memorystore with transit encryption disabled inside the private VPC.

A plaintext request to the edge is refused rather than redirected. A redirect makes a client configured with `http://` work, so a client that sends its credential on every request, such as `dnf` reading a `.repo` file, sends it in the clear each time without anyone noticing.

For the GitLab.com beta these three plain hops carry no application-level TLS. Each is authenticated (service credentials on gRPC, AUTH on Redis), the network is private, and [Google encrypts traffic that crosses a physical boundary it controls](https://cloud.google.com/docs/security/encryption-in-transit); within one boundary, physical security stands in.

Self-Managed and Dedicated assume no platform guarantee, and some operators mandate encryption on every hop. Serving TLS on these hops is therefore an optional capability of each service, not a deployment assumption: the operator provides file-based key pairs and turns it on. It is first needed for Self-Managed GA; GitLab.com runs with it off today and may adopt it like any operator. Verification stays optional until an operator enforces it, so enabling a certificate authority cannot break a working hop.

Mutual TLS with workload identity is an open direction, not a decision; [ADR-020](020_authentication_flow.md) records it under future work. Two events reopen it: a per-hop encryption or workload-identity mandate from a supported deployment model, or the authentication architecture settling the Unified Request Token direction.

title: 025 Garbage Collection
text:
<!-- Design Documents often contain forward-looking statements -->
<!-- vale gitlab.FutureTense = NO -->

## Summary

When a client deletes a tag, a version or a cached file, the Artifact Registry removes the metadata, but the content-addressed blob and its storage object stay.
Without garbage collection (GC), storage grows without bound.

The Artifact Registry reclaims storage with per-namespace, online, deferred GC.
A blob becomes a candidate when its last reference in its namespace goes.
The candidate waits out a review delay, is checked again under a lock on the blob's row, and only then is its object deleted, before the row.
A re-push during the delay rescues it.
GC never decides which artifact to keep, and it never reads a manifest or a package.

## Motivation

Blobs are content-addressed ([ADR-008](008_content_addressable_storage.md)) and deduplicated within a namespace ([ADR-002](002_storage_deduplication_scope.md), [ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md)).
[ADR-010](010_data_retention.md) gives GC its contract: reclaim the blobs nothing references, and leave every decision about which artifacts to keep to the formats, lifecycle and retention.
Every delete and every expiry already removes references; nothing turns those removals into freed storage.

Two properties make GC hard, and neither depends on scale:

1. **A reclaim must never break a live artifact.** Deleting a blob an artifact references, or one a push is about to reference, loses data for good.
1. **A delete cannot be undone.** A GC bug does not corrupt a record someone can repair. It destroys bytes.

The GitLab Container Registry is the production precedent.
It moved from offline mark-and-sweep to an [online model](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/container-registry/-/blob/master/docs/spec/gitlab/online-garbage-collection.md): a review queue with a delay, so a re-push can rescue a blob before it goes.
The Artifact Registry keeps that shape.
Its narrower deduplication boundary lets it close what the Container Registry left open: deduplicating instance-wide made the delete-time lock that closes the worst push-versus-GC race too costly there, so that race stayed.

### Goals

1. Reclaim every blob that nothing in its namespace references, without blocking writes.
1. Never delete an object a committed reference points at, or one a push in progress relies on.
1. One mechanism for every format: Maven, npm and Container/OCI, hosted and remote.
1. Operators can halt blob reclamation at once, see the queue, and see which blobs keep failing.

We know GC works when deduplicated storage per namespace drops a review delay after deletes, the queue drains, and no pull ever finds a missing object.

### Non-Goals

1. Deciding which tags, manifests, versions or cached files to keep. Formats, lifecycle, retention and cleanup policies own that, including untagged manifests, which stay retained artifacts.
1. Expiring soft-deleted artifacts, or evicting remote caches by size or age. Those remove references, and GC reclaims what they leave.
1. Finding leaks GC cannot see from the database: an orphaned reference row, or an object with no blob row. The reconciliation service in [ADR-011](011_data_reconciliation.md) owns those.
1. Purging a whole namespace.

## Proposal

GC is online, because it learns a blob is unreferenced from the delete that removed the reference, not by walking storage.
It is deferred, because a reclaim never runs with the delete: a delay, a recheck and a lock close the race with a re-push.
It is per namespace, because deduplication is, so every reference count, lock and reclaim stays inside one namespace and needs no global coordination.

### What must always hold

| # | Constraint | Machine-checkable? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **The reference count is the attachment count.** A blob is reclaimable only when no attachment in its namespace references it. GC keeps no reference tables, computes no reachability and parses no artifact, so a crafted manifest cannot steer it. | Yes: whether a blob is reclaimable depends only on its attachments |
| 2 | **One lock serializes every race.** Every write that adds or removes an attachment, and every reclaim, first locks the blob's row. Writes take blob rows in one fixed order. | Yes: no attachment write or reclaim runs without the blob-row lock |
| 3 | **Only the zero transition captures.** Removing the last attachment records a candidate in the same transaction. A new attachment clears it in the same transaction. A missed capture leaks storage; it never deletes early. | Yes: removing the last attachment records a candidate, and a new attachment clears it |
| 4 | **Review, then recheck.** A candidate waits a review delay of at least one hour. Then cleanup, under the lock, confirms the candidate is still due and rechecks attachments before any delete. | Yes: a review delay under one hour is refused, and no blob is deleted before its candidate's delay ends, or while it has an attachment |
| 5 | **A fresh blob is never reclaimed.** A blob younger than a fixed grace window, measured from its row's creation, is never captured by the backstop scan or deleted by cleanup. The window is not configurable. | Yes: neither the backstop scan nor cleanup takes a blob younger than the grace window, and no setting changes the window |
| 6 | **Storage first, then the row.** Cleanup deletes the object before the blob row, in one transaction. A crash leaves the row and its candidate, and a live candidate tells the next upload to check storage before it trusts the row. | Yes: a crash in cleanup never leaves an object without its blob row, and the next upload then checks storage before it trusts the row |
| 7 | **A deduplicated upload trusts nothing a reclaim may have touched.** When an upload finds an existing blob row with a live candidate, it checks storage again under the lock and clears the candidate at commit. For a fixed window after a timed-out delete, it answers a retryable `503` instead of trusting the object. If the object is gone, it deletes the row under the lock and commits, then uploads as a new blob, so no lock is held across the upload. | Yes: an upload never commits against a blob row whose object is gone, or inside the window after a timed-out delete |
| 8 | **No caller waits without a bound.** A request waits a bounded time for the lock and answers a retryable `503` on timeout or deadlock. Cleanup never waits: it requeues. Every storage call made under the lock is time-bounded. | Yes: a lock wait past its bound, or a deadlock, answers a retryable `503`; cleanup requeues instead of waiting; and a storage call under the lock stops at its bound |
| 9 | **Persistent failure backs off, and nothing is set aside.** Every failed delete, a definite error or a timeout, counts a failure and moves the candidate's next attempt out by a per-candidate backoff that doubles to a daily cap, and cleanup keeps retrying. GC cannot tell an outage from one object nobody can delete, so it treats both the same way. A candidate at ten failures counts as stuck for the status route and an alarm, and a delete-error rate is the fleet-wide signal. | Yes: no failed delete ends a candidate's retries, each failure waits longer than the last up to the cap, and a candidate at ten failures is counted as stuck |
| 10 | **Blob reclamation can be stopped, and starts off.** Configuration turns reclamation on, and it is off by default. Where a flag service exists, a kill-switch flag also halts it without a deploy, and fails closed. The staging sweep is not gated: an expired upload never became a blob, so nothing can rescue it. | Yes: reclamation is off by default, and where a flag service exists, the flag halts it, also when the service does not answer |

### Pros

1. No stop-the-world: GC reclaims continuously and never blocks writes.
1. One lock closes the capture race, the push race and the crash case.
1. One mechanism for every format, with no per-format reference tracking.
1. A wrong delete upstream stays recoverable for the whole review delay.
1. The per-namespace boundary bounds any contention or mistake to one tenant.

### Cons

1. **Space comes back late.** Storage frees a review delay after the delete, so users and operators must be shown pending reclamation.
1. **A lock on the write path.** Two writes that share a blob in one namespace serialize briefly. Its cost under real traffic is unmeasured until production.
1. **Two data-loss paths stay open.** A publish slower than the grace window, with no upload session open in its namespace, can have its fresh blob reclaimed before it attaches. Closing it needs the storage layer to let a format protect a blob until a deadline. The second path: once the window after a timed-out delete closes, a deduplicated upload can trust an object that the delete still removes later.
1. **A blob in constant use is never reclaimed.** If its last reference keeps coming back inside the review delay, it stays. That is intended: it costs one blob's storage and protects the next push.
1. **The backstop scan is the only safety net at launch**, because [ADR-011](011_data_reconciliation.md) defers reconciliation.

## Design and implementation details

### Candidate lifecycle

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Tracked: last attachment removed
    Tracked --> [*]: attachment added again
    Tracked --> Due: review delay elapses
    Due --> [*]: recheck finds an attachment
    Due --> Reclaimed: no attachment, past the grace window
    Due --> Tracked: lock busy, delete failed, or inside the grace window
    Reclaimed --> [*]: object deleted, then the blob row
```

The review queue is its own table, not the job backend's.
The delay has to be re-evaluated against live attachments at dequeue, and the candidate has to outlive any single job attempt to serve as the crash marker.

### Jobs

GC runs as background jobs on the job backend chosen in [ADR-006](006_technology_stack.md):

1. A sweep feeds due candidates to cleanup, oldest first, in bounded batches.
1. Cleanup locks, rechecks and deletes. It is the only job that destroys blob bytes.
1. A low-frequency backstop scan finds zero-attachment blobs older than the grace window that capture missed.
1. A staging sweep deletes the staging objects of expired uploads, which never became blobs.

### Lock order and contention

A delete locks its artifact row, then its blob rows.
A push locks its blob rows first, in ascending digest order, because its artifact row does not exist yet.
The two orders can deadlock; the database aborts one side, and that side answers `503`.
A caller that cannot wait, such as a cache fill that runs after the response, skips its write instead.

### Operations

Operators see GC through queue metrics, lock-wait timing, and an event for every object delete.
Alarms cover a queue that stops draining, a delete-error rate, a rising count of stuck candidates, a reclaim spike, and a halt.
Per-namespace status, with a stuck count, is on the platform-only API, and the runbook query lists stuck candidates by namespace and digest.

### Adoption

1. **Capture only.** Candidates are recorded, the backstop scan runs, and nothing is deleted. Metrics show the re-reference timing.
1. **Recheck and discard.** Cleanup runs end to end except the storage delete.
1. **Delete.** The irreversible delete turns on only once the team has shown that every write path takes the lock and loses no race with cleanup, that cleanup never reclaims a blob inside the grace window, and that the review delay fits observed re-push timing.

## Alternative Solutions

### Do nothing

Storage grows without bound, and users pay for bytes no artifact references.
Rejected: [ADR-010](010_data_retention.md) commits the registry to reclaiming them.

### Offline mark-and-sweep

Walk all storage, mark what live metadata reaches, and delete the rest.
Rejected: it must stop writes or risk deleting a blob a push is about to reference, its cost grows with total storage rather than with churn, and an interrupted sweep cannot resume cleanly.

### Synchronous deletion

Delete the object when its last reference goes.
Rejected: it races a re-push that relies on the object, at any scale.

### Database triggers for capture

Record candidates with triggers on the attachment table.
Rejected: every attachment write already goes through one store, where capture is testable and observable, and a missed capture only leaks.
Revisit if a write path ever bypasses the store.

### Lock the queue row, not the blob row

Keep the write path lock-free, as the Container Registry does.
Rejected: the blob row is the durable invariant, so one lock covers every race; a queue-row lock needs separate answers for the push race and the crash case.

### An advisory or Redis lock on the digest

Rejected: it is an extra acquisition that nothing enforces, an advisory key can collide across digests, and Redis adds a failure domain to an irreversible path.
Revisit if blob-row waits prove to be a bottleneck.

### Delete the row first, the object later

Commit the metadata change, then delete the object out of band, so no transaction holds the lock across a storage call.
Rejected: a crash between the steps leaks an object with no row, which nothing in GC can find.
It is the first option to revisit if the bounded hold hurts write latency.

### Materialized manifest-to-layer edges

Rejected: reachability is not GC's to compute, and reading manifests would let a crafted one influence what GC reclaims.

title: 027 Replicating Registry Data To Orbit
text:
<!-- Design Documents often contain forward-looking statements -->
<!-- vale gitlab.FutureTense = NO -->

## Status

**Proposed.**

## Context

### What Orbit is and why it matters here

Orbit is the GitLab knowledge graph. It stores GitLab entities as nodes and edges so that people and AI agents can ask
questions that cross entities. The graph is built in the
[knowledge-graph repository](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/orbit/knowledge-graph).

The monolith's packages are already in Orbit: `Package`, `HAS_PACKAGE`, `BUILT_BY`, and
`HAS_VULNERABILITY`. Artifact Registry data should follow the same pattern. The work is tracked in
[gitlab#605695](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/605695) and
[epic 22707](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/epics/22707).

### What only the graph can answer

The Artifact Registry API answers questions about its own data. The graph earns its place when a question crosses the
Artifact Registry and the monolith.

**v0 answers**:

- Which projects published into this repository?
- What did this project publish across all Artifact Registry repositories?
- What does the Artifact Registry hold for these monolith projects and groups, in one query, scoped to an
  organization?

**Later answers**, once dependencies and vulnerabilities are in the Artifact Registry graph:

- Which Artifact Registry versions are affected by this vulnerability?
- Which virtual repositories serve a vulnerable version from an upstream?

v0 alone gives limited value. The case for the graph grows with dependencies and vulnerabilities. Orbit's
`HAS_VULNERABILITY` covers monolith packages today, not Artifact Registry versions.

### How data reaches Orbit today

Orbit gets monolith data through Siphon:

1. Siphon reads the monolith Postgres database with logical replication.
1. A Siphon producer publishes the changes to NATS.
1. A Siphon consumer writes them to ClickHouse.
1. The Orbit indexer builds the graph's nodes and edges from those tables.
1. At query time, Rails redacts the results.

Two constraints matter for the Artifact Registry:

- **Siphon sources are monolith databases only.** Siphon replicates the monolith's `main`, `ci`, and `sec` databases,
  and nothing else.
- **Redaction fails closed.** Rails checks every result with `Ability.allowed?`. An unknown type or a missing row is
  denied.

### Why the Artifact Registry does not fit today

| Orbit expects | Artifact Registry has |
| --- | --- |
| A source database inside the monolith (`main`, `ci`, `sec`) | A separate Postgres database ([ADR-006](006_technology_stack.md), [ADR-024](024_infrastructure_delivery.md)) |
| `Int64` ids for nodes and edges | UUIDv7 ids ([ADR-007](007_database_schema.md)). Orbit needs native UUID support. |
| A `traversal_path` on every namespaced row (`org_id/ns/.../`) | No `traversal_path`. Every table carries `namespace_id`. |
| Authorization through `Ability.allowed?` on an ActiveRecord model | Authorization inside the Artifact Registry ([ADR-021](021_authorization.md)) |

Four details sit behind the table:

- **First external producer.** Siphon supports only PostgreSQL. To add a source, we need network connectivity between
  Siphon and the database, a new Siphon producer, and metadata about which tables to pull. The Artifact Registry would
  be the first producer against a database outside the monolith.
- **No organization column.** The Artifact Registry has no organization column. The organization's UUID sits in
  `namespaces.entity_id` when `entity_type = 'organization'` ([ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md)).
- **Opaque roles.** The Artifact Registry stores its roles (Artifact Viewer, Contributor, Manager, Admin) as tuples in
  the auth platform's Relationships API. A GLAZ policy-engine sidecar evaluates them ([ADR-021](021_authorization.md)).
  Rails and Orbit cannot see them. Today every Artifact Registry row would be hidden from every user.
- **No event stream.** The Artifact Registry has no outbox or domain events table. It emits only usage events to
  Snowplow ([ADR-012](012_usage_data_collection.md)).

### The Cells constraint

The GitLab ClickHouse is cell-local. A global service cannot feed a cell-local ClickHouse. The Orbit team confirmed two
points:

- In the short and mid term, a connection to the legacy SaaS instance's ClickHouse is possible. Orbit already indexes
  from that instance. No data flows into that ClickHouse from other cells.
- If the Artifact Registry becomes cell-local, it fits the current Cells and Siphon design.

New environments will be deployed over the next year. Data migrates from the legacy SaaS instance, which eventually
goes away. Whether Orbit itself is cell-local or global is not decided.

## Decision

**Replicate a fixed set of Artifact Registry tables into the legacy SaaS ClickHouse with Siphon CDC. Orbit indexes the
graph from there. Authorization stays in the Artifact Registry.**

### 1. Replicate with Siphon CDC

We add the Artifact Registry Postgres database as a new Siphon source. Siphon reads it with logical replication. The
rows land in the legacy SaaS ClickHouse as `siphon_ar_*` tables. Orbit indexes from those tables, as it does for
monolith tables.

- **Scope**: GitLab.com only, in the near term.
- **Direction**: data flows only from Postgres. Nothing in this path depends on where the Artifact Registry runs.
- **Freshness**: CDC is near-real-time. Freshness equals Siphon lag. We agree on a target with the Orbit team.

This answers the emit-mechanism question in [gitlab#605695](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/605695).
The mechanism is continuous replication, not periodic reconciliation.

### 2. The replicated table list is a contract

The set of replicated tables, and the columns Orbit reads, is a contract between the Artifact Registry and the
Orbit/Siphon teams. The exact v0 list is tracked in
[gitlab#605695](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/605695).

- A schema change to a replicated table needs Orbit/Siphon review.
- The list is versioned with the Artifact Registry migrations.
- A table joins the list only after Orbit agrees to index it.
- The Artifact Registry soft-deletes rows ([ADR-010](010_data_retention.md#soft-delete)). A soft delete replicates as an update,
  not a delete. The node extract must filter soft-deleted rows, and rows under a deleted namespace, or the graph keeps
  them.

### 3. v0 graph model

The domain is `artifact_registry`. v0 covers repositories, packages, versions, upstream links between virtual and
upstream repositories, and a link from versions to the monolith project that published them.

Container images, remote cache tables, files and blobs, and dependencies are out of v0. The exact node and edge names,
and the implementation plan, are tracked in [gitlab#605695](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/605695)
and [epic 22707](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/epics/22707).

This answers the entity and edge question in
[gitlab#605695](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/605695). `gitlab_project_id` is opaque text with no
foreign key, so the link to the monolith project depends on Orbit resolving it to a monolith `Project` node.

### 4. Orbit must support UUID ids natively

Orbit must support UUID node and edge ids natively. This is a requirement, and a dependency on the Orbit team.

- **Hashing is rejected**: we do not hash UUIDs to `Int64`, even for v0. A collision makes one node silently replace
  another, possibly from another organization. Safety would then depend on every query path redacting perfectly.
- **A `bigint` column is rejected**: adding one to the Artifact Registry tables means migrations on the partitioned
  tables and a second id.
- **UUID keys are an Artifact Registry requirement**: see [ADR-007](007_database_schema.md#namespace-id-type) (the
  Namespace ID type section). Every service that leaves the monolith brings UUID keys.

Artifact Registry data cannot land in Orbit until native UUID support exists. Whether it is planned, and when, is an
open question for the Orbit team.

### 5. Graph rows use an org-root path

Graph rows use an org-root `traversal_path` (`<org_id>/`), not global nodes. The org-root path gives a cheap filter
before redaction, so Orbit makes fewer calls to the Artifact Registry.

`traversal_path` encodes `organization_id`
([structure](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/database/clickhouse/clickhouse_table_design_with_siphon/#traversal_path-structure)).
ClickHouse needs a map from the organization UUID to the numeric organization id. Rails holds the namespace UUID row
([gitlab#603023](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/603023)), which could be replicated.

Still open: confirming that Rails grants org-root paths.

### 6. Authorization stays in the Artifact Registry

Orbit does not copy Artifact Registry permissions. Orbit redaction asks the Artifact Registry.

- Redaction gets a non-ActiveRecord branch for Artifact Registry resource types. The branch sends the resource ids to
  the Artifact Registry.
- The branch calls as the end user, with the end user's token ([ADR-020](020_authentication_flow.md)). It never uses a
  service token to assert a user identity. [ADR-021](021_authorization.md) forbids that, and this ADR keeps the rule.
- Redaction needs a new Artifact Registry endpoint. The GLAZ `BatchCheck` contract is internal to the Artifact
  Registry. Today Rails only gets verdicts embedded in namespace-scoped reads, and only for namespaces and
  repositories.
- The new endpoint checks a list of ids, of any type, for one user. It must also hide disabled, suspended, and blocked
  registries.
- Rails never mirrors Artifact Registry roles.
- The branch fails closed. An unknown type, an unreachable Artifact Registry, a timeout, or a missing verdict denies
  the row.

This direction is consistent with the no-callbacks constraint in [ADR-020](020_authentication_flow.md) and
[ADR-021](021_authorization.md). That constraint forbids the Artifact Registry from calling the GitLab instance while
it processes a request. It does not forbid the GitLab instance from calling the Artifact Registry. Redaction is a
GitLab to Artifact Registry call. No new Artifact Registry to GitLab call appears.

This answers the permission question in [gitlab#605695](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/605695).
Enforcement happens at query time, in redaction. The graph layer holds no Artifact Registry permissions.

New node types must also be registered in the EE redaction service, or they return zero rows.

### 7. Go/no-go: authorization latency

If every Orbit answer that touches Artifact Registry data needs a permission call to the Artifact Registry, the graph
could end up as slow as an agent calling the Artifact Registry API directly. It would also have staler data and more
moving parts.

**Gate**: an Orbit query that touches Artifact Registry data, permission check included, must beat the same answer built
from direct Artifact Registry API calls at p95.

- We measure it in the first local spike, before production work.
- We agree on the absolute number with the Orbit team before the spike.

If we miss the gate, we fall back in this order:

1. Filter by the org-root path first, then cache permission verdicts within a request.
1. Replicate role tuples (Alternative 4).
1. Keep Artifact Registry data out of the graph. Agents use the Artifact Registry API.

### 8. Database requirements

The Artifact Registry database needs the following. No `wal_level` or publication configuration exists yet.

- **Logical decoding**: enable it on the Runway CloudSQL instance ([ADR-024](024_infrastructure_delivery.md)).
- **Publication and users**: a publication and Siphon users, following the monolith's Siphon setup
  ([`gitlab:siphon:setup`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/master/lib/tasks/gitlab/siphon/setup.rake)).
- **Network path**: connectivity between the Siphon infrastructure and the database.
- **WAL safeguards**: if Siphon stalls, the replication slot keeps WAL on the instance and can fill the disk. That
  would take the Artifact Registry down. We add three safeguards:
  - Set `max_slot_wal_keep_size` to about 10% of the provisioned disk, as we do for the monolith databases.
  - Enable Siphon
    [emergency mode](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/analytics-section/siphon/#emergency-mode-nats-unavailable). It
    buffers WAL data on object storage when NATS is unavailable, so WAL does not pile up in Postgres.
  - Add a replication slot lag alert.

Partitioned tables replicate without `publish_via_partition_root`, as the Siphon team confirmed for the consumer.
Default replica identity works because every replicated table has a primary key.

### 9. Cells

If the Artifact Registry becomes cell-local, this design holds without a rewrite. Postgres stays the source of truth.
When an organization moves to another cell:

1. The target cell receives INSERTs.
1. The source cell later runs DELETEs.
1. Siphon replicates both.
1. ClickHouse and Orbit follow.

The design is described in the
[Siphon table design doc](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/database/clickhouse/clickhouse_table_design_with_siphon/#working-in-cells-environment).

| Holds | Changes |
| --- | --- |
| The replicated table list and the graph model | Siphon runs one producer per cell instead of one for the legacy instance |
| Postgres as the only source | The ClickHouse target moves from the legacy SaaS instance to cell-local ClickHouse |
| Authorization in the Artifact Registry | Redaction must reach the Artifact Registry in the right cell |
| Org-move behavior (INSERT, then DELETE) | Orbit's own placement (global or cell-local) decides how the graph is queried across cells |

## Consequences

### Positive

1. **Reuses a proven pipeline**: the same Siphon, ClickHouse, and indexer path serves monolith packages.
1. **No Artifact Registry runtime change for data**: replication reads the write-ahead log. No new events or jobs on
   the request path. Authorization needs one new endpoint.
1. **Near-real-time**: CDC gives freshness equal to Siphon lag.
1. **One source of truth for permissions**: the Artifact Registry stays the only place that decides access. No role
   mirror can drift.
1. **Nothing thrown away on the Cells move**: data flows only from Postgres, so the path carries over.
1. **Deletes replicate**: Siphon turns deleted rows into soft rows, so the graph drops purged rows.

### Negative

1. **First external producer**: Siphon has never read a database outside the monolith. The first time needs a sit-down
   with the Orbit team.
1. **Schema coupling**: ClickHouse schema for Siphon tables lives in the monolith today (moving it out is planned).
   Adding a replicated Artifact Registry table, or changing one, needs a matching ClickHouse migration in the
   monolith. This slows Artifact Registry migrations on those tables.
1. **Latency on every Orbit query that touches Artifact Registry nodes**: redaction adds a call to the Artifact
   Registry, made as the end user. The go/no-go gate in Decision 7 limits this risk.
1. **New Artifact Registry load**: Orbit queries become a caller of the new authorization endpoint.
1. **Dependency on the Orbit team**: Artifact Registry data cannot land in Orbit until Orbit supports UUID ids natively.
1. **Infrastructure work**: logical decoding, a publication, a replication user, and network access all need Infra
   work.
1. **GitLab.com only**: self-managed and Dedicated get no Artifact Registry data in Orbit.
1. **A stalled replication slot can fill the database disk**: that would take the Artifact Registry down. The WAL
   safeguards in Decision 8 limit it.

## Alternatives Considered

| Alternative | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| API-based periodic sync | Not chosen |
| Domain-event outbox in the Artifact Registry | Not chosen |
| Reuse Snowplow to Snowflake | Not chosen |
| Replicate role tuples into ClickHouse | Not chosen for v0 |
| Rails mirrors Artifact Registry resources as ActiveRecord models | Not chosen |

### Alternative 1: API-Based Periodic Sync

#### Approach

The Artifact Registry exposes list endpoints. A job on the GitLab side, or in Orbit, calls them on a schedule and
writes the results into the graph.

#### Why Not Chosen

1. **Freshness**: the graph is only as fresh as the poll interval. CDC is near-real-time.
1. **Deletes**: a poll must diff full listings to find removed rows. CDC reports deletes directly.
1. **New code on both sides**: it needs new list endpoints, paging, and a sync job. Siphon already exists.
1. **Load**: scans across namespaces compete with request traffic.

### Alternative 2: Domain-Event Outbox in the Artifact Registry

#### Approach

The Artifact Registry writes an event row in the same transaction as each change. A relay publishes the rows to Orbit.

#### Why Not Chosen

1. **No outbox exists**: the Artifact Registry has no outbox or domain events table. Only usage events go to Snowplow.
1. **New write-path code**: every mutation path would write an event. A missed path means a silent gap in the graph.
1. **Relay needed**: Siphon already reads the write-ahead log. An outbox adds a second change feed for the same data.
1. **Not foreclosed**: if Orbit needs semantic events instead of row changes, an outbox can come later.

### Alternative 3: Reuse Snowplow to Snowflake

#### Approach

Send registry state through the usage-event pipeline from [ADR-012](012_usage_data_collection.md) and build the graph
from the warehouse.

#### Why Not Chosen

1. **Wrong data**: [ADR-012](012_usage_data_collection.md) events describe actions (push, pull, delete). They do not
   describe current state. Orbit needs state and relationships.
1. **Wrong consumer**: the Snowplow pipeline feeds Snowflake for product analytics. Orbit indexes from ClickHouse.
1. **Pseudonymization**: the pipeline pseudonymizes data. The graph needs real identifiers.
1. **Opt-out coverage**: administrators on self-managed and Dedicated can turn Snowplow off, so it would not give full coverage anyway.

### Alternative 4: Replicate Role Tuples into ClickHouse

#### Approach

Replicate the Artifact Registry's role assignments into ClickHouse. Orbit filters rows by those tuples and never calls
the Artifact Registry.

#### Why Not Chosen

1. **Second evaluator**: the tuples live in the auth platform's Relationships API, and GLAZ evaluates them. Orbit
   would need its own evaluator that matches GLAZ exactly.
1. **Drift risk**: a mismatch between the two evaluators is a data leak, not a bug.
1. **Large scope**: it needs a new replication source for the Relationships API and a new filter path in Orbit.
1. **Not foreclosed**: it is the second fallback in the go/no-go gate (Decision 7) if the authorization call is too
   slow.

### Alternative 5: Rails Mirrors Artifact Registry Resources as ActiveRecord Models

#### Approach

Rails keeps a read-only ActiveRecord model for each Artifact Registry resource. The existing redaction service
loads those models and runs `Ability.allowed?`.

#### Why Not Chosen

1. **Duplicated state**: Rails would hold a second copy of the Artifact Registry's data and keep it in sync.
1. **Duplicated permissions**: `Ability.allowed?` would need Artifact Registry roles, which Rails does not hold.
   Mirroring them means mirroring the role tuples (see Alternative 4).
1. **Against the decoupling goal**: [ADR-022](022_namespace_decoupling.md) keeps Rails identifiers out of the
   Artifact Registry. Rails already stores only the namespace UUID, one row per namespace
   ([gitlab#603023](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/603023)).

## Open Questions

1. **Native UUID support in Orbit.** Is it planned, and when? Artifact Registry data cannot land in Orbit until it
   exists. This needs
   the Orbit team.
