Deployments per zone, Service"] hub_haproxy --> ci_images hub_busybox --> ci_images agent_src --> ci_images ci_images --> ar charts --> ops_reg ops_reg --> argocd apps --> argocd argocd --> release ar -.-> release renovate -.-> ci_images renovate -.-> charts renovate -.-> apps classDef new fill:#c8e6c9,stroke:#2e7d32,color:#1b3d1f class release new ``` ### What the chart renders - Per zone: a Deployment, an HPA on CPU and memory, and a PodDisruptionBudget. - Per release: one `LoadBalancer` Service, a PodMonitor, cert-manager Certificates for the hostnames the fleet certificates do not cover, the Reloader annotation that rolls the pods when a mounted Secret changes, and the HTTP error pages. - The agent as a sidecar. Its image tag is a value so Renovate can bump it. - A preStop hook that disables the check frontends, waits for the load balancer health check to notice, then sends `SIGUSR1` for a soft stop. The termination grace period covers `hard-stop-after 30m` (ADR 008). ### Where the config lives The chart accepts the config as one string through `tpl`. The template and its parameters are argocd/apps values. They were ported from the cookbook templates a section at a time and diffed against the VM config. Until the VMs are decommissioned the config exists twice, in the cookbook for the VMs and in argocd/apps for the pods, and a change to one has to be made in the other. A diff of the two rendered configs detects drift. The rendered config is written to a ConfigMap. A checksum annotation on the pod template makes a config change a rolling deploy (ADR 008). The review check is the rendered diff in the MR. A config HAProxy rejects fails the startup probe, and the rollout stops with the old pods still serving. Cloudflare's origin-pull CA is a public CA and a cookbook file today. It ships in the chart and is written to the config ConfigMap. ### What changes in the config for a container - The kernel runs with its defaults, with two exceptions. The VMs set a dozen `net.*` sysctls that date from before Cloudflare was in front. There is no record of what any of them changed. The socket buffer maximums go on the node pool. The listen backlog sysctls (`somaxconn`, `tcp_max_syn_backlog`) are pod sysctls because the pod network namespace default of 1024 caps every listener backlog at 1024 against 50000 on the VMs. Congestion control is not settable on Dataplane V2 clusters, so cubic runs behind Cloudflare instead of BBR. Anything else is added only where `gstg` under load shows a difference. - HAProxy runs as non-root without `daemon` or `chroot`, and binds IPv4 only. The VMs render an IPv6 bind on every port, but they have no global IPv6 address and every backend is IPv4, so those binds see no traffic today. Pages IPv6 is still served by its TCP proxy LB, which connects to the pods over IPv4. - `stats auth` and `stats admin` are removed. The stats port is only reachable inside the cluster, and the agent-check control plane overwrites any admin action at the next check anyway. The registry `peers` section is dropped. The VMs render it with the local node only, so it replicates nothing. - The `check_http`, `check_https`, and `check_ssh` monitor frontends become the readiness probe and the preStop drain target. The kas releases have a new `check_kas` on `nbsrv(kas)`, where the VM's load balancer check looks at `/-/available-http`. - Config from the cookbook that does nothing is dropped. The evidence is in the MR: `tfo` on the binds, which the VMs never negotiated, the unused `stick-table` in the `kas` and `ssh` frontends, and the second stats bind. ### Images ci-images builds three images. They are published to Artifact Registry like the rest of the fleet's images and pulled from there: - `haproxy` wraps the official `haproxy:3.0` image with nothing added. The official image has the prometheus exporter, Lua, and OpenSSL compiled in and ships `socat` for the preStop hook. The pods run the 3.0 LTS branch because the VMs run it, so the platform and the version do not change in one step. 3.0 has the JSON log encoding the request log uses (ADR 006). `init-state` arrived in 3.1, so the startup probe still needs its initial delay (ADR 008). Renovate bumps the tag within 3.0. Moving past 3.2 later means renaming the `ssh` and `kas` frontends: 3.3 rejects a frontend and a backend under one name, and the backend names are in the dashboards and the agent-check keys. The official image is built on Debian with a newer OpenSSL than the PPA build on the VMs. The TLS comparison on `gstg` covers that difference. - `gitlab-haproxy-agent` wraps the image the agent project publishes, so the sidecar also comes from Artifact Registry. It is the same binary as on the VMs. It talks to the Consul client on the same node through the node address instead of `localhost`. - `haproxy-init` is the init container image of the pods. Today it wraps the official `busybox` image with nothing added. The `ci` release uses its `ip` to add the second interface's route (ADR 007). ## Consequences - The cookbook's templates are ported incrementally into argocd/apps values, and the two renderings can be compared line by line while both fleets exist. - Each release has its own config template in its shard values. The backend pools, hostnames, thread count, and resources are environment values. The log formats and Cloudflare ranges are global values. A backend change is one edit for every release. - Pulls never go to Docker Hub or `registry.gitlab.com` at runtime. - The client address handling depends on the pod seeing the real source address: `set-src` from `CF-Connecting-IP` on 80 and 443, and `expect-proxy` on 22 and 8150. `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` on a passthrough NLB provides it. ## Alternatives considered ### Upstream haproxytech/haproxy chart The [haproxytech/haproxy chart](https://github.com/haproxytech/helm-charts/tree/main/haproxy) runs one HAProxy Deployment or DaemonSet from a `config: |` string. It has `includes` for map files, `sidecarContainers`, `initContainers`, `extraVolumes`, HPA or KEDA, a PDB, a `LoadBalancer` Service, and a ServiceMonitor. It accepts the config as a string like ours does. Rejected because the Kubernetes objects it renders do not fit the releases: - It renders one Deployment and one Service that selects that Deployment's pods. The releases need three Deployments, one per zone, behind one Service. - Sidecars are raw container specs pasted into values and repeated per release. There is no image tag Renovate can bump. - It has no preStop drain sequence. Adding one means wrapping the chart in another chart, at which point the wrapper is the chart. ### Official image straight from Docker Hub Nothing has to be built. Rejected because every pull under HPA and node churn would depend on Docker Hub's availability and rate limits, Wiz would not scan the image, and GKE image streaming only works for images in Artifact Registry. Wrapping it means a small Dockerfile and one more image to keep up to date. ### Agent image from its own registry The agent project publishes its own image to `registry.gitlab.com` through goreleaser. It works as is. Rejected because every other workload image comes from Artifact Registry and the argocd/apps values assume that. A wrapper in ci-images follows the pattern.

title: 003 Release Topology
text:
## Status

Accepted, in progress.

## Stakeholders

- Networking and Incident Management: the split and the HPA settings
- Fleet Management: the node pools on the consolidation clusters and the cluster features the releases need
- Delivery, release managers in particular: the canary backends, weights, and `/chatops gitlab run canary` behave the same on pods
- Environments (kas): the separate kas release and the 30 minute grace period

## Context

Each `haproxy-main` VM runs one HAProxy process that serves every
frontend: 80 and 443 for the web, api, and git-https backends, 22 for
ssh, 8150 for kas, and 11443 for clients inside the network. The
frontends differ in three ways:

- Clients: Cloudflare, runner managers, Gitaly, and the job router.
- Load: TLS termination is CPU-bound, ssh passthrough and kas tunnels
  are connection-bound.
- Tolerance for reloads: kas tunnels run up to two hours, and a reload
  older than `hard-stop-after 30m` cuts them.

Two frontends already have a path of their own:

- The internal gateway on 11443 has its own internal load balancer and
  serves Gitaly's API callbacks to Rails. It shares the process with
  public 443.
- ci-gateway on 8989 has its own VMs in the ci-gateway network. In the
  cookbook, `haproxy-ci` is the `main` flavor with `ci-gateway.enabled`
  and origin-pull verification off.

## Decision

One release per protocol group and address. Each release has its own
`LoadBalancer` Service, one Deployment per zone
([ADR 004](004_zone_locality.md)), and a 30 minute termination grace
period. Eight releases per environment.

| Release | Ports | PROXY protocol | Load |
|---|---|---|---|
| `main-http` | 80, 443 | no | TLS, CPU-bound |
| `main-ssh` | 22 (altssh is forwarded to 22) | Spectrum | TCP passthrough, connection-bound |
| `main-kas` | 8150 | Spectrum | long-lived tunnels, connection-bound |
| `main-internal-http` | 80, 443, 11443, internal LB | no | TLS, CPU-bound |
| `main-internal-kas` | 8150, internal LB | no | long-lived tunnels, connection-bound |
| `registry` | 80, 443 | no | TLS, CPU-bound |
| `pages` | 80, 443 | no | TCP passthrough on 443, connection-bound |
| `ci` | 8989, internal LB in the ci-gateway network | no | TLS, CPU-bound |

### Scaling

Each zone Deployment has an HPA on CPU. Memory is not a signal: the
config has `no-memory-trimming` so that `malloc_trim` does not stall
the process at tens of thousands of connections, and RSS therefore
plateaus at the peak instead of following the connection count. If
CPU turns out not to follow load for the connection-bound releases,
the next step is the sessions metric through KEDA (see Alternatives).
Scale-down is slow: a 15 minute stabilization window, then at most 10
percent of the pods every 5 minutes.

`gprd` peaks at about 165k HTTPS requests per second, and the 60
`main` VMs average 94 percent CPU at that peak, about 450 busy cores.
The pods are `nbthread 4` with a 3.4 CPU request, which fits two
pods per `n4d-standard-8` node next to the daemonsets. We can
increase the machine size to fit more pods.

The HPA min and max are set per release. For gprd, the max and the
node pool max are set above the VM capacity.

For `main-http` the traffic share is the http-router feature flag's
rollout percentage, which grows in steps. The min grows with it, with
a factor two as a buffer:

```plaintext
min(VM capacity × rollout percentage × 2, VM capacity)
```

The other releases have no gradual steps. The Spectrum origin list and
the DNS record go from 0 to 50 percent in one step, the pages and
registry address handover from 0 to 100 percent. Their min is set to
the full VM capacity right before the switch. Until then they run with
one pod per zone, enough to check them against the VMs.

Once the pods have served production traffic for a few weeks, the
mins are lowered step by step against the observed utilization.

### Cluster

The pods run on the new regional clusters from the cluster
consolidation
([production-engineering#29065](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/gl-infra/production-engineering/-/work_items/29065)):
`gitlab-36dv2` in `gstg`, `gitlab-3okls` in `gprd`. The existing
regional clusters are on the legacy dataplane, and GKE cannot switch
a cluster to Dataplane V2 in place, which is why the consolidation
created new ones.

GKE cluster requirements:

- **Standard mode**: dedicated node pools, pod sysctls, the node-local
  Consul client
- **Dataplane V2**, **GKE 1.36 or later**, and **L4 ILB subsetting**:
  multi-network `LoadBalancer` Services
  (ADR 007)
- **`externalIPs` allowed on Services** during the pages and registry
  address handover ([ADR 001](001_traffic_cutover.md)), disallowed
  again once the handover is done

### Node pools

- One dedicated node pool per zone, tainted and labelled like the
  other dedicated pools, with a minimum of one node so a node exists in
  every zone before the pods need one. The cluster autoscaler can
  only add a node in the zone of a pinned Deployment's pending pod
  when the pool is zonal.
- GCP stockouts leave some zones short of nodes. A GKE
  `CapacityBuffer` per zone, the size of two HAProxy pods, keeps enough
  slack for the surge pods of a deploy.
- A pool's maximum has to cover the HPA max of every release in the
  zone plus the buffer.
- The machine type is `n4d-standard-8`, two generations newer than
  the VMs' T2D, which is being phased out and has no committed use
  discount and no quota room.
- n4d has been short in us-east1 more than once, and a Deployment
  pinned to a zone cannot scale elsewhere. Each pool has a fallback
  pool on `n4-standard-8` with the same taint and label and zero
  nodes until needed: `haproxy-n4-1` and `haproxy-ci-n4-1`. The
  cluster's default ComputeClass ranks n4d above n4. The fallback is
  used only when n4d is short.
- Machine type is fixed per pool. If `gprd` needs a different one, a
  pool with it is added next to the existing ones.
- The pools use the cluster's pod range. A dedicated secondary range
  for the HAProxy pools would let backend allowlists name a range that
  contains only HAProxy pods instead of the cluster's pod /16, and it
  is immutable on a pool. Not done. Backend allowlists name the
  cluster's range, and a cluster move repeats that work
  ([ADR 001](001_traffic_cutover.md)). The `ci` pods have a second
  address in the pod range of the `ci-gateway` subnet
  (ADR 007).
- The pods have a CPU request and no CPU limit. The HAProxy threads
  can use idle cores on the node.
- The PodDisruptionBudget is `maxUnavailable: 1`, which on a zone with
  one pod lets a node drain evict it. `minAvailable: 1` is open.

## Consequences

- Each release is isolated from the others, where the VMs served
  every frontend from one process. A config change, a rollout, a
  traffic spike, or a scale-down in one release does not touch the
  others. kas pods roll only for their own changes, and the 30 minute
  cutoff for tunnels on a draining process is unchanged. ssh has its
  own replica minimum, which also sets the effective value of its
  per-process session rate limit.
- `main-internal-http` is the `main` config without origin-pull
  verification behind an internal load balancer. Only 11443 has
  traffic. `main-http` serves Cloudflare traffic only, without the
  11443 bind.
- `main-internal-kas` is kas on an internal address without PROXY
  protocol, for the job router's Relay path over Private Service
  Connect. The PSC service attachment still targets the VM fleet's
  internal load balancer in both environments. Moving it is a cutover
  step of its own ([ADR 001](001_traffic_cutover.md)). Once the
  attachment targets the release's forwarding rule, it is a Terraform
  reference to a GKE object that lasts, and the Service is not
  recreated lightly.
- `ci` is the `https_git_ci_gateway` frontend alone, with the api,
  git-https, canary, and packhorse backends and the ci-gateway
  certificate. The VM fleet's load balancers only ever forwarded 8989
  to those hosts. The rest of the `main` config they render receives
  no traffic and is left out. `ci` is its own release because
  it is in the ci-gateway network
  (ADR 007).
- The per-port cutover ([ADR 001](001_traffic_cutover.md)) maps onto
  the releases: each protocol group has its own address, and the
  Spectrum origin switch is per port.
- The cookbook already renders each frontend from its own template, so
  the split follows boundaries the config already has.
- Five Services and addresses for `main` instead of one, and 24
  Deployments per environment instead of one process per VM. kas's
  only backend is one regional ILB and its three Deployments render
  the same server list. It follows the per-zone pattern anyway, and
  every release drains and scales the same way.

## Alternatives considered

### One process per pod, as on the VMs

A direct port: one release per fleet, one Deployment per zone, every
frontend in one process. Fewer objects, and the closest match to what
runs today. Rejected because the frontends' reload tolerance and
scaling signals differ enough that one HPA and one rollout schedule
serve none of them well, and because Gitaly's write path would be in
the same process as public 443.

### kas as one regional Deployment

kas's backend is a single regional ILB. There is no zone ordering to
preserve, and one Deployment with `topologySpreadConstraints` would
do. Rejected because every other release is per zone, and one release
that drains and scales differently is one more thing to know during an
incident.

### An Ingress or Gateway in front of the releases

One Gateway with a route per hostname and port, the releases as its
backends. Rejected because it is a proxy hop in front of HAProxy for
routing HAProxy already does, and the TCP frontends would need
`TCPRoute` with proxy protocol passed through both hops. A
`LoadBalancer` Service per release is the same L4 load balancer
without the hop.

### A dedicated load balancer cluster

A cluster of its own for the load balancers removes the circular
dependency between the pods and the ILBs of the cluster they run in,
which the consolidation creates once canary and kas move onto the same
cluster. Rejected because the dedicated node pools already isolate the
pods from node failures, pool upgrades, and other workloads. A
separate cluster adds isolation from the control plane and the
cluster network only. It protects only the path to the zonal clusters'
backends, since canary and kas are down in that incident either way,
and it is one more cluster to run and upgrade while the fleet is being
consolidated.

### Custom metrics from the start

A KEDA scaler on `haproxy_frontend_current_sessions` for the
connection-bound releases. The clusters run KEDA already.
Rejected because it adds a metrics dependency to the scaling path
before `gprd` has shown that CPU is not enough. If it is not, KEDA is
the next step.

## References

- [GKE custom ComputeClasses](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-custom-compute-classes)
- [GKE capacity buffers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/capacity-buffer)

title: 004 Zone Locality
text:
## Status

Accepted, in progress.

## Stakeholders

- Networking and Incident Management
- Fleet Management: the consolidation clusters decide which of the alternatives becomes possible later

## Context

Each VM sends traffic to the GKE cluster in its own zone and treats
the other two zones as `backup`. The cookbook reads the node's zone
from the GCE metadata and picks the matching server list from the role
JSON. Cross-zone traffic is billed and adds latency. This limits it to
the failover case, and the pods have to do the same.

The application backends are ILBs of three zonal GKE clusters, one per
zone. To the HAProxy pods every backend is an address outside their
cluster, and Kubernetes' own zone-aware routing does not apply. GKE's
L4 controller creates one backend service per Service in one cluster,
and no single backend service spans all three zones either. The
cluster consolidation
([production-engineering#29065](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/gl-infra/production-engineering/-/work_items/29065))
changes both once the application runs on the regional cluster.

## Decision

One Deployment per zone per release. Each is pinned to its zone with
a `nodeSelector` and renders that zone's servers as primary and the
other two as `backup`. Backup edges are shown for zone c only. b and d
have the same.

```mermaid
graph TB
    nlb["passthrough NLB"]
    subgraph zb ["us-east1-b"]
        pb["haproxy Deployment b"]
        gb["GKE cluster b"]
    end
    subgraph zc ["us-east1-c"]
        pc["haproxy Deployment c"]
        gc["GKE cluster c"]
    end
    subgraph zd ["us-east1-d"]
        pd["haproxy Deployment d"]
        gd["GKE cluster d"]
    end
    nlb --> pb
    nlb --> pc
    nlb --> pd
    pb -->|"primary"| gb
    pc -->|"primary"| gc
    pd -->|"primary"| gd
    pc -.->|"backup"| gb
    pc -.->|"backup"| gd
    classDef new fill:#c8e6c9,stroke:#2e7d32,color:#1b3d1f
    class pb,pc,pd new
```

The chart accepts the zone list as a value. A release can be one
Deployment or three without a chart change if the cluster
consolidation makes one of the alternatives below available.

The node pools have a minimum of one node per zone
([ADR 003](003_release_topology.md)) because a soft spread
constraint never scales a pool up from zero: a pod is only Pending
when no existing node has room for it. A hard spread would block a rollout in a
zone with a stockout. Where a spread constraint is used at all, it is
soft.

## Consequences

- This ports the current mechanism and depends only on this
  migration's own chart and values.
- The rendered config is reviewable per zone. A zone is drained by
  scaling one Deployment down, which matches today's zonal drain
  workflow.
- Three Deployments and three HPAs per release instead of one.
- A zone loss is a scale-up on the remaining two zones, with no
  provisioning and no bootstrap, and the dead zone's backends are
  served by the `backup` servers. That is the failure the HAProxy game
  day exists for, and it is no longer a rebuild.

## Alternatives considered

### One Deployment that discovers its zone at startup

An init container reads the zone from the metadata server and renders
the config. One HPA per release, `topologySpreadConstraints` for zone
balance. Rejected because the rendered config is no longer reviewable
per zone, and a zone cannot be drained by scaling one Deployment.

### Regional ILBs with zonal affinity between HAProxy and the backends

GCP's internal passthrough load balancers can prefer backends in the
client's zone and spill over to other zones when the local one is
unhealthy or too small. We already use this in front of `haproxy-ci`
through the `regional-internal-lb-zonal-affinity` module. With one such
ILB per application backend, HAProxy needs one server line per backend
and no primary and backup ordering. The config is then the same
in every zone, and one Deployment per release is enough.

Rejected because it needs one backend service spanning all zones,
which GKE's L4 controller only creates for a Service in one cluster,
and with the application on three zonal clusters there is no such
Service. Once the application runs on the regional cluster, this or
Kubernetes topology-aware routing (below) can replace the per-zone
Deployments with one per release, as a separate decision.

### Kubernetes topology-aware routing

`trafficDistribution: PreferClose` on a Service (or the older
topology-aware hints) sends traffic from a client pod to endpoints in
the same zone and falls back to other zones when there are none.
Rejected because it only works between a pod and a Service in the same
cluster, and HAProxy's backends are ILBs of other clusters.

Once HAProxy and the application share the regional cluster, HAProxy
can target the Services inside the cluster directly and Kubernetes
provides the zone locality, with no ILB hop and no zone ordering in
the HAProxy config. That is the simplest of the four options and the
one to evaluate first, ahead of the zonal-affinity ILBs.

title: 005 Configuration Inputs
text:
## Status Accepted, in progress. ## Stakeholders - Networking and Incident Management - Security (SIRT, anti-abuse): the publish job in `front-end-security` - Fleet Management: Vault paths and External Secrets ## Context HAProxy depends on files besides the rendered config. On VMs, these are: - TLS certificates, issued through SSLMate with the key stored in Vault, where the Certificates Updater renews them. - The Cloudflare origin-pull CA, a cookbook file. - The deny lists from the `front-end-security` repository and the captcha list from the `recaptcha` repository. - The Cloudflare IP ranges, fetched by URL. - Per-incident deny rules and the URI blocklist, inline in chef-repo role JSON. On the VMs, Chef refreshes the clones and the ranges every 30 minutes. The GKE clusters already run External Secrets against Vault and cert-manager with DNS-01 challenges, which the pods can use instead. ## Decision Everything HAProxy reads from disk that is private or changes on its own comes from Vault through External Secrets, mounted as files. Everything else can be defined as chart values in argocd/apps. ```mermaid graph TB fes["front-end-security repo
deny lists, URI blocklist, captcha list"] cf["Cloudflare IP ranges"] ssl["SSLMate certificates"] vault["Vault KV"] eso["External Secrets
refresh every 5 minutes"] secret["Secrets, mounted as files"] values["argocd/apps values"] pod["haproxy pod"] fes -->|"publish job"| vault cf -->|"daily check, then an MR"| values ssl -->|"Certificates Updater"| vault vault --> eso --> secret --> pod values --> pod classDef new fill:#c8e6c9,stroke:#2e7d32,color:#1b3d1f class pod new ``` - Lists: `front-end-security` has every list, with its review flow, including the captcha list and the per-incident deny rules, which moved there. A `publish` job on its default branch writes them to one Vault KV entry, and each release mounts them from there through an External Secret. - Cloudflare ranges: one chart value, rendered into the list files the config reads and into `loadBalancerSourceRanges` on every Service, which a Secret cannot feed. A daily CI job in argocd/apps compares the value with the Cloudflare API and fails when they differ. The fix is an MR. The ranges change rarely and Cloudflare announces additions in advance. - `loadBalancerSourceRanges` is the admission control on 22 and 8150. On the VMs only 443 checks who connects: the firewall is open on 22 and 8150, and `expect-proxy` only determines whether to read a PROXY header. A connection straight to the origin address bypasses Spectrum. That is pre-existing and is raised with the Spectrum owners separately. On the pods only Cloudflare can connect. - Origin-pull CA: a public CA, ships in the chart ([ADR 002](002_chart_and_images.md)). - Certificates: the pods use the same SSLMate certificates as the VMs, read from the same Vault secret through an External Secret. The per-release origin hostnames that exist only for the pods have cert-manager certificates from Let's Encrypt. Moving everything to cert-manager is the follow-up once the VMs are decommissioned. ## Consequences - One delivery mechanism for certificates, credentials, and lists. No extra sidecar images, no deploy tokens in the pods, no `.git` directories on disk. - External Secrets refreshes the Secret every 5 minutes and Reloader then rolls every release, since every release mounts the lists (ADR 008). A merge in `front-end-security` is on the pods within about ten minutes, against a 30 minute converge on the VMs. The geoblock bot merges about weekly. - The list delivery is a prerequisite for a cutover. Until the publish job existed, the `gstg` pods served with empty lists: no deny list, no URI blocklist, and no captcha list. - A pod starting needs only the Secrets, and no access to the ops git mirrors or cloudflare.com. ## Alternatives considered ### git-sync sidecars and an init container git-sync sidecars for the two repositories and an init container fetching the Cloudflare ranges by URL, the direct equivalent of what Chef does. Rejected because it is two more images, deploy tokens in the pods, and a startup dependency on hosts outside the cluster, for the same files. ### cert-manager for the public names during the migration Technically ready: cert-manager with DNS-01 is on the clusters and every name is in a public zone. Rejected for the migration so that both fleets present the same certificate while both are live, and the TLS comparison between them has one variable. ### Lists as chart values argocd/apps is a public repository, while `front-end-security` and chef-repo are private. Rejected because putting the deny lists, the captcha list, or the per-incident rules into values would publish every blocked address, user agent, and path, make every change a rolling deploy, and move the review out of the security team's repository.

title: 006 Observability
text:
## Status Accepted, in progress. ## Stakeholders - Networking and Incident Management - Observability: the `haproxy` service in the metrics catalog, the PodMonitor, the log format and the Cloud Logging sink - Delivery: the `canary up` promotion check - Cloud cost utilization: the `gl_service` and `gl_shard` labels and the feature category model for `haproxy` - The consumers of the HAProxy BigQuery tables ## Context ### Metrics The VMs are scraped through GCE service discovery in the `prometheus-scrape-configs` service, which adds `type=frontend`, `tier=lb`, `stage=main`, `shard=default`, `environment`, and `fqdn` from GCE labels and rewrites the exporter's `proxy` label into `frontend` or `backend` by metric name. The `frontend` service in the metrics catalog and the dashboards select on those labels. ### Logs HAProxy logs to the journal, rsyslog writes `/var/log/haproxy.log`, fluentd tails it, parses each line into fields with a regex, and sends it to Cloud Logging. A Cloud Logging sink from 2018, not in Terraform, exports to the `haproxy_logs` dataset in BigQuery as sharded `haproxy_YYYYMMDD` tables in `gstg` and `gprd`. The logs are in BigQuery only, not in Elasticsearch. GKE workload logging is on. Pod stdout is in Cloud Logging as `k8s_container`. ### Cost attribution The VMs have the GCP label `gl_service=frontend`, and the billing export attributes their cost to it. `frontend` is one of the largest cost lines on GitLab.com, most of it network data transfer out through the peerings. The [cloud cost attribution design](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/cloud_cost_attribution/) splits each `gl_service` further by feature category, from a usage metric declared on the service in the metrics catalog, whose `type` label maps to `gl_service`. The cost team asked for one `gl_service` per release, so that HAProxy for `registry` is attributed with `registry`. ## Decision ### Labels The pods are their own service, `haproxy`, with one shard per release. Their labels are `type=haproxy`, `tier=lb`, `stage=main`, and `shard=` (`main-http`, `main-ssh`, `main-kas`, `main-internal-http`, `main-internal-kas`, `registry`, `pages`, `ci`). The same values go on the pods as `gl_service=haproxy` and `gl_shard=`. `gl_shard` is new. The runner shards in the `ci` environment have it already, and the pod label `shard` arrives in the billing export as `k8s-label/shard` either way. `frontend` remains the service of the VMs until they are decommissioned. The two fleets are told apart by `type`. Both have the same `backend` and `frontend` label values, which lets a panel put them side by side per backend. ### Metrics ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph vm[VM] v1[HAProxy exporter] end subgraph pod[Pod] p1[HAProxy exporter] p2[agent sidecar] end v1 --> sd[GCE service discovery
type=frontend, shard=default
fqdn from GCE labels] p1 --> pm[PodMonitor
type=haproxy, shard=release
pod] p2 --> pm sd --> prom[Mimir] pm --> prom prom --> c1[metrics catalog] prom --> c2[dashboards] prom --> c3[release-tools canary check] ``` The PodMonitor puts the same labels on the pod series as the VM scrape config puts on the VM series, `backend` and `frontend` included. The one difference is the instance label: `pod` instead of `fqdn`. The `haproxy` service in the metrics catalog has the same SLIs as `frontend`, per shard, and tracks the Deployments, HPAs and node pools of the pods. ### Logs ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph vm[VM] v1[HAProxy] -->|syslog| v2[rsyslog
/var/log/haproxy.log] v2 --> v3[fluentd
regex parse] end subgraph pod[Pod] p1[HAProxy
JSON per request] -->|stdout| p2[GKE workload logging] end v3 --> cl[Cloud Logging] p2 --> cl cl -->|sink from 2018| t1[(haproxy_logs.haproxy_YYYYMMDD)] cl -->|sink in Terraform| t2[(haproxy_logs.stdout
partitioned, 30 day expiry)] ``` HAProxy writes one JSON object per request to stdout, with the fields the fluentd regex extracts today plus the request timers, TLS details, and the pod name. A Cloud Logging sink per environment, in Terraform, writes them to a partitioned table in the `haproxy_logs` dataset, next to the VM tables. The logs are not ingested into Elasticsearch, which matches the status quo, chosen mainly for cost reasons. ### Cost attribution GKE cost allocation writes node cost (vCPU, RAM, disk, by resource request) to the billing export with the cluster, namespace, workload name, and every pod label as `k8s-label/`. The fleet's compute cost is one `gl_service=haproxy` line, split per release by `gl_shard`. Network egress is not among the SKUs cost allocation covers. The feature category split of the whole `haproxy` line comes from a usage metric declared on the `haproxy` service, as the cost attribution design describes. The metric is bytes out per backend (`haproxy_backend_bytes_out_total`), which both fleets emit. Which backend maps to which feature category is worked out with the cost team and is not part of this record. ## Consequences ### Labels - The chart sets `type` and `gl_service`, the release's values set `shard` and `gl_shard`. The `gstg` pods change from `type=frontend` to `type=haproxy` when this rolls, and their series move from the `frontend` service to `haproxy`. - Cost allocation data is in the detailed billing export only, from about three days after a label exists, with no backfill. ### Metrics - Stats UI: `kubectl port-forward` to 7331 per pod, same UI, no credentials ([ADR 002](002_chart_and_images.md)). `kubectl exec` with `socat` and `show stat` replaces `ssh` to the node and `hatop`. Manual state changes through the socket are overwritten at the next agent check, as on the VMs. ### Logs - The fluentd regex and the rsyslog step are gone once the VMs are decommissioned. - BigQuery remains the only place to query HAProxy logs. ## Alternatives considered ### Keep the pods in `frontend` The first plan: the pods take the VM label set, `type=frontend` and `shard=default`, and both fleets are one service. Rejected because `frontend` is a confusing name for a load balancer, and the migration is the one chance to change it without renaming a running service. Also the fleets could not be told apart in the catalog. ### One service per release `gl_service` and `type` per release, `haproxy-main-http` and so on, with a catalog entry each, as the cost team first asked. Rejected because that is eight services, eight SLI sets, and eight dashboard sets for one piece of software, and `shard` gives the cost team the same split under one service. ### Ship logs through vector-agent to PubSub The clusters run `vector-agent` with presets that route other containers' logs to PubSub topics and on to Elasticsearch. Adding a `haproxy` preset would put one line per gitlab.com request on that path, which nothing there is sized for. Today's path is Cloud Logging with a BigQuery sink, which pod stdout already feeds. ### Keep the fluentd parsing A fluentd sidecar tailing a shared file and parsing with the existing regex would preserve the BigQuery schema without touching the HAProxy config. Rejected because the regex is fragile and hard to read, and HAProxy can emit the fields itself. This is the chance to drop it. It would also be one more container per pod. ## References - [GKE cost allocation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/cost-allocations)

title: 007 Ci Network Placement
text:
## Status Accepted, in progress. Running in `gstg`, where the pods serve the job VMs' ci-gateway traffic. ## Stakeholders - Networking and Incident Management - Runners Platform: the ci-gateway clients and the runner egress firewall - Fleet Management: multi-networking on the Dataplane V2 cluster and the node pools with a second network ## Context Job VMs in the `gitlab-ci` project fetch git repositories and upload artifacts through `us-east1.ci-gateway.int.gprd.gitlab.net`. That hostname resolves to an ILB in a dedicated `ci-gateway` VPC in `gitlab-production`, which the job VM networks are peered with. The `haproxy-ci` VMs have one interface there and one in the `gprd` VPC, and route between the two. The runner managers do not use ci-gateway any more. They talk to the API and kas through Private Service Connect endpoints ([ADR 001](001_traffic_cutover.md)). ```mermaid graph TB subgraph ci ["gitlab-ci project"] runners["job VMs"] mgr["runner managers"] end subgraph cigw ["ci-gateway VPC (gitlab-production)"] ilb["ci-gateway ILB"] nic2["haproxy-ci VMs
second interface"] end subgraph gprd ["gprd VPC (gitlab-production)"] nic1["haproxy-ci VMs
first interface"] gke["GKE cluster
pods have interfaces here only"] igw["internal gateway ILB"] be["application ILBs"] end runners -->|"VPC peering"| ilb mgr -->|"Private Service Connect"| igw ilb --> nic2 nic2 -.->|"same VM"| nic1 nic1 --> be gke -->|"reachable"| be runners -.-x|"no route: peering is not transitive"| gke classDef old fill:#ffcdd2,stroke:#b71c1c,color:#4a0d0d classDef blocked fill:#bbdefb,stroke:#0d47a1,color:#0b2a4a class nic1,nic2 old class gke blocked ``` The cutover is a DNS change: the hostname gets the pod load balancer's address ([ADR 001](001_traffic_cutover.md)). For that to work, the pod load balancer has to be in a network the job VMs can route to. That is what this record decides. ## Decision The `ci` pods get a second interface in the `ci-gateway` VPC, same as the VMs. This is accomplished through [GKE multi-networking](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/setup-multinetwork-support-for-pods): the `haproxy-ci` node pools have an interface in `ci-gateway`, each pod gets an address from a pod range on that subnet, and a Service on that network gives us an internal load balancer there. The existing hostname points at that load balancer. ```mermaid graph LR subgraph ci ["gitlab-ci project"] jobs["job VMs"] end subgraph cigw ["ci-gateway VPC (gitlab-production)"] fw["firewall
runner ranges"] ilb["ci-gateway ILB (GKE)"] nic2["ci pods
second interface"] end subgraph gprd ["gprd VPC (gitlab-production)"] nic1["ci pods
first interface"] be["application ILBs"] end jobs -->|"VPC peering, as today"| fw fw --> ilb --> nic2 nic2 -.->|"same pod"| nic1 nic1 --> be classDef new fill:#c8e6c9,stroke:#2e7d32,color:#1b3d1f class nic1,nic2 new ``` - The runner networks, their peerings, and the isolation between them and `gprd` are as today. The pods see the runner address, and the frontend's `src` ACLs are unchanged. - The runner egress firewall allows the GKE subnet in `ci-gateway`, next to the VM subnet. - Multi-network Services need Dataplane V2, which the legacy clusters (`gprd-gitlab-gke`) do not have and cannot be switched to. The `ci` release is built on the new cluster of each environment ([ADR 003](003_release_topology.md)). ## Consequences - The chart renders the second interface: pod annotations for the two interfaces, an init container that adds a routing table so traffic from the second pod range leaves through the second interface, and a Service that selects the network. The Service is one internal `LoadBalancer` with `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`, which GKE requires on a secondary network. - The `Network` objects are their own argocd/apps service, one per cluster, and are immutable. A pool's networks are fixed at creation. - The pods have two interfaces and a routing table to reason about in an incident, and a second pod range, on the `ci-gateway` subnet, that backend allowlists have to include next to the cluster pod range ([ADR 001](001_traffic_cutover.md)). - The cutover is a DNS record change, no runner config changes. The legacy zonal ILBs and hostnames are not recreated. The dual-interface VMs and the multi-NIC routing recipe are removed with the VM fleet. - The `ci` release serves the job VMs: git fetches, the job API calls for traces and artifacts, and redirects, as the VM frontend does. ## Alternatives considered ### Peer the runner networks with gprd Peer the ephemeral job VM networks with `gprd` directly, as the `ci` VPC with the runner managers already is, and put the ci-gateway ILB in front of the pods in `gprd`. No second interface, no new GKE feature, and the `ci-gateway` VPC is removed. Rejected because a job VM network can reach one address in `gitlab-production` today, and peered with `gprd` it could route to any internal address there, with a firewall rule as the only boundary. Job VMs run customer code. Whether that is acceptable is a Runners Platform decision, and this migration does not depend on it. ### Peer ci-gateway with gprd Rejected because it does not work: runner VPC to `ci-gateway` is one peering and `ci-gateway` to `gprd` is another, and peering is not transitive. ### A GKE cluster with nodes in the ci-gateway VPC A node pool cannot span VPCs. This is a separate cluster in `ci-gateway`, plus a peering from `ci-gateway` to `gprd` so the pods can reach the application backends. Today's isolation exactly. Rejected because the cluster needs its own Consul access for the agent, monitoring, ArgoCD registration, and node pools, for one release, and it goes against the cluster consolidation. ### Private Service Connect PSC as the way into the `ci-gateway` VPC instead of a second interface: the `ci` release's ILB published as a service attachment, and an internal TCP proxy load balancer in the `ci-gateway` VPC with a PSC NEG as its backend, sending PROXY protocol so the pods see the job VM's address. It works and needs nothing from the runner side. Rejected because PSC and the proxy each charge per GB, and `ci` serves job artifacts and git fetches. The runner managers' PSC endpoints for the API and kas are a different path with far less traffic, and stay. ### Leave haproxy-ci on VMs Nine VMs with one purpose and a narrow interface, which could remain on Chef until the Envoy Gateway migration reaches them. Rejected because the VM fleet would keep its Chef roles, patching, and the multi-NIC routing recipe for one release. ## References - [GKE multi-network support for Pods](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/setup-multinetwork-support-for-pods)

title: Index
text:
## Introduction

In 2023 GitLab launched a new fully managed private solution, [GitLab Dedicated](https://about.gitlab.com/dedicated/), our single tenant
SaaS offering completely managed by GitLab Inc. These internal instances run public GitLab versions limiting the ability to deploy security
fixes before a public disclosure. To guarantee the [safety and availability](/handbook/engineering/development/principles/#prioritizing-technical-decisions)
on single tenant SaaS instances, Delivery has an increasing need to prepare private packages to remediate high-severity issues within [specific SLAs](/handbook/security/product-security/vulnerability-management/sla/).

There is no official release process available to remediate these private instances. Given the [GitLab open core](/handbook/company/stewardship/#business-model)
and public by default nature, GitLab releases were designed to be public from the beginning of time.
In case of a high-severity issue release managers must manually operate the release tooling available to remediate the single tenant SaaS instances
within the remediation SLAs, impacting GitLab customers and the ability to remediate them on time:

* Elevated coordination between release managers and all the stakeholders involved.
* The current release tooling lacks the flexibility to perform simultaneous releases, for example, if a vulnerability is found near the
  monthly release week preparation, a release candidate must be created earlier on the development cycle, renouncing features and bug fixes for the active monthly release.
* Existing release process are not adept to remediate single tenant Saas instances putting at risk their availability and integrity.

![current remediation strategy](/images/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/internal-releases/current_remediation_strategy.png)

## Goal

Introduce an internal release GitLab process focused on releasing private packages targeted to private GitLab SaaS managed instances.
Private packages will contain remediations for the high-severity issues before disclosing them to the general audience. Due to the nature of
[GitLab business model](/handbook/company/stewardship/#business-model) addressing internal releases brings unique
long-term challenges that will be driving Delivery-Releases work during the upcoming quarters:

1. **Understanding the internal release nature**. Introducing a private release on top of the GitLab’s open nature by default
is a unique challenge that starts by understanding the problem, vision, scope, and challenges. The outcome of this first step
is this blueprint that documents the internal release roadmap.
2. **Remove the blocking nature of releases**. Engineering constraints prevent preparing a patch release in the middle of the
monthly release week preparation. Establishing a private release process requires removing this constraint with flexible tooling
to allow simultaneous releases without leaking vulnerabilities before they're disclosed.
3. **Introduce a GitLab Dedicated remediation process into the GitLab release strategy**. GitLab SaaS single tenant instances are
remediated by manually operating the critical patch release process. This involves considerable toil from release management, security and
engineering stakeholders. Internal releases aim to upgrade the GitLab Dedicated remediation process to be at the same level as GitLab.com
and self-managed remediation processes.

![goal](/images/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/internal-releases/goal.png)

## Key terms

* Internal releases: New private release strategy to remediate GitLab SaaS single tenant instances within [specific SLAs](/handbook/security/product-security/vulnerability-management/sla/).
* GitLab SaaS single tenant instances: SaaS instances managed by GitLab, Inc. At the moment limited to [GitLab Dedicated](https://about.gitlab.com/dedicated/).
* High-severity issues: Bugs or security vulnerabilities defined as ~"severity::1" having an impact on [availability](/handbook/product-development/how-we-work/issue-triage/#availability), [functionality](/handbook/product-development/how-we-work/issue-triage/#severity) or [critical for security](/handbook/security/product-security/vulnerability-management/sla/) on GitLab SaaS single tenant instances.
* See [release terminology](/handbook/engineering/releases/#terminology) for additional definitions.

## Goals and non-goals

### Vision

#### Short-term

Align the internal releases effort into the GitLab Delivery strategy. Outline a vision, effort, and an understanding of the
challenges and requirements to embed an internal release process as part of the GitLab releases. We will deliver this by:

* Documenting a blueprint detailing the roadmap and iterative steps to achieve the internal release vision.
  * Epic: https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-com/gl-infra/-/epics/1292

#### Medium-term

Release Managers will kick off an automated process to create a private release version with the relevant fixes required
to remediate GitLab Dedicated without disclosing the vulnerabilities to the public. After the GitLab Dedicated team has
sent an acknowledgement that all instances are upgraded, the publish process is then kicked off. We will deliver this by:

* Designing an internal release process to remediate high-severity issues on GitLab SaaS single tenant instances.
  * Epic: https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-com/gl-infra/-/epics/1201
* Bridging the patch release process to account for the current GitLab Dedicated remediation strategy. This will
  permit the generation of a private package with a different tag from the public patch.
  * Epic: https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-com/gl-infra/-/epics/1373
* Decouple the current auto-deploy strategy. This will transform release tooling into highly flexible tools and
  allow to cleanly separate the private and public parts of this process to ensure GitLab Dedicated is running a patched
  version before any fixes are communicated/released publicly.
  * Epic: https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-com/gl-infra/-/epics/1050.

#### Long-term

An internal release process to remediate high-severity issues on GitLab SaaS single tenant instances is part of the GitLab
release strategy. Release managers will be able to perform an internal release process to remediate high-severity issues
in GitLab SaaS single tenant instances. The outcome of this process will allow GitLab to iteratively deliver fixes to GitLab Dedicated
based on the remediation SLAs or when there is a pressing need (short critical remediation targets).

The internal release process should be automated end-to-end, only paging engineers when manual intervention is required, and it should
remove the blocking nature of GitLab releases: multiple release types should be performed simultaneously.

* Use advanced package deployment strategies to prepare a private package without blocking an existing release process.
* Emitting private packages without disclosing the vulnerabilities to the general audience.
* Enabling the auto-upgrade of Dedicated tenants via Switchboard API.

### Scope

Internal releases are limited to introducing a new release process to SaaS instances managed by GitLab, Inc. At the moment,
this is limited to GitLab Dedicated.

### Out of scope

* Internal releases are not intended to create releases with custom functionalities that diverge from the standard GitLab product offering.
* Internal releases are limited to mitigate critical vulnerabilities or bug fixes that impact the availability of
  GitLab SaaS single tenant instances. Issues with lower severity stick to the [patch release cadence](/handbook/engineering/releases/patch-releases/#patch-release-cadence).
* GitLab.com and GitLab self-managed instances are not considered for internal releases. On these instances,
  auto-deploy, patch and monthly releases remediate bug and vulnerabilities within the [remediation SLAs](/handbook/security/product-security/vulnerability-management/sla/).
* GitLab Cells is not considered for internal releases, subject to change in the future.
* Internal release channels for self-managed customers are not considered on the initial roadmap. Product analysis and validation will be performed on upcoming stages.

## Proposed plan of action

Aside from understanding the internal releases concept and introducing a new internal release strategy, two
main requirements must be addressed:

1. Remove the blocking nature of GitLab releases.
2. Elevate the GitLab Dedicated remediation process to a first-class citizen.

These two requirements can be addressed simultaneously, the work for each will span throughout multiple quarters.

![roadmap](/images/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/internal-releases/roadmap.png)

### Remove the blocking nature of GitLab releases

The mitigation of a high-severity issue on GitLab.com requires a fix to be merged into the GitLab security repository
and deployed to the GitLab production environment. This operation breaks the mirroring between the GitLab canonical and security
repositories impeding the monthly release preparation: Performing a monthly release with an undisclosed security vulnerability
tampers our ability to remediate GitLab Dedicated and GitLab self-managed instances. Due to this limitation, patch and monthly
releases can't be performed simultaneously without leaking the vulnerability to the public.

The auto-deploy strategy must be adapted to be highly flexible allowing the delivery of packages to all GitLab instances without
breaking the mirroring between GitLab repositories and without initiating a patch release. This work will be done in iterations
spanning multiple quarters:

1. **First iteration: Decouple auto-deploy tagging from rollout** - Removes the strong coupling between building packages
   and rolling them out to GitLab.com production environments by establishing two independent processes: one for building packages
   and another for rolling them out. This iteration paves the way for advanced package selection strategies.
2. **Second iteration: Filter and selection of auto-deploy packages** - With the decoupling of the auto-deploy process,
   packages can be configured to be built with specific requirements, for example requiring a minimum SHA in all upcoming packages.
   This ability can be used to guarantee the mitigation of production incidents.
3. **Third iteration: Ability to create custom auto-deploy packages** - The flexibility of auto-deploy should be focused on
   allowing the creation of packages with experimental features (Ruby/Rails upgrades) or with unmerged changes (security fixes)
   preventing the mirroring divergence between GitLab repositories.

### Introduce a GitLab Dedicated remediation process into the GitLab release strategy

Establish a new private release model for GitLab Dedicated and elevate it to the same standard as GitLab.com and self-managed
remediation processes. Considering GitLab open-core nature this is an uncharted territory that will require multiple iterations:

1. **First iteration: Bridge the patch release process to account for GitLab Dedicated remediation strategy** - Adjusts the release
   tooling to generate self-managed packages without interfering with the patch release process.
2. **Second iteration: Introduce an internal release process** - Design and introduce an internal release process to remediate
   GitLab Dedicated instances.
3. **Third iteration: Automate the internal release process end-to-end** - With an established internal release process and
   with the ability to create custom internal packages:
   * The highly flexible auto-deploy process will be used to deploy security fixes without breaking the mirroring between GitLab repositories.
   * The internal release process will guarantee predictability and results, and minimize the human factor from the process. The remediation of high severity
   issues in GitLab Dedicated instances will be automated from start to end by using the Switchboard functionality to perform an auto-upgrade of Dedicated tenants.

title: 001 Unify Kev And Epss As Cve Enrichments
text:
## Context

We are implementing support for KEV data in GitLab.
Initially, we considered storing KEV data separately from EPSS data.
However, after [discussion](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/11912#note_2075459748),
we realized that unifying KEV and EPSS data as CVE
enrichments could provide benefits in terms of performance and simplicity.

The unified approach simplifies data management and querying. By consolidating
KEV and EPSS data into a single table, we create a more efficient structure for
these CVE-based enrichments. This design allows for more efficient DB queries by reducing the
number of joins.

It's important to note that while KEV data includes around 1,000 records, EPSS
data includes around 250,000 records (these numbers will increase over time).
KEV data is limited to a boolean value indicating whether a vulnerability is
known to be exploited.
The small size of this additional boolean field and the relatively small number
of KEV records compared to EPSS records support the decision to combine these
datasets, as it adds minimal overhead to the existing EPSS data structure.

The current EPSS implementation already has a design in place, which we can
leverage and extend for this unified approach. In addition, the API remains
unaffected by these backend changes, maintaining its current structure and
usability.

## Decision

We have decided to:

1. Maintain separate tables for KEV and EPSS data in PMDB.
2. Export both KEV and EPSS data into a single, shared GCP bucket.
3. Implement a single process for syncing and ingesting the unified data into a
   new `pm_cve_enrichments` table in GitLab DB.
4. Structure the `pm_cve_enrichments` table to include:
    - cve_id
    - epss_score (nullable)
    - has_known_exploit (nullable)
5. Use GraphQL queries to access enrichment data exclusively from
   the `pm_cve_enrichments` table.

## Consequences

### Positive

- Enhanced SQL query performance for CVE enrichment data retrieval by storing
  EPSS and KEV in a unified table, requiring only a single join instead of two.
- Reduces the complexity of the data model on the backend.
- Eliminates code duplication by using shared feature flags, sync, ingestion, and
  export processes for both KEV and EPSS data.
- Minimal impact on upsert queries and the [Write Ahead Log](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-intro.html)
  since KEV data is restricted to a single boolean column.

### Negative

- Loss of cursor functionality for KEV, requiring full data export each time due
  to EPSS data always being fully exported.
- One-time performance cost during PMDB's export due to joining KEV and EPSS
  tables.

## Alternatives

1. Store KEV data separately:
    - Advantages:
        - Maintains separation of concerns.
        - Preserves cursor functionality for KEV.
        - Less frequent KEV data updates in GitLab DB (due to smaller dataset
          and less frequent changes compared to EPSS).
        - Reduces the [Write Ahead Log](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-intro.html)
          during the ingestion of KEV data and EPSS data.
    - Disadvantages:
        - GraphQL queries trigger SQL queries that JOIN two tables.
        - Increased complexity in ingestion and synchronizing two separate
          datasets.

2. Denormalize KEV data into vulnerabilities tables:
    - Advantages:
        - Fast access to KEV data when querying vulnerabilities.
    - Disadvantages:
        - Data redundancy.
        - Different approach between EPSS and KEV, leading to inconsistent data
          management.
        - Duplicated ingestion and sync processes.

3. Store KEV data in `pm_advisories`:
    - Advantages:
        - Keeps advisory-related data together.
        - Leverages current exporting, ingestion, and sync processes for
          advisories, lessening the need for new implementations.
    - Disadvantages:
        - Requires joining with advisories for GraphQL querying, which may
          impact performance.
        - May introduce complexity if KEV data needs to be accessed
          independently of advisory data.

title: 001 Http Routing Approach
text:
## Context

As part of LabKit v2 development, we evaluated whether to adopt
[go-chi/chi](https://github.com/go-chi/chi) as the standard HTTP router for
all Go services at GitLab, and whether LabKit should expose a `Router`
interface that abstracts the underlying framework.

The discussion ([team-tasks#4311](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/quality/quality-engineering/team-tasks/-/issues/4311))
was an open discussion where senior technical leaders and Go service maintainers
could raise concerns, suggest alternatives, or approve the direction.

An investigation with benchmarks was conducted in
[team-tasks#4294](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/quality/quality-engineering/team-tasks/-/issues/4294).

## Decision

1. LabKit does not own the routing layer. LabKit v2 provides
   observability middleware (tracing, access logging, correlation IDs, health
   probes) that works with any `net/http`-compatible handler. Services bring
   their own router.

1. No Router interface in LabKit. The original `v2/httpserver.Router`
   interface is removed. Abstracting a router behind a LabKit API adds
   maintenance cost without clear gain. Per
   [Hyrum's Law](https://www.hyrumslaw.com/), consumers will inevitably
   depend on the concrete implementation, making the abstraction difficult to
   honor in practice.

1. Go 1.22+ standard library `ServeMux` is sufficient for most services. Modern
   `ServeMux` supports method-based routing (`GET /path`) and path
   parameters (`/items/{id}`), covering the needs of services with simple
   routing requirements.

1. Chi is recommended when advanced routing is needed. For services
   requiring route grouping, scoped middleware, or sub-router mounting,
   `go-chi/chi` is the recommended choice. It depends only on the standard
   library, uses `http.Handler` throughout, and is already in use at GitLab
   (Container Registry migration, Zoekt indexer).

1. LabKit middleware must compose with any standard library-compatible router.
   Middleware signatures use `func(http.Handler) http.Handler`. This works
   with standard library `ServeMux`, chi, or any other `http.Handler`-compatible
   router.

1. Lab Bench owns higher-level HTTP abstractions. If a structured service
   chassis requires a routing abstraction (for capability analysis,
   convention enforcement, or the three-layer service model), that
   abstraction belongs in Lab Bench, not LabKit.

## Consequences

- Services adopting LabKit v2 are not locked into a specific router. They
  choose the router that fits their complexity level.
- LabKit's API surface is smaller and more stable. Middleware is the
  extension point, not routing.
- Cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, circuit breakers, auth) are
  delivered as middleware that composes with any router, rather than being
  tied to a specific routing framework.
- Services that already use chi (Container Registry, Zoekt) or standard library
  (Workhorse, Runner) do not need to change their routing to adopt LabKit v2
  middleware.
- If a future need arises for a routing abstraction, it can be introduced
  in Lab Bench with full knowledge of the service chassis requirements,
  rather than prematurely in LabKit.

## Alternatives

1. Adopt chi as the default router in LabKit and expose a `Router`
   interface. This was the original proposal in
   [team-tasks#4283](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/quality/quality-engineering/team-tasks/-/issues/4283).
   Rejected because the abstraction adds maintenance cost without clear
   benefit, and Hyrum's Law makes swapping implementations impractical.

1. Mandate chi for all services. Rejected because many services have
   simple routing needs fully served by the standard library, and mandating a dependency
   for services that do not need it conflicts with the
   "minimal API surface" principle.

1. Do nothing. Rejected because the lack of shared middleware leads to
   fragmented observability setups across services, as documented in the
   DX survey results referenced in the
   [LabKit North Star Strategy](../_index.md).

## References

- [Discussion issue: team-tasks#4311](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/quality/quality-engineering/team-tasks/-/issues/4311)
- [Router investigation: team-tasks#4294](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/quality/quality-engineering/team-tasks/-/issues/4294)
- [Lab Bench proposal](https://docs.google.com/document/d/11Zj918LuZeY3fPcU50ZPhzJtcqzvyXaO0SDamW7cDc8/)
- [LabKit North Star Strategy](../_index.md)

title: Alternative Solutions
text:
## Alternative Solutions

### Option 1 - using service accounts

In addition to the current proposal, we also considered the following additional
features:

#### System-generated service accounts

To support internal features and automation, some service accounts will be
created and managed automatically.
These system-generated service accounts differ from user-created service
accounts in terms of control and visibility.

To prevent accidental disruption of application flows, system-generated service
accounts will not be directly manageable by users or admins:

- they cannot be edited, deleted, or modified.
- their membership is automatically managed: the membership is added or removed
  based on the lifecycle of the feature or integration that depends on them.

This protects critical application flows from being broken due to
misconfigurations or malicious actions (eg. removing a necessary system account
from a project).

#### Creation and membership allowlists

Allowlists enable group or instance administrators to define and enforce
boundaries on where service accounts can be created and used.
They can restrict:

- Creation: Define which groups or projects are permitted to create new service
  accounts.
- Membership: Define which groups or projects a service account may be added to
  as a member.

This mechanism helps ensure that service accounts are not unintentionally or
maliciously created, or granted access to unrelated or sensitive parts of the
hierarchy.
It also allows top-level owners to retain control over the footprint of service
accounts created under their domain.

Note: these restrictions apply only to user-created service accounts.
System-generated service accounts can be created regardless of the allowlist to
avoid disrupting internal features and integrations.

#### Downsides

- Introduces 2 implicit types of service accounts (user-created vs
  system-generated).
  This distinction could be made explicit (see Option 2).
- Access model issues persist: while allowlists mitigate them to an extent, they
  don't fully resolve the problem, and increase the risk of misconfiguration.
  If a service account is added to multiple projects, neither the project
  owners, nor the service account owner (top-level group owner) has visibility
  into where it's used or what access it has.
- Allowlists and the 2 implicit types adds significant complexity to both user
  experience and the codebase.

### Option 2 - introduce a simplified user type

Service accounts have introduced significant complexity over time:

- It's a licensed feature
- They support multiple memberships, increasing the potential for accidental
  access sprawl.
- Ownership and membership are decoupled, with ownership limited to creation
  time and lacking visibility into access.
- User experience: administrative overhead

  The current model requires a project owner to go through the following steps:
    1. contact the instance admin and request a service account
    2. instance admin creates a service account
    3. project owner adds the service account as a project member
    4. contact the instance admin again, and request a PAT for the service
       account
    5. instance admin creates the PAT for the service account
    6. instance admin has to securely transfer the token to the project owner as
       this cannot be done in `gitlab-rails`

Option 1 adds further complexity:

- It introduces a distinction between user-created and system-generated service
  accounts.
- It relies on allowlists to partially mitigate the downsides of multiple
  memberships and limited visibility into access.

Since service accounts are already generally available, we cannot change their
behavior without disrupting existing user flows.
Instead:

- Preserve existing service accounts as-is for backward compatibility and as a
  machine identity option for users.
- Introduce a new user type (eg. service user) for all internal machine identity
  use cases, including token consolidation.

This service user would align more closely with the
[original proposal of service accounts](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/284393):

- Available in the `CE`
- Single membership: a service user can only belong to a single group or project
- No distinction between ownership and membership: the namespace that creates
  the service user retains full control.

This approach results in a significantly cleaner access model, avoids the
pitfalls of the existing service account implementation, and provides a
lightweight path forward for automation needs.

Cross-group or cross-project operations would still be supported with this
approach.
They would simply require a separate token for each group / project the service
user needs to access.
If those groups belong to different organizations, cross-organization access
using a single access token wouldn't be possible anyway, due to organization
isolation.

Via introducing breaking changes over time, we could be simplify the existing
service account model and eventually merge the two user types to reduce
maintenance overhead.

#### Downsides

- Builds on 2 user types for machine identity, instead of consolidating under a
  single one.
- Despite the access model being simpler, it introduces some challenges.
  Eg. Amazon Q integration would require adding the service account to the
  top-level group, granting it access to all projects in the hierarchy.

### Option 3 - some combination of 1 & 2

As an example: starting from a defined cutoff date, new memberships for service
accounts cannot be created.
This preserves current access while simplifying future behavior without
introducing a new user type.

title: 001 Tooling Repository Strategy
text:
## Context

The UI Platform team owns shared tooling packages (TypeScript config,
ESLint config, Vitest setup, build helpers, publish scripts) and
standalone utility libraries (`@gitlab/frontend-utils`, `@gitlab/frontend-tests`).
These packages are consumed by the monolith, by LabBench modules that
carry their own MFE, and by MFEs that have no module of their own.

We need to decide where these packages live on the spectrum between:

- **(A) Polyrepo:** each package is its own repository, small and
  self-contained.
- **(B) Monorepo:** a single repository with multiple packages managed
  via workspaces.

This decision is about **tooling packages only**. Where MFE application
code lives is a [separate question](001_tooling_repository_strategy.md#mfe-application-code-open).

### Monorepo pros

- **Atomic cross-package changes.** A change that touches multiple
  packages is one MR, not a chain of releases and Renovate bumps.
- **Shared CI improvements.** Pipeline configuration, caching, and
  tooling upgrades happen once and apply to every package.
- **Shorter feedback loop.** Changing a shared package immediately
  surfaces breakage in downstream packages within the same repo.
- **Less infrastructure.** No Renovate chains between packages, no
  project templates, no per-repo CI duplication.
- **Discoverability.** Contributors find all tooling in one place
  instead of searching across repositories.

### Monorepo cons

- **CI complexity.** Pipelines need change-detection to avoid running
  every package's tests on every MR. Tools like Turborepo and Nx help
  but add their own maintenance cost.
- **Maintainer / CODEOWNERS mismatch.** GitLab project maintainers have
  access to the entire project. CODEOWNERS provides granular approval
  but not granular merge permissions.
- **CODEOWNERS upkeep.** Keeping the CODEOWNERS file correct in a
  multi-package repo is painful and error-prone.
- **Larger agent context.** AI agents need to load more context to
  understand the repo, though this can be mitigated with
  per-package AGENTS.md files.

### Polyrepo pros

- **Clear boundaries.** Each repo has exactly one owner, one pipeline,
  one set of maintainers.
- **Small surface for agents.** The smaller the repo, the cheaper it is
  to get an agent up to speed and the more likely it is to propose
  patterns that match.
- **Fast, focused pipelines.** No change-detection logic needed; every
  push runs the full pipeline and it finishes quickly.
- **No permission sprawl.** Maintainer access is scoped to exactly the
  code that person owns.

### Polyrepo cons

- **Renovate chains.** A change in package A that affects package B
  becomes: release A, Renovate bumps B, release B. Auto-merge reduces
  the cost but the chain remains.
- **CI duplication.** Each repo needs its own pipeline configuration,
  linting setup, and publish workflow.
- **Cross-package testing.** Verifying that a change in one package
  does not break consumers requires multi-project pipelines or manual
  testing.

## Decision

**Tightly coupled tooling packages** (TypeScript config, ESLint config,
Vitest setup, build and publish helpers) go in a **single monorepo**
with pnpm workspaces. These packages have strong interdependencies:
changes frequently span multiple packages, and the cost of Renovate
chains outweighs the CI complexity of a monorepo.

[ADR 004](004_packages_group_and_shared_setup.md#context) amends this: the
tooling configs always change together, so they ship as a single
package, `@gitlab/frontend-config`, with one subpath export per config
instead of a pnpm workspace.

**Standalone utility packages** (`@gitlab/frontend-utils`,
`@gitlab/frontend-tests` etc.) remain in **separate repositories**.
These packages have
minimal dependencies on each other, change independently, and gain
little from co-location. The polyrepo cons (Renovate chains,
cross-package testing) are near zero for these packages.

The dividing line: if a package regularly changes together with other
packages, it belongs in the monorepo. If it changes independently and
has a stable public API consumed by many, it stays standalone.

## Consequences

- The UI Platform team creates a single tooling monorepo under
  `gitlab-org/frontend/` with CODEOWNERS covering each package.
  Superseded by [ADR 004](004_packages_group_and_shared_setup.md#where-do-packages-live):
  `@gitlab/frontend-config` and the standalone packages live in
  `gitlab-org/frontend/toolkit`.
- Standalone packages keep their own repositories under the same group.
- Both the monorepo and standalone repos follow the same versioning and
  publishing conventions (changesets, npm publish, Renovate for
  consumers). [ADR 004](004_packages_group_and_shared_setup.md#how-do-we-publish-packages)
  defines the publishing gate, the release flow and the maintainer model.

---

## MFE application code (open)

Where MFE application code lives is a **separate decision** that has
not been made. The constraints differ from tooling:

- LabBench modules **must** carry their own MFE in the module's
  repository. This is polyrepo by construction and the UI Platform
  team must support it regardless.
- MFEs with no module of their own (Duo Chat, Compliance Center) could
  live in a shared monorepo or in separate repositories.

### Monorepo for MFE apps: pros

- Shared infrastructure (federation config, dev proxy, Storybook) is
  maintained once.
- Cross-MFE changes (shared layout, navigation integration) are atomic.
- The existing
  [`gitlab-mfe`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/frontend/gitlab-mfe)
  repo demonstrates this approach with working CI, Turborepo, and
  Module Federation.

### Monorepo for MFE apps: cons

- The team must support polyrepo anyway (LabBench modules). Maintaining
  both a monorepo and polyrepo developer experience doubles the
  infrastructure work.
- MFE-specific concerns (bundle size, Vue version drift, security
  backports) apply to shipped code, unlike dev-time tooling.
- An MFE that ships with a module changes together with that module's
  backend. Putting it in a separate monorepo adds a cross-repo
  coordination step.

### Polyrepo for MFE apps: pros

- Each MFE is owned and released by the team that owns the surface.
- Aligns with LabBench's module-per-repo model, so the same tooling
  works everywhere.
- Pipelines are scoped to one MFE; no cross-MFE blast radius.

### Polyrepo for MFE apps: cons

- More infrastructure per MFE (CI, federation config, dev proxy).
- Cross-MFE changes require coordinated releases.
- Discoverability: no single place to see all MFEs.

This decision will be revisited once we have more experience with the
first MFE deliveries and a clearer picture of how many surfaces will
not have a LabBench module.

title: 002 Reusable Testing Approach
text:
## Context Every micro-frontend (MFE) application should be testable within the confines of its own package. Most of the current test setup will therefore be shared across apps, and no package should have to rebuild or copy/paste the same testing strategies. At a high level, the three testing levels must be easy to consume from any package: - Unit tests - Integration tests - Browser-driven tests This document proposes a single test package, `@gitlab/frontend-tests`, that holds the shared setup and utilities for every GitLab frontend package. The repository is split into one `src/` directory per test layer, plus a shared `utils/` directory, and offers the bootstrapping and utilities needed to test MFE apps. Proposed structure: ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph repo["gitlab-org/frontend/tests · @gitlab/frontend-tests"] direction LR unit["unit/
shared Rstest config, mount helpers"] integ["integration/
MSW server, fixtures, variants, request capture
(exists today)"] e2e["e2e/ (proposed)
Playwright host page, fixture route helper"] utils["utils/
cross-layer helpers: fixture loading, DOM waiters, matchers"] end unit --> utils integ --> utils e2e --> utils repo -->|"@gitlab/frontend-tests/<layer>"| mono["gitlab monolith"] repo -->|"@gitlab/frontend-tests/<layer>"| mfe["MFEs / LabBench modules"] ``` ### Requirements The test setup itself is only one concern. Each layer must also provide every tool an MFE app needs to be fully tested. MFE applications will no longer have direct access to the GitLab Rails API, so they can become fully isolated, without a meaningful means to keep their tests coherent with the exposed API. The requirements are therefore: 1. Unit, integration and E2E layers are easy to set up for any MFE app. 1. MFE applications can be tested holistically with as little reliance on the GitLab Rails monolith as possible. 1. Semantically meaningful mock data is made accessible. ## Options per layer ### Unit tests #### Tools The monolith currently uses Jest as its test environment, which leverages jsdom. In terms of **config**, however, Jest requires a lot of logic related to Babel transformers. This makes it a poor choice to scale across many MFE applications: each app would need to keep its own list of modules to exclude from the Jest transform, which is time consuming and hard to maintain as dependencies evolve. The proposed solution is to use Rstest for the reusable test setup. Rstest has a Jest-compatible API, so existing test knowledge carries over, and it supports jsdom. With `@rstest/adapter-rspack` it reuses the Rspack config, so build and test share one toolchain. Its Module Federation plugin lets us test MFE compatibility, described in [Module Federation compatibility](#module-federation-compatibility) below. Rstest is still pre-1.0 and less mature than Vitest, and we accept that tradeoff. The Jest configuration for unit tests in the GitLab monolith is mostly (~90%) specific to that project, so we probably do not need to port its setup, aliases, or other tooling to the test package. New applications benefit from a leaner Rstest config from the start. #### New systems One of the biggest foreseeable issues with MFE unit tests is the need to re-define every API mock the consumer cares about, and the potential drift from the defined schema. This has always been the case, but it becomes more apparent (and harder to catch) when living in an external package. A possible solution is a mock data generator in the test package, built in four layers: 1. Get the GraphQL schema from the monolith. 1. Create a map of types to generators for the core types of the schema, such as User, WorkItem, MergeRequest, Pipeline, etc. 1. Use FakerJS to generate the data. 1. Match GraphQL operations to the schema shape to get the right mocks out. The generator only needs a published schema, not the monolith itself. If the GraphQL or REST API later moves to separate backend modules, the download step points at the new publisher and nothing else changes.
