The end result is similar to [proof-of-concept merge request for schema-based mock generation](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/257929), where data is generated from the schema and consumed for the right operation. If the schema changes, the repository can re-generate its mocks quickly, and if tests break as a result, they can be addressed in the same merge request before it ever reaches the monolith. #### How it would work This is roughly what the POC does. The test package has a script that downloads the GraphQL schema from the package that the monolith CI already publishes on every `master` pipeline, so there is no need for a Rails environment. From there, a spec passes its real `.graphql` query to a `generateOperationResponse` helper and gets back a response that matches the query shape, aliases and fragments included. The query is checked against the schema first, so if the schema changed and the query no longer fits, the test fails right there instead of passing with stale data. The values themselves come from FakerJS with a few GitLab rules on top: ids look like `gid://gitlab//`, dates are real dates, enums come from the schema, and fields like `name`, `title` or `webUrl` get something that looks like the real thing. The same query always gets the same data, so tests stay stable. When a spec needs a specific value, it passes an override object shaped like the response, and an override that points to a field that does not exist throws. The data is valid for the schema but it has never been through the backend, so it knows nothing about permissions or licensing. This is why the integration layer keeps using recorded fixtures. Recorded Rails fixtures are also fine in unit tests, and we do not discourage them. They help when a test needs realistic, complex relationships between several entities, such as a merge request with its pipeline and approvals, which a generator would fake independently. The same download script the integration layer uses provides them. #### REST The generator targets GraphQL first because the schema already exists. REST is supported, not discouraged. Options for REST mock data: 1. Reuse the recorded Rails fixtures, with the same download script as the integration layer. This is costly for a simple unit test that needs new data, but cheap when the core fixtures already cover the case. 1. Plain hand-written mocks. Boring, but valid for unit tests and a small burden for a first version. 1. Generate a REST schema from the Rails endpoint helper, which lists every known endpoint, and build a generator on it the same way as for GraphQL. Options 1 and 2 are supported natively in the first iteration. Option 3 only makes sense once there are many REST consumers. #### Open questions - Whether schema-based REST generation (option 3) is worth building. ### Integration tests #### Tools Integration tests are very new and were already built with reuse by different consumers in mind. They use Mock Service Worker (MSW) to intercept API calls and serve fixture data. They currently rely on fixtures generated by Rails, and can keep doing so through a reusable download script that gets the latest fixtures from Rails. One huge advantage of fixtures over the generated mocks proposed for unit tests is that fixtures inherently carry authentication and authorization. Fixtures can be generated for any user role: guest, developer, maintainer, admin, and so on. Each role yields a different payload, so we can test the UI against each one and verify it matches that role's permissions. If permissions change, the test fails with the latest fixture and the regression is caught in time. #### New systems - Ability to download the latest fixtures from Rails, including in CI. This creates a small dependency on the monolith, but it is currently better than using mocks or generating disconnected data. #### Open questions - None at this time. ### Module Federation compatibility #### Tools The Module Federation plugin for Rstest, `@module-federation/rstest`. See the [Rstest 0.12 announcement](https://rstest.rs/blog/announcing-0-12#module-federation). #### How it would work An MFE is built into a bundle that the host (the monolith) loads at runtime. For that to work, the two sides have to agree on a few things: which libraries they share, like Vue and `@gitlab/ui`, and how the host mounts the MFE. If they disagree, the MFE renders nothing, or two copies of Vue end up on the page. Today we only find out in a browser or in production. Rstest has a Module Federation plugin that closes that gap. It lets a jsdom test load the MFE's real built bundle the same way the host would, with the same shared libraries declared. So a plain unit test can import the MFE, mount it, and check that it rendered. No browser needed, and it is fast. We would run it on both sides. In the MFE's pipeline, we build the bundle, download what the monolith expects (shared library versions and the mount contract) from monolith CI output, and run the test against that build. This is the same idea as the GraphQL schema and the Rails fixtures. A broken build or a version mismatch shows up on the MR that caused it, with no monolith checkout. On the monolith side, the same test runs against the published MFE package when we bump its version and on `master`. That catches the monolith changing something the MFE relied on. ```ts // rstest.config.ts import { defineConfig } from '@rstest/core'; import { federation } from '@module-federation/rstest'; export default defineConfig({ testEnvironment: 'jsdom', plugins: [ federation({ remotes: { 'work-items-app': 'work-items-app@https://example.com/remoteEntry.js' }, shared: { vue: { singleton: true }, '@gitlab/ui': { singleton: true } }, }), ], }); // work_items_app.test.ts it('exposes a mount function', async () => { const { mount } = await import('work-items-app/WorkItemsApp'); expect(mount).toBeInstanceOf(Function); }); ``` #### New systems - The monolith publishes what it expects from an MFE (shared library versions and how it mounts one) as a CI artifact, next to the GraphQL schema. - The test package provides a preset that reads that file and sets up the Rstest federation plugin, so an MFE does not write that config by hand. - A CI job on each side: the MFE tests against its own build, and the monolith tests against the latest published package. #### Open questions - Should an MFE MR also trigger a monolith pipeline to test the real thing? It would be the most faithful check, but it costs a full monolith pipeline per MFE MR and ties the two CI setups together. - Which version of the monolith's expectations does an MFE test against: latest `master`, or a tagged version? ### Browser-driven tests #### Tools In the GitLab monolith, we currently use Capybara to run what we call feature tests and E2E tests. Both are "browser-driven" tests (technically [graphical user interface testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphical_user_interface_testing)). MFEs will not have access to the existing Capybara tests, so it makes sense to offer our own solution. The GitLab monolith would still want to test that consuming the package works as intended. The proposed tool is Playwright. #### What a browser layer adds over integration tests Browser-driven tests in the package would replay the same Rails GraphQL fixtures as the integration layer. The data is not the differentiator. What jsdom cannot see is: - Real chunk loading: the federation smoke tests cover the remote entry and shared singletons in jsdom, so the browser adds loading chunks over the network through the browser's own module loader. - Layout: jsdom has no box model, so virtual scroll, sticky headers, overflow and responsive breakpoints go untested. - Browser APIs that jsdom stubs: `IntersectionObserver`, `ResizeObserver`, clipboard, drag and drop, file inputs, focus trapping. - Visual regression and accessibility checks in a real browser. Everything else (Apollo, routing, permission-bound fixtures, user flows) the integration layer already covers, and faster. A browser layer in the package is therefore best scoped as a smoke layer: load the built bundle in a real browser, mount it, render, run axe. Apps that need real layout or browser APIs opt in to more. #### How it would work Playwright intercepts the API in the browser with `page.route`, the same way MSW does in jsdom. The fixture utilities (`loadFixturesMap`, `matchFixture`, variants) are plain TypeScript and run in the Node side of Playwright, so they are reused as-is; only the MSW-bound `buildHandlers` and `createServer` are replaced. ```ts import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test'; import { loadFixturesMap, getActiveVariant } from '@gitlab/frontend-tests/integration'; const fixtures = loadFixturesMap('./tmp/fixtures/graphql'); test('renders work item list', async ({ page }) => { await page.route('**/api/graphql', async (route) => { const { operationName } = route.request().postDataJSON(); const fixture = getActiveVariant(operationName) ?? fixtures[operationName]; if (!fixture) return route.fulfill({ status: 400 }); await route.fulfill({ json: fixture }); }); await page.goto('/host.html?remote=/dist/remoteEntry.js&module=./WorkItemsApp'); await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Work items' })).toBeVisible(); }); ``` `host.html` is a static page shipped by the package: a mount element, the base `@gitlab/ui` CSS, and a script that loads the federation remote and calls its mount function with the injected config. It implements the host mount contract (mount element, injected config, emitted events, shared dependencies, base CSS) that the monolith and LabBench modules also implement. #### New systems 1. A host page to mount MFE apps on, plus a Playwright fixture that wires `page.route` to the downloaded Rails fixtures. 1. Possibly a GitLab skeleton generated from an existing contract. #### Open questions **Should browser-driven tests live in the package at all?** The alternative is to rely on the integration layer alone and let the host own browser-based testing. The case for the package is the list above (bundle, layout, browser APIs) and the fact that LabBench modules have no Capybara, so for them the package is the only place a browser test can live. The case against is one more layer to maintain for data the integration layer already exercises. **What does the MFE mount on?** Options: 1. An empty host page implementing the mount contract, where we only test our application. 1. A shell of the GitLab monolith that contains navigation and a few skeleton elements, to smoke test the integration. 1. A full GitLab page pulled or generated from the CI output of the repository. Option 1 is probably enough to start. Anything more and we risk adding too much tooling early on. The GitLab monolith can retain the responsibility to test how the packages work together. ## How a package consumes it A package adds `@gitlab/frontend-tests` as a devDependency and wires each layer the same way the other shared configs are wired in [ADR 004](004_packages_group_and_shared_setup.md#how-do-we-keep-packages-in-sync): import the base, spread it, override locally. Nothing from the test setup is copied into the package. ```json { "scripts": { "test": "rstest", "fixtures:download": "frontend-tests fixtures download", "test:integration": "rstest -c rstest.integration.config.ts", "test:e2e": "playwright test" }, "devDependencies": { "@gitlab/frontend-tests": "^2.0.0" } } ``` ```ts // rstest.config.ts import { defineConfig } from '@rstest/core'; import base from '@gitlab/frontend-tests/unit'; export default defineConfig({ ...base, include: ['src/**/*.spec.ts'], }); ``` ```ts // rstest.integration.config.ts import { defineConfig } from '@rstest/core'; import base from '@gitlab/frontend-tests/integration'; export default defineConfig({ ...base, include: ['spec/integration/**/*.spec.ts'], setupFiles: [...base.setupFiles, './spec/integration/setup.ts'], }); ``` `@gitlab/frontend-tests/unit` carries the jsdom environment, the Rspack adapter and the mount helpers. `@gitlab/frontend-tests/integration` adds a setup file that starts the MSW server from the fixtures under `tmp/fixtures/`, which `fixtures:download` fills from the latest monolith `master` pipeline. The download is a separate script on purpose. Locally it runs once and `test:integration` is then fast and offline; the setup file fails fast with a message naming the script when `tmp/fixtures/` is missing, and deleting the directory forces a refresh. In CI, `ci/base.yml` always runs `fixtures:download` before `test:integration`, so every pipeline tests against the latest fixtures and catches API drift. The script does not skip when fixtures exist: stale fixtures passing silently is worse than an explicit refresh. A spec then imports from the layer as shown in the sections above, for example `getActiveVariant` and `loadFixturesMap` from `@gitlab/frontend-tests/integration`. `new-gitlab-module` from ADR 004 writes these three files when it creates a package, and `ci/base.yml` from `@gitlab/frontend-config` runs `test` and `fixtures:download && test:integration` as separate jobs. ## Decision 1. Use Rstest as the unit test environment and provide a shared Rstest config to import. 1. Have the test package provide a mock data generator based on the GraphQL schema. 1. Smoke test Module Federation compatibility on both sides with Rstest: the MFE against its own build and the host against the published package, importing each MFE's exposed module through its real built remote entry in jsdom. 1. Keep MSW for integration tests and add a reusable script to download the latest Rails fixtures. 1. Treat the integration layer as the primary layer for MFE behaviour. 1. Use Playwright for browser-driven tests, if the package offers them. **Open**: schema-based REST generation; whether an MFE MR should trigger a monolith pipeline; which version of the monolith's expectations an MFE tests against; whether browser-driven tests belong in the package; what the MFE mounts on. ## Consequences - The `gitlab-org/frontend/tests` repository gains `unit/`, `utils/` and possibly `e2e/` next to the existing `integration/`. - The repository moves to `gitlab-org/frontend/toolkit` and consumes `@gitlab/frontend-config` for its CI, ESLint and TSConfig setup, see [ADR 004](004_packages_group_and_shared_setup.md#migrating-the-existing-packages). The npm package name does not change. - Each layer is published as a subpath, `@gitlab/frontend-tests/`, and consumed by the monolith, MFEs and LabBench modules alike. - The test package takes a build-time dependency on the monolith for the GraphQL schema, the Rails fixtures, and the host contract, including in CI. - The host (monolith, LabBench module) keeps one browser smoke test per MFE against the published package.

title: 003 Module Carried Packaging And Serving
text:
## Context

The [design document](../_index.md) lists one goal the first two ADRs do not
touch: a LabBench module, a separately deployed service, needs a standard way
to put UI into the GitLab shell. Today each module would invent its own
integration. The marketplace that will later distribute standalone MFEs is
itself such a module, so whatever we decide has to work before any marketplace
or registry exists.

This ADR records the decisions validated by the first end-to-end
module-carried MFE on a Caproni rig. A module built with `bench` contains a
Vue application and an API. GitLab finds the application, puts it in the
Admin sidebar and in a page slot, serves it through its own origin, and in
development reloads it from the module's dev server. GitLab did not change
for the application.

Implementation and discussion:

- Validation issue with the demo video and the known problems:
  [work item 634099](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/634099)
- GitLab side: [merge request 262539](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/262539)
- Module side (`bench`): [merge request 192](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/lab-bench/bench/-/merge_requests/192)
- Reference module: [bench-mfe-demo](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/frontend/playground/bench-mfe-demo)

### Constraints

- **No module discovery.** The monolith cannot discover deployed modules.
  The list of sources is monolith configuration, and the design must work
  with nothing but that list.
- **No single domain yet.** Until GATE delivers routing, the browser may
  only reach what the monolith can serve or proxy. Sources may be
  cluster-internal.
- **No registry.** The marketplace is a module that has not shipped. The
  protocol must let a module appear without a prior registration step,
  otherwise the marketplace cannot bootstrap itself.
- **Module-owned release cycle.** A module and its UI release together,
  from the module's repository. ADR 001 already treats this as polyrepo by
  construction.

## Decisions

### 1. One source protocol for every surface

Every MFE source, whether a LabBench module, the future marketplace, or a
static directory, serves the same three things:

- `/-/mfe/index.json`: the applications the source carries, each with its
  version, manifest path, and manifest SHA-256.
- `/-/mfe/<app>/<version>/gitlab-mfe-manifest.json`: the sidecar manifest
  (schema 1) with the entry file, the files with their digests, and the
  placement block.
- `/-/mfe/<app>/<version>/*`: the files. A version's files never change.

The protocol is the integration surface. Anything that serves these paths is
a source, so a pure static source works for everything except an API proxy.
This is also what lets the monolith test the mechanism against a fixture
source instead of a running module (decision 5).

**Alternative not taken:** a registry that must know an application before
GitLab shows it. It adds a service between a module and its UI, and it
cannot host the marketplace, which has to appear first.

**Deliberately open:** the exact manifest fields beyond what the JSON schema
in the monolith requires today. The LabBench `Assembly.ui` field is recorded
separately as an LB-D in LabBench.

### 2. Catalog in the monolith, pull model

`mfe.sources` in `gitlab.yml` lists the sources. The catalog reads each
source's index, validates each manifest against the JSON schema, verifies the
manifest's digest, and caches manifests by digest. The merged list is cached
briefly and rebuilt on read.

**Alternative not taken:** modules push their registration into GitLab, or a
sources table in the database. Both need a registration step that does not
exist yet. Either may replace the pull model once module discovery lands in
the monolith; that is outside this platform's scope, and the manifest
protocol does not change when it does.

**Known shortcut:** the demo refreshes the catalog inside a web request with a
one-minute TTL and a five-second timeout per source. A slow or stopped source
stalls a page once a minute. Refresh moves to a Sidekiq cron before any
non-demo use; see Consequences.

### 3. Delivery through the GitLab origin

Workhorse serves `/-/mfe/<app>/<version>/*` and `/-/mfe/<app>/api/*` with
`send_url` from the source the catalog resolved. The browser speaks only to
GitLab. A module can stay inside the cluster network, and the CSP does not
grow per module.

**Alternative not taken:** the browser loads files from the module with
CORS, or delivery through GitLab Pages. Both expose the module's origin to
the browser and need per-module CSP and network reachability.

GATE may later provide the same property at the routing layer. If it does,
this decision is replaced at the edge and nothing above Workhorse changes.

### 4. The module declares its placement; the monolith owns the vocabulary

The `gitlabMfe.placement` block in the UI's `package.json` has `navigation`,
`routes`, and `slots`. The build copies it into the manifest. GitLab reads it
from the manifest and contains no application name in its code.

The split of responsibility is:

- **The monolith owns the vocabulary.** Which panels exist (`admin` today),
  which slots exist (`dashboard_top` today), which permissions an entry may
  require (`admin` today). A page reserves a slot with `= mfe_slot('name')`.
  A manifest can only name spots the monolith has published.
- **The module declares its claim.** Which panel entries it adds, which
  slots it fills, and which expose mounts where.
- **The monolith arbitrates.** A reserved list in the monolith names the
  spots that first-party surfaces own (a route, a slot, a sidebar
  `item_id`). A manifest entry that lands on a reserved spot is dropped with
  a warning, and the registered application renders. On open spots, source
  order in `mfe.sources` wins, and every collision is logged and counted.
  Silent precedence is not acceptable.

The reserved list and the collision metric are not in the demo. They are the
first follow-up on the monolith side; see Consequences.

**Why the module declares.** When someone installs a module they expect it to
appear at a predictable place without a monolith release. Jira extension
modules, VS Code `contributes.menus`, and Backstage plugins all have the
extension name the host's public contribution points, and the host owns the
set of points and arbitrates. Without this, the marketplace cannot add its
own Admin entry, and each new module waits on a monolith MR to be visible.

**Alternative not taken:** placement configuration in GitLab for each
application. It gives the consumer a central map of what mounts where, which
is easier to read and to test, and it is the right model for first-party
surfaces that must never be displaced. That is what the reserved list keeps.
As the only model it breaks the marketplace bootstrap and reintroduces a
monolith MR per module.

### 5. Testing ownership follows the protocol

Monolith specs never depend on a live module. The monolith tests the
mechanism against a fixture source that serves a static index and manifest:
an application that declares slot X mounts in slot X, a reserved spot is
protected, a collision is logged. A module tests its manifest against the
published JSON schema as a contract test in its own pipeline. A first-party
application that must be present is listed in the monolith's reserved list,
and its absence fails loudly there.

This keeps a change in a module repository from breaking the monolith's
`master`, which was the main objection to module-declared placement. It is
consistent with ADR 002, which already has each side test against the
other's published contract rather than a checkout.

### 6. One application, several exposes

An application exposes `./App`, `./DashboardWidget`, and other entry points.
The manifest places each expose. A navigation entry can name its expose; the
default is `./App`. Rule: one application per thing that is operated and
versioned independently.

**Alternative not taken:** one application per placement. It multiplies
versions and manifests for things that always ship together.

### 7. Mount contract and shared runtime

Each expose exports `mount(el, props)` and `unmount(el)`. One Module
Federation runtime serves all applications on a page. GitLab builds the
injected clients from its own instances, so an application neither imports
GitLab internals nor builds its own HTTP client.

**Open:** what the host injects, and whether an application declares what it
needs. The demo passes an `axios` instance bound to the application's API
proxy as a placeholder. The concern on record is that "the shell gives
everything, the application takes what it needs" repeats the growth of HAML
data attributes. The preferred direction is that the manifest, which is
already the declaration surface, lists the clients an application requires,
and the host instantiates lazily. The first contract is fixed in a later ADR
once a second consumer exists.

### 8. CSS isolation with a selector prefix

The build prefixes each selector with `.mfe-<app>`. `:root`, `html`, and
`body` become that class. The host adds the class to the mount element.
`@keyframes` names stay global. Styles an application adds at run time are
not isolated.

Monolith styles still reach into an application. The mitigation is to keep
reducing global selectors at the monolith level, which the Frontend
Decomposition work already pursues, rather than build a second mechanism at
the MFE level. A reset at the `.mfe-<app>` boundary is a possible partial
mitigation and is not adopted here.

**Alternative not taken:** `@scope`, which is not Baseline before mid-2028
on the browsers GitLab supports. Shadow DOM was not examined; it isolates
styles fully but cuts off `@gitlab/ui` global styles and complicates focus
and portal behaviour.

### 9. Trust model

A module-carried application has the trust of its module. It is first-party
JavaScript on the GitLab origin. Each user who can reach the proxy can call
the module's API, so authorization is the module's responsibility behind
that proxy.

The digests in the manifest are verified for the manifest itself and are
used as cache keys for files. GitLab does not compare the bytes Workhorse
streams with the digests listed in the manifest. This is a deliberate
scoping, not an oversight: a source is instance-operator configuration, and
integrity checking of module bytes against a module-published digest adds no
trust. Readers should not assume subresource integrity exists on this path.

## Consequences

- A LabBench module gains a UI unit through `bench ui create`, and
  `bench build` writes the sidecar manifest and embeds `dist/` into the
  binary, which serves the source protocol. Only Go assemblies serve files
  today.
- The monolith gains the catalog, the Workhorse routes, the host runtime,
  `mfe_slot`, and a per-panel menu that reads the catalog. All behind the
  existing `mfe_enabled` kill switch.
- Follow-ups on the monolith side, in order: catalog refresh in a Sidekiq
  cron; the reserved list and collision metric from decision 4; the fixture
  source and the specs from decision 5; application names prefixed by module
  name to remove cross-source name collisions; a short overlap where a module
  keeps serving its previous version so a release does not 404 for one
  catalog TTL.
- Follow-ups on the module side: `bench build` rebuilds the UI on content
  change rather than on a version bump, and writes the one version into the
  manifest, the index, and the binary.
- Development reload depends on an external tool (portless) and its route
  file. GitLab reads it only in development, and when it is absent GitLab
  loads the deployed application. This dependency is accepted until a
  replacement needs no per-developer configuration either.
- The LabBench `Assembly.ui` schema field is recorded as an LB-D with GitLab
  as the named consumer.
- A later ADR fixes the mount contract (decision 7) and the shared-module
  strategy; the demo ships a Vue 3 per application on purpose.

title: .gitlab-ci.yml
text:
## Context

As we start working on modularity, the polyrepo approach to smaller repositories can give us great speed, but it is essential that there are tools and guardrails in place to make sure that all of our packages stay aligned and require minimal maintenance in the longer run.

Based on the decision in [ADR-001](./001_tooling_repository_strategy.md#decision), it is already agreed that standalone utils packages are polyrepos, where each one gets to be more or less independent from others, while tooling packages that have tight dependencies would live in a single package, such as eslint, TSconfig, CI config helpers, etc.

This ADR aims to clarify these packages, where they live, how they are created, how they remain discoverable and how they are maintained.

ADR-001 called the tightly coupled tooling a pnpm workspace. Since those configs always change together, we make them one package instead, `@gitlab/frontend-config`, with a subpath per config (`@gitlab/frontend-config/eslint`, `@gitlab/frontend-config/tsconfig`) and the CI templates under `ci/`. One version then serves both the npm dependency and the CI `include`, see [How do we keep packages in sync?](#how-do-we-keep-packages-in-sync). We looked at separate `@gitlab/eslint-config`, `@gitlab/tsconfig` and `@gitlab/ci-templates` packages, but three bumps per consumer is not worth it. If we ever need independent versions, the subpaths can become workspace packages later.

## Package lifecycle

The flow below is the whole ADR in one picture, from creating a package to consuming it. Each step is detailed in its own section.

```mermaid
%%{init: {"flowchart": {"curve": "linear"}}}%%
flowchart TB
    settings([Toolkit group settings]) --> project
    config([Configs from toolkit/config]) --> project
    group[Toolkit group] --> create{Run new-gitlab-module}
    create --> project[Project C]
    project --> mr[First merge request]
    mr --> merge{UI Platform or project Maintainers merge}
    mr --> blocked{Policy blocks the merge}
    blocked --> fix[Get the required approval]
    fix --> mr
    merge --> request[New package request in the toolkit group]
    request --> trust{npm maintainers trust the package}
    request --> deny{Request denied}
    deny --> why[Clear explanation with next steps]
    trust --> tag{Maintainer tags vX.Y.Z}
    tag --> publish[CI publishes]
    publish --> pkgC[Package C]
    pkgC --> consume{Consumed by other projects}

    consume --> pkgB[Package B]
    consume --> unused{No consumer left}
    unused --> retire[Retire the package]
    configRelease[New toolkit/config release] --> renovate{Renovate opens a bump MR in each consumer}

    renovate --> pkgB
    renovate --> pkgC

    style unused stroke:#dd2b0e,color:#dd2b0e
    style retire stroke:#dd2b0e,color:#dd2b0e
```

## Where do packages live?

We want a central group that holds all of the packages that we consider are reusable. The first two packages that were created ended up in `gitlab-org/frontend/` which is a good landing place, but it lacks the single purpose. A lot of projects in this group are not related to our new UI platform effort, and so it becomes noisy as we cannot have a single spot to see all packages.

### Decisions

1. Create a new group called `gitlab-org/frontend/toolkit` (we avoided `packages` as a name because, like `utils`, it invites everything in).
1. Migrate both `@gitlab/frontend-utils` and `@gitlab/frontend-tests` to this new group.
1. Create a new project `gitlab-org/frontend/toolkit/config` that publishes `@gitlab/frontend-config` and holds the shared setup. Projects in the group are named after what they publish (`tests`, `utils`), so `config`, even though it also ships the CI template and the bootstrap script.
1. Add a clear description to the group that new projects added here are intended to become reusable packages.
1. Ensure that these packages still ship to our npm registry.

### Migrating the existing packages

We transfer `@gitlab/frontend-utils` and `@gitlab/frontend-tests` as projects, so history, issues and MRs come along. For each package:

1. Transfer the project to `gitlab-org/frontend/toolkit` from its general settings. GitLab redirects the old path as long as nothing else claims it.
1. Update the trusted publisher on npmjs to the new project path, otherwise the next release fails.
1. Check that the group settings from [What rules does this group need?](#what-rules-does-this-group-need) are inherited and that no leftover project-level settings conflict with them.
1. Replace any CI `include` or link that uses the old path, then cut a release to confirm publishing works.

The npm package names do not change, so consumers are not affected.

## What rules does this group need?

There are common settings that all packages should inherit. New package authors should not have to check them, and they should not be able to turn them off when convenient: no self-approval, required reviews, no push to `main`. Nobody should have to read documentation to find the right configuration for their package. Nobody should be able to create 100k lines of code, merge them unreviewed, then enable our standards after the fact in the name of speed or iteration.

### Decisions

GitLab can push settings from the group down to every project, including future ones. We use four layers.

1. Group settings that projects cannot override.
   - A group-level protected branch on `main`: nobody can push, Maintainers can merge, code owner approval required.
   - Group push rules: reject unsigned commits and require the commit author to be a GitLab user.
   - Default branch protection set to fully protected so new projects start right.
   - Merge request approval settings only exist on top-level groups, so the policy below handles those.
1. A security policy project, `toolkit/security-policies`, with one merge request approval policy for every MR in every project: one Maintainer approval, no approving your own MR or commits, approvals reset on new commits, no pushing to or editing protected branches. Projects cannot turn it off. Which Maintainers count is up to each package's CODEOWNERS, see [How do we define maintainers?](#how-do-we-define-maintainers).
1. A compliance framework `frontend-compliance` applied by default to every project in the group. The Compliance Center then shows each project and whether it still follows the rules above.
1. The bootstrap script for the rest. Protected tags `v*` are project-level, so `new-gitlab-module` sets them when it creates the project. A scheduled job in the tooling project compares every project against this baseline and opens an issue when something drifted.

We cannot stop someone from importing an existing repository with its history. What we can do is make `main` protected the moment it lands, require the policy approval on every change after that, and only publish once the request in [How do we publish packages?](#how-do-we-publish-packages) is approved, which is when someone actually looks at what came in.

### Considered and rejected

A pipeline execution policy that injects `ci/base.yml` into every pipeline in the group. It would guarantee the base jobs run even if a project removes the include, but it pins one `ref` for the whole group, and we want each package to bump when it makes sense to them. CODEOWNERS on `.gitlab-ci.yml` already makes removing the include a reviewed change.

## How do we create new packages?

It should be possible to bootstrap a new package quickly without relying solely on AI to scaffold. Ideally, we would want the developer experience to look something like this:

1. Developer needs to create a new reusable package.
1. They run `npx new-gitlab-module`.
1. This script asks a few questions through a TUI such as package name, purpose, stack, etc.
1. The script is dynamically loading its configuration from the `@gitlab/frontend-config` package with latest Eslint, TSConfig, CI, etc
1. The repository is created with `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `eslint.config.js` and `tsconfig.json` already wired to `include` and `extends` the `@gitlab/frontend-config` base, see [How do we keep packages in sync?](#how-do-we-keep-packages-in-sync)

This way, creating a new package is trivial and controlled through the TUI setup. As we add package defaults, these options appear in the TUI.

It is a Node script in `@gitlab/frontend-config`, run with `npx`, so there is nothing else to install. On top of rendering the files it creates the project in the group and sets the protected `v*` tags, see [What rules does this group need?](#what-rules-does-this-group-need).

LabBench modules use `copier`, a Python templating tool, for scaffolding. We are not reusing it for the frontend part: it would bring Python into every package and pipeline, and its update feature is the copy-and-diff approach we reject in [How do we keep packages in sync?](#how-do-we-keep-packages-in-sync). The LabBench template calls `new-gitlab-module` for the UI instead, so one script owns the frontend setup everywhere.

## How do we keep packages in sync?

Once a package is created, it has essentially broken free from the constraints of our code standards and best practices. Ideally, each of these consumers is wired to consume `@gitlab/frontend-config` so that the shared setup is never copied into the package, only referenced:

1. CI is remote. The package `.gitlab-ci.yml` is a small stub that `include`s the base file from the tooling project at a pinned `ref` and adds its own jobs below it. Changing the base in the tooling repository and cutting a new tag is enough for every consumer to pick it up on their next bump.
1. Config files are extended. `eslint.config.js` imports the base config from `@gitlab/frontend-config/eslint` and spreads it, `tsconfig.json` uses `extends`. Packages override a few rules on top, in their own file, so overrides never collide with the base.

In practice a package carries three small files and nothing else from the shared setup:

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
include:
  - project: gitlab-org/frontend/toolkit/config
    ref: v1.4.0
    file: ci/base.yml

package-specific-job:
  script: pnpm run some-extra-check
```

```js
// eslint.config.js
import base from '@gitlab/frontend-config/eslint';

export default [
  ...base,
  {
    files: ['src/**/*.vue'],
    rules: { 'vue/multi-word-component-names': 'off' },
  },
];
```

```json
// tsconfig.json
{
  "extends": "@gitlab/frontend-config/tsconfig",
  "include": ["src"]
}
```

Since both the npm dependency and the CI `ref` point to the same release, an update is a version bump. Package maintainers do it when it makes sense to them, through an MR, and Renovate can open that MR for them: its `npm` manager bumps the dependency and its `gitlabci-include` manager bumps the `ref`, grouped together.

### Considered and rejected

We considered a Shadcn style of update, where the package owns some original version of the config files, we allow the package to iterate on it, and an `update-gitlab-module` script pulls the new source and diffs it against the local copy. This is too complex for our needs: it requires tracking what the package changed, merging it with upstream changes, and resolving conflicts in files that `extends` and `include` already keep separate. We drop the update script. The only files that would still be copied are `.gitignore` and `.tool-versions`, which rarely change and are small enough to update by hand.

## What does the frontend-config package include?

1. Eslint config
1. TsConfig
1. Base `gitlab-ci.yml` template
1. Base `package.json` scripts and dependencies, see [Base scripts](#base-scripts)
1. Test setup wired to `@gitlab/frontend-tests` from [ADR-002](./002_reusable_testing_approach.md), with Rstest as the default framework
1. The reusable script for setup `new-gitlab-module` (name TBD)
1. `.gitignore` for a typical JS/Vue repository.
1. `.tool-versions` for `mise` or equivalent if we ever change tooling manager.
1. (less certain) A .claude directory with frontend-wide directives. This would mean moving the distillation for the frontend docs into this package, and then the monolith would inherit our frontend-wide directives, while retaining the ability to overwrite them as needed.

### Default test framework

ADR-001 named Vitest as an example. ADR-002 settled on Rstest for `@gitlab/frontend-tests` because it aligns with Rspack and tests Module Federation remotes. The toolkit makes Rstest the default: `new-gitlab-module` adds `@gitlab/frontend-tests/unit` and a `test` script that runs it. A package can opt out in the TUI and bring its own framework, at the cost of maintaining that setup itself and losing the shared mount helpers. Deviating should have a reason written in the package README.

### Base scripts

The base CI template calls scripts by name, so every package needs the same entry points. The toolkit ships a `package.json` fragment that `new-gitlab-module` merges into the new package:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "rslib build",
    "test": "rstest",
    "fixtures:download": "frontend-tests fixtures download",
    "test:integration": "rstest -c rstest.integration.config.ts",
    "lint": "eslint .",
    "typecheck": "vue-tsc --noEmit"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@gitlab/frontend-config": "^1.4.0",
    "@gitlab/frontend-tests": "^2.0.0"
  }
}
```

`test:integration` runs the integration layer from [ADR-002](./002_reusable_testing_approach.md#how-a-package-consumes-it) with a config that extends `@gitlab/frontend-tests/integration`, which starts the MSW server and serves the Rails fixtures under `tmp/fixtures/`. `fixtures:download` fills that directory and is separate so that developers run it once locally, while `ci/base.yml` runs it before every integration job to test against the latest fixtures. A package gets unit and integration jobs without writing CI.

The build tool and its config are part of this: `ci/base.yml` runs `pnpm run build`, so the toolkit exposes `@gitlab/frontend-config/rslib` as the base build config in the same `extends` style as ESLint and TSConfig. Mixing reference files such as `.gitignore` and `.tool-versions` with the extendable configs is accepted for now. If packages opt out of the copied files often, they move behind a TUI question or out of the toolkit.

## How do we publish packages?

As of now, whenever a new package is created, we need to create a version and ask for someone to configure GitLab's npm trusted publish list with the namespace of the project and the CI file. There is currently little to no one with access, and as such a more formal process should be in place to allow a more systemic review of a new package and a list of owners who can decide the package is warranted, approve and let us publish from the registry.

The registry is the real gate. Nothing reaches npmjs without someone with access on the `@gitlab` scope, and only the approvers have that. So anyone can create a project in the group and iterate on it, we just do not publish it until the request is approved. No CI guard needed, and no need to restrict project creation.

### New package request

Open a work item in `gitlab-org/frontend/toolkit` from the `New package request` template. It must include:

1. The list of developers and maintainers who will work on the package.
1. The consumers of this package and an explanation of why and how it will be reused.
1. A forward looking plan for the next 6 months, how the package is expected to grow.
1. For packages over a certain size (threshold TBD), proof that the code has been reviewed before we publish. A large package merged without review does not get published because it is now convenient to do so.

Rejections should be rare and always come with a clear why from the UI Platform maintainers, written in the issue. The most common reason we expect is "this is not a package, it is a monolith util": code with a single consumer and no reuse plan belongs in the monolith. The other expected reason is that an existing package already covers the need, in which case the proposal becomes a contribution to that package instead.

### Decisions

1. Add a `New package request` issue template to `gitlab-org/frontend/toolkit` that captures the purpose, the owner, and an overlap check with existing packages, and a `Deprecate package` template for [How do we retire packages?](#how-do-we-retire-packages).
1. The approvers are the UI Platform maintainers plus a few Frontend Foundations team members, who are also the people with maintainer rights on the `@gitlab` npm scope.
1. Once approved, an approver does the first publish, from their own npm account or with a short-lived token in a masked CI variable that they delete afterwards. They then set the project up as a trusted publisher so that every following release ships from CI.

### How are versions cut?

We release from tags, the same way `@gitlab/frontend-tests` does today, and `ci/base.yml` ships the job:

1. A package Maintainer creates tag `vX.Y.Z` on `main`, from the Releases page or with `git tag`, and writes the release notes in the release description or the tag message. Nothing is committed, `package.json` keeps a placeholder version such as `0.0.0-dev`.
1. The tag pipeline runs the `publish` job, which sets the version from the tag in the job workspace, publishes to npmjs with provenance through trusted publishing, and creates the GitLab Release with the notes.
1. Protected tags `v*` are open to project Maintainers and the UI Platform team.

```yaml
publish:
  stage: publish
  id_tokens:
    NPM_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: npm
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+/
  script:
    - pnpm version "${CI_COMMIT_TAG#v}" --no-git-tag-version   # workspace only, nothing is committed
    - pnpm publish --provenance --access public --no-git-checks
    - release-cli create --tag-name "$CI_COMMIT_TAG" --description "$CI_COMMIT_TAG_MESSAGE"
```

So a Maintainer tags `v1.3.0`, npmjs shows `1.3.0` with a provenance badge pointing at the pipeline, and the GitLab Release carries the notes. How often a package releases is up to the package.

### Considered and rejected

1. Changesets, which ADR-001 mentions. Every MR adds a changeset file, and a release job turns them into a version bump, a `CHANGELOG.md` and a release MR that a Maintainer merges when they want to ship. It reviews the bump size with the code, but it needs a release bot, a release MR per release and a changeset file per MR, and the tag flow gets us the same timing control with less machinery.
1. Conventional commits with semantic-release, where the version is derived from commit prefixes. Squash merges and the monolith's commit style make the prefixes unreliable, and the bump is invisible during review.
1. A single granular token scoped to `@gitlab/*` stored as a group-level CI variable. It removes the per-package admin step, but every project in the group could publish with it, which bypasses the review above. It is also a long-lived secret with no provenance.
1. Publishing to the GitLab package registry of the group instead of npmjs. Publishing would only need `CI_JOB_TOKEN`, but an npm scope maps to a single registry in `.npmrc` and `@gitlab/*` already lives on npmjs for the monolith, so it would require a new scope or a proxy.

## How do we retire packages?

Packages that nobody consumes still cost reviews, dependency bumps and security fixes. Two scenarios need a process.

### Unused package

A package is unused when a reverse dependency search across the monolith and the other packages in the group finds no consumer. npm download counts are only a secondary signal, since CI mirrors inflate them. The drift job from [What rules does this group need?](#what-rules-does-this-group-need) reports both.

1. As soon as a package is flagged unused, remove its trusted publisher on npm so nothing ships unnoticed, and open an issue from the `Deprecate package` template, noting that publishing again means going through the request process again. Existing versions stay installable.
1. After 6 months without activity and still unused, post in `#frontend` and on the issue, pinging every maintainer, with two weeks to claim the package before we move it out of `toolkit`.
1. If nobody answers, the project moves to `gitlab-org/frontend/archive` and is archived, read-only with its history and a URL redirect. If the code is small and still useful, it is folded into `@gitlab/frontend-utils` instead, and if the monolith was its only consumer, it moves back into the monolith.
1. In all three cases the package is deprecated on npm with `npm deprecate` and a reason, so stale installs warn.

We considered archiving in place inside `toolkit`. It is simpler, but the group exists to be the single spot to see live packages, and archived projects would still show up in it. Deleting the project loses history while the npm versions remain anyway.

### Used but unmaintained package

Since the UI Platform team is on every project, see [How do we define maintainers?](#how-do-we-define-maintainers), a package never has zero maintainers. When its listed maintainers leave or stop responding, we look for new owners by posting in `#frontend` and pinging the teams that consume the package. If no team takes it, the UI Platform team keeps it in maintenance mode, security fixes and dependency bumps only, until a consumer steps up or the package becomes unused.

## How do we define maintainers?

Each of these packages is going to require a list of active maintainers. We could either re-use the existing @frontend-maintainers group from the monolith and give merge rights to everyone, CODEOWNERS rules that would make certain reviewer review mandatory, or creating a smaller pool of maintainers for the tooling packages. Rules might also differ per project.

### Option 1: Frontend maintainers for all packages

Make the monolith frontend maintainers group also the maintainers of `gitlab-org/frontend/toolkit` and let each package define a CODEOWNERS rule if they think they need more controls.

#### Pros

1. The pool of maintainers is large, easy to get reviewers and to merge.
1. We can enforce no-self merge rules and other safety from the get go and not block the author.
1. Knowledge spread stays wide for the whole company.

#### Cons

1. Less control over who gets to contribute. Since packages are wide-impacting, the risk of allowing anyone to merge is much higher.
1. With the push to have "everyone" a maintainer in the monolith, domain expertise is not guaranteed.
1. AI can work faster than we can filter. Anyone allowed to merge and release packages can derail the scope of a package quickly.

### Option 2: UI Platform maintainers + each package additional domain experts

Tooling packages could all be owned by the UI platform team, and each individual package could get more maintainers when they are actively contributing to the package.

### Option 3: Each package define its own maintainers

No assumption is made and each package gets to define who has merge rights.

Note: CODEOWNERS is always an option to weave in any of the options. We could have every Frontend maintainer of the monolith also own the package, but enforce CODEOWNERS of the UI platform team.

### Decision

Option 2, set up so that no package can go below the group's rules:

1. The UI Platform team is the `gitlab-org/maintainers/frontend-toolkit` group, same convention as the other maintainer groups. It is Owner on `gitlab-org/frontend/toolkit` because group settings need that. The team owns the group settings, approves new packages and is the default maintainer of a package until it has its own. Inherited membership cannot be removed at project level, so a package cannot lock the team out.
1. Monolith frontend maintainers inherit Maintainer from `gitlab-org/frontend` and we cannot lower that in a subgroup. So they can merge, and what keeps the bar up is the approval policy and CODEOWNERS, not the role.
1. Each package adds its domain experts as project Maintainers. A project can add members, not remove inherited ones.
1. `new-gitlab-module` writes a CODEOWNERS with `* @gitlab-org/maintainers/frontend-toolkit` as the default, plus one line per shared file for the same group: `.gitlab/CODEOWNERS`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `package.json`, `tsconfig.json` and `eslint.config.js`. When a package has its own maintainers, it changes the default line and leaves the shared ones. Code owner approval is on for `main`, so these entries are enforced.
1. Protected tags `v*` are open to project Maintainers and the UI Platform team, see [How are versions cut?](#how-are-versions-cut).
1. No self-approval and no editing of approval rules come from the policy in [What rules does this group need?](#what-rules-does-this-group-need), since group approval settings do not reach a subgroup.

Option 1 is rejected because AI can work faster than we can filter, and the push to make everyone a maintainer in the monolith means the pool is not vetted for package work. Option 3 is rejected because without a baseline an author can approve their own work.

Consequence: the UI Platform team is the reviewer of last resort for every package in the group. This is fine while the group is small and should be revisited once it is not.

## Decision

1. Reusable packages live in `gitlab-org/frontend/toolkit`. `@gitlab/frontend-utils` and `@gitlab/frontend-tests` move there.
1. `@gitlab/frontend-config` is a single package with subpath exports that holds the ESLint config, TSConfig, CI templates and the bootstrap script.
1. Packages reference the shared setup through `include` and `extends` at a pinned version. Renovate opens the bump MRs.
1. Group settings, a merge request approval policy and a compliance framework enforce reviews, protected `main`, and no self-approval on every project, including future ones.
1. Publishing is gated by a request issue reviewed by the UI Platform maintainers plus a few Frontend Foundations team members, who also hold the `@gitlab` npm scope. After the first publish, a release is a `v*` tag by a package Maintainer and CI does the rest.
1. The UI Platform team is `gitlab-org/maintainers/frontend-toolkit`, Owner on the group. It owns the settings, approves new packages and is the default maintainer of a package until it has its own. Monolith frontend maintainers inherit Maintainer from `gitlab-org/frontend`. CODEOWNERS protects the shared files.
1. Unused packages lose trusted publishing right away and move to `gitlab-org/frontend/archive` after 6 months of inactivity and an unanswered call in `#frontend`. Used but unmaintained packages fall back to the UI Platform team until new owners are found.

## Consequences

1. The UI Platform team is the reviewer of last resort for every package and the approver of every new one. This works while the group is small and should be revisited once it is not.
1. Every package needs a CODEOWNERS approval when shared files change, and a release is one tag by a package Maintainer.
1. Two one-time asks outside the team: an Owner of `gitlab-org/maintainers` creates `maintainers/frontend-toolkit`, and an Owner of `gitlab-org` creates the compliance framework. The UI Platform team does the rest.
1. Owners inherited from `gitlab-org/frontend` can still change group settings or unlink the policy project. The compliance dashboard would show it, it does not block it.
1. ADR-001's pnpm workspace for tooling becomes a single package, and its mention of changesets becomes tag-driven releases. The rest of ADR-001 still applies.

## Open questions

Collected here for review. Questions a section already answers keep a pointer.

1. Can we enforce some form of restriction on project creation to prevent non-related packages being created? Answered in [How do we publish packages?](#how-do-we-publish-packages): creation stays open, publishing is gated.
1. How can we audit this repo for usage and make sure we don't have dead packages? Answered in [How do we retire packages?](#how-do-we-retire-packages).
1. How can we enforce these settings by default? Answered in [What rules does this group need?](#what-rules-does-this-group-need).
1. How can we make sure users cannot disable these rules? Answered in the same section through locked group settings and the approval policy.
1. How to make sure users cannot clone a package from an existing repo to this group to bypass the rules? Partially answered: import cannot be prevented, the publish gate is the control.
1. What is the size threshold above which a package must show prior code review before its first publish?
1. Is Renovate already configured on `gitlab-org/frontend/*`, or does this ADR need to request it?
1. Which GitLab group represents the UI Platform team in CODEOWNERS and protected tags? Answered in [How do we define maintainers?](#how-do-we-define-maintainers): `gitlab-org/maintainers/frontend-toolkit`.
1. Does `@gitlab/frontend-config` also ship the `.claude` directory, and if so how do consumers pick up changes to it, since it cannot be extended?

title: Bounded Contexts
text:
## Historical context

Until May 2024 the GitLab codebase didn't have a clear domain structure.
We have [forced the creation of some modules](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/212156)
as a first step but we didn't have a well defined strategy for doing it consistently.

The majority of the code was not properly namespaced and organized:

- Ruby namespaces used didn't always represent the SSoT. We had overlapping concepts spread across multiple
  namespaces. For example: `Abuse::` and `Spam::` or `Security::Orchestration::` and `Security::SecurityOrchestration`.
- Domain code related to the same bounded context was scattered across multiple directories.
- Domain code was present in `lib/` directory under namespaces that differed from the same domain under `app/`.
- Some namespaces were very shallow, containing a few classes while other namespaces were very deep and large.
- A lot of the old code was not namespaced, making it difficult to understand the context where it was used.

In May 2024 we [defined and enforced bounded contexts](decisions/002_bounded_contexts_definition.md).

## Goal

1. Define a list of characteristics that bounded contexts should have. For example: must relate to at least 1 product category.
1. Have a list of top-level bounded contexts where all domain code is broken down into.
1. Engineers can clearly see the list of available bounded contexts and can make an easy decision where to add
   new classes and modules.
1. Define a process for adding a new bounded context to the application. This should occur quite infrequently
   and new bounded contexts need to adhere to the characteristics defined previously.
1. Enforce the list of bounded contexts so that no new top-level namespaces can be used aside from the authorized ones.

## Mapping bounded contexts to feature categories

Bounded contexts are anchored on feature categories. A feature category represents a
product area large enough for a module to be **deep**, which keeps us from proliferating
small top-level modules. Anchoring on feature categories also keeps the codebase aligned
with the product's [ubiquitous language](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/development/software_design.html#use-ubiquitous-language-instead-of-crud-terminology)
and helps new contributors — GitLab team members and the wider community — navigate the
code.

A team can be responsible for multiple feature categories, and therefore own the vision
for multiple bounded contexts. When a feature category changes ownership, remapping the
bounded context to its new owners is cheap.

Feature categories and bounded contexts are not always one-to-one:

- If multiple feature categories are strongly related, they may be grouped under a single
  bounded context.
- If a feature category is only relevant within a parent feature category, it may be folded
  into the parent's bounded context — for example, build artifacts exist within the
  Continuous Integration feature category and may be merged under a single bounded context.

## Iterations

1. [Extract libraries out of the `lib/` directory](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/4c6e120069abe751d3128c05ade45ea749a033df/doc/development/gems.md).
    - This step is non blocking to modularization but the less generic code exists in `lib/` the
      easier will be to identify and separate bounded context.
    - Isolate code that could live in a separate project, to prevent it from depending on domain code.

1. [ADR-001: Modularize application domain](decisions/001_modular_application_domain.md)? Start with modularizing
1. [ADR-002: Define bounded context around feature categories](decisions/002_bounded_contexts_definition.md) as a SSoT in the code.
1. [ADR-003: Assign stewards to all modules and libraries](decisions/003_stewardship.md).
1. [Publish the list of bounded contexts](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/development/software_design.html#use-namespaces-to-define-bounded-contexts).
    - Define a SSoT list of bounded contexts.
    - Enforce enforce it using RuboCop static analyzer.
    - Autoload non-standard Rails directories based on the given list.

title: 001 Modular Application Domain
text:
## Context

Before we modularize a codebase we first needed to define how we are going to divide it.

## Decision

We start by focusing on the application domain (backend business logic) leaving the
application adapters (Web controllers and views, REST/GraphQL endpoints) outside the
scope of the modularization initially.

The reasons for this are:

1. Code in application adapters may not always align with a specific
   domain. For example: a project settings endpoint or a merge request page contains
   references to many domains.
1. There was a need to run separate Rails nodes for the SaaS architecture using different
   profiles in order to save on memory.
   For example: on SaaS we wanted to be able to spin up more Sidekiq nodes without the need
   to load the whole Rails application. The assumption is that for running Sidekiq we don't
   need ActionCable, REST endpoints, GraphQL mutations or Rails views.
   We only need the application domain and infrastructure code.
   This could still be true even with the introduction of [Cells](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/architecture/blueprints/cells/index.html) but
   we need to re-evaluate this assumption.
1. Keep the scope and effort smaller. Tackling only domain code is easier to understand than
   the complexity of how to breakdown the application adapters and all their edge cases.

The decision to scope out application adapters is not final and we decided to defer
it to later.

Finally, the infrastructure code containing technical concerns (typically the `lib/`) will
be part of a common "platform" layer that every domain module will depend on in order to function.

The "platform" layer can be broken down into independent libraries extracted as gems.

## Consequences

We focus on modularizing business logic, defining rules and guidelines for engineers.
We can apply the same set of patterns across modules.

## Alternatives

We looked into including application adapters to the modularization effort but noticed that
modularizing adapters is more delicate as we need to preserve user-facing dependencies like routes.

title: 002 Bounded Contexts Definition
text:
## Context

With the focus primarily on the application domain we needed to define how to
modularize it.

## Decision

The application domain is divided into bounded contexts which define the top-level
modules of GitLab application. The term bounded context is widely used in
Domain-Driven Design.

Defining bounded contexts means to organize the code around product structure rather than
organizational structure.

From the research in [Proposal: split GitLab monolith into components](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/365293)
it seems that following [product categories](/handbook/product/categories/), as a guideline,
would be much better than translating organization structure into folder structure (for example, `app/modules/verify/pipeline-execution/...`).

However, this guideline alone is not sufficient and we need a more specific strategy:

- Bounded contexts (top level modules) should be [sufficiently deep](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/development/software_design.html#use-namespaces-to-define-bounded-contexts)
  to encapsulate implementation details and provide a smaller interface.
- Some product categories, such as Browser Performance Testing, are just too small to represent
  a bounded context on their own.
  We should have a strategy for grouping product categories together when makes sense.
- Product categories don't necessarily translate into clean boundaries.
  `Category:Pipeline Composition` and `Category:Continuous Integration` are some examples
  where Pipeline Authoring team and Pipeline Execution team share a lot of code.
- Some parts of the code might not have a clear product category associated to it.

Despite the above, product categories provide a rough view of the bounded contexts at play in the application.
For that we use product categories to sketch the initial set of bounded contexts.
Then, group related or strongly coupled categories under the same bounded context and create new bounded contexts if missing.

## Consequences

In May 2024 we completed the [Bounded Contexts working group](../../../../company/working-groups/bounded-contexts/)
which completed the first phase of modularization, described in this page.

We defined a list of [bounded contexts in code](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/development/software_design.html#use-namespaces-to-define-bounded-contexts)
and started enforcing them with RuboCop, in order to move towards a fully namespaced monolith.
Team members can edit this list by creating and deleting bounded contexts explicitly and the decision is reviewed
by Staff+ engineers.

## Alternatives

We evaluated whether to align the code to the organizational structure but we decided it wasn't viable:

- Product categories can change ownership and we have seen some pretty frequent changes, even back and forth.
  Moving code every time a product category changes ownership adds too much maintenance overhead.
- Teams and organization changes should just mean relabelling the ownership of specific modules.
- Coupling and complexity are directly correlated to business logic and product structure.
  A code organization that aligns to organizational structure could generate unnecessary complexity and
  much more coupling.

title: 003 Stewardship
text:
## Context

How do we assign stewardship to domain and platform layer? We have a large amount of shared code
that does not have explicit stewards who can provide a vision and direction on that part of code.

## Decision

We use the term **stewards** instead of **owners** to be more in line with GitLab principle of
**everyone can contribute**. Stewards are care takers of the code. They know how a specific
functionality is designed and why. They know the architectural characteristics and constraints.
However, they welcome changes and guide contributors towards success.

A module, whether is from a domain bounded context or platform layer, must have at least 1 group of stewards.
This group can be a team name (or GitLab group handle). Optionally, the list of stewards can include
single IC entries.

We have not yet decided on the code-structure mechanism for modules (e.g. Packwerk packages
or gems). Until that decision is made, we indicate stewardship using the existing `CODEOWNERS`
file, assigning the module's directory to one or more groups (and optionally individual ICs):

```text
/ci/ @gitlab-org/maintainers/pipeline-execution @gitlab-org/maintainers/pipeline-authoring @grzesiek @ayufan
```

If we later adopt a code-structure mechanism that carries metadata (such as a Packwerk
`package.yml` or a gemspec), stewardship can move into that metadata and the relevant
`CODEOWNERS` sections can be generated from it.

Gems extracted from the platform layer (e.g. `Gitlab::Redis`) should also have stewards assigned.

## Consequences

Stewardship defined in code can be very powerful:

- Review Roulette or Suggested Reviews features use `CODEOWNERS` to route reviews to stewards.
- Engineers can easily identify stewards and have design conversations early.

## Alternatives

Instead of using `CODEOWNERS`, we could rely on each team to informally know what bounded contexts
they are responsible for, without recording stewardship anywhere. For the "shared code" in the
platform modules we would expect maintainers to fill the role of stewards.

- Pros: we give trainee maintainers a clear development path and goals. Today it feels unclear what they must
  learn in order to become successful maintainers.
- Cons: The amount of "shared" code is very large and still hard to understand who knows best about
  a particular functionality. Without an explicit record, stewardship stays tribal knowledge — invisible
  to new contributors and to agents — which is exactly what modularization aims to remove.

title: 004 Library Extraction
text:
## Context

[ADR-001](001_modular_application_domain/) established that the "platform" layer —
the technical, cross-cutting code that today largely lives in `lib/` and
`ee/lib` — can be broken down into independent libraries extracted as gems. This
ADR commits to how we do that.

`lib/gitlab/` has become a junk drawer mixing three kinds of code: genuinely
generic utilities, GitLab-specific but isolated libraries, and code that is
tightly coupled to ActiveRecord models and the Rails runtime. The last category
is domain code, not platform code.

The detailed extraction pattern, candidate tiers, and sequencing guidance live
in the [Extracting cross-cutting libraries into gems](../library_extraction.md)
page, which is the single source of truth for this topic.

## Decision

We extract cross-cutting **platform** libraries out of `lib/`/`ee/lib` into Ruby
gems under `gems/`, referenced via `path:` in the Gemfile, with the following
commitments:

- **Libraries must be ActiveRecord-free.** Only true cross-cutting concerns
  (logging, error reporting, metrics, rate limiters, parsers, generic utilities
  like `Banzai`) become gems. Needing to inject AR data into a "library" is a
  signal that it is not generic.
- **Domain code will follow the bounded context strategy.** AR-coupled code pulled
  out of `lib/gitlab/` moves to its
  [bounded context](../bounded_contexts.md) namespace per
  `config/bounded_contexts.yml` — it does not keep the `Gitlab::` prefix.
  Platform code may keep `Gitlab::`.
- **Gem extraction is an atomic refactor**, optionally Packwerk-assisted for
  code that can only be isolated gradually. Packwerk is a complementary tool,
  not the main path.
- **Start fine, from the bottom.** Begin from the lowest-level dependency-free
  code and extract small, focused gems one at a time. That proves the extraction
  pattern and CI wiring sooner.

## Consequences

- Dependencies that were implicit become explicit and enforced at the gem
  boundary; hidden coupling surfaces as errors.
- Each gem carries an explicit `feature_category:` and a clearer owner, and runs
  its own isolated CI suite.
- The CI speedup is modest in practice — `lib/gitlab/` libraries are stable and
  gems remain interconnected — so the primary value is establishing the pattern,
  tooling, and isolation rather than CI time saved.
- The exercise forces a useful classification: code that resists AR-free
  extraction is revealed as domain code and routed to its bounded context.

## Alternatives

- **Leave platform code in `lib/`** and rely only on static analysis to enforce
  boundaries. Rejected as the primary path: keeping everything in `lib/` does not
  improve the design — interfaces stay blurred and coupling unconstrained — and
  it does not let us run fewer CI tests, since the code stays part of the
  monolith's suite. A gem gives code an explicit, isolated dependency declaration
  and its own CI suite that `lib/` cannot.

title: Persistence only — scopes and AR persistence, nothing else. Private to the domain.
text:
This page is the single source of truth for isolating the **application domain** —
the business logic at the core of the [hexagonal monolith](hexagonal_monolith/index.md) —
into bounded, independently-owned modules.

It covers domain code only. Extracting cross-cutting **platform** code is covered in
[Extracting cross-cutting libraries into gems](library_extraction.md); extracting the
**transport layer** (Web, REST, GraphQL, Sidekiq) is covered in
[Decomposing the transport layer into adapters](transport_layer.md). How domains are
identified and named is covered in [Defining bounded contexts](bounded_contexts.md).

Domain isolation is the hardest part of modularization. The platform and transport
layers have relatively clean seams; the domain is where the coupling actually lives.

## What domain isolation means

A domain is isolated when:

- **Nothing crosses its boundary except through its public API.** Other domains call
  a documented, intentional interface — they never reach into internals, AR models,
  or private services.
- **It exclusively owns its data.** The domain owns its database tables and the
  ActiveRecord models that map them. No other domain queries those tables or holds
  references to those models.

A well-designed domain module is also **deep** — it encapsulates a large amount of
internal logic, state, and data behind that small interface — and **cohesive**, acting as
the single source of truth for the feature it describes. It follows the
[guideline on naming namespaces](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/development/software_design.html#use-namespaces-to-define-bounded-contexts)
and uses [ubiquitous language](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/development/software_design.html#use-ubiquitous-language-instead-of-crud-terminology)
rather than CRUD terminology. How domains are identified and mapped to feature categories
is covered in [Defining bounded contexts](bounded_contexts.md).

Everything below is about the work required to get there.

## The hard part: cross-domain coupling

Our modular-monolith research surfaced the coupling that makes this difficult. In the
current codebase:

- **Policies depend on other policies** — for example `PipelinePolicy` delegates to
  `ProjectPolicy`.
- **Services depend on shared components** — publishing events, sending mail, system
  notes, auditing, and so on.
- **Domains depend on each other's AR models**, both explicitly (`Ci::Pipeline.find_by_id`)
  and implicitly through associations (`security_scan.pipeline`).
- **Circular dependencies** between domains are common.

This is why domain isolation cannot be a mechanical file move the way library and
transport extraction largely can. Most of the effort is *refactoring away the coupling*,
not relocating code.

## Owning the data

Exclusive data ownership is the core of isolation. Each domain owns its tables and the
AR models that map them, and is the only code allowed to query them.

Two enforcement problems follow:

**Cross-domain AR associations.** Today any domain can call `project.ci_pipelines` and
walk straight into CI's data. Isolation requires removing cross-domain associations and
going through the owning domain's public API instead — `Ci::Pipeline.all(project)` rather
than `project.ci_pipelines`. A prerequisite is
[Taming Omniscient Classes](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/software_design/#taming-omniscient-classes):
classes like `Project` and `User` accrete associations and methods from every domain and
must be slimmed down.

**Direct model references.** Even with associations gone, any code can reference
`Ci::Pipeline` directly. One option is to keep the AR model private to the domain — for
example `Ci::Internal::Pipeline` — so it cannot be referenced from outside, exposing
pipeline data only through the `Ci::*` public interface.

### Repository-pattern option

A more structured variant uses AR strictly as a persistence/repository layer, separate
from the domain object:

```ruby
# Persistence only — scopes and AR persistence, nothing else. Private to the domain.
Ci::Repository::Pipeline

# Domain object wrapping the record, exposing behaviour. The public type.
Ci::Pipeline   # #builds, #cancelable?, ...
```

The AR model is never used outside its domain object. This makes the domain trivially
stubbable in tests and removes the AR dependency from callers. The cost is significant:
it is a large, invasive refactor regardless of whether we ultimately extract gems.

## Cross-domain data and shared models

The thorniest question is what happens to shared entities like `Project` and `User`,
which nearly every domain touches.

**Strip shared models to identity objects.** If a cross-domain accessor returns the full
`Project` AR object, it drags in that object's entire surface and re-couples the domains.
Shared data should be reduced to a minimal identity object, not the full model.

**Domain-specific representations.** Rather than every domain consuming a shared
`Project`, a domain can wrap the data it needs behind its own facade:

```ruby
project = Ci::Internal::Project.new(project_id) # PORO or record local to the CI domain
project.variables       # internal to CI
project.public_builds?  # CI-specific project setting
project.pipelines       # pipelines queried via Ci::Project, not Project
```

This keeps `project.pipelines` inside the CI domain instead of on the global `Project`.
A related idea is per-domain owner objects — for example `Ci::JobOwner` wrapping a
`user_id` and delegating to `User` only for identity-specific concerns.

**Prefer direct dependencies over monolith callbacks.** Where a domain needs data from
another domain, prefer a direct, declared dependency on that domain's public interface
over wiring callbacks back into the monolith. Direct dependencies are trackable — we can
render a cross-domain dependency graph and use it in CI to run only the affected tests —
whereas callbacks hide the coupling.

**A stable client interface, swappable to gRPC later.** A domain can be treated as
external from the start: it exposes a Ruby client interface and keeps everything else
private. The backend behind that interface can later move to gRPC without changing
callers.

**Avoid chatty domains.** Once boundaries are enforced we will find components that are
too dependent on each other — Rails makes everything available all the time, so a single
business transaction reaches across many domains. Avoiding chatty cross-domain calls
(a real problem once domains become services) means denormalizing or duplicating data,
keeping local representations, and applying interface segregation — for example a slim
`Ci::Internal::User` that wraps a basic identity object instead of the full `User`.

> The shared "scaffolding" every domain needs — `Project`/`User` lookups, permission
> checks, and similar — might instead live in a coarse `gitlab-platform`/`gitlab-core`
> gem that every domain depends on, rather than being injected per-domain. That
> trade-off is tracked as an
> [open question on the library-extraction page](library_extraction.md#open-questions).

## What must be resolved before extraction

Domain isolation is mostly unanswered design work. Before extracting a domain — into a
gem **or** a package — we need reproducible guidelines, so the refactor is not left to
per-engineer or per-agent interpretation, for at least:

1. What happens to cross-domain **AR associations**.
1. What logic lives on the **AR model** versus the **domain object**.
1. What data is allowed to **cross a boundary**, and in what shape.
1. What to do when a caller receives a data object but needs a method on a **domain
   object** (for example `Ci::Pipeline#merge_request`) — without creating chatty domains
   or over-serializing responses (a current pain in REST).
1. Who **owns database migrations**, and where they live.
1. Whether `Project` is a **shared model** or becomes a `Projects` **domain**.
1. How **EE and JH** extensions are isolated alongside the domain — the same extension
   problem the library and transport layers face.
1. How **tests** decouple. Factories are global and heavily coupled. As domains decouple,
   each should expose a public interface for specs/factories, or callers should stub
   rather than build cross-domain records:

  ```ruby
  RSpec.describe Ci::Pipeline do
    let(:user)    { Gitlab::Platform::Specs.create_user }
    let(:project) { Gitlab::Platform::Specs.create_project }
  end
  ```

The glue code that bridges domains during the transition could be very large. We likely
need a proof of concept to learn what it actually contains before committing to a
strategy.

## Where domain code lives: `domains/` vs `gems/`
