Auto-confirmation without review creates an Org structure the customer may not recognize or trust.

**Skipping or shape-varying the workflow by deployment type.** Rejected. Two variants were considered and rejected: (a) SM/Dedicated skip the workflow entirely with platform auto-confirmation, which bypasses informed consent; (b) SM/Dedicated walk through only Steps 1 and 4 with Steps 2 and 3 auto-completing invisibly, which creates a deployment-specific workflow shape and weakens consent. The adopted model is universal: every customer walks through all four steps, with content adapting to context (interactive reconciliation, fast-path verification, or read-only acknowledgment) but structure staying the same. This keeps the workflow simple and the customer's consent meaningful, regardless of deployment type.

---

## Review and Approval Required

This ADR requires review and approval from the following before implementation begins on any step.

| Reviewer | Area | Required for |
|---|---|---|
| Tenant Scale Engineering Lead | Data model, state machine, atomic writes, forward compatibility | All steps |
| UX and Technical Writing | Orientation content, reconciliation wizard, entitlements summary screen with owner designation, help link affordance, confirmation screen | Steps 1, 2, 3, 4 |
| AR Team | Entitlement scoping to organization_id, purchasing flow integration | Step 3 |

---

## References

- New Isolation upgrade ADR: Isolation Upgrade Workflow (downstream of a confirmed Org)
- Organizations Onboarding Step Specs: Steps 1 through 4 (this initiative)
- Organizations and Billing issue: gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/597957
- Non-Isolated Organizations Onboarding epic: gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/21394
- Organizations Onboarding Workflow for Artifact Registry Enablement: gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/21393
- AR Usage Billing Integration MR: gitlab.com/gitlab-org/architecture/usage-billing/design-doc/-/merge_requests/27
- ADR 008: Non-Isolated Organizations on GitLab.com: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/organization/decisions/008_non_isolated_organizations_gitlab_com/
- Cells: Organization Migration design document: https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/organization-data-migration/
- Cells: Organization Migration design document

title: 012 Organization Space
text:
## Context

An Organization is a **logical boundary** — more than a data boundary, it is a
self-contained space that owns its own resources, names, and features. That
boundary shows up in three independent ways:

- **Scoped space** — the boundary in the address space (names, routes). Always
  present.
- **Isolation** — whether the data layer actually prevents data from crossing
  between Organizations (see [Organization Isolation](../isolation.md)). Enforced
  gradually, so a [non-isolated](008_non_isolated_organizations_gitlab_com.md)
  Organization already has its space even if its data boundary is not yet enforced.
- **Cell placement** — the boundary realized in physical infrastructure.

These are orthogonal. Scoped space is the logical boundary made addressable, so
it exists whether or not the data is isolated or the Organization lives on its
own Cell.

## Decision

Every Organization occupies its own scoped space, including non-isolated ones.
Scoping is an addressing and ownership decision, so it does not wait on isolation
being enforced or on a move to a dedicated Cell. Concretely, this means:

1. **Its own namespace.** Today every routable name (e.g. Groups and Projects)
   must be unique across one shared global namespace (cluster-wide on GitLab.com). Two customers cannot both have a "Marketing" group; they
   contend for the same global name. An Organization space partitions that
   namespace, so names need only be unique within the Organization.
2. **A single, predictable point of change.** Legacy URLs are retained, but the
   URL format changes once a resource enters an Organization. We make that change
   at one logical point — entering the Organization — rather than later when the
   Organization moves to a Cell. The path does not encode the Cell, so Cell moves
   never change URLs.
3. **A home for Organization-level features.** Organizations own features, such
   as security dashboards, that need a place to live in the URL space, just as
   Groups, Projects, and Users do.

## Consequences

- Non-isolated Organizations are scoped from creation, not retrofitted later.
- The URL mechanism for this is the `/o/<organization>/` scope decided in
  [ADR 004](004_path_scope.md).
- The transition away from the legacy system to the Organization system does come
  with complications — for example, legacy global routes and scoped routes
  coexisting — but these are essentially unavoidable.

title: 013 Warn On Tlg Creation
text:
## Context

Subscriptions (Free, Premium, Ultimate), credits, and related billing entitlements are scoped to a Top-Level-Group, not to an organization.
When a Top-Level-Group is transferred into an organization, its existing license remains attached to that Top-Level-Group. However, if a user creates another Top-Level-Group under the same organization, the new Top-Level-Group does not inherit the sibling Top-Level-Group's subscription or credits.

For example, the owner of the `acmea` Top-Level-Group creates a new organization (also named `acmea`) and transfers the Ultimate-licensed Top-Level-Group into it:

```text
acmea (org)
└── acmea (Top-Level-Group)
```

If the organization owner then creates a new Top-Level-Group called `tlg-new`, they may expect it to behave the same way as `acmea`. It does not, because billing is currently tied to each Top-Level-Group until [organization-level billing](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/customers-gitlab-com/-/merge_requests/15263) exists.

```text
acmea (org)
├── tlg-new
└── acmea (Top-Level-Group)
```

As Organizations become the primary structure users interact with, this distinction becomes easier to miss: creating a group directly under an organization produces a sibling Top-Level-Group rather than extending the billing scope of an existing one.

## Decision

When a user creates a Top-Level-Group inside an organization, we surface a warning during that flow. The warning communicates that:

- Subscription tier (Free, Premium, Ultimate) is scoped to each individual Top-Level-Group and is not shared with sibling Top-Level-Groups in the same organization.
- Credits are also scoped per Top-Level-Group, so a new Top-Level-Group does not inherit credits from its siblings.
- Billing for the new Top-Level-Group is separate from its siblings until [organization-level billing](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/customers-gitlab-com/-/merge_requests/15263) ships.

The warning remains in place until [organization-level billing](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/customers-gitlab-com/-/merge_requests/15263) ships, after which it can be removed.

## Consequences

- Customers retain flexibility to structure their organization with multiple Top-Level-Groups, which is a core value proposition of Organizations.
- Billing remains scoped per Top-Level-Group until [organization-level billing](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/customers-gitlab-com/-/merge_requests/15263) ships. The affected population is small today, but expected to grow as Organizations roll out, so surfacing the distinction early reduces avoidable confusion without blocking adoption.
- The broader plan to roll all existing Top-Level-Groups into organizations is unblocked. Multi-Top-Level-Group organizations remain able to adopt new features (such as Artifact Registry) and to be migrated between cells.
- We avoid one-way-door decisions that would later require building organization-merging, registry-merging, or organization-affinity tooling.
- A user may dismiss the warning and still create a Top-Level-Group whose billing differs from its sibling, leading to surprises later. Clear, specific warning copy reinforced in onboarding mitigates this risk but does not eliminate it.

## Alternatives Considered

1. **Do nothing**: users would create new Top-Level-Groups with no signal that licensing and credits are not shared. Rejected because the divergence only becomes visible later when a feature or credit is unexpectedly unavailable, creating UX papercuts and support load.
1. **Share entitlements**: if one Top-Level-Group has credits or a license attached, share those entitlements across all Top-Level-Groups in the same organization. Rejected because entitlements are currently modeled and audited at the Top-Level-Group boundary, and sharing them across sibling Top-Level-Groups would require significant changes in downstream billing and entitlement systems such as CustomersDot.
1. **Block creation of new Top-Level-Groups inside organizations**: prevent the creation of any new Top-Level-Group in an organization until [organization-level billing](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/customers-gitlab-com/-/merge_requests/15263) exists. Rejected because:
   - It is inconsistent with the existing path that allows multi-Top-Level-Group customers to reconcile into a single organization.
   - It blocks the broader rollout where existing Top-Level-Groups become organizations, since "you cannot create a Top-Level-Group" is a regression for those customers.
   - It blocks multi-Top-Level-Group organizations from adopting features such as Artifact Registry, and from being migrated between cells.
   - It creates one-way-door decisions: forcing customers into separate organizations would later require building organization-merging, registry-merging, and organization-affinity tooling.
   - It undermines a core value proposition of Organizations: letting customers flexibly structure their groups and projects. Self-Managed and Dedicated customers commonly operate with hundreds or thousands of Top-Level-Groups today, suggesting Top-Level-Groups will become the natural unit of organizational structure inside Organizations.

title: 015 Non Isolation Is Permanent
text:
## Context

[Organization Isolation](../isolation.md) assumes every Organization
eventually isolates, and [Non-isolated organizations on GitLab.com](008_non_isolated_organizations_gitlab_com.md) treats
non-isolation only as a starting point on the way there. Whether
non-isolation is temporary or a valid, permanent outcome has been
ambiguous until now. This ADR makes it explicit.

## Decision

A non-isolated Organization is a permanent, valid state. An Organization
is never required to isolate. Isolation is something an Organization's
owner opts into, if and when it makes sense for them — not a
destination every Organization is expected to reach.

## Consequences

1. [Organization Isolation](../isolation.md)'s opening claim, that all
   Organization data will be isolated, is corrected as part of this
   ADR. Its phased rollout further down still describes engineering
   milestones as though every Organization eventually isolates;
   revising that is a separate piece of work.
1. A non-isolated Organization may remain on the legacy Cell
   indefinitely, not only until it isolates. A separate, upcoming
   Organization-scoped request context blueprint works out what this
   means for Cell placement in full.
1. Multi-Organization membership is not a temporary side effect of an
   in-progress migration. It is a permanent capability for any
   Organization that stays non-isolated.

## Alternatives considered

1. **Treat non-isolation as a temporary migration state, with every
   Organization eventually isolating** — rejected. Isolation means no
   data crosses the boundary, so an isolated Organization gives up all
   interop with other Organizations. Many Organizations rely on that
   interop today. Isolating every Organization anyway would break real
   workflows for them; assuming it will happen assumes a replacement
   interop capability that does not exist yet. One idea, sometimes
   called "Org Connect," could someday fill that gap, but it remains a
   long way off.

title: 016 User Context
text:
## Context

See [Request Context](../contexts.md) for the three contexts every
request or process resolves to: Organization context, User context, and
Nil context.

Today, `organization_id` is required, and membership in that
Organization is always treated as exclusive, whether or not the
Organization is isolated. This blocks User context for every User:
every User's identity is always bound to one Organization.

Today, routing also treats "no Organization" the same as "Default
Organization." This blocks Nil context the same way, and causes bugs
(see [issue #605747](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/605747)).

[ADR 015: Non-isolation is a permanent Organization state](015_non_isolation_is_permanent.md)
established that some Organizations stay non-isolated indefinitely. User
context and Nil context only make sense given that fact: they need
Users whose membership is not exclusive, not just Users who have not
isolated yet.

The isolated-Organization work moved straight from "every User belongs
to one Organization" to "every Organization is isolated." It did not
define the states in between. This decision fills that gap.

## Decision

### Isolation, not presence, decides whether membership is exclusive

`organization_id` stays required. It is also the `users` table's
Cells sharding key, so every User needs a concrete value; that cannot
change.

```text
User.organization_id: org_id
```

What changes is the rule for what that value means. Isolation gates
User context, not whether `organization_id` points at an
Organization — it always does. This field only affects User context —
Nil context has no User to apply it to.

Ownership — `organization_id` itself — is always exclusive: it points
at exactly one Organization. What isolation decides is whether
membership is exclusive too:

1. Points at a **non-isolated** Organization — the User has User
   context. Membership is not exclusive: the User can be a member of
   any number of other non-isolated Organizations too, with the same
   account, and User context aggregates across all of them.
1. Points at an **isolated** Organization — required for every member.
   The User has no User context: the Organization is a real boundary,
   and the User's identity does not exist outside it.

Invariant: membership in an isolated Organization implies
`organization_id` points at it, with no exceptions. A User's
`organization_id` points at, at most, one isolated Organization at a
time. It is reassigned once, at isolation, for members not already
pointing at it. It does not change as memberships change afterward.

### Query scoping

Org-scoped finders apply an Organization filter when the Organization
acts as a real boundary:

```ruby
apply_org_filter = org.present? && org.isolated?
```

This is the core rule. There is a separate, secondary optimization for
instances with only one Organization: when `Organization.count == 1`,
filtering is a no-op, so we skip it. This is a performance detail, not
part of the scoping rule.

Self-managed and Dedicated instances have exactly one Organization, the
Default Organization, so `Organization.count == 1` is true for every
install there, and the filter stays a no-op, at no cost.

### Routing must decide, per route, which context applies

Today, a path with no Organization prefix (for example
`/dashboard/...`) implies the Default Organization. A path with an
Organization prefix (for example `/o/acme/...`) implies that
Organization instead.

User context and Nil context are real, separate values now, not
variants of "no Organization" that fall back to the Default
Organization. An unprefixed path like `/dashboard/...` could mean User
context, or it could still mean Organization context bound to the
Default Organization. A path like `/explore` could mean Nil context, or
it could likewise still mean the Default Organization today.

We must choose, one route at a time, which context applies. Some routes
(for example, a personal to-do list) likely want User context. Some
routes (for example, `/explore`) likely want Nil context. Other routes
may still want the Default Organization. This decision does not resolve
that choice. It only makes the three contexts real enough to choose
between.

## Consequences

On .com, every existing User's `organization_id` already points at
the Default Organization, which is non-isolated. No backfill is needed.
User context is available: a User's to-do list, and other User-context
views, span every non-isolated Organization they are a member of — for
example, an open-source contributor who is also a member of a company
Organization.

title: 017 Organization Roles Permissions Artifact Registry
text:
## Context

Organizations is the vehicle for delivering Artifact Registry (AR). AR customers
will use Organizations to manage their data and need custom roles to support
user access during the initial launch. Organizations was deliberately designed
with limited org-level user types (Org Admin and Org User, see
[Organizations ADR 014](014_organization_roles_renamed_to_organization_user_type.md))
to avoid repeating previous mistakes with cascading Group permissions. We should
avoid repeating those mistakes while finding a route to deliver AR-scoped roles
as an interim measure until Teams is delivered.

### Why Groups became a permissions system

GitLab's existing permissions model has at least 6 overlapping systems (base
RBAC, custom roles, settings-based overrides, visibility controls,
authentication layers, and approval/cap systems) with 52+ modifiers that
interact in contradictory and unpredictable ways. A single user action can be
blocked by up to 6 different settings at different levels, with no visibility
into which one is the blocker.

This did not happen by design. Groups were the only available organizational
entity, so every feature that needed access management attached itself to
Groups. Over time, Groups became simultaneously an organizational hierarchy, a
permission inheritance mechanism, a billing unit, a namespace, and a visibility
boundary. Users cannot form a reliable mental model of what they are allowed to
do, and administrators cannot answer "who can do what, where, and why."

Organizations is the successor entity to Groups at the top level, so there is
pressure to attach permissions to it. It is the path of least resistance:
Organizations exists, users exist within it, so why not use it to manage
access? A permissions system tightly coupled to an organizational entity
accumulates modifiers over time. Today it is "Org Admin can manage AR."
Tomorrow it is "Org Admin can manage AR, unless the repo is flagged private,
unless the user was invited externally, unless..." The endpoint is the same
place Groups arrived.

### AR's authorization model

[Artifact Registry ADR 021](../../artifact_registry/decisions/021_authorization.md)
is the best available specification given what was possible to agree on. It is
not a foundation that can be built on indefinitely without revisiting, and
Teams is the mechanism by which the current compromises can be unwound. ADR 021
does not require Organizations to own permissions, and its structure is
compatible with the Teams direction. The model has three layered mechanisms:

1. **Role assignment** via the Auth platform's Relationships API. A principal
   is assigned one of four product-specific roles at the organization level,
   with optional repository-level overrides.
1. **Access rules**. For artifact operations, the set of roles that hold a
   permission can be tightened at the namespace or repository level. Rules can
   only tighten, never expand.
1. **Bootstrapping**. Organization Owners receive full access automatically, so
   someone can assign roles before any explicit assignments exist. This stays in
   sync as ownership changes (a removed owner loses access too), rather than
   being a one-time grant at first activation. It is already built (see
   [Create Org Owner role assignments for organisation owners](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/601665)).

The four AR roles are independent permission buckets, entirely distinct from
platform roles. See
[AR ADR 021](../../artifact_registry/decisions/021_authorization.md) for what
each role can do.

Organization membership grants none of these. Access is closed-by-default,
aligned with GCP, AWS, and Azure, and is what enterprise customers require as a
condition of purchase.

The Auth platform stores role assignments (Relationships API) and provides the
policy evaluation engine (GLAZ/Cedar). AR owns the role definitions, permission
model, and access rules, and evaluates every decision locally without calling
back to GitLab during request processing. Organizations owns the UI for making
and viewing those assignments. The UI is shown to any Artifact Admin, and
write authorization (not an Org Admin check) decides what they can change, so
Organizations does not make an authorization decision of its own.

### The access-assignment problem

The AR closed-by-default model with product-specific roles is correct for the
first product. It becomes a scaling problem by the third or fourth. Each add-on
product that follows AR will define its own roles, its own assignment surface,
and its own management UI. Without a shared mechanism, Org Admins will manage
access across a growing list of product-specific role systems, each with its
own mental model, UI, and assignment overhead. This is the same dynamic that
produced Group-based permissions complexity, replicated at the modular product
level.

The UX team has already documented that the choices made for AR's auth MVC set
the pattern for all subsequent add-on products on Organizations. Branch rules
and settings-related technical debt are an example of how insular, short-term
access management decisions accumulate.

### Auth team capacity and Cells

The Auth team (Sec:SSCS) owns GATE, GLAZ/Cedar, the IAM service, Cloud Connector
v2, and OAuth for Organizations. These workstreams compete for the same small
group of engineers. AR and Cells/OAuth for Organizations have been competing for
that capacity, and the April 24 review escalated this to leadership. The
resolution was an interlock change request moving GATE to FY27 Q4, which
favoured AR by deferring the GATE-dependent OAuth work.

A proof of concept ([MR !236139](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/236139))
demonstrates an alternative for Cells' cross-cell OAuth problem using the
Topology Service. It publishes OAuth application data as Topology Service
claims, uses routable token prefixes for HTTP Router-level routing, and queries
the Topology Service to resolve which cell owns a user account. It avoids
implementing a full-stack IAM service and instead unblocks OAuth for a specific
subset of customers and functionality, accepting a known level of technical
debt in exchange for earlier progress.

The Auth team's assessment identifies three categories of that debt:

1. Work that becomes redundant once IAM is authoritative (Rails/Doorkeeper
   overrides).
1. Work that conflicts with IAM implementation already landing (Workhorse proxy
   for `/oauth/*`, token issuance/revocation APIs).
1. Work requiring cleanup (DB schema, non-persisted records hydrated from
   Topology Service claims).

The architectural objection is that the Topology Service was scoped to routing
only, and the November 2025 architecture decision explicitly excluded auth data
from it. Pressure to deliver Cells is leading us to consider an exception to
that decision. The disagreement over the size of the debt is for Cells
leadership to resolve. GATE has been in development since at least April 2025
and its timeline has already slipped to FY27 Q4.

## Decision

1. **Organizations does not own permissions.** The scope of Organizations is
   deliberately and permanently narrow: **user membership** and **user
   administration**. Any permissions work on Organizations recreates the
   technical debt that Group-based permissions accumulated over a decade. This
   is the intended design, not a temporary limitation, and it should be held as
   a firm boundary.

   Organizations owns:

   1. User membership: which users belong to an Organization.
   1. User administration: the ability for an Org Admin to manage that
      membership.
   1. User onboarding (TLG to Organization migration).
   1. The minimum viable UI for Artifact Admins to assign AR roles to users.
   1. Sending owner changes to the AR bootstrapping sync (see
      [Revoke Artifact Registry owner role on organization removal](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/253370)).

   Organizations does not own:

   1. Role definitions or permission policies of any kind.
   1. Inherited access to any module (AR access is closed-by-default).
   1. The long-term permissions platform, which belongs to AuthZ and Teams.
   1. General-purpose RBAC, role cascading, or permission inheritance.

1. **Teams is the mechanism for access assignment, and must be funded.** Teams
   is the long-term solution to GitLab's access-assignment problem: it replaces
   the practice of overloading Groups as ad-hoc sets of people, which today
   diverges, conflicts, and accumulates debt across every product. Teams is
   **not** a permissions platform. Roles and the authorization model remain
   AuthZ's responsibility, and Teams complements that platform by providing a
   reusable **principal** for those mechanisms to assign access to.

   A Team is a new authorization principal (a named set of users) that behaves
   exactly like the User principal does today, with one added rule: granting an
   access level or role to a Team applies it to every member. Instead of
   assigning AR roles to individual users, then Duo roles to individual users,
   then Security Scanner roles to individual users, an Org Admin assigns users
   to a Team and assigns the Team to a resource. Products define what a Team
   member can do within their scope. Teams introduces no new roles, only a new
   principal, so the number of assignment operations scales with the number of
   Teams, not with the product count.

   Anywhere a user can be assigned today (Groups, Projects, and later
   org-level resources like Artifact Registry), a Team can be assigned using
   the same role and access-level catalog. How a Team is assigned to an
   org-level resource is therefore the same question as how a user is assigned
   to it. That is a resource-model and AuthZ question, not a Teams question.
   In short, Teams is a principal provider (membership), not a permissions
   owner.

1. **AR's delivery path does not depend on resolving Cells' OAuth approach.**
   Whichever way Cells resolves cross-cell OAuth, AR needs only two components
   from the Auth team, and Cells should not compete with them for capacity:

   1. **IAM Data Access** for the Relationships API
   1. **GLAZ** as the policy engine sidecar

   [AR ADR 021](../../artifact_registry/decisions/021_authorization.md) already
   uses both in closed beta (roles assigned through the Relationships API,
   evaluated by GLAZ), so GLAZ is a closed beta need as well as monetized beta.

## Alternatives considered

Without Teams, there are three alternatives:

1. **Each product builds its own role management.** This is what is happening
   now with AR, and it produces fragmentation, inconsistent UX, and an Org Admin
   experience that degrades with every new product.
1. **Permission logic migrates back to Organizations.** This is the mistake
   described in Decision 1.
1. **Access management stays broken at scale.** This is where GitLab's
   Group-based model already is, and where enterprise customers are already
   applying pressure.

## Consequences

### Positive

- Organizations stays small and avoids accumulating the modifiers that made
  Group permissions unmanageable.
- Teams and AR are compatible. ADR 021 was designed with Teams in mind: role
  assignments made through the Relationships API in the first iteration are
  structured as relation tuples, the same primitives Teams will use. When Teams
  is ready, the assignment surface changes (a Team principal rather than an
  individual user) but the underlying authorization model does not, because a
  Team is a new principal type that the existing assignment primitives already
  understand. No migration cost is introduced by the first-iteration
  implementation. The cost comes only from workarounds that bypass the
  Relationships API.
- Each team's boundary is clear: Auth stores assignments and evaluates policy,
  AR owns roles and access rules, and Organizations owns membership and the
  assignment UI.

### Negative

- Teams is currently unfunded. The cost of not funding it is deferred, not
  avoided, and it will be paid in every add-on product shipping decision until
  Teams exists.
- Organizations must deliver an assignment UI for AR roles without owning the
  roles behind it, and that UI is currently without a confirmed engineering DRI.
- AR's four roles are a compromise rather than a principled design. Teams is
  the route to revisiting them.

### AR milestone requirements

These are the requirements this decision places on the AR betas.

**Closed Beta (API-only, design partners):**

1. Relationships API operational (on the critical path).
1. AR implements first-iteration role resolution (querying the Relationships
   API directly).
1. Bootstrapping mechanism for Organization Owners implemented (R6, done).
1. [Interface agreement](../../artifact_registry/agreements/auth.md) updated to
   reflect product-specific roles from Artifact Registry ADR 021.
1. AR team manages onboarding manually, so no Organizations UI is required yet.

AR needs two GATE components for the closed beta: IAM Data Access (the
Relationships API) and GLAZ. The rest of GATE (such as identity federation and
key serving) is not needed in beta, where the interim uses Cloud Connector v1.

**Monetized Beta:**

1. Relationships API stable and production-validated from closed beta.
1. GLAZ/Cedar policy evaluation engine operational.
1. Organizations user management UI, so Artifact Admins can view and update AR
   role assignments.
1. Internal visibility semantics resolved.
1. Bootstrapping confirmed at scale.

title: 018 Isolation Is Four Facts
text:
## Context

Today an Organization has one isolation setting,
`organization_isolations.isolated`, which is true or false. Code checks
it for three different reasons:

- To keep an Organization's Users from joining other Organizations.
- To block new links into or out of the Organization, such as outside
  members or MR dependencies.
- To decide whether the background validator checks the Organization's
  data. When the validator finds a cross-Organization link, it sets
  `isolated = false`.

One setting cannot serve all three. For example, an owner who wants to
try blocking new links before committing must set `isolated = true`,
which also locks their Users into the Organization. Docs share the
problem: [Request Context](../contexts.md) and
[ADR 016](016_user_context.md) say "isolated" without saying which
meaning.

## Decision

Isolation is four independent facts. Docs and code always say which one
they mean, for example "enforced isolation" rather than "isolation."

| Term | Means | Reversible |
|------|-------|------------|
| **Requested isolation** | The owner has asked to isolate, which starts severance. | Until committed |
| **Enforced isolation** | GitLab blocks writes that would create new cross-Organization links. | Until committed |
| **Committed isolation** | The owner has committed, and severance has completed. | No |
| **Verified isolation** | The background validator found no cross-Organization links. | Lapses on drift |

Committed isolation requires requested and enforced isolation. Enforced
isolation stays on from commitment onward.

The table below shows example rules, one or more per fact. It is a
sample, not a complete list: many more rules depend on isolation, and
each one names the fact it reads.

| Example rule | Reads |
|--------------|-------|
| Starting severance | Requested isolation |
| Blocking new cross-Organization links: outside members, MR dependencies, imports | Enforced isolation |
| Organization context ([Request Context](../contexts.md)) | Committed isolation |
| Exclusive membership and `organization_id` reassignment ([ADR 016](016_user_context.md)) | Committed isolation |
| Organization filter on Organization-scoped finders ([ADR 016](016_user_context.md)) | Committed isolation |
| Reporting drift to the owner, naming the link to fix | Verified isolation |
| Moving to another Cell | Committed and verified isolation |

## Consequences

1. An owner can turn on enforced isolation to try it out, then turn it
   off again. Membership, User context, and query filtering do not change.
1. When the validator finds a new cross-Organization link, only verified
   isolation lapses. Committed isolation stays, so the Organization keeps
   Organization context, exclusive membership, and the Organization
   filter while the owner fixes the link.
1. Each `isolated?` caller moves to the fact it means.

## Alternatives considered

1. **One boolean**: forces preview, severance, and drift to share one
   answer.
1. **Isolation levels** (Fully, Resource, or Not Isolated): describe
   only how much data is contained, which is verified isolation alone.
1. **Merging committed into verified isolation**: drift would undo a
   one-way decision.

title: 019 Isolation Severance Process
text:
## Context

[Organization Isolation](../isolation.md) describes isolation as a
constraint the application enforces, but not how an Organization that
is non-isolated today reaches that state, or what happens to the data
already crossing its boundary.

[ADR 008](008_non_isolated_organizations_gitlab_com.md) and
[ADR 015](015_non_isolation_is_permanent.md) establish that
non-isolation is a valid, permanent state.
[ADR 016](016_user_context.md) defines the Organization filter rule for
org-scoped finders. The transition _itself_ remains undefined.

Isolation exists to serve Cell migration. The Cells architecture has no
general shared, cluster-wide data layer, and isolation is what lets an
Organization move without one.

Enforcement has so far been pursued mainly as automatic scoping of all
read queries via the `gitlab-database-data_isolation` gem. That is
untested, because no Organization is isolated yet, and does not produce
a guarantee on its own. This ADR records a different emphasis.

## Decision

### Isolation is an application-enforced boundary

Isolation gives us an assertable boundary around an Organization's data
so it can be moved, and reduces unwanted interaction from outside. It
is a governance and visibility control and a layer of defence in depth,
comparable to group and project visibility. It is not a hard boundary
(such as a separate database per customer, or row-level security) and we
will not describe it as one. Customers whose requirement is a hard
tenancy guarantee are served by GitLab Dedicated. An application-enforced
boundary can be established incrementally and verified by inspection;
a hard boundary could not.

### Severance creates isolation; enforcement preserves it

An Organization becomes isolated through **data severance**: a one-way,
customer-initiated process that removes every relationship reaching
across the boundary, leaving the data self-contained. In priority
order:

1. **Severance** makes the data an island. Without it, the Organization
   arrives on its Cell carrying references it cannot resolve.
1. **Write protection** keeps the island intact. The Organization
   boundary must be protected on database writes so that no bridging
   occurs, before and after the crawl. Policies have a role to play:
   they are the right place to block cross-boundary actions that users
   take through the UI and API, with a clear message. They do not cover
   background jobs or console access, so the database layer is the
   backstop that protects the write itself. The mechanism is still to be
   decided (see Consequences).
1. **Read scoping** is applied to the specific surfaces where outside
   data is otherwise user-visible.

Read scoping is targeted, not generic. Automatic scoping of all reads
at the Rails application level is no longer a precondition of isolation;
query isolation becomes opt-in per code path, covering mentions,
invites, related items, group and project sharing, and autocomplete.

These are product correctness problems regardless. Identifying the full
set of affected code paths is the substantive work. The rule in
[ADR 016](016_user_context.md) is unchanged; this concerns the broader
rewriting of reads.

### Isolation state is asserted by crawling the data graph

An Organization is marked isolated only on the evidence of a completed
crawl that enumerates every relationship leaving its data graph. The
crawl does not assume sharding keys are correct, so it validates
sharding rather than depending on it. Sharding remains required for
aligning and moving data, but is not a precondition for assessing
isolation.

Correct sharding is also not sufficient. A table can be sharded
correctly and still represent data that crosses the boundary. For
example, `group_group_links` rows are sharded, but each one links two
groups that can belong to different Organizations. The crawl therefore
follows relationships between records, and does not stop at checking
that each record carries the right sharding key.

Organizations that have never formed an external
relationship are identified by the same crawl and need no severance.

### What the boundary includes

Included: all data reachable from the Organization's sharding keys
(`organizations`, `namespaces`, `projects`) across the `main`, `ci` and
`sec` databases; its top-level groups and their contents; and the
accounts of consenting members, with the personal namespaces and
projects those accounts own.

Excluded: accounts of members who have not consented and anything they
own, and resources that must stay unique cluster-wide, as described in
[Organization Isolation](../isolation.md).

Severance resolves the rest: memberships held by non-members, forks of
external projects, contributions authored outside the Organization, and
references to data in another Organization. The customer is shown what
severance will remove, as a report generated from the crawl, rather
than a reversible preview of an isolated state.

Severance is not automated end to end. Many of these relationships need
a decision only the customer can make, and removing them is
destructive, so it needs careful handling. The customer reviews the
report and vets or resolves the relationships it lists before anything
is removed. Tooling reduces the effort of that review but does not
replace it.

### Account ownership is opt-in and independent of isolation

Account ownership is a sub-process of severance, but does not depend on
isolation and will not be sequenced behind it. An Organization may take
ownership of its users while remaining non-isolated.

1. Consent is opt-in and given per account. Absence of consent is not
   consent.
1. Without consent we do not move the account or its data. We create a
   new Organization-owned account and link it to the prior one where we
   can. Email addresses must be unique, so the new account cannot reuse
   an address still held by the prior account. How the two are
   reconciled is not decided here and needs its own decision.
1. A personal namespace cannot be detached from the account owning it,
   so consent is not collected per project. A user who wants to retain
   content moves it out before consenting.
1. An Organization with an incomplete consent process cannot be
   isolated or migrated.

## Consequences

1. Severance, write protection and the crawl become the critical path
   for Cell migration. Generic read scoping does not. The crawl is part
   of the severance work, not a separate workstream.
1. The `gitlab-database-data_isolation` gem is retained and applied
   selectively. The work shifts to finding the code paths that need it.
1. Organizations that are already isolated can migrate with no
   customer-facing severance step.
1. Account ownership can be offered on the legacy Cell as a feature in
   its own right, in parallel with isolation work.
1. Isolation must not be positioned as a hard security or data
   segregation guarantee. It can be described as governance, visibility
   and defence in depth.
1. The phased rollout in [Organization Isolation](../isolation.md) still
   describes enforcement as a global constraint on reads. Revising it is
   follow-up work under
   [Phase 2](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/epics/11838) and
   [Phase 3](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/epics/11839).
1. The mechanism for blocking cross-boundary writes remains undecided.
   The existing mechanism detects such a write asynchronously and marks
   the Organization non-isolated after the fact. Blocking requires an
   in-transaction check with a cost on write performance, and needs its
   own decision record.

## Open questions

These need an end-to-end proof of concept to answer.

1. How long does it take to crawl the data graph for Organizations of
   different sizes?
1. How is the crawl triggered, and by whom?
1. How long does the severance process take? It cannot take so long that
   only a handful of Organizations ever become isolated. The goal is for
   isolation to be the default state.
1. Where does write protection sit and how is it enforced? See the
   undecided write-blocking mechanism above.

## Alternatives considered

1. **Automatic scoping of all read queries as the primary enforcement
   mechanism** - rejected as a precondition, retained as a possible
   later step. The production cost is unknown and unmeasurable until an
   Organization is isolated, and it produces no guarantee on its own
   because it can be bypassed and does not cover hard-coded SQL. The
   surfaces that leak are enumerable product features, better fixed
   directly.
1. **Treating isolation as a hard security guarantee** - rejected. The
   available mechanisms do not support the claim, and making it would
   expose us to a worse failure than not making it.
1. **Deriving isolation state from sharding keys alone** - rejected.
   Sharding keys describe where data is expected to belong, not what
   references it. Using them to assert isolation means trusting the
   thing we most need to verify.
1. **A reversible isolation preview** - rejected in favour of the
   severance report. A preview faithful enough to be useful would
   require the application to behave as though the Organization were
   isolated, which is the state the customer is deciding about.

title: 020 Organizations Charter And Invariants
text:
## Purpose

This document defines what Organizations are, what they are not, and the rules that govern how to build features. It is the source of truth for architectural and product decisions about the Organizations layer.

The charter exists so the team can move fast without fragmenting. When a partner team proposes a feature, when an engineering decision surfaces a tradeoff, or when a stakeholder pushes for a scope change, the answer lives here. If the charter does not cover the situation, that is a signal to add to the charter rather than improvise.

Partner teams should use this charter together with the Organizations handbook design document and the relevant ADRs. The charter is the decision framework. The handbook is the implementation design reference.

Changes to this document require sign-off from the Tenant Scale PM and engineering lead. Changes to the invariants section in particular require sign-off from engineering leadership and product leadership.

## User types and terminology

The Organizations layer defines two core customer user types at the Org level: Org Admin and Org Member. User types describe who a person is at the tenant level. They are distinct and separate from roles, which are the access-granting mechanism. Neither user type on its own is a role. An Org Admin holds standing authority by virtue of being an Org Admin; an Org Member holds no access by virtue of Org membership alone.

**Org Admin.** The elevated Org user type. Org Admin holds standing full CRUD across the entire Organization estate: the admin area (billing, settings, user management, entitlement), tenant-wide policy configuration, and read, create, update, and delete authority on every resource attached to the Organization, including resources owned by partner products. This preserves functionality customers already have under TLG Owner (on GitLab.com) and Instance Admin (on Self-Managed and Dedicated), from which Org Admins are seeded at launch. Org Admins gain nothing they did not already hold and lose nothing. On GitLab.com SaaS, the Org Admin and the GitLab Instance Admin are expected to be different users, and the Instance Admin can overrule Org Admin actions when necessary. Instance Admin retains additional infrastructure provisioning and configuration privileges that Org Admin does not hold. The Org Admin is the highest customer authority inside the tenant, but not above GitLab-operated instance administration. We use "Org Admin" rather than "Org Owner" deliberately, because "Owner" collides with the access-granting Group Owner role and reintroduces the access confusion the permission model is built to avoid.

**Org Member.** The baseline Org user type. Being an Org Member means belonging to the Organization. A user becomes an Org Member by belonging to a Group or Project within the Organization. Org Member is the required precondition for holding any Group or Project membership inside the Org, but it does not grant access to any Group, Project, or resource by itself, including read. It is the first gate, not the grant. Access comes from roles: product feature roles scoped to a single product, and the existing Group and Project role model. Org Admin can remove an Org Member, which deactivates that user's effective permissions everywhere inside the Org via universal revocation.

These user types are used consistently throughout this document. The word "role" is reserved for access-granting mechanisms and is never used to describe an Org user type. Breakglass and admin-mode language is reserved for the exceptional access pattern described in the invariants, not for the default user type definition.

## 1. What Organizations are

Organizations is the tenant container for GitLab. It is the unit at which a customer relationship exists with GitLab as a product.

Organizations are:

The entitlement boundary. The Organization defines what a customer is licensed for: subscription tier, seat allocations, credits across their GitLab estate, and any features or add-on capabilities they are entitled to.

The governance, administration, and visibility layer. The Organization is the administrative spine across the customer's estate. Org Admins set organization-wide policy, configure Organization-level settings, manage Org membership, and are responsible for billing, credit management, and entitlement decisions. Org Admin also holds standing full CRUD across the estate, including the contents of Groups, Projects, and partner-product resources attached to the Org (see I5). Org membership itself grants no access to Groups, Projects, or resources; access at the Group and Project level continues to route through the standard permissions model (see I6).

The single deployment unit. The Organization is the unit of deployment across every deployment type: GitLab.com SaaS, Self-Managed, and Dedicated. It is the abstraction customers, admins, and developers interact with regardless of where it physically runs, whether that is a Cell on .com, a Self-Managed instance, or Dedicated infrastructure. This primitive carries a baseline engineering requirement: all features must be org-compatible across all deployment types. A feature that works on one deployment type but breaks the Organization primitive on another is not shippable. Org-compatibility is the recently published engineering requirement that operationalizes this, and it is the single most important constraint partner teams inherit from the Organizations layer.

The identity scope for Org-level constructs. SSO configuration, SCIM provisioning, audit events, compliance settings, and Org-wide policies are scoped to the Organization.

The ultimate parent in the object hierarchy. The structural model is Organization to Groups to Projects. Groups and Projects continue to function as they do today, with Organizations as the new administrative parent layer. Projects are not created directly in an Organization. Groups and Projects remain the operational levels underneath it.

The migration unit. When a customer moves between Cells, between tiers, or platforms, the Organization is the thing that migrates.

That is the affirmative scope. Everything else is described by what follows.

### A note on non-isolated and isolated Organizations

On GitLab.com, an Organization begins as non-isolated. Isolation is a state an Organization can reach later, not a precondition for the model. Features that depend on organization-scoped data must check the current organization state before enforcing organization boundary rules, rather than assuming isolation is always in effect. Proposals that depend on isolation-only assumptions should route to review under the workflow in section 4.

### Where settings live

This is illustrative rather than exhaustive. It anchors the rest of the document's language about governance, workflow, and feature location.

| Level | What lives here |
|---|---|
| Organization | Tenant-wide governance, Organization-level settings, SSO and SCIM, audit and compliance configuration, entitlement state. Most former instance-level and select top-level-group functionality moves here. |
| Group | Permissions, workflow, project hierarchy, team navigation, Group settings. Operates as it does today. |
| Project | Repositories, issues, merge requests, pipelines, and Project settings. Operates as it does today. |

## 2. What Organizations are not

This section is the more valuable half of the charter. The most expensive scope mistakes come from features that sound like they belong to Organizations but actually belong somewhere else, or do not belong anywhere yet.

Organizations are not:

A replacement for Groups. Groups remain the primary structural unit inside an Organization. Permissions, workflow, project hierarchy, and team navigation continue to operate at the Group level. Organizations do not flatten the Group structure or take over its responsibilities.

A permissions root through membership. Membership in an Organization does not imply membership in any Group or Project inside it. Org membership grants no access to any Group, Project, or resource; access at the Group and Project level continues to route through explicit grants under the standard permissions model. Org Admin holds standing full CRUD across the estate as an admin authority tied to the Org Admin user type (see I5), not as an implication of Organization membership. This distinction is load-bearing: it preserves TLG Owner and Instance Admin functionality without turning Org membership itself into an access mechanism.

A resource attachment point. Issues, epics, merge requests, repositories, pipelines, and other work artifacts do not attach to the Organization node. The Organization holds governance, configuration, and visibility. Work lives at User, Group and Project level. Attach to these existing anchor points. New anchor points need careful design and require architectural review. Approved exceptions exist but are rare by design.

The workflow boundary. Issues, merge requests, CI/CD, deployments, and other workflow constructs operate at Project and Group level. There is no Organization-level issue tracker, Organization-level pipeline, or Organization-level board.

The default place for cross-cutting features. When a feature spans multiple Groups inside an Organization, the default answer is to scope it at Group level with cross-Group navigation, not to invent an Org-level version. Org-level scope is reserved for features that materially require global scope across the tenant. The bar is high.

A user identity provider in itself. Users belong to Organizations through membership. SSO and SCIM operate at the Organization level. The underlying user identity model continues to be governed by the existing identity architecture.

A billing UI for end users. The Org Admin sees billing. Project members do not see billing through the Project. Group members do not see billing through the Group. Billing lives in one place inside the Organization.

A vehicle for resolving today's escalations. When a customer or partner team requests a feature framed as "this needs to be at the Org level," the first question is whether it actually requires Org-level scope or whether it would work at Group level with appropriate UX. Most requests resolve at Group level. The ones that do not become candidates under the extension model in section 4.

A feature flag or entitlement system. Organizations is the tenant model. Capabilities that vary by tier, entitlement, or rollout state continue to be governed by the existing feature flag and entitlement systems. The Organization holds entitlement state. It does not become the entitlement system.

## 3. Invariants

These are architectural commitments that cannot be changed without formal review. They exist because the Organizations layer is the foundation for the next several years of GitLab's tenant model, and architectural drift at this layer is expensive to reverse.

If a proposal violates an invariant, the default answer is no. The burden is on the proposer to make the case for changing the invariant, not for the team to make the case for keeping it.

**I1. The hierarchy is Organization to Group to Project.** Organizations sit above Groups. Groups sit above Projects. There is no flattening, no inversion, no alternative structural layer between them.

**I2. One Organization, one deployment.** On GitLab.com, an Organization lives on exactly one Cell. On Self-Managed and Dedicated, the Organization is the instance. In all cases an Organization occupies a single deployment and is never split across Cells or instances. Cross-Cell and cross-instance features are out of scope at the Organization level.

**I3. The Organization is the entitlement boundary; billing anchoring is transitional.** Entitlements scope to the Organization. Billing does not yet anchor to the Organization and remains on the top-level group at launch. The target state moves billing to the Org layer, but until that work with the Billing team lands, both models coexist: Org-level entitlement and TLG-level billing. Features in this space must not assume Org-level billing exists and must remain compatible with the existing TLG billing constructs. Changing the eventual target, for example deciding billing should not move to the Org, goes through architecture review.

**I4. Settings inheritance flows downward.** Organization settings cascade to Groups and Projects. Group settings cascade to subgroups and Projects. There is no upward inheritance and no peer inheritance across Groups.

**I5. Org Admin is the highest customer authority inside the tenant, and holds standing full CRUD across the entire Organization estate.** No customer user type or role inside the Organization has authority above Org Admin for tenant-level policy, configuration, and administration. Org Admin authority is standing read, create, update, and delete across every resource attached to the Organization, including resources owned by partner products. This preserves the functionality customers have today under TLG Owner (on GitLab.com) and Instance Admin (on Self-Managed and Dedicated); Org Admins are seeded from those roles at launch and gain nothing they did not already hold and lose nothing. Partner products must accept Org Admin as an authorized actor on any of their resources without a targeted grant, and must attribute Org Admin authority correctly in their audit events. On SaaS, GitLab Instance Admin sits above Org Admin for instance administration and can overrule Org Admin actions when necessary. Cross-Organization administration, where it exists, is a construct operated by GitLab itself, not by customers. 

**I6. Org membership is not access.** Membership in an Organization does not grant access to any Group, Project, or resource inside it, including read. Access is granted explicitly through the existing permissions model at the Group and Project level, or through product-specific roles at the Org<>Product surface. Features that attempt to bypass this with implicit Org-level access require architecture review and are denied by default. This invariant is paired with I5: Org Admin authority is a property of the Org Admin user type, not of Org membership. Org membership itself is a gate, not a grant.

**I7. The Organization is not a resource attachment point.** Issues, epics, merge requests, repositories, pipelines, and other work artifacts attach to Groups or Projects, not to the Organization. Work lives at User, Group, and Project level. Features that propose attaching new work resources to the Org node require architecture review and a documented reason why the resource cannot live at Group level. Approved exceptions exist but are rare.

**I8. Org-level entities are namespaced inside the Org.** Anything created at Org level (settings, integrations, policies, audit configurations) belongs to that Organization and does not leak across Organizations.

**I9. Migration is the contract.** Any change to the Organizations data model or hierarchy must include a defined migration path for existing customers. We do not ship Org-level changes that require customers to recreate state.

**I10. Org-compatibility across all deployment types is non-negotiable.** Features built at Org level must work on GitLab.com SaaS, Self-Managed, and Dedicated. Deployment-type-specific Org features are not permitted. Where a feature genuinely cannot work on all three, it does not ship at Org level. This is enforced through the org-compatibility engineering requirement and its associated checks.

Adding, removing, or modifying an invariant goes through architecture review, not through partner team negotiation. Sign-off required from engineering leadership, product leadership, and Tenant Scale PM.

## 4. Extension model: alignment and review workflow

Partner teams should not need to stop and schedule a review every time they touch Organizations. The default should still be to build independently when the work fits the model. This workflow exists for the smaller set of cases where a team is unsure, where a proposal may stretch the model, or where a new Org pattern is being introduced.

The simple model is this: if a proposal may create or change Org-level behavior, open a PREP review. PREP is the intake path. Tenant Scale triages it. Most items should get a quick in-alignment answer and move on. Only the narrower set of proposals that introduce a new pattern or push on an invariant should go to architecture review.

Partner teams should use this workflow together with the Organizations handbook design document and the relevant ADRs, which carry the implementation-level detail this charter does not duplicate.

### How the workflow works

**1. The partner team does a quick self-check.**
Owner: Partner PM and EM. Timing: before solutioning is locked.

The self-check is intentionally simple. The team asks:

- Does this actually need Org-level scope, or would Group-level scope with better UX solve the problem?
- Does it introduce a new Org-level entity, setting, permission, or workflow?
- Does it attach a work resource or system of record directly to the Org node?
- Does it depend on changing a charter rule around hierarchy, inheritance, billing, identity, or access?
- Does it depend on isolation-only assumptions rather than checking current organization state?
- Does it introduce a pattern that other teams are likely to copy?

If the answers are clearly no, the team should just build. If any answer is yes or maybe, the team should open PREP.

**2. PREP is the intake path.**
Owner: Partner PM. Timing: as soon as the team sees possible Org-level impact.

The PREP issue should be short. It does not need to be a mini design doc. It just needs enough context for Tenant Scale to route it correctly:

- what the team wants to build
- why Org-level scope may be needed
- which part of the charter seems relevant
- whether the team believes this is an existing pattern, a new pattern, or a possible exception
- links to draft UX or technical notes if they exist

The important thing is timing. Teams should open PREP early, not after implementation is already underway.

**3. Tenant Scale triages the PREP issue.**
Owner: Tenant Scale PM and engineering lead. Timing: initial triage within 3 business days.

Tenant Scale reviews the issue and routes it into one of three paths.

| Path | What it means | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| In alignment | The proposal fits the charter and uses an existing pattern. | Tenant Scale confirms alignment in PREP and the team proceeds. |
| Focused review | The proposal is probably fine, but one part needs discussion or clarification. | Feedback stays in PREP. The team updates the proposal and moves on once the concern is resolved. |
| Architecture review | The proposal introduces a new pattern, pushes on an invariant, or creates material tension with the model. | PREP becomes the handoff into architecture review, and the final decision is recorded back in the same thread. |

This keeps the common case light, while still giving teams a clear path when the work is less obvious.

**4. What always needs architecture review.**

A few categories should never self-clear because they are not just implementation choices. They are proposals to change the model itself.

These always route to architecture review:

- changing the Organization to Group to Project hierarchy
- granting access to Groups, Projects, or resources through Org membership (versus through Org Admin standing CRUD, which is the sanctioned path per I5)
- attaching issues, epics, merge requests, pipelines, repositories, or similar work resources directly to the Org node
- bypassing the inheritance model
- introducing cross-Org visibility by default
- assuming Org-level billing exists before that model ships
- proposing Org-level scope for something that should stay at Group level
- inventing a product-local authority that outranks Org Admin

These are the high-cost mistakes the charter is meant to prevent.

### A note on automation

Over time, parts of this workflow should be automated. The obvious examples are checks that a feature is not attaching work resources directly to the Org node, or that it is not assuming unsupported billing behavior. But the process should not depend on a tool that does not yet exist. The workflow should work today, using PREP, and get more automated over time.

### Decision record

PREP is the system of record. The final state of the issue should make it easy to tell whether the proposal was:

- in alignment
- approved after focused review
- escalated to architecture review
- declined, with rationale

If a proposal establishes a reusable Org pattern, Tenant Scale should add that pattern back into the charter or the supporting guidance. If teams repeatedly hit the same gray area, the document should get better rather than forcing every team through the same debate again.

### Practical rule of thumb

- If the work clearly fits the model, build.
- If the team is unsure, open PREP.
- If the proposal changes the model, send it to architecture review.

That is the whole workflow.

## 5. Decision rights

- Charter changes (non-invariant sections): Tenant Scale PM and engineering lead.
- Invariant changes: Engineering leadership, product leadership, Tenant Scale PM. Goes through architecture review.
- PREP triage: Tenant Scale PM and engineering lead, within 3 business days of intake.
- Architecture review decisions: Architecture review attendees, recorded with rationale in PREP.
- Pattern additions to the charter or supporting guidance: Tenant Scale engineering lead, with PM sign-off on user-facing implications.
- Org-versus-Group judgment: Tenant Scale PM when the self-check and charter do not resolve it.
- Roadmap prioritization: Tenant Scale PM, informed by partner team demand and platform capacity.
- Permissions strategy (Org-level roles, assignment logic, refinement of standing CRUD): AuthZ PM, in coordination with Tenant Scale PM. The charter invariants (I5, I6, I7) frame the boundary; AuthZ owns the model inside it. 

## 6. Deliberately out of scope for v1 of this charter

Items deferred to a later revision:

- Isolation roadmap and architectural treatment.
- Multi-Organization features (cross-Org navigation, cross-Org reporting). Not on the roadmap and not addressed here.
- Org-to-Org migration, merge, and split flows. Acknowledged as a future need, not specified here.
- The specific data model for Teams. Covered in the Teams design doc, referenced but not duplicated.
- Org-level billing: credit pooling, entitlement review and adjustment through the admin area, and the move of the billing anchor from the TLG to the Organization. This is active work with the Billing team, not in the initial launch. Billing remains anchored to the TLG until this lands, and the eventual design must account for a transitional state where Org-level entitlement and TLG-level billing coexist.
- Groups and Projects role model changes. Out of scope at launch. Any collision surfaced by the Org<>Product role UI routes through PREP.

## 7. How to use this document

For Tenant Scale team members: this is the spine of every architectural conversation. If a decision feels load-bearing and the charter does not cover it, propose an addition rather than deciding in a one-off channel.

For partner teams: read sections 1 through 4 before proposing Org-related work. The extension model in section 4 is the right entry point for most requests. Use it alongside the Organizations handbook design document and the relevant ADRs.

For leadership and stakeholders: section 3 is the place to push back on or extend the architectural commitments. The rest of the document follows from there.

Questions, proposals, and disagreements go to `#g_organizations` channel. Disagreement with the charter is valuable input. Working around it is not.

## 8. References

- Organization | The GitLab Handbook
- Organizations ADR 006: Administration and Settings | The GitLab Handbook
- Organizations ADR 007: Self-managed and Dedicated Single Organization | The GitLab Handbook
- Organizations ADR 008: Non-isolated organizations on GitLab.com | The GitLab Handbook
- Organizations ADR 011: Universal Onboarding Workflow | The GitLab Handbook
- Organization Lifecycle | The GitLab Handbook
- Permissions Framework for Org-Anchored Products | Organizations Trackers and Roadmaps

title: Faq
text:
## Do we expect large SaaS customers to be licensed at the Organization level?

Yes. At the moment billing will move to the Organization level. We will continue to update [Organization and Billing](billing.md).

## Will Self Managed and Dedicated allow for multiple Organizations?

Yes, most likely. Initially our focus will be on GitLab.com but we understand there is demand for multiple Organizations on other platforms and anticipate rolling this feature out eventually.

## How will Organizations affect Self Managed?

Self Managed will remain relatively unchanged. The Organization will be exposed to Self Managed just like other platforms, and features may shift up or down to the Organization level.

Eventually we expect all platforms will provide the ability to operate multiple Organizations.

Our goal is to minimize disruption to Self Managed and Dedicated while we try to bring GitLab.com to parity with the other platforms.

In the longer term, we anticipate faster feature development by having Organizations as a common top level entity across all platforms.

## Can a user be a member of multiple Organizations?

Yes, as long as those Organizations are non-isolated. Ownership (`organization_id`) always points at exactly one Organization, but membership is only exclusive to that Organization once it isolates (see [The User's Home Organization](users.md#the-users-home-organization)); before that, the same account can be a member of any number of non-isolated Organizations. See [Request Context](contexts.md) for the full model. Membership in a single isolated Organization is the long-term goal once isolation ships for a given Organization.

## Do we expect to be able to configure alternate GitLab domain names for Organizations (such as `customer.gitlab.com`)?

There is no plan at this point to allow configuration of alternate GitLab domain names.
GitLab Dedicated will be a much better fit for that at this moment.

## Do we expect Organizations to have visibility settings (public/private) of their own?

Visibility is documented on the main [Organization page](_index.md#visibility).

## What would the migration of a feature from the top-level Group to the Organization look like?

We will provide more information at a later date. It won't be possible to build a feature completely at the Organization level until the Organization feature is released.

However, data at the top-level group will still need to be linked back to an Organization for Organization data isolation purposes.

## How many Cells and Organizations do we expect to exist on GitLab.com?

At this time we can only make rough estimates of how many Organizations or Cells may exist.

As the Cells will be multi-tenanted, with many Organizations belonging to one Cell, there will inevitably be more Organizations than Cells.

There will likely be thousands of Organizations spread across the Cells.
Possibly even millions of Organizations, if most top-level groups get converted to their own Organization.

There will also likely be hundreds or even thousands of Cells.

At the start however, there will be far fewer of each, as we gain operational experience in production with customer data and decide how much to scale.

title: Isolation
text:
This blueprint details requirements for Organizations to be isolated.
Read more about what an Organization is in [Organization](_index.md).

Isolation is four independent facts, described in [Isolation States](#isolation-states). They are orthogonal to the Organization lifecycle (`unconfirmed`, `confirmed`, `active`, etc.) described in [Organization Lifecycle](lifecycle.md), with one dependency: requested isolation requires the organization to be `active`.

## What?

An Organization can reach committed isolation, where data and features
stay within that Organization's boundary. Non-isolation is also a
valid, permanent state on its own. See [ADR 015: Non-isolation is a permanent Organization state](decisions/015_non_isolation_is_permanent.md).

Below is a depiction of multiple Organizations within a single instance called "Cell 1".

![Organization Isolation](/images/engineering/architecture/design-documents/organization/diagrams/organization-isolation.drawio.png)

Many features in GitLab can link data together.
A few examples of links that enforced isolation blocks:

1. [Related issues](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/project/issues/related_issues.html): Users would not be able to take an issue in one Project in `Organization A` and relate that issue to another issue in a Project in `Organization B`.
1. [Share a project/group with a group](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/members/sharing_projects_groups/#invite-a-group-to-a-group): Users would not be allowed to share a Group or Project in `Organization A` with another Group or Project in `Organization B`.
1. [System notes](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/project/system_notes.html): Users would not get a system note added to an issue in `Organization A` if it is mentioned in a comment on an issue in `Organization B`.

An Organization becomes isolated through data severance, and the isolation boundary is application-enforced rather than a hard guarantee. See [ADR 019: Data severance and the scope of Organization isolation](decisions/019_isolation_severance_process.md).

## Isolation States

Isolation is four independent facts: requested, enforced, committed, and
verified isolation. [ADR 018: Isolation is four facts, not one](decisions/018_isolation_is_four_facts.md)
defines each one, with example rules. Every rule says which one it
reads, for example "enforced isolation" rather than "isolation."

A typical path:

1. **Preview (optional).** The owner turns on enforced isolation.
   Membership, User context, and query filtering stay unchanged.
1. **Request.** Requested isolation starts severance and turns on
   enforced isolation, so removed links stay removed.
1. **Commit.** Severance completes. Committed isolation brings
   Organization context, exclusive membership, and the Organization
   filter.
1. **Verify.** The validator keeps checking. A lapse in verified
   isolation calls for fixing the specific link; committed isolation
   holds throughout.

Where older documents say "isolated," read committed isolation.

## Why?

There are two primary purposes for Organization Isolation:

1. Organization Portability.
2. Customer data segregation.

### Organization Portability

By establishing clear boundaries around data and features, we can manage Organizations as self-contained structures. This allows Organizations to become portable between our various SaaS and Self Managed platforms, and also internally across our Cells.

In the case of Cells, data association between Organizations could mean crossing Cell boundaries which won't work.

![Broken Organization Isolation](/images/engineering/architecture/design-documents/organization/diagrams/organization-isolation-broken.drawio.png)

If today we allowed users to create Organizations that linked to data in other Organizations, these links would suddenly break when an Organization is moved.
For this reason we need to ensure from the very beginning of rolling out Organizations to customers that it is impossible to create any links that cross the Organization boundary, even when Organizations are still on the same instance.
If we don't, we will create even more mixed up related data that cannot be migrated between instances.
Not fulfilling the requirement of isolation means we risk creating a new top-level data wrapper (Organization) that cannot actually be used as a sharding key.

### Customer Data Segregation

On GitLab.com there is demand for customers to have their own private data collection that is not part of the shared data pool. They want hard boundaries between their data and outside users, and also do not want to be distracted by data outside of their interests.

Secondly, there is also demand for multi-tenant facilities within the Self Managed and Dedicated platforms. Organization isolation will allow these platforms to operate distinct GitLab data segments within the same instance.

## How?

Multiple POCs have been implemented to demonstrate how we will provide robust developer facing and customer facing constraints in the GitLab application and database that enforce the described isolation constraint.
These are:

1. [Enforce Organization Isolation based on `project_id` and `namespace_id` column on every table](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/133576)
1. [Enforce Organization Isolation based on `organization_id` on every table](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/129889)
1. [Validate if a top-level group is isolated to be migrated to an Organization](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/131968)

The major constraint these POCs were trying to overcome was that there is no standard way in the GitLab application or database to even determine what Organization (or Project or namespace) a piece of data belongs to.
This means that the first step is to implement a standard way to efficiently find the parent Organization for any model or row in the database.

The proposed solution is ensuring that every single table in the database except for those in cell-local schemas must include a valid sharding key that is a reference to `projects`, `namespaces` or `organizations`. This will mean that all Organization specific data will be directly or indirectly associated with an Organization.
At first we considered enforcing everything to have an `organization_id`, but we determined that this would be too expensive to migrate large Organizations.
The added benefit is that more than half of our tables already have one of these columns.
Additionally, if we can't consistently attribute data to a top-level Group, then we won't be able to validate if a top-level Group is safe to be moved to a new Organization.

Once we have consistent sharding keys we can use them to validate all data on insert are not crossing any Organization boundaries.
We can also use these sharding keys to help us decide whether:

- Existing namespaces in the default Organization can be moved safely to a new Organization, because the namespace is already isolated.
- The namespace owner would need to remove some links before migrating to a new Organization.
- A set of namespaces is isolated as a group and could be moved together in bulk to a new Organization.

## Detailed steps

### Organization Isolation - Phase 1

[Organization Isolation - Phase 1](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/epics/11837) [Status: Completed]

1. Implement developer facing documentation explaining the requirement to add these sharding keys and how they should choose.
1. Add a way to declare a sharding key in `db/docs` and automatically populate it for all tables that already have a sharding key
1. Implement automation in our CI pipelines and/or DB migrations that makes it impossible to create new tables without a sharding key.
1. Implement a way for people to declare a desired sharding key in `db/docs` as
   well as a path to the parent table from which it is migrated. Will only be
   needed temporarily for tables that don't have a sharding key
1. Attempt to populate as many "desired sharding key" as possible in an
   automated way and delegate the MRs to other teams
1. Fan out issues to other teams to manually populate the remaining "desired
   sharding key"

### Organization Isolation - Phase 1.5

[Organization Isolation - Phase 1.5](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/epics/13678) - [Status: In Progress]

1. Start manually creating then automating the creation of backfill migrations for
   tables to populate sharding keys from "desired sharding key".
1. Wait for the migration of ~300 tables that are missing a sharding key to finish:
   1. The Tenant Scale team migrates the first few tables.
   1. We build a dashboard showing our progress and continue to create
      automated MRs for the sharding keys that can be automatically inferred
      and automate creating issues for all the sharding keys that can't be
      automatically inferred

### Organization Isolation - Phase 2

[Organization Isolation - Phase 2](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/epics/11838) - [Status: Pending]

1. Once all tables have sharding keys we ship an
   evolved version of the
