and containers happens in the same background job. This lack of isolation could mean
that if attestation of OCI images fails, this failure can spread to the
attestation of artifacts within that same build. Other builds would not be
affected.

This can be mitigated by appropriate [exception handling](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/logging/#exception-handling)
 and [proper abstractions](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/reusing_abstractions/).

Proper abstractions and reusable code will be produced for the final
implementation.

## Testing, Performance and Availability

To ensure high-levels of availability and robust performance, several
measures will be put in place by the SSCS stage's Pipeline Security team:

- Manual testing of the attestation process in production behind a feature flag,
  to prevent accidental impacts to other GitLab users.
- End-to-end tests for our `cosign` integration will provide assurance
  for our `cosign` upgrade.
- We will implement extensive test coverage, particularly for scenarios
  involving registry failures, as well as Sigstore failures. This will ensure
  the appropriate measures are in place to allow for the graceful handling of
  outages.
- Sidekiq jobs will be configured to retry as appropriate to ensure that sporadic
  outages of Sigstore infrastructure or registries do not lead to persistent
  failures in SLSA attestation generation.
- This feature will only be enabled for users who specifically opt-in.
- We will use Sidekiq's default [retry configuration](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/sidekiq/#retries) for
  dealing with Sigstore transient failures. We have also flagged our worker as
  having [external dependencies](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/sidekiq/worker_attributes/#jobs-with-external-dependencies).

title: Example values, in seconds. The CA must outlive every leaf certificate it issues.
text:
## Background

The ~"group::build security" group, part of the SSCS stage, is working towards
providing users with
[SLSA Level 3 Provenance Attestations](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/slsa_level_3/).
As a simplified summary, in the [context of GitLab](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/slsa_level_3/),
a provenance statement is a JSON document that correlates the SHA-256 sum of an
artifact or an OCI container with the build information. A worker then performs a
[digital signature](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/slsa_level_3/decisions/004_attestation_in_sidekiq/),
called a provenance attestation, stored as a "Sigstore Bundle" blob.

These digital signatures are kicked off by the background worker, but they
leverage what is known as the "public-good" Sigstore infrastructure. More
information is available in the [Sigstore Overview](https://docs.sigstore.dev/about/overview/)
page. This "public-good" infrastructure is not suitable for private
repositories, and self-managed and dedicated deployments for reasons highlighted
below.

This ADR captures our decision to perform signatures using a per-project
certificate authority (CA) whose key is stored within PostgreSQL, and documents
our rationale for doing so. Additionally, this ADR contains information
regarding our decision to not use Rekor, or any other transparency log or
timestamp authority, in these cases, while a permanent decision is made
regarding its usage.

Additionally, it highlights the new UX our users will leverage in order to use
this functionality, as well as what technical mechanisms will be used in this
integration.

### Why this change is required

The points highlighted below, specifically the disclosure of information to
Rekor and the difficulty of the integration with Sigstore for self-managed and
Dedicated deployments, show that our current implementation is not viable for
these kinds of customers.

By implementing the changes in this ADR, we are able to sign attestations in
the control plane for every repository type and deployment type, by leveraging
already existing infrastructure in a cost-effective way. By using the proposed
solution our users are able to easily configure their pipelines to generate
attestations which can then be verified before consumption, preventing supply
chain attacks for our most security conscious users.

### References

- [[Discussion] UX to enable SLSA provenance generation (#547903)](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/547903#note_2748278333)
- [ADR 002: Generate SLSA Provenance in GitLab Rails backend](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/slsa_level_3/decisions/002_provenance_generation_location/)
- [ADR 004: Bundle cosign with GitLab Rails, perform attestation in GitLab Rails backend](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/slsa_level_3/decisions/004_attestation_in_sidekiq/)
- [ADR 006: Enable the creation of SLSA Level 3 Attestations for OCI images](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/slsa_level_3/decisions/006_signing_with_sbom_and_provenance_in_oci/)
- [Cosign Image Signatures. The protocol format explained!](https://medium.com/sigstore/cosign-image-signatures-77bab238a93)
- [Phase 5: OCI Containers Attestation (#20683) · Epic · gitlab-org](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/20683)
- [Signing artifacts, attesting builds, and why you should do both](https://some-natalie.dev/blog/signing-attesting-builds/)
- [SLSA • Build: Requirements for producing artifacts](https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.2/build-requirements)
- [SLSA • Provenance](https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.1/provenance)
- [SLSA Level 3 Provenance Attestations](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/slsa_level_3/)
- [OpenBao chart | GitLab Docs](https://docs.gitlab.com/charts/charts/openbao/)
- [GitLab Secrets Manager (OpenBao) | GitLab Docs](https://docs.gitlab.com/administration/secrets_manager/#openbao-architecture)

## Desired user experience (UX)

Changes will be required to the UX specified in the [SLSA level 3 provenance attestations](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/pipeline_security/slsa/level_3/)
page.

A new CI/CD variable controls whether to use a local CA. This optional
variable, `ATTEST_METHOD`, accepts two possible values: `SIGSTORE`, or
`LOCAL_CA`. This value defaults to `SIGSTORE` for public projects in GitLab.com,
and `LOCAL_CA` for private repositories, GitLab dedicated and self-managed.

`ATTEST_METHOD` applies to both `ATTEST_BUILD_ARTIFACTS` and
`ATTEST_CONTAINER_IMAGES`. Like those variables, it's read only from the
`variables` keyword in `.gitlab-ci.yml`. Variables set anywhere else, such as
project, group, instance or pipeline variables, are ignored. The value is
case-insensitive and surrounding whitespace is ignored. Any other value falls
back to the default.

GitLab creates a project's CA the first time the project produces a `LOCAL_CA`
attestation.

Specifically, the new UX will look as follows:

```yaml
build-job:
  stage: build
  variables:
    ATTEST_BUILD_ARTIFACTS: true
    ATTEST_METHOD: LOCAL_CA
  script:
    - echo "Hello, $GITLAB_USER_LOGIN!"
    - echo "Hello, $GITLAB_USER_LOGIN!" > test.txt
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - test.txt
```

Here's an example of the UX with the optional value not included. In this case
the behavior will be to use the default value.

```yaml
build-job:
  stage: build
  variables:
    ATTEST_BUILD_ARTIFACTS: true
  script:
    - echo "Hello, $GITLAB_USER_LOGIN!"
    - echo "Hello, $GITLAB_USER_LOGIN!" > test.txt
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - test.txt
```

Users of this feature can override this default value. The rationale for
allowing users to override this value is twofold. Firstly, this gives users who
are able to use Sigstore in a self-managed instance the choice to use Sigstore.
Secondly, making this value explicit allows us to add other values, such as
other BYOK providers.

Our current behavior is to disallow `SIGSTORE` for private projects, which is
preserved: a non-public (private or internal) project that sets
`ATTEST_METHOD: SIGSTORE` is not attested. Public projects can choose
`LOCAL_CA`.

## Technical background

Largely, the Sigstore public good infrastructure authenticates with OIDC, and
then if the authentication is successful, performs a signature. The identity of
the signature, will be dependent on what identity is used to authenticate
against that OIDC server. An example of an identity would be a username or
email, although in this process we authenticate as a repository/branch
combination.

The threat model clarifies what the signature means:

> Under normal operation (no Sigstore compromise), verifying a "keyless" signature from `user@example.com` using the ExampleIdP identity provider at a given timestamp guarantees that the signature was created by a signer who successfully authenticated to Sigstore using that identity at that time.

### On the usage of the above mechanism for private repositories on GitLab.com

While this is suitable for public projects, where the artifacts and container
images are known to the public and not sensitive, private projects within
GitLab.com may not wish to disclose this information publicly. Here is an
example attestation for a container: [Rekor Search](https://search.sigstore.dev/?uuid=108e9186e8c5677a23c91a821a2732ffad83e22d730c98dee8af822aaaaac5fe512fdc8eabebc6fd).
Information disclosed is: hash of the binary, name of the organization, name of
the project, name of the repository and builder, among other details.

As of this point, the assumption is that disclosure of information is acceptable
for public projects, but unacceptable for private projects. Due to this,
`SIGSTORE` attestations are only allowed for public projects. `LOCAL_CA`
attestations are never sent to public infrastructure, so they're allowed for
every project.

### On the usage of the above mechanism for self-managed and dedicated deployments

In addition to the point above about information disclosure for private
projects, there is an additional constraint that prevents the usage of
"public-good" Sigstore infrastructure for self-managed and dedicated
deployments.

In the explanation above, there is a mention of the "OpenID Provider". These are
restricted by default, and Fulcio maintains an allowlist. In the case of
GitLab.com, we've performed specific work to ensure our OIDC provider is added
to the list, as tracked in the "[Use GitLab.com as an OIDC provider for cosign (#10254)](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/10254)"
ticket.

In the case of self-managed and dedicated deployments, each of our customers
would need to create an MR similar to [this one](https://github.com/sigstore/fulcio/pull/1327)
in order for their instance to be allowed. This is not practical or advisable to
do, and the changes highlighted in this ADR would prevent our customers from
having to go through this process.

### On Rekor

#### What is Rekor

From: [An Introduction to Rekor — Chainguard Academy](https://edu.chainguard.dev/open-source/sigstore/rekor/an-introduction-to-rekor/):

> Rekor stores records of artifact metadata, providing transparency for
> signatures and therefore helping the open source software community monitor
> and detect any tampering of the software supply chain. On a technical level,
> it is an append-only (sometimes called "immutable") data log that stores
> signed metadata about a software artifact, allowing software consumers to
> verify that a software artifact is what it claims to be. You could think of
> Rekor as a bulletin board where anyone can post, and the posts cannot be
> removed, but it's up to the viewer to make informed judgements about what to
> believe.
> [...]
> Users of Rekor also have an offline method for determining whether a
> particular entry exists in a Rekor log by leveraging inclusion proofs, which
> are enabled through Merkle trees. Merkle trees are a data structure that
> enable a party to use cryptographic hash functions — a way of mapping
> potentially large values to relatively short digests — to prove that a piece
> of data is contained within a much larger data structure. This proof is
> accomplished by providing a series of hashes to the user, hashes that if
> recombined prove to the user that an entry is indeed in the Rekor log.
> Sigstore users can "staple" such an inclusion proof to an artifact, attaching
> the inclusion proof next to an artifact in a repository, and therefore proving
> that the artifact is indeed included in Rekor. For a detailed description of
> Merkle trees and inclusion proofs, refer to the helpful resources section at
> the end of this chapter.

Key characteristics of Rekor are:

- Immutable
- Tamper-resistant

More information on the role that Rekor plays in public infrastructure is
available in the [Threat Model](https://docs.sigstore.dev/about/threat-model/)
page. Additional research into Rekor, and how to potentially replicate that behavior
in-house, can be found in the [Explore designs for multi-tenant attestations (#21881)](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/21881)
page.

#### Is use of an immutable, tamper-resistant log a requirement for SLSA L3?

There is an additional [potential requirement around a replacement for Rekor](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/590549#note_3326516370).
Fundamentally though, the use of Rekor is associated with the usage of Sigstore
and not a requirement under SLSA L3. The only two requirements exclusive to L3
are "Unforgeable", and "Isolated":

- **Unforgeable**: Provenance MUST be strongly resistant to forgery by tenants.
- **Isolated**: The build platform ensured that the build steps ran in an isolated environment, free of unintended external influence.

More discussion in https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/590549#note_3326516370

## Decision: Perform signing using a key stored in PostgreSQL

A full discussion of the options reviewed can be found on the "[Investigate Options for self-managed/customer owned Sigstore. (#590549)](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/590549)"
ticket.

After carefully reviewing our options, considering aspects such as complexity of
implementation, ease of use for our customers, as well as security and other
aspects, we've decided to:

- Perform signing using a per-project root CA whose key is stored in
  PostgreSQL, and a new leaf certificate and key for every attestation. More
  detail below.
- Hold off on the decision to implement a tamper-resistant log of attestations,
  based on the discussion [in this comment](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/590549#note_3326516370).
  In the meantime, `LOCAL_CA` attestations do not use Rekor or a timestamp
  authority (TSA) until a decision is made on the issue.

### Disabling Rekor and timestamp authorities

`LOCAL_CA` signing is configured so that cosign doesn't contact any
transparency log or timestamp authority.

Without a transparency log or TSA, there is no trusted record of when an
attestation was signed. Verifiers check the signing certificate against the
current time, so the certificate has to stay valid for as long as the
attestation needs to be verifiable. This is why leaf certificates are
long-lived.

### Key generation and storage

At a high-level, there are two types of keys in this solution:

- A root certificate authority (CA) key for each project.
- A leaf key and certificate for each attestation. The leaf certificate is
  issued by the project's CA, and its private key is discarded after signing.
  See [Generation of ephemeral keys for signing](#generation-of-ephemeral-keys-for-signing).

Each project's CA is stored in PostgreSQL, with the private key encrypted at
rest. Handling of these keys is done in accordance with the
[Secure coding development guidelines](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/secure_coding_guidelines/#handling-credentials),
specifically the "Handling Credentials" section, as private keys are explicitly
mentioned there. Also relevant to this decision are the
[GitLab Cryptography Standard](/handbook/security/policies_and_standards/cryptographic-standard/) and
the [Encryption Standard](https://internal.gitlab.com/handbook/security/policies_and_standards/standards/encryption-standard/).

Keys use ECDSA on the P-256 curve, and certificates are signed with SHA-256.
RSA was also viable, but we chose ECDSA for its security and performance
characteristics. Both meet the policies linked above.

The following example creates a CA certificate with these algorithms and
the extensions a CA needs. It runs as plain Ruby, for example in `irb`, and
its validity periods are examples. See the
[CA Certificate section of the OpenSSL documentation](https://ruby.github.io/openssl/OpenSSL.html#module-openssl-ca-certificate)
for background.

```ruby
require 'openssl'
require 'securerandom'

# Example values, in seconds. The CA must outlive every leaf certificate it issues.
ca_validity = 5 * 365 * 24 * 60 * 60 # 5 years
clock_skew = 5 * 60 # 5 minutes, backdates not_before

ca_key = OpenSSL::PKey::EC.generate('prime256v1')
ca_name = OpenSSL::X509::Name.new([%w[CN ca], %w[DC gitlab]])

ca_cert = OpenSSL::X509::Certificate.new
ca_cert.version = 2 # X.509 v3
ca_cert.serial = SecureRandom.random_number(1...(2**159))
ca_cert.not_before = Time.now - clock_skew
ca_cert.not_after = Time.now + ca_validity
ca_cert.public_key = ca_key
ca_cert.subject = ca_name
ca_cert.issuer = ca_name

extension_factory = OpenSSL::X509::ExtensionFactory.new
extension_factory.subject_certificate = ca_cert
extension_factory.issuer_certificate = ca_cert

ca_cert.add_extension(extension_factory.create_extension('basicConstraints', 'CA:TRUE', true))
ca_cert.add_extension(extension_factory.create_extension('keyUsage', 'keyCertSign,cRLSign', true))
ca_cert.add_extension(extension_factory.create_extension('subjectKeyIdentifier', 'hash'))

ca_cert.sign(ca_key, OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'))
```

CA operations sit behind an abstraction, so that a different key store, such
as a cloud KMS, can be added later to support BYOK without changing how leaf
certificates are built.

Each attestation records which method signed it, so the method stays known
even if the CA that signed it is later removed.

Key rotation and revocation are out of scope for this ADR.

### Generation of ephemeral keys for signing

This section is superseded by
[ADR 008: Signing LOCAL_CA attestations](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/slsa_level_3/decisions/008_signing_local_ca_attestations/).

In summary, each attestation is signed with a new ECDSA P-256 key. The
project's CA issues a leaf certificate for that key, with the identity in a URI
Subject Alternative Name, for example
`https://gitlab.example.com/my-group/my-project//.gitlab-ci.yml@refs/heads/main`.
The certificate is long-lived and stored in the attestation's bundle, and the
private key is discarded after signing.

ADR 008 also records how cosign is configured to sign offline, how signing
material is kept private, and what each attestation records about how it was
signed.

### Signature verification

The verification of a signature can be performed manually, or through
GitLab's `glab` tool. Calling `glab` will look identical to how it is documented
in the [SLSA level 3 provenance attestations](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/pipeline_security/slsa/level_3/#verifying-attestations)
page. For example:

```bash
glab attestation verify gitlab-org/gitlab filename.txt
```

Code for this command-line endpoint is available at [internal/commands/attestation/verify/verify.go](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cli/-/blob/main/internal/commands/attestation/verify/verify.go).
This will be modified slightly for key verification.

This tool will do the following:

1. Get the project metadata.
2. Calculate the digest of the artifact/container.
3. Retrieve the provenance metadata, with the [Attestations API](https://docs.gitlab.com/api/attestations/).
   This metadata will be indicative of whether the verification needs to happen
   with Sigstore or with the solution indicated in this ADR. If the latter is
   true, the endpoint will return the signed public key associated with the
   ephemeral key.
4. Retrieve the bundle associated with the attestation.
5. Retrieve a list of valid Certificate Authorities.

With this information, we will perform the following verifications.

1. We will call the `cosign` binary referencing the key and bundle file,
   similarly to how we verify with Sigstore. This will ensure the provenance is
   signed by the key associated with it.
2. We will ensure the ephemeral key is signed by a valid "Root CA". This will be
   done with the information returned by step 5 above.
3. We will ensure the `subject` field matches the `ci_ref_uri` of the
   repository. This field is documented in [OpenID Connect (OIDC) Authentication Using ID Tokens](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/secrets/id_token_authentication/).

Step 1 can be completed with the instructions provided in the [Signing with Self-Managed Keys](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/key_management/signing_with_self-managed_keys/)
page. Steps 2 and 3 can be achieved with the following code in Ruby:

```ruby
cert.verify ca_key.public_key
=> true
cert.subject == name
=> true
```

An attacker without access to this key cannot generate a valid certificate for
repositories they cannot control. This is because the CN of the certificate is
set to `ci_ref_uri` and the certificate is generated using the `ca_key`, which
is securely stored in the database.

To clarify, if a user generates a `SupplyChain::Attestation` for `RepoA` and
`main` branch, this will have a different subject to the one generated for
`MaliciousRepo` `main` branch. This ensures that if a user does not have write
access to the specific branch, the attestations generated by our system for
other branches cannot be used to bypass verification procedures.

### Positive Consequences

- No external services for this feature, it is entirely self-contained.
  `LOCAL_CA` signing contacts no Sigstore, Rekor or TSA service, and uses the
  `cosign` binary that GitLab already ships for Sigstore attestations
  ([ADR 004](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/slsa_level_3/decisions/004_attestation_in_sidekiq/)).
- Would work well in combination with
  [BYOK](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/590549#note_3326459572)
  in a future iteration, through the abstraction described above.
- Relatively small engineering footprint and cost.
- Does not require any new services to be created or maintained.
- Supports all environments and all repository types.
- Each project has its own CA, so one project's CA can't issue certificates
  that verify for another project.
- No instance or project configuration is required.

### Negative Consequences

- Does not include a solution in terms of a tamper-proof, immutable record of
  signatures, such as Rekor, or a trusted signing time. This is a temporary
  situation until a permanent solution is found. See [this comment](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/590549#note_3326516370)
  for more information.
- CA private keys are encrypted with the instance's encryption keys. As with
  other encrypted data, backups must include the instance's secrets.
- Signing relies on a recent version of `cosign` being available wherever
  attestations are signed.

## Testing, Performance and Availability

To ensure high-levels of availability and robust performance, several
measures will be put in place by the SSCS stage's Build Security team:

- Manual testing of the attestation process in production behind a feature flag,
  to prevent accidental impacts to other GitLab users.
- End-to-end tests for our `cosign` integration will provide assurance
  for our `cosign` upgrade.
- We will implement extensive test coverage, particularly for failure scenarios.
  This will ensure the appropriate measures are in place to allow for the
  graceful handling of outages.
- Sidekiq jobs will be configured to retry as appropriate to ensure that sporadic
  outages do not lead to persistent failures in SLSA attestation generation.
- This feature will only be enabled for users who specifically opt-in.
- We will use Sidekiq's default [retry configuration](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/sidekiq/#retries) for
  dealing with transient failures. We have also flagged our worker as having
  [external dependencies](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/sidekiq/worker_attributes/#jobs-with-external-dependencies).
  This applies to `SIGSTORE` attestations. `LOCAL_CA` attestations don't depend
  on Sigstore services.

title: ca_cert and ca_key come from the CA example in ADR 007.
text:
## Context

[ADR 007](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/slsa_level_3/decisions/007_attestations_private_dedicated_self_hosted/)
decided that attestations which can't use public Sigstore infrastructure are
signed by a certificate authority (CA) whose key is stored in PostgreSQL. We
call this the `LOCAL_CA` attest method. Each project has its own CA, and every
attestation is signed with a new key. A leaf certificate issued by the
project's CA binds that key to the project, the CI configuration file and the
ref.

This ADR records how we build that leaf certificate and how we sign with it.
The goal is for `LOCAL_CA` signing to work the same way on GitLab.com, GitLab
Dedicated and self-managed instances, including offline ones. On GitLab.com,
public projects use Sigstore by default, as described in ADR 007.

Two things about cosign shaped most of the decisions below. First, cosign v3
is built around a signing configuration. It reads the Sigstore services to use,
such as Fulcio, Rekor and timestamp authorities, from a signing configuration,
and uses the public Sigstore one if none is given. Older versions skipped the
transparency log with `--tlog-upload=false`. cosign v3 deprecates that flag in
favor of a signing configuration with no log, so that's what we pass, and we
don't use the flag. Second, cosign works with files, so the key, the
certificate, the trusted root and the signing configuration all have to be on
disk before cosign can use them.

## Decision

We sign each `LOCAL_CA` attestation with cosign, offline, using a new key and a
leaf certificate issued by the project's CA. The sections below go through each
part of that.

### Signing identity in a URI SAN

The leaf certificate has an empty subject and a single, critical URI Subject
Alternative Name (SAN). For example:

```plaintext
Subject: (empty)
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: critical
    URI:https://gitlab.example.com/my-group/my-project//.gitlab-ci.yml@refs/heads/main
```

The URI is the pipeline's `ci_config_ref_uri`, prefixed with the instance's
protocol. GitLab generates this value, not the job, and it has the same format
as the `ci_config_ref_uri` claim in
[CI/CD ID tokens](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/secrets/id_token_authentication/).

We put the identity in a URI SAN rather than the CN for a few reasons:

- The identity is a URI, and
  [RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280.html#section-4.2.1.6)
  defines the URI SAN for this purpose.
- It's what [Fulcio's certificate profile](https://github.com/sigstore/fulcio/blob/main/docs/certificate-specification.md#issued-certificate)
  does. cosign reads the identity from the SAN and doesn't fall back to the CN,
  so `cosign --certificate-identity` works on our certificates as they are.
- [RFC 5280 Appendix A.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280.html#appendix-A.1)
  limits a CN to 64 characters, and the example above is already 78.
- A URI inside a distinguished name has to be escaped when we issue the
  certificate and parsed carefully when we verify it. A typed SAN avoids that.

We always issue exactly one absolute URI in the SAN, and mark the extension
critical, as RFC 5280 requires when the subject is empty. The CN is never used
for the identity. Verifiers compare the SAN with an identity they work out for
themselves, never with a value read from the certificate itself.

The leaf certificate also carries the Fulcio issuer extension (OID
`1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.8`), set to the instance URL, for example
`https://gitlab.example.com`. No Fulcio server or OIDC exchange is involved.
GitLab sets the value itself, so verifiers can check it with
`--certificate-oidc-issuer` in the same way they do for Sigstore attestations.

### Long-lived leaf certificates

Leaf certificates are valid for several years, so an attestation stays
verifiable for several years after it's signed.

The certificate is stored in the attestation's Sigstore bundle, which GitLab
keeps with the attestation and users download with the
[Attestations API](https://docs.gitlab.com/api/attestations/). The private key
is ephemeral. We generate a new one for each attestation, use it once and
discard it, and it's never stored.

A CA only issues a leaf certificate if the CA itself stays valid for at least
the leaf certificate's lifetime.

### A new key and certificate for every attestation

We generate a new leaf key and certificate for every attestation, including one
for each artifact when a job produces several. A key signs one attestation and
is never reused.

The main benefit is that there's no long-lived signing key to store or protect.
The CA key is the only key that needs long-term protection. It also matches
Sigstore, which uses a new key for every signature, so both attest methods
behave the same from a user's point of view. And because each attestation
carries its own certificate, attestations don't depend on each other.

### Offline signing with an explicit signing configuration

We create a signing configuration with
[`cosign signing-config create`](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/doc/cosign_signing-config_create.md),
with no service flags, and pass it to cosign with `--signing-config`. The
configuration lists no transparency log and no timestamp authority:

```json
{"mediaType":"application/vnd.dev.sigstore.signingconfig.v0.2+json", "rekorTlogConfig":{}, "tsaConfig":{}}
```

We also unset `COSIGN_FULCIO_URL` and `COSIGN_REKOR_URL` for the
`cosign attest-blob` command. cosign reads `COSIGN_<FLAG>` variables as flags
and won't accept service URLs next to `--signing-config`, so a Sigstore URL set
on the host would otherwise break `LOCAL_CA` signing.

`LOCAL_CA` signing makes no network calls, so it works the same on an air-gapped
self-managed instance as on GitLab.com, and nothing about a private project
reaches a public log. If we later add a transparency log or timestamp authority
that GitLab runs, that's a change to the signing configuration rather than to
the signing flow.

### Certificate chain check at signing time

We build a trusted root that contains only the project's CA, with
[`cosign trusted-root create`](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/doc/cosign_trusted-root_create.md),
and pass it to `cosign attest-blob` with `--trusted-root`:

```shell
cosign trusted-root create \
  --fulcio 'url=https://gitlab.example.com,certificate-chain=ca.crt.pem' \
  --no-default-fulcio --no-default-rekor --no-default-ctfe --no-default-tsa \
  --out trusted-root.json
```

| Flag | Why |
|---|---|
| `--fulcio url=...,certificate-chain=...` | Adds the project's CA as the only certificate authority. The URL is the instance URL, the same value as the leaf certificate's issuer extension. |
| `--no-default-fulcio`, `--no-default-rekor`, `--no-default-ctfe`, `--no-default-tsa` | Leave out public Sigstore's certificate authority, transparency logs and timestamp authorities, so the trusted root contains nothing but the project's CA. |
| `--out` | Writes the trusted root next to the other signing material. |

cosign splits the `--fulcio` value on commas, so we reject a file path or
instance URL that contains one.

With the trusted root in place, cosign checks the leaf certificate against the
project's CA before it writes the bundle. A leaf certificate that doesn't chain
to that CA fails at signing time, so we never store an attestation that can't
be verified. Because the trusted root holds only the project's CA, a
certificate from public Sigstore or from another project's CA can't pass the
check. Signing and verification also use the same trust material in the same
format (ADR 009).

### Leaf certificate embedded in the bundle

We pass the leaf certificate to `cosign attest-blob` with `--certificate`, so
the Sigstore bundle carries it. This follows from the verification approach in
ADR 009, where cosign checks the certificate and the identity.

The bundle ends up self-contained: one file holds the signed provenance and the
certificate that ties it to an identity. We don't need a separate store or API
for leaf certificates or public keys, and `LOCAL_CA` bundles have the same
format as Sigstore bundles, so the same tools read both.

### Private, short-lived signing material

Because cosign works with files, we prepare the signing material for each
attestation like this:

- Each attestation gets its own new temporary directory, which only the
  operating system user running GitLab can open. It's deleted when signing
  finishes, whether signing succeeds or fails.
- The leaf key is converted to cosign's encrypted key format with
  [`cosign import-key-pair`](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/doc/cosign_import-key-pair.md).
  We write the plaintext key to cosign's standard input, so it never touches
  disk. The encrypted copy is protected by a random password generated for that
  one attestation.
- The password reaches cosign through its environment, not on the command line,
  where other users of the host could see it.
- The provenance reaches cosign on standard input, so it isn't written to disk
  either.
- cosign always runs directly from an argument list, never through a shell, and
  every value we pass to it, such as digests, file names and paths, is
  validated first. Sigstore signing uses the same pattern, which follows the
  [shell command development guidelines](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/shell_commands/).

Key material only exists while one attestation is being signed, in a directory
other users on the host can't read, and it's gone afterwards even when signing
fails.

### Signing method and issuing CA on every attestation

Every attestation records its `signing_method`, which is `sigstore` or
`local_ca`. A successful `LOCAL_CA` attestation also records
`signing_certificate_id`, a reference to the CA that issued its leaf
certificate.

Failed attestations record the method too, but no CA reference. Signing logs
include the method as well.

If a CA is ever deleted, its attestations keep their history, lose only the
reference, and still say `local_ca`. While its CA exists, every successful
`LOCAL_CA` attestation points at the CA that vouches for it, even when a project
has had more than one CA. A verifier can choose between the Sigstore and
`LOCAL_CA` verification paths from the attestation alone (ADR 009), and
failures can be grouped by method, so a problem with one path stands out.

## Certificate profile

Each leaf certificate has:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Subject | Empty |
| Subject Alternative Name | One URI, critical |
| Issuer | The project's CA |
| Validity | Long-lived, see [Long-lived leaf certificates](#long-lived-leaf-certificates) |
| Public key | ECDSA P-256, new for each attestation |
| Signature | ECDSA with SHA-256, by the project's CA |
| Basic constraints | Not a CA |
| Key usage | Digital signature |
| Extended key usage | Code signing |
| `1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.8` | The instance URL |

The example below builds a leaf certificate with this profile. It continues
from the CA example in ADR 007, so run it in the same Ruby session. The
validity periods are only examples.

```ruby
require 'openssl'
require 'securerandom'

# ca_cert and ca_key come from the CA example in ADR 007.
# Example values, in seconds. The leaf certificate must expire before the CA.
leaf_validity = 3 * 365 * 24 * 60 * 60 # 3 years
clock_skew = 5 * 60 # 5 minutes, backdates not_before

identity = 'https://gitlab.example.com/my-group/my-project//.gitlab-ci.yml@refs/heads/main'
instance_url = 'https://gitlab.example.com'

leaf_key = OpenSSL::PKey::EC.generate('prime256v1')

leaf_cert = OpenSSL::X509::Certificate.new
leaf_cert.version = 2 # X.509 v3
leaf_cert.serial = SecureRandom.random_number(1...(2**159))
leaf_cert.not_before = Time.now - clock_skew
leaf_cert.not_after = Time.now + leaf_validity
leaf_cert.public_key = leaf_key
leaf_cert.subject = OpenSSL::X509::Name.new([])
leaf_cert.issuer = ca_cert.subject

extension_factory = OpenSSL::X509::ExtensionFactory.new
extension_factory.subject_certificate = leaf_cert
extension_factory.issuer_certificate = ca_cert

leaf_cert.add_extension(extension_factory.create_extension('basicConstraints', 'CA:FALSE', true))
leaf_cert.add_extension(extension_factory.create_extension('keyUsage', 'digitalSignature', true))
leaf_cert.add_extension(extension_factory.create_extension('extendedKeyUsage', 'codeSigning'))
leaf_cert.add_extension(extension_factory.create_extension('subjectKeyIdentifier', 'hash'))
leaf_cert.add_extension(extension_factory.create_extension('authorityKeyIdentifier', 'keyid:always'))

# Built as ASN.1, so the URI is never parsed as an OpenSSL config string.
san = OpenSSL::ASN1::Sequence.new([OpenSSL::ASN1::ASN1Data.new(identity, 6, :CONTEXT_SPECIFIC)])
leaf_cert.add_extension(OpenSSL::X509::Extension.new('subjectAltName', san.to_der, true))

issuer = OpenSSL::ASN1::UTF8String.new(instance_url)
leaf_cert.add_extension(OpenSSL::X509::Extension.new('1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.8', issuer.to_der, false))

leaf_cert.sign(ca_key, OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'))
```

## Signing command

For each artifact or image digest, we get a new leaf key and certificate from
the project's CA, prepare the
[signing material](#private-short-lived-signing-material), and sign the
provenance:

```shell
cosign attest-blob \
  --new-bundle-format \
  --predicate - \
  --type slsaprovenance1 \
  --hash <SHA-256 digest> \
  --key cosign.key \
  --certificate leaf.crt.pem \
  --trusted-root trusted-root.json \
  --signing-config signing-config.json \
  --yes \
  --bundle attestation.bundle \
  -- ./<artifact name or digest>
```

| Flag | Why |
|---|---|
| `--key` | The leaf key, new for this attestation and in cosign's encrypted format. |
| `--certificate` | Embeds the leaf certificate in the bundle. |
| `--trusted-root` | Makes cosign check the leaf certificate against the project's CA before writing the bundle. |
| `--signing-config` | Keeps signing offline, with no transparency log and no timestamp authority. |
| `--predicate -` | Reads the SLSA provenance from standard input, so it isn't written to disk. |
| `--type slsaprovenance1` | Marks the predicate as SLSA provenance v1. |
| `--hash` | Signs the SHA-256 digest that GitLab computed, so cosign doesn't need to read the artifact. |
| `--new-bundle-format` | Writes a standard Sigstore bundle. |
| `--bundle` | Where cosign writes the bundle, which GitLab then stores with the attestation. |
| `--yes` | Skips cosign's confirmation prompt, because signing runs in the background. |
| `-- ./<name>` | The subject name in the provenance: the artifact's file name, or the image digest. The `--` and `./` stop a name from being read as a flag. |

Compared with Sigstore signing, `LOCAL_CA` replaces `--identity-token`,
`--oidc-issuer` and `--use-signing-config=false` with `--key`,
`--certificate`, `--trusted-root` and `--signing-config`. Everything else is
shared, so both methods produce the same kind of bundle from the same
provenance. We don't pass the job's CI/CD ID token to cosign for `LOCAL_CA`,
because the identity comes from the certificate GitLab issues.

## Consequences

### Positive

- `LOCAL_CA` signing works the same on GitLab.com, GitLab Dedicated and
  self-managed instances, including air-gapped ones, with no external service
  and no setup.
- Details of private projects don't reach a public log.
- Attestations are standard Sigstore bundles that cosign verifies with one
  trusted root, so users don't need any GitLab-specific tooling.
- cosign's existing identity checks work on `LOCAL_CA` certificates, because
  we follow Fulcio's certificate profile. Anyone who knows Sigstore will find
  the certificates familiar, and standard X.509 tools can read them.
- The CA key is the only long-lived secret. Leaf keys exist only while one
  attestation is being signed, and never leave a private, temporary directory.
- Each attestation is signed with its own key and certificate, so attestations
  don't depend on each other.
- Mistakes surface at signing time, through the chain check, instead of when a
  user tries to verify.
- Every attestation can be traced to the method that signed it, and every
  successful `LOCAL_CA` attestation to the CA that issued its certificate,
  while that CA exists.

### Negative

- An attestation verifies only until its leaf certificate expires. Keeping it
  verifiable for longer would need re-signing. A leaked leaf key or CA key
  could also produce certificates that verify until they expire. Short-lived
  leaf certificates would reduce both (see
  [Future considerations](#future-considerations)).
- A CA must outlive every leaf certificate it issues, so it stops issuing well
  before its own expiry and has to be replaced before then. Key rotation is out
  of scope for ADR 007 and this ADR.
- Each artifact needs a few extra local cosign commands, the encrypted leaf key
  is briefly on local disk, bundles are slightly larger, and signing relies on
  cosign v3.

### Future considerations

As a follow-up, we want to move to short-lived leaf certificates, paired with a
trusted signing time from a timestamp authority (TSA,
[RFC 3161](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3161.html)) or a transparency log.
Verifiers would then check that the certificate was valid when the attestation
was signed, rather than when it's verified. This would:

- Limit how long a leaked leaf key stays useful.
- Let the CA lifetime shrink too.
- Keep attestations signed after the change verifiable once their leaf
  certificates expire.

It needs a TSA or log that self-managed and Dedicated instances can run, so
we'll pick it up together with the transparency log decision in ADR 007.

## Alternatives considered

### Identity in the subject CN

The identity could go in the CN, as `/CN=<identity>/DC=gitlab`. But the
identity is a URI that's usually longer than a CN allows, it would need
escaping inside the distinguished name, and cosign doesn't read identities from
the CN, so its identity checks wouldn't work.

### Skipping the transparency log with `--tlog-upload=false`

This is the older way to sign without Rekor, and it's deprecated in cosign v3.
It also leaves cosign's other defaults in place, and in that mode cosign signs
without checking the certificate chain at all. A signing configuration on its
own isn't enough either: without `--trusted-root`, cosign checks the leaf
certificate against public Sigstore's trust root, which doesn't contain the
project's CA. We pass a signing configuration with no log and a trusted root
with only the project's CA instead.

### Storing the public key with the attestation

We could store the leaf's public key with the attestation, verify the
signature with `cosign --key`, and check the certificate separately. That needs
separate storage and an API for keys or certificates, and certificate checks
that GitLab would own. Embedding the certificate avoids both. ADR 009 compares
the two verification approaches.

### Inferring the signing method

We could infer the method from whether an attestation references a CA, but
deleting a CA clears that reference, and its attestations would then look like
Sigstore ones. We could also read it from the certificate in the bundle, but
that needs every bundle to be downloaded and parsed, so it can't be queried.
Recording the method explicitly avoids both problems.

## References

- [ADR 007: Attestations for private repositories, GitLab dedicated and self-managed instances](/handbook/engineering/architecture/design-documents/slsa_level_3/decisions/007_attestations_private_dedicated_self_hosted/)
- [cosign attest-blob](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/doc/cosign_attest-blob.md)
- [cosign import-key-pair](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/doc/cosign_import-key-pair.md)
- [cosign signing-config create](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/doc/cosign_signing-config_create.md)
- [cosign trusted-root create](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/doc/cosign_trusted-root_create.md)
- [Fulcio certificate specification](https://github.com/sigstore/fulcio/blob/main/docs/certificate-specification.md)
- [RFC 5280: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280.html)
- [Shell command development guidelines](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/shell_commands/)
- [Sigstore: Trusted time](https://blog.sigstore.dev/trusted-time/)

title: Decision Log
text:
Read more about SDD in [Spec-Driven Development](_index.md).

**Maturity: Still defining**

## Summary

The decision log is a record of the decisions made about a work item. It keeps the reason for each decision next to the work item, so the history is not lost in chat or in comment threads. Humans and agents both read it and write to it.

When a complex work item needs a lot of alignment, pending questions get lost, and adding every resolved decision to the description makes it too long. Someone who joins later spends a long time catching up. With agents, collaboration moves faster, and humans and other agents need to see the decisions made in conversations between humans and agents.

For this iteration, the decision log is not a long-lived artifact. Its lifespan is tied to the work item.

Epic: [WS-5: Decision log](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/21552)

User documentation: [Decision log](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/work_items/workplan/#decision-log)

## Scope

- Available on issues and tasks, and on custom work item types based on them.
- A work item does not need a Workplan or AI planning to have a decision log.
- Viewing and recording decisions is available to the Planner, Reporter, Security Manager, Developer, Maintainer, and Owner roles. A stricter permission model is still being discussed.
- The decision log opens in a side panel from the work item header. The header button counts resolved, non-archived decisions. Open decisions are stored but hidden from the panel for this iteration ([issue 631883](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/631883)).

## Data model

Decisions are stored in their own tables, `work_item_decisions` and `work_item_decision_options`, joined to the work item. The backend work is tracked in the [data model and backend epic](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/22374).

The existing model derives a decision's state from its timestamps:

- `active`: An open decision, with no resolution or archive timestamp.
- `resolved`: A decision with a resolution timestamp and no archive timestamp.
- `archived`: A decision with an archive timestamp.

This lifecycle supports creating an open question with options and resolving it later. A decision can also be created already resolved to record an outcome directly.

The API and model use `question` for the question a decision answers. Create and update mutations accept it alongside the legacy `title` argument during the transition ([merge request 259900](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/259900)). The database column rename is a separate follow-up.

## Interactions

First iteration, tracked in the [frontend epic](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/22375):

- Record a decision manually. Required fields are the decision, who decided, and the context. Optional fields are the reasoning and a source link.
- Show each decision as a card with the decision, the open question it answers, who settled it and when, where it came from, and the context and reasoning.
- Link a decision to the thread and comment that produced it.
- Edit the decision text and decider, delete a decision, or archive it. Archived decisions can be shown with a visibility toggle.
- Resolving a Duo question through the work item UI resolves its matching decision. A general action to resolve any thread by creating or picking a decision is still tracked in [issue 603073](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/603073).
- A decision quick action and a resolve-with-decision option are proposed in [issue 634656](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/634656). The proposal is still under discussion and not yet decided. The current direction in that issue is that creating a decision from a thread should not have to resolve the thread, because one thread can produce several decisions.
- Recording or resolving a decision creates an activity-feed system note linking directly to its card. The note follows the decision log's visibility rules ([merge request 259191](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/259191)).
- A link to an archived decision turns on the archived visibility toggle and scrolls the card into view. A link to a decision that does not exist shows a dismissible warning, and the other decisions still show ([merge request 263112](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/263112)).

Deferred to a later iteration:

- An approval lifecycle beyond the existing active, resolved, and archived states, including negative decisions.
- Decision assignees and the to-do items they create.
- Cascading decisions from child work items up to the root epic.
- Decision categories, ordering, and superseding a decision.

## Agents

- The backend creates an open decision when the workplan flow's service account posts a valid clarifying question. It stores the question, options, discussion, and workflow reference.
- The frontend resolves the matching decision when the user resolves the question thread through the work item UI. This requires the decision log to be available on the work item. See [Human in the loop](human-in-the-loop.md#relationship-to-the-decision-log) for failure handling and older questions.

## Observability

Internal events track a decision being recorded as already resolved, an open decision being resolved, and the decision-log panel being opened. Resolution events include how the decision was settled. Creating an open question alone is not counted as a resolved decision ([merge request 261013](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/261013)).

Editing, archiving, and deleting an open decision also send events. They carry the work item, the decision, and the request source: the web UI, the API, or an AI workflow ([merge request 263772](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/263772)). The panel view event carries the work item ID and whether the panel was opened from a deep link or the header button ([merge request 264363](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/264363)).

## Decisions

| Date | Decision | Who |
| ---- | -------- | --- |
| 2026-09-09 | The decision log is independent of the Workplan and of AI planning. Its rendering is split from the AI planning widget ([issue 624791](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/624791)). | WS-5 |
| 2026-09-15 | The decision log can be offered in the Free tier, but this is not a priority ([issue 628417](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/628417)). Until then, it stays behind the `ai_workflows` licensed feature. | @gweaver, @nickbrandt |

## Open questions

- How to expose open decisions and their options in the panel ([issue 631615](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/631615)).
- Whether reopening a resolved decision should modify it in place or supersede it ([issue 632762](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/632762)).
- Requiring both work-item update permission and internal-note access, including behavior on archived projects ([issue 632270](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/632270)).

title: Downstream Consumers
text:
Read more about SDD in [Spec-Driven Development](_index.md).

**Maturity: Still defining**

## Summary

The Workplan's value comes from being consumed by downstream agents. This page covers how Duo Developer implements a Workplan, and how validation against the Workplan could work later.

## Duo Developer handoff

When a Workplan exists, a user selects **Implement** on the Implementation widget or in the Workplan panel. This starts the Duo Developer flow (`developer/v1`) asynchronously, without opening Duo Chat ([issue 628801](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/628801)).

Duo Developer treats the Workplan as the primary specification. It uses the work item description and comments only for additional context. It also treats every point in the [readiness](readiness.md) feedback, including non-blocking ones, as a finding to resolve. For each point, it either resolves it or explains in the merge request description why it did not ([merge request 265980](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/265980)).

Prerequisites: Duo Agent Platform remote flows must be enabled. When the Developer flow is not configured, the **Implement** button is disabled with a tooltip ([issue 629904](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/629904)).

The **Implement** button is hidden on closed work items in both the widget and the Workplan panel ([merge request 261747](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/261747)). Starting the Developer flow also requires the CI flow permission; aligning it with work-item action permissions is tracked in [issue 634208](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/634208).

Showing the implementation phase and the merge request status on the Implementation widget remains open in [issue 628976](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/628976). Handling repeated **Implement** clicks while a run is active, while still allowing an intentional restart, is part of that ongoing design work.

## Duo Review validation (deferred)

The Duo Review agent could validate merge request changes against the originating Workplan, using it as evaluation criteria. This depends on the [work item to merge request relationship](wi_mr_relationship.md). It is not part of the current epic.

Epic: [Workstream 1: MR spec enforcement](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/21514)

## Merge check in MR (deferred)

Validating the Workplan at merge time as a merge check is not part of the current epic. It may be covered by the [Code Review Lifecycle Transformation](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1BsdLonLqNyB0QSdEiUaJJ5GNQLkr-gKx_uQNTApdfCA/edit?tab=t.0) initiative instead of SDD.

## API surface

Downstream agents read the Workplan through the work item GraphQL API and the MCP work item tools. See [Workplan](workplan.md#api-surface).

## Structured vs raw Markdown

Downstream agents consume the Workplan as raw Markdown. If the Workplan evolves to a richer structure, such as sections, acceptance criteria, or test cases, serialization and backward compatibility will need to be addressed.

## Decisions

| Date | Decision | Who |
| ---- | -------- | --- |
| 2026-04-17 | The Workplan format consumed by downstream agents is **Markdown** (not YAML or structured JSON). Markdown is human-readable, already the common format of GitLab descriptions, and avoids serialization overhead for consumers. | @fredericcaplette |
| 2026-09-23 | **Implement** runs Duo Developer asynchronously instead of opening Duo Chat. | WS-7 |

title: Human In The Loop
text:
Read more about SDD in [Spec-Driven Development](_index.md).

**Maturity: Still defining**

## Summary

When the [async workplan flow](workplan-flow.md) hits a decision it should not make alone, it asks a clarifying question in the work item discussions. A human answers there, and the flow picks up the answer and continues. Examples are whether something is free or paid, who can see it, or whether a change breaks existing behavior. A plan built on a wrong guess is worse than no plan.

Epic: [WS-4: HITL and notifications](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/22772)

Designs: [SDD iteration path in Figma](https://www.figma.com/design/uJb85wjoRaj7MMvjxAmdHf/SDD-Iteration-Path?node-id=46-27205)

## Why work item discussions

- A question in a discussion is durable. A chat session is not.
- Other people can see the question and weigh in.
- The work item already holds everything else about the work, so the decision sits next to what it affects.
- Any flow that needs to ask something can use the same surface, not only workplan generation.

## Interaction

1. The flow posts a comment with its question and attaches a small machine-readable payload that describes the question, the options, and its recommendation.
1. The work item renders the question as a card in the thread. The card shows up to five options and which one the flow recommends. Cards render only for notes authored by the Duo bot. They don't depend on the `workplan` feature flag: a valid question payload renders as a card, including in board drawers. A question posted while the flag was on stays answerable after the flag is turned off, while generating and resuming stay blocked by the backend ([merge request 264177](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/264177)).
1. A user answers by choosing an option. Some questions accept more than one answer. A user can also give a free-text answer.
1. If none of the options are right, a user can reject them. An explanation is required, because that is what the flow acts on next.
1. Answering posts the choice as an ordinary reply and resolves the thread. The thread is resolved only if the user has permission to resolve it. The chosen answers remain visible; options that were not selected can be expanded in a disabled state after resolution ([merge request 260428](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/260428)).
1. The user selects **Continue** on the Implementation widget to resume the flow with the answers and open the session in the Duo drawer.

Permission to resume and eligibility to supply answers are separate. The resume service checks work-item update permission and project remote-flow availability, then uses the original flow owner's identity. Starting a new CI flow has a separate Developer-level permission check; aligning the role policy is tracked in [issue 634208](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/634208). The resume service includes replies only from users with a project role above Guest. Replies from Guest and lower roles are excluded, even when the author can update the work item and select **Continue**.

Thread resolution is not required to resume. The service collects eligible replies to question payloads from both resolved and unresolved threads. Unanswered questions do not block a resume; if there are no eligible replies, the flow is instructed to continue with its best assumptions. A request to expand the description follows a separate path: the user edits the description, and **Continue** resumes research with the original goal.

Because the answer is a normal comment and a normal thread resolution, everything stays visible. The payload is stripped from note emails.

## Question navigation

While a flow awaits input, the Implementation widget shows its open-question count and previous/next navigation. The sticky header also exposes question navigation. Resolved threads are skipped, and answering from a card refreshes the widget without waiting for its next poll ([issue 608855](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/608855), [issue 628347](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/628347), and [issue 631032](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/631032)).

The backend counts unresolved flow-note threads across all runs, while navigation filters for question payloads. Progress notes and context requests can therefore inflate the count. A Guest can also resolve a thread whose reply is excluded from the resume goal. The counter is a navigation aid, not an authorization check or a prerequisite for resuming.

## Notifications

When the flow pauses for input, the user is notified. This was implemented in the AI Gateway in [merge request 6711](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/modelops/applied-ml/code-suggestions/ai-assist/-/merge_requests/6711).

## Relationship to the decision log

Automatic recording of clarifying questions and their answers in the [decision log](decision_log.md) is implemented in two parts:

1. The backend creates an open decision with the question, options, and discussion ID when the flow posts a clarifying question ([issue 630439](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/630439)).
1. The frontend resolves that decision when the thread is resolved through the work item UI, recording the selected options or free-text rationale and linking the answer reply ([merge request 259195](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/259195)).

This integration requires the decision log to be available for the work item's license and type. If no matching decision exists, such as for an older question, the frontend skips recording. Resolving without an answer records a fixed rationale rather than selecting an option. Reopening and resolving the thread again does not replace the first decision resolution. Resolving a thread outside this UI does not automatically resolve its decision.

Open decisions are stored but hidden from the decision-log panel until resolved. Recording a decision is separate from resuming the flow: **Continue** does not resolve threads or decisions, and a decision-log mutation failure does not prevent the answer from being posted.

## Open questions

- **Approval requests**: A single run can produce real questions and requests to approve a tool call. The current thinking is that discussions carry questions only, and approvals stay where the person running the flow can see them.
- **Updating the spec**: Automatically updating the description from a resolved Duo decision is in development ([issue 633224](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/633224)). A backend service that applies an AI-generated description update from a resolved Duo decision exists. It strips quick actions and escapes new mentions, but nothing calls it yet ([merge request 262147](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/262147)). The proposed backend event and worker that trigger it and link the description version to the decision are still open. The frontend diff presentation and whether manual decisions should also update the description remain under discussion in [issue 629471](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/629471).
- **Unanswered questions**: The flow waits for an explicit **Continue** action, which can resume it without answers. Nothing chases an unanswered question or cleans it up.
- **Resolving without replies**: The work item UI can resolve a discussion before anyone replies. It shows the collapsed reply box with a **Resolve thread** button, and the **Resolve thread** checkbox in the reply form ([merge request 259967](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/259967), [merge request 263718](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/263718)). Plain comments still become resolvable only after a reply, and the flow currently posts plain comments. Posting discussions directly is tracked in [issue 633575](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/633575). This is a prerequisite for [Resolve all questions](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/631563).
- **Answer eligibility**: Aligning resolved-question counts with the resume service's reply permissions ([issue 631546](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/631546)).

title: Readiness
text:
Read more about SDD in [Spec-Driven Development](_index.md).

**Maturity: Still defining**

## Summary

Readiness communicates how ready a work item is for agent execution. It is a lightweight quality gate before the handoff to Duo Developer. Without it, anyone can start an agent on a poorly scoped work item, which wastes tokens and produces low-quality output, and there is no signal of whether a work item is good enough to hand off.

Readiness applies to the whole work item, not only to the Workplan. It is backed by a numeric readiness score, but the user interface shows only the readiness level, not the number. The rename from confidence is implemented in [merge request 259555](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/259555).

Epic: [WS-6: Work item readiness score](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/23050)

User documentation: [Readiness](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/work_items/workplan/#readiness)

## Scoring model

The score is a number from 0 to 100. The scoring stage evaluates the saved Workplan against the work item description and comments. Its supervisor coordinates two rounds of three evaluators:

1. A rubric evaluator scores coverage, groundedness, specificity, feasibility and ordering, and completeness. A coverage evaluator maps requirements to plan steps in both directions. A falsifier looks for a wrong premise, wrong target, or success criteria that could pass without solving the problem.
1. Three cross-examiners reassess those findings against each other. The supervisor combines the revised scores and caps the result when a material defect remains plausible or confirmed.

Each round is designed for parallel delegation, with sequential fallback if the execution environment does not support it. An incomplete first round does not produce a score. These scoring caps affect the assessment, not the user's permission to implement.

The supervisor also writes Markdown recommendations, ordered by impact. It lists up to three recommendations and does not invent issues to fill the list. The gate's amendment, when a gate fired, and any finding a cross-examiner confirmed are marked blocking. Blocking items are listed first, non-blocking items are dropped first when trimming to three, and minor cons are skipped. Every scoring run writes feedback, using an empty string when there is no genuine recommendation, so a new score always replaces the previous feedback ([merge request 7554](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/modelops/applied-ml/code-suggestions/ai-assist/-/merge_requests/7554)). The implementation is in the [workplan scoring configuration](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/modelops/applied-ml/code-suggestions/ai-assist/-/blob/main/duo_workflow_service/agent_platform/v1/flows/configs/workplan/1.1.0.yml). Further simplification is tracked in [issue 2913](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/modelops/applied-ml/code-suggestions/ai-assist/-/work_items/2913).

## Computation

Scoring runs inside the [async workplan flow](workplan-flow.md), after the planner writes the plan, rather than launching a separate workflow. The scoring stage fetches the saved work item and non-system notes, evaluates them, and writes only the score and feedback; it does not rewrite the plan ([merge request 7039](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/modelops/applied-ml/code-suggestions/ai-assist/-/merge_requests/7039)). A scoring fetch failure ends the scoring stage without turning a successfully written plan into a failed planning run.

The score and feedback are stored with the Workplan and exposed through `readinessScore`, `readinessScoreFeedback`, and `readinessScoreFeedbackHtml`. The AI Gateway work item tool persists both the score and feedback ([merge request 7144](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/modelops/applied-ml/code-suggestions/ai-assist/-/merge_requests/7144)). The MCP work item tools support the score; feedback support remains tracked separately in [issue 627234](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/627234).

## Display

The Implementation widget shows the readiness indicator only after a numeric score exists, including zero.

| Score | Level | Indicator color |
| ----- | ----- | --------------- |
| 0–39 | Low | Error |
| 40–79 | Medium | Warning |
| 80–100 | High | Success |

The indicator bar fills to the score, clamped to 0–100, so a score of 85 does not look the same as 100. The level, color, and label still follow the thresholds above ([merge request 263153](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/263153)).

**Readiness details** opens an overlay drawer titled **Readiness**. The title stays the same for every score state. When feedback exists, the drawer body shows it under a **How to improve readiness** heading, which leaves room for other per-state content, such as a 100% state ([merge request 263908](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/263908)). The drawer fetches rendered feedback with its own query, which is skipped while the drawer is closed and then served from the cache. The feedback is refetched when the score changes or a workplan run finishes, so the drawer shows the latest feedback without a page reload ([merge request 265399](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/265399), [merge request 265706](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/265706)). While feedback loads, the drawer shows a skeleton. If loading fails, it shows an inline error with **Try again**. The readiness explanation is pinned to the drawer footer ([merge request 264391](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/264391)). The readiness level stays in the widget. Opening the drawer does not resize the work item or change its URL. Closing it restores focus to the trigger ([merge request 259135](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/259135)).

When no score exists, the UI does not yet distinguish evaluating, failed, canceled, and not evaluated states. A dedicated `readinessScoreStatus` field is proposed in [merge request 262079](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/262079), with the UI tracked in [issue 633076](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/633076).

## Behavior

In this iteration, readiness is advisory. Users can start implementation regardless of the readiness level. This avoids hard approval gates while still signaling when a work item needs more refinement.

Future iterations might add:

- Approval gates for handoff below a threshold, restricted to specific roles.
- Project-level policies, such as automatic handoff above a threshold.
- Score history.
- Criteria configurable by project owners.
- A separate score for how well the merge request matches the Workplan.

## Open questions

- Whether to also score before plan generation, and how to support scoring independently of a planning run.
- How to show a score without feedback. The scoring stage can now write empty feedback, and the drawer has no body for that case yet ([issue 633996](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/633996)).
- Default thresholds for any warning before handoff.
- Whether to store score history or only the current score.

title: Wi Mr Relationship
text:
Read more about SDD in [Spec-Driven Development](_index.md).

**Maturity: Not for now**

This design is deferred. It is not part of the current [parent epic](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/22445). It is kept for when Duo Review validation or merge checks against the Workplan are picked up.

## Summary

SDD requires a first-class, bidirectional relationship between work items and merge requests. The Workplan lives on the work item. Duo Developer and Duo Review operate on the merge request. Without a strong link, downstream agents cannot reliably find the Workplan they should follow or validate against.

## Current state

Today the work item to merge request link is loose:

- **Closing references**: A merge request description containing `Closes #123` adds a closing reference.
- **Mentioned reference**: When a comment links to an issue, it adds a `Mentioned` reference.
- **No programmatic lookup**: There is no reliable API to ask "given this merge request, what is the originating work item and its Workplan?"

In the current iteration, the Duo Developer handoff from a work item links the merge request through the work item's **Development** section. Showing the merge request status on the Implementation widget is part of [WS-2](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/22703).

## What SDD needs

1. **Duo Developer** starts a coding session from a work item. The resulting merge request must be automatically linked back to that work item.
1. **Duo Review** receives a merge request and needs to fetch the originating Workplan. It must be able to traverse merge request, linked work item, and Workplan in a single, deterministic path.
1. **Merge checks** may eventually validate the merge request against the Workplan. This requires the link to be queryable on the merge request page.

## Proposed approach

Strengthen the existing work item to merge request association so it is:

- **Automatic**: When Duo Developer creates a merge request from a work item, the link is created as part of the flow.
- **Explicit**: The relationship can be created or removed through the API and the UI.
- **Bidirectional**: Queryable from both the work item side (`workItem.mergeRequests`) and the merge request side (`mergeRequest.workItems`).
- **Typed**: Distinguishable from other merge request references, for example "created by agent from this plan" and "manually linked".

The exact data model (extending the existing `MergeRequestsClosingIssues` table, a new association table, or work item links) is TBD.

## Downstream impact

- [Downstream consumers](downstream_consumers.md): Duo Review validation and merge checks depend on this link.

title: Workplan Flow
text:
Read more about SDD in [Spec-Driven Development](_index.md).

**Maturity: Still defining**

## Summary

The async workplan flow refines a work item and generates its [Workplan](workplan.md) in the background, without Duo Chat. It replaces the earlier plan for an interactive builder, a Duo Chat and live preview UI for iterating on a plan. Instead of one user shaping one plan in a chat session, a user can start several flows in parallel, leave the page, and come back when a flow needs input. Collaboration happens in the work item discussions. See [Human in the loop](human-in-the-loop.md).

Epic: [WS-3: Crafting the Workplan](https://gitlab.com/groups/gitlab-org/-/work_items/22702). The initial [work plan refinement loop](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/605157) is complete; follow-ups continue in the workstream.

## Requirements

1. **Agents make their own suggestions.** When a question comes up, the flow does not stop at the first unknown. It lists its questions, gives options for each, and states its recommendation. This supports both users who trust the agent's recommendations and users who want to review and iterate before handoff.
1. **Notifications are mandatory.** When the flow needs input, the user must be notified.
1. **Research happens upfront.** The Workplan contains as much research as possible, so cheaper models can implement it and humans can review it accurately.
1. **Parallel work is considered.** If tasks should be done by different sub-agents, the Workplan says so.

## Flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    participant WI as Work item
    participant Rails as GitLab Rails
    participant DAP as Duo Agent Platform (workplan/v1)

    User->>WI: Select Plan
    WI->>Rails: WorkItemGenerateWorkplan
    Rails->>DAP: Create and start workflow (runs in CI)
    DAP->>WI: Read work item, comments, and project
    alt Decision needed
        DAP->>WI: Post clarifying question and mention user
        DAP-->>Rails: Status input_required (NEEDS_INPUT)
        User->>WI: Reply to question
        User->>WI: Select Continue
        WI->>Rails: WorkItemResumeWorkplan
        Rails->>DAP: Resume with eligible replies or best-assumptions instruction
    else More context needed
        DAP->>WI: Ask user to expand the description
        DAP-->>Rails: Pause at context_gate
        User->>WI: Update description and select Continue
        WI->>Rails: WorkItemResumeWorkplan
        Rails->>DAP: Resume research with the original goal
    end
    DAP->>WI: Write Workplan
    opt Readiness scoring available
        DAP->>WI: Read plan and context, write score and feedback
    end
    DAP-->>Rails: Status COMPLETED
```

1. A user selects **Plan**. The frontend calls the `WorkItemGenerateWorkplan` mutation.
1. `Ai::DuoWorkflows::GenerateWorkplanService` starts the `workplan/v1` foundational flow for the work item's project. The flow runs in CI through the Duo Agent Platform. The goal only names the target work item. The flow's system prompt in AI Gateway defines the plan format, how to handle ambiguity, and when to ask questions.
1. Research gathers requirements, comments, and repository context through GitLab API tools, then passes its findings to the planner. Either stage can post a clarifying question, mention the user, and pause in the `input_required` state.
1. For clarifying questions, a user replies and selects **Continue**. The frontend calls `WorkItemResumeWorkplan`, which forwards eligible replies from users with a project role above Guest. Only flow notes with question payloads are included as questions; progress notes and context requests are excluded. Thread resolution is not required to resume, and unanswered questions do not block it. If there are no eligible replies, the flow is instructed to continue with its best assumptions.
1. If the description lacks enough context to research, either stage routes to `context_gate`. The user expands the description and selects **Continue**. The resume service sends the original goal, so research reads the updated work item instead of treating a missing reply as permission to guess. This is implemented in [merge request 257208](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/257208).
1. The planner writes the Workplan and posts a completion comment. When readiness scoring is available, the same flow continues into a [scoring stage](readiness.md#computation) that writes the score and feedback.

The widget shows progress through `generationStatus`: `NOT_STARTED`, `GENERATING`, `NEEDS_INPUT`, `COMPLETED`, `CANCELED`, or `FAILED`. Cancellation is distinct from failure ([merge request 258021](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/merge_requests/258021)). Starting or resuming a run opens its session in the Duo drawer.

## Lifecycle and safety

- **Single flow per work item**: Only one workplan flow in a non-terminal state can exist per work item. An exclusive lease prevents two concurrent requests from both starting a flow.
- **Concurrent flows across work items**: Flows on different work items can run at the same time, so a user can refine several work items in parallel.
- **Permissions**: The work item mutations check `update_work_item`, but starting a CI flow additionally requires `create_duo_workflow_for_ci` (currently Developer or above). Resume checks work-item update permission and project remote-flow availability, and keeps the original flow owner's identity. These boundaries are not yet aligned; the role policy is tracked in [issue 634208](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/634208).
- **Answer eligibility**: The resume service excludes replies from Guest and lower roles and collects eligible replies regardless of thread resolution. This differs from the question counter, which uses thread resolution.
